XIII.
### BOOK ONE.

Among the angelic ranks as well, the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels, whose name is derived from the Hebrew word for "burning."</note>, the Virtues, and the Powers are of fire; the Cherubim are of earth; the Thrones and the Archangels are of water; and the Dominions and Principalities are of air. Regarding the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The "Archetypal World" is the original divine blueprint of the universe in the mind of God.</note> itself, the Creator of all things, do we not read: "Let the earth open and bring forth a Savior" <note>original: "Aperiatur terra, et germinet salvatorem"</note>? Is it not said of the same, He is a "fountain of living water" <note>original: "fons aquae vivae"</note> that purifies and regenerates? Is He not the same Spirit breathing the "breath of life" <note>original: "spiraculum vitae"</note>? And as both Moses and Paul testify, is He not also a "consuming fire" <note>original: "ignis consumens est"</note>? Therefore, no one can deny that the elements are found everywhere and in all things in their own way: first in these lower realms, though they are foul and coarse; in the celestial realms, however, they are purer and bright; while in the super-celestial realms they are living and blessed in every part. Thus the elements exist: in the Archetype as ideas of things to be produced; in the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>Higher spiritual beings or purely intellectual minds.</note> as distributed powers; in the heavens as virtues; and in the lower regions as coarser forms.

->### Of the natural virtues of things depending immediately on the elements. Chapter IX.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' depicting a scholar or philosopher in a study, surrounded by books and scientific instruments.</image-desc>
The natural virtues of things are partly elemental, such as heating, cooling, moistening, and drying; these are called primary operations or qualities, and are active in the second degree. For these qualities alone transform the entire substance, which none of the other qualities can do. Some virtues, however, are present in things composed of elements, extending even beyond the primary qualities. These include qualities that are ripening, digesting, dissolving, softening, hardening, <term>styptic</term> <note>Astringent; used to stop bleeding.</note>, cleansing, corrosive, caustic, opening, evaporating, strengthening, soothing, bonding together, obstructing, expelling, retaining, attracting, repelling, numbing, expanding, lubricating, and many others. For an elemental quality has much to do in a mixture that it cannot perform by itself. And these operations are called secondary qualities, because they follow the nature and measure of the mixture of the primary virtues, as is treated extensively in the books of physicians. For instance, ripening is the operation of natural heat according to a certain measure in the substance of matter; hardening is the operation of cold; likewise with freezing, and so on with similar effects. And these operations sometimes act upon a specific limb or organ, such as those that provoke urine, or milk, or menses; these are called tertiary qualities, which follow the secondary just as the secondary follow the primary. According to these primary, secondary, and tertiary qualities, many diseases are both cured and induced. 

Many things are also made artificially which men greatly admire, such as the fire that burns in water, which they call <term>Greek fire</term> <note>A legendary incendiary weapon used in medieval warfare that continued to burn even when doused with water.</note>. Aristotle teaches several compositions for this in his treatise on this singular subject. In a similar way, a fire is made that is extinguished by oil and ignited by cold water when it is sprinkled over it; there is also fire ignited by rain, or wind, or the sun. And a fire is made which is called <term>burning water</term> <note>original: "aqua ardens." This likely refers to distilled alcohol or brandy, which was a novelty that burned with a "cool" flame.</note>, the preparation of which is very well known, which consumes nothing but itself. There are also made inextinguishable fires, incombustible oils, and perpetual lamps which can be extinguished neither by wind, nor water, nor by any other means. This would seem utterly incredible, were it not for that most famous lamp that once shone in the temple of Venus, in which burned an <term>asbestos</term> <note>Agrippa refers to the ancient belief that asbestos was a "stone" that, once lit, would never go out.</note> stone; for once it is truly ignited, it is never extinguished.

### Of the Hidden Virtues of Things. Chapter X.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial I featuring floral scrolling and a seated figure holding a staff or instrument.</image-desc>

<margin>Why they are called occult properties.</margin>
In addition, there are other virtues in things which do not belong to any element, such as driving away poison, dispelling carbuncles <note>A type of severe skin infection or boil, often associated with the plague in historical texts.</note>, attracting iron, or other such effects. This virtue is a consequence of the <term>species</term> <note>In the Aristotelian sense, the "species" is the specific essence or "flavor" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> and the form of this or that thing. Hence, even in a tiny quantity, it has a significant effect in its action, which is not granted to an elemental quality. For these virtues, because they are highly "formal" <note>Meaning they derive from the "form" or spiritual blueprint of the object rather than its physical bulk.</note>, can accomplish much with very little matter. An elemental virtue, however, because it is material, requires a great deal of matter to act strongly. These are called <term>occult properties</term> because their causes are hidden, such that the human intellect cannot fully investigate them. For this reason, philosophers have acquired the greatest part of them through long experience rather than through the investigation of reason. For just as food is digested in the stomach by heat, which we recognize, it is likewise transformed by a certain occult virtue which we do not understand. It is certainly not transformed by heat alone, for if that were the case, it would be transformed better in a hearth by a fire than in the stomach. Thus, beyond the elemental qualities that we know, there are certain other innate virtues in things, created alongside them by nature. We admire these and are often amazed by them, as they are unknown to us or rarely, if ever, seen—as we read in Ovid concerning the Phoenix, that unique bird that renews itself:

> There is one bird that restores and reseeds itself; 
> The Assyrians call it the Phoenix. <note>original: "Una est quae reparat, sese ipsa reseminat ales, Assyrii phoenica vocant." From Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note>

->And elsewhere:<-

> Egypt gathers at the miracle of such a sight, 
> And the cheering crowd greets the rare bird. <note>original: "Conuenit Aegyptus tanti ad miracula uisus, Et raram uolucrem turba salutat ouans."</note>

<margin>The beast of Matreas.</margin>
Matreas <note>A famous wandering philosopher and joker of antiquity mentioned by Athenaeus.</note> once caused great wonder among both the Greeks and Romans; he used to say that he nourished a beast that would devour itself. Because of this, even today many people anxiously search for what the "beast of Matreas" might be. Who would not marvel at fossilized fish found in the earth, of which Aristotle, Theophrastus, and the historian Polybius have written? And the things Pausanias recorded about singing stones—all of these are the works of occult virtues. In the same way, the ostrich bird cooks and digests cold and very hard iron for the nourishment of its body; it is said that its stomach is not even harmed by glowing iron. Likewise, that little fish, the <term>echines</term> <note>The Remora or "suckerfish," which ancient writers believed could stop a ship's progress by simply clinging to its hull.</note>, so restrains the force of the winds and tames the fury of the sea that, no matter how much the storms command and rage, even with infinite sails stretched by the wind, it nevertheless checks the ships by its touch alone and forces them to stand still so that they cannot be moved in any way. Similarly, salamanders and <term>pyraustae</term> <note>Mythical insects or small creatures said to live and dance in the heart of a fire.</note>, small beasts, live in fire; and though they may sometimes seem to burn, they are nevertheless not harmed. It is similar with a certain bitumen with which the weapons of the Amazons were said to have been smeared, which...

### Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'P' depicting a seated figure within a landscape and architectural frame.</image-desc>The Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, specifically the Neoplatonists who merged his ideas with later mystical traditions.</note> maintain that all lower things are patterned after superior <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic thought, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things that exist in the physical world.</note>. They define an Idea as a form above bodies, souls, and minds—one, simple, pure, unchanging, indivisible, incorporeal, and eternal—and they hold that the nature of all Ideas is the same. However, they place Ideas first in the Good itself, which is God, by way of cause; here they are distinguished among themselves only by certain relative reasons, so that everything in the world is not a single, characterless thing. Yet they agree in essence, so that God is not a multiple substance. Secondly, they place them in the <term>Intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure thought or intellect.</note> itself, which is the <term>World Soul</term> <gloss>Anima Mundi</gloss> <note>The "Anima Mundi" was thought to be an intrinsic spiritual force that animated all nature, acting as a bridge between the divine and the material.</note>, through forms properly speaking, and moreover differing from one another as absolute forms, so that while Ideas in God are all one form, in the World Soul they are many. They are then placed in the subsequent minds, whether joined to a body or separated from a body, by a certain participation, and are step-by-step more and more distinct. They place them in Nature as certain lowest "seeds" of forms infused by the Ideas. Finally, they place them in matter as shadows. Added to this is the fact that there are as many <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes rerum seminales" — the formative "seeds" or principles that govern how a thing grows and functions.</note> of things in the World Soul as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind. By these reasons, the World Soul built for itself figures in the heavens beyond the stars and impressed properties upon all of them. From these stars, figures, and properties, all the virtues and properties of the lower species depend, so that every species has a celestial figure suitable to it, from which also proceeds its wonderful power in operation, a dowry which it receives from its Idea through the seminal reasons of the World Soul. For Ideas are not only the causes of a species' existence, but also the causes of every virtue that dwells within that species. This is what many philosophers say: that by certain virtues—namely those having a certain and stable reason, not accidental or by chance, but effective, powerful, and unfailing, doing nothing in vain or fruitlessly—the virtues existing in the nature of things are moved. These virtues are the operations of the Ideas, which do not err except by accident, namely from the impurity of

Indeed, all celestial influences can be hindered by the confusion and incapacity of matter. Hence it was a proverb among the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato, who believed that the physical world is a reflection of higher, perfect "Ideas."</note> themselves that celestial virtues are infused according to the "merits of the matter." We know, therefore, that the position and figure of the heavenly bodies are the cause of every noble virtue found in the lower species.

### How different virtues are infused into different individuals, even of those of the same species. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' containing a landscape scene with a figure.</image-desc>
Individual things also possess singular gifts; many are as wonderful as those found in entire species, likewise arising from the figure of the heavens and the position of the stars. For every individual, when it begins to exist under a determined <term>horoscope</term> <note>The specific configuration of the heavens at the moment of birth or creation.</note> and celestial constellation, contracts along with its existence a certain wonderful virtue for acting and enduring. This is a marvelous thing, even beyond the virtue it has from its species, arising both through the influx of the heavens and through the obedience of "generatable" matter to the <term>Soul of the World</term>. <note>The "Anima Mundi," a classic Neoplatonic concept of a spiritual essence that connects the entire universe like a single living organism.</note> This obedience is exactly like the obedience of our own bodies to our souls. For we feel within ourselves that whatever form we conceive in our minds, our body is moved accordingly—either with delight, or with horror, or by fleeing. In the same way, the celestial souls frequently conceive various things, and then matter is moved through obedience to that conception. Thus, many wonders appear in nature from the "imagination" of the superior movements. In this way, not only natural things, but sometimes even artificial things <note>Items made by human craft, like talismans or tools.</note> conceive different virtues, especially if the soul of the person performing the work is focused on the same goal. Hence Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a highly influential Persian polymath and philosopher.</note> says: whatever happens here must pre-exist in the motions and conceptions of the stars and the celestial spheres. Thus, various effects, inclinations, and characters are produced in things, not only from the varied disposition of matter (as many believe), but from a varied influx and a diverse form—not indeed a diversity of the species, but one that is particular and unique. The degrees of these are distributed in various ways by God, the first cause of all, who remaining the same distributes to each as He wills; yet the secondary causes—the angelic and celestial—cooperate with Him, disposing corporeal matter and other things committed to them. Therefore, all virtues are infused by God through the Soul of the World, yet through the particular virtue of the presiding <term>images and intelligences</term>, <note>Spiritual beings or "angels" believed to govern specific stars or regions of the sky.</note> and through the meeting of the rays and aspects of the stars in a certain peculiar and harmonious concord.

XVII.
BOOK ONE.
b iii

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' featuring a portrait of a bearded man in a circular frame within a square border.</image-desc>

It is known to everyone that there is a certain power in the **magnet** by which it attracts iron, and that the **diamond** <note>original: "adamas"</note> by its presence takes away the power of the magnet. In the same way, **amber** <note>original: "electrum"</note> and **balagius** <note>Likely a balas ruby or a similar reddish stone.</note>, when rubbed and warmed, draw straws to themselves. The **asbestos** stone, once set on fire, is never or hardly ever extinguished. The **carbuncle** <note>A term used for red gemstones, like rubies or garnets, believed to glow in the dark.</note> shines in the darkness. The **eagle-stone** <note>original: "aëtites," a stone found in eagles' nests, believed to assist in pregnancy.</note>, when placed above, strengthens the fetuses of women and plants; when placed below, it draws them forth. **Jasper** stops the flow of blood. The **remora** <note>original: "echineis," a small fish or mythical stone said to be able to stop a ship in its tracks.</note> halts a ship. **Rhubarb** expels yellow bile. The **liver of a Chameleon**, burnt on the highest roof-tiles, stirs up rains and thunders. The **heliotrope** stone <note>Also called bloodstone; ancient authors claimed it could make the wearer invisible when combined with certain herbs.</note> dazzles the sight and renders the wearer invisible. The **lynx-stone** <note>original: "lyncurius," believed to be formed from the urine of a lynx.</note> takes away illusions from the eyes. The smoke of the **lipparis** stone calls forth all wild beasts. **Synochitides** <note>An ancient magical stone used to summon shades from the underworld.</note> brings out the shadows of the dead. **Anachitides** <note>A stone used for hydromancy or summoning divine images.</note> makes images of the gods appear. **Ennectis**, when placed under those who are dreaming, returns oracles. There is an **Ethiopian herb** by which, it is said, lakes are dried up and all closed things are opened. We read that the **Latace** herb <note>An herb mentioned by Pliny the Elder as providing abundance and plenty.</note> was given by the kings of the Persians to their ambassadors so that, wherever they went, they might abound in plenty. There is also a **Spartan** or **Scythian herb**, which, if tasted or even held in the mouth, they say allows the Scythians to endure hunger and thirst for twelve days. And **Apuleius** <note>Lucius Apuleius, a Roman philosopher and author of "The Golden Ass."</note> says that he was taught by a divinity that there are many kinds of herbs and stones by which humans can even grant themselves perpetual life; but it is not lawful for men to know their science because, since they live for only a short time and yet eagerly pursue evils and dare every crime, if they were to receive a great length of time, they would not even spare the gods themselves.

Indeed, from where these virtues come, none of those who have published huge volumes on the properties of things has revealed: not **Hermes**, not **Bochus**, not **Aaron**, not **Orpheus**, not **Theophrastus**, not **Thebith**, not **Zenothemis**, not **Zoroaster**, not **Euax**, not **Dioscorides**, not **Isaac the Jew**, not **Zacharias the Babylonian**, not **Albertus**, not **Arnoldus**. <note>Agrippa lists a "who's who" of ancient and medieval authorities on medicine, magic, and natural history, including Albertus Magnus and Arnaldus de Villa Nova.</note> And yet all these have confessed, as **Zacharias** writes to **Mithridates**, that a great power and the very fates of humans are contained within the virtues of stones and herbs. From where, then, these things come requires a deeper contemplation.

**Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>, not departing from his senses and physical qualities, thinks that these things come from the elements and their qualities. This might perhaps be thought true, if those qualities were of the same kind; however, the operations of stones are many, agreeing neither in species nor in genus. Therefore, the **Academics** with their **Plato** attribute these virtues to the **Ideas**, the formative patterns of things. **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian polymath and philosopher.</note>, however, traces such operations back to the **Intelligences** <note>Celestial spirits or angelic beings that move the spheres.</note>; **Hermes** to the stars; **Albertus** to the "specific forms" of things. And although these authors seem to oppose one another, none of them, if understood correctly, departs from the truth, since all their sayings agree toward the same effect in most things. For **God**, in the first place, the end and origin of all virtues, provides the seal of Ideas to his ministers, the Intelligences; who, like faithful executors, mark each thing committed to them with an "ideal" virtue through the heavens and the stars, as if using instruments, while matter in the meantime is disposed to receive those forms which reside in the Divine Majesty (as Plato says in the *Timaeus*) to be drawn down through the stars.

### XVIII.
### CONCERNING OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

The Author of forms distributes them through the ministry of the **intelligences** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "intelligences" refer to angelic or spiritual beings that govern the celestial spheres and natural world.</note>, whom he has appointed as rulers and guardians over his works. To these beings is entrusted the faculty over the things committed to them, so that every virtue of stones, herbs, metals, and all other things originates from these presiding intelligences. Thus, form and virtue proceed first from the **Ideas** <note>Platonic "Ideas" or divine blueprints in the mind of God.</note>, then from the presiding and ruling intelligences, then from the aspects of the heavens that dispose them, and further from the arranged temperaments of the elements corresponding to the influences of the heavens, by which the elements themselves are ordered. 

Therefore, these operations are found in these lower things through distinct forms; in the heavens through disposing virtues; in the intelligences through mediating reasons; and in the **archetype** <note>The "archetype" refers to the original model or God Himself, from whom all creation is patterned.</note> through ideas and exemplary forms. It is necessary for all of these to coincide in the execution of the effect and virtue of every thing. Thus, there is a virtue and a wonderful operation in every herb and stone, but a greater one in a star, beyond which each thing acquires much from the presiding intelligences; but most especially from the Supreme Cause, to whom all things correspond in mutual and perfect agreement, harmonizing in their own rhythmic accord—much like hymns—always praising that highest Maker. This is just as those holy children in the Chaldean furnace <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the fiery furnace from the biblical Book of Daniel.</note> are invited to do while singing:

> Bless the Lord, all things growing in the earth, and all things that move in the waters, all birds of the heavens, beasts and cattle together with the sons of men. <note>original: "Benedicite dominum uniuersa germinantia in terra, & omnia quæ mouentur in aquis, omnes uolucres cœli, bestiæ & pecora simul cum filiis hominum."</note>

There is, therefore, no other cause for the necessity of effects than the connection of all things with the First Cause, and their correspondence to those divine examples and eternal Ideas, from which every thing has its particular place determined in the archetype, whence it lives and draws its origin. Every virtue of herbs, stones, metals, animals, words, and prayers—and of all things that are from God—is implanted there. 

Although God operates in these lower things through intelligences and the heavens, sometimes—omitting these mediums or suspending their ministry—God does those things immediately by Himself. These works are then called **miracles**. For while the **secondary causes** <note>The natural laws and spiritual intermediaries (like stars and angels) that usually carry out God's will.</note> (which Plato and others call "ministers") necessarily act and produce their effects by the command and order of the First Cause, God sometimes releases or suspends them according to His pleasure, so that they utterly cease from the necessity of that command and order. These are the greatest miracles of God. 

Thus, the fire in the Chaldean furnace did not burn the boys; thus, at the command of **Joshua**, the sun moved backward from its course for the space of one day; thus, at the petition of **Hezekiah**, it went back ten lines or hours; and thus, while **Christ** was suffering, the sun underwent an eclipse during the full moon <note>A solar eclipse naturally only occurs during a new moon; its occurrence during the Passover full moon was cited by theologians as a miracle.</note>. The reasons for these operations cannot be investigated or reached by any discourse of reason, nor by any magic or any science however occult or profound, but are to be learned and sought out only from divine oracles.

XIX.

### **BOOK ONE.**

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a scholar or a philosopher seated at a desk with an open book, framed by ornate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

**D**emocritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans, having most diligently investigated the powers of the heavens and the natures of the lower things, said that all things are full of gods. And this was not without reason, for no thing is of such outstanding strength that it could be content with its own nature if it were deprived of divine help. However, they called the "gods" those divine virtues diffused throughout things; these are what Zoroaster called "divine charms" <note>original: *illices*</note>, Synesius called "symbolic attractions" <note>original: *symbolicas illecebras*</note>, others called "lives," and others even "souls." They said that the virtues of all things depend on these, because it belongs to the soul alone to be extended from one matter into other things upon which it acts—just as a human extends their intellect toward things that can be understood, and their imagination toward things that can be imagined. 

This is what they meant when they said that the soul of one being goes out and enters into another, enchanting it and hindering its operations; just as a diamond <term>adamas: a diamond or exceptionally hard mineral believed in antiquity to have the power to nullify magnetism</term> hinders a magnet so that it cannot attract iron. Since the soul is the "prime mover" and, as they say, is mobile by its own will and of itself—whereas the body or matter is by itself ineffective for movement and falls far short of the soul's nature—they say for this reason there is need of a more excellent medium. This medium must be something which is, as it were, not quite a body and yet almost a soul, or not quite a soul and yet almost a body; it is the link by which the soul is connected to the physical body. 

They imagine such a medium to be the **Spirit of the World** <term>spiritus mundi: a subtle, ethereal substance that acts as the "glue" between the spiritual and physical realms</term>, which we call the **Fifth Essence** <note>original: *essentiam quintam*; also known as the "quintessence," the pure element of the heavens</note>. This is so named because it is not made of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water), but is a certain fifth thing subsisting through them or beyond them. Such a spirit is therefore necessarily required as the medium by which celestial souls may inhabit a thicker, physical body and bestow wonderful gifts upon it. This spirit is almost the same in the "body" of the world as our own spirit is in the human body; for just as the powers of our soul are applied to our limbs through our spirit, so the virtue of the **World Soul** <note>original: *anima mundi*; the soul of the universe</note> is spread through all things by the Fifth Essence. 

Indeed, nothing is found in the whole world that lacks a spark of this virtue. However, it is most especially infused into those things that have "inhaled" the most of this kind of spirit. It is inhaled through the rays of the stars, insofar as things make themselves conformable to them. Therefore, through this spirit, every **occult property** <term>occulta proprietas: hidden qualities or "magical" powers that cannot be explained by physical temperature or moisture</term> is propagated into herbs, stones, metals, and living creatures, via the sun, the moon, the planets, and by stars even more sublime than the planets. 

This spirit can be of more use to us if one knows how to separate it from the other elements, or at least how to use those things that are most abundant in this spirit. For those things in which that spirit is less submerged in the body and less restrained by matter act more powerfully and perfectly; they also generate their own likeness more promptly. Every generative and "seeding" virtue is contained within it. For this reason, the **Alchemists** strive to separate that spirit from gold and silver. If this spirit is properly segregated and extracted, and then applied to any matter of the same kind—that is, to any of the metals—they will immediately produce gold or silver. We know how to do that, and have sometimes seen it; but we could not manufacture more gold than the weight of the gold from which we first extracted the spirit. For since that spirit is an "extended" and not an "intense" form, it cannot change an imperfect body into a perfect one beyond its own measure; though I do not deny that this can be done by another artifice <note>The author suggests that while simple extraction has limits, higher alchemical secrets might allow for true transmutation</note>.

XX.

<header>ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

## How we must investigate and test the virtues of things, by way of similarity. Chapter XV.

It is clear, therefore, that the hidden properties in things are not derived from their elemental nature <note>The "elemental nature" refers to the four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, but are instead implanted from heaven. They are hidden from our senses and barely known even to our reason. These properties proceed from the life and spirit of the world through the very rays of the stars, and we can only track them down through experience and conjecture. 

Therefore, O seeker who desires to work in this study, you must consider that every single thing moves and turns toward its own likeness. It inclines toward itself with all its might, both in its "property"—that is, its hidden virtue <term>virtue: in this context, an inherent power or medicinal/magical efficacy</term>—and in its "quality"—that is, its elemental power. Sometimes this happens even in the substance itself, as we see with salt; for whatever stays with salt for a long time becomes salt. Every active force, when it begins to act, does not move toward something inferior to itself, but as much as possible toward its equal and its like. We see this clearly in sentient animals, where the nutritive power does not transform food into grass or a plant, but converts it into sentient flesh. 

Therefore, in whatever things there is an excess of some quality or property—such as heat, cold, boldness, fear, sadness, anger, love, hatred, or any other passion or virtue (whether it is in them by nature, or sometimes even by art or chance, such as boldness in a prostitute)—these things most strongly move and provoke that same quality, passion, or virtue. Thus, fire moves toward fire, water moves toward water, and the bold person moves toward boldness. 

It is well known among physicians that "brain helps brain" and "lung helps lung." Thus they say that if the right eye of a frog is hung from the neck in a cloth of its natural color, it heals bleary eyes in the right eye, and the left eye of the frog for the left eye. They say the same regarding the eyes of a crab. Likewise, the feet of a tortoise benefit those suffering from gout <term>podagra: a painful form of arthritis, traditionally called gout, often affecting the feet</term>, if they are tied on so that foot is joined to foot and hand to hand—the right to the right and the left to the left. 

In this same way, they say that any sterile animal provokes sterility, and this is especially true of the testicles, the matrix <note>The "matrix" refers to the uterus or womb.</note>, or the urine. Thus they say a woman will not conceive if she takes some of the urine of a mule every month, or something soaked in it. Therefore, if we wish to work toward a certain property or virtue, let us seek out animals or other things in which such a property exists most excellently. From these, let us take the part in which that property or virtue is most vigorous. For example, if we wish to promote love, let us seek an animal that loves most intensely, such as the dove, the turtledove, the sparrow, the swallow, or the wagtail. From these, we should take the members or parts in which the "Venereal" <note>Refers to Venus, the goddess of love; meaning sexual or amorous desire.</note> appetite is most vigorous: which are the heart, the testicles, the matrix, the penis, the sperm, or the menses. And this should be done at that time when these animals are most captured and intent upon such an affection, for then they strongly provoke and bring about love. 

In a similar way, to increase boldness, let us seek a lion or a rooster, and from these take the heart, or the eyes, or the forehead. And so we must understand what Psellus the Platonist <note>Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine scholar and philosopher whose works on demons and Greek philosophy were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> says: that dogs, crows, and roosters contribute to wakefulness; also...

<summary>Agrippa explains the "Law of Similarity," arguing that natural and magical effects are produced by using objects or animals that naturally possess the desired trait in excess. He provides specific examples of sympathetic healing and the creation of love charms or charms for boldness using animal parts.</summary>

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

the nightingale <note>original: "philomela"</note>, the bat, and the little owl, and from these especially the head, the heart, and the eyes. Therefore they say that if someone carries the heart of a crow or a bat upon themselves, they will not sleep until it is put down. A dried bat’s head tied to the right arm of a person who is awake does the same thing; for if it is placed upon a sleeper, it is said they will not be woken until it is removed. In the same way, the frog and the horned owl <note>original: "bubo"</note> make one talkative, and from these especially the tongue and the heart: thus the tongue of a water frog placed under the head makes one speak in their sleep. The heart of a horned owl placed upon the left breast of a sleeping woman is said to make her reveal all her secrets. The heart of a little owl <note>original: "noctua"</note> and the fat <note>original: "sepum"</note> of a hare placed upon the chest of a sleeper is said to do the same. In the same way, all long-lived animals contribute to a long life; and whatever things have a restorative power in themselves contribute to the renewal of our body and the restoration of youth, which physicians have shown themselves to know many times over—as is evident regarding the viper and serpents. It is well known that stags renew their old age by eating serpents. In the same way, the phoenix is renewed by the funeral pyre which it builds for itself, and a similar power is in the pelican, whose right foot, if placed under warm dung, after three months a pelican is regenerated from it. Therefore, certain physicians, with certain preparations made from viper and hellebore, and from the flesh of such animals, promise to restore youth, and they sometimes do restore it—occasionally even such as Medea promised and restored to the old man Pelias <note>In Greek myth, the sorceress Medea demonstrated her power to rejuvenate the elderly, though she used this promise to trick the daughters of Pelias into killing him.</note>. It is also believed that the blood of a bear, drunk with the mouth directly from a fresh wound, provides an increase in bodily strength through this kind of drink, because that animal is made most robust.

## How the operations of various virtues are transfused from one thing to another, and are communicated mutually to each other.

### Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling vines and floral patterns.</image-desc> You should know that the power of natural things is so great that they not only affect all things near them by their own virtue, but beyond this, they infuse into them a similar power, through which these things also affect others with this same virtue—just as we see in the magnet. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but also infuses a force into the rings themselves, by which they are able to do the same thing, which Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> and Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> report having seen. In this way, it is reported that a public harlot, in whom there is boldness and banished modesty, affects all things near her with this same property, which then return it to others. Therefore, they say that if someone puts on the garment or shirt of a harlot, or has with them the mirror in which she daily looked at herself, they will be made bold, fearless, shameless, and lustful. In a similar way, they say a cloth that has been at a funeral conceives from this a certain property of sadness and of Saturn <note>In astrology, the planet Saturn is associated with melancholy and death.</note>; and the noose of a hanged man similarly has some marvelous properties. Similar is what Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 'Natural History'</note> relates: if someone lays earth under a blinded green lizard, and together in a glass vessel includes rings made of solid iron or gold, when it appears the lizard has recovered its sight, the rings—having received the virtue through the glass—act against...

### How through strife and friendship, the virtues of things are to be investigated and experienced. Chapter XVII. ###

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial R at the beginning of the text block featuring foliage patterns.</image-desc>
It remains now to see how all things have among themselves friendship and enmity <note>The concepts of "amicitia" and "inimicitia" are the foundations of natural magic, suggesting that objects have natural attractions (sympathies) or repulsions (antipathies) toward one another.</note>: and every thing has something to be feared and dreaded, as an enemy and a destroyer; and on the contrary, something exulting, gladdening, and comforting. Thus in the elements, fire is opposed to water, and air to earth; yet in other ways they agree with one another. Again, in the heavens, the friends of Saturn are Mercury, Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon; his enemies are Mars and Venus. All planets are friends of Jupiter except Mars; so too all hold Mars in hatred, except Venus. Jupiter and Venus love the Sun, while Mars, Mercury, and the Moon are its enemies. All love Venus except Saturn. Mercury’s friends are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; his enemies are the Sun, the Moon, and Mars. Finally, the Moon’s friends are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; her enemies are Mars and Mercury. There is another enmity of the stars, namely when they have opposite houses <note>term: "domus" (houses); in astrology, these are the signs of the zodiac over which a planet has primary rule.</note>: such as Saturn to the luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>, Jupiter to Mercury, and Mars to Venus. And the enmity is stronger for those whose exaltations <note>term: "exaltatio" (exaltation); the specific zodiac sign where a planet's influence is considered most powerful.</note> are opposite: such as Saturn and the Sun, Jupiter and Mars, and Venus and Mercury. However, the strongest friendship is between those who agree in nature, quality, substance, and power, such as Mars with the Sun, Venus with the Moon, and similarly Jupiter with Venus. There is also friendship between those whose exaltation is in the house of another: such as Saturn with Venus, Jupiter with the Moon, Mars with Saturn, the Sun with Mars, Venus with Jupiter, and the Moon with Venus. And just as these friendships and enmities exist among the higher things, such are the inclinations of the things subject to them here in the lower world. Therefore, these conditions of friendship and enmity are nothing other than certain inclinations of things toward one another—desiring such and such a thing if it is absent, moving toward it unless hindered, and resting once it is obtained; or conversely, fleeing the contrary, dreading its proximity, and never finding rest in its presence. Led by this opinion, Heraclitus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who argued that the universe is in a constant state of flux and that "strife is the father of all things."</note> declared that all things come to be through strife and friendship. Truly, these inclinations of friendship exist in plants and minerals, such as the attraction the magnet <note>original: "magnes"</note> has for iron; the emerald <note>original: "smaragdus"</note> for riches and favor; jasper <note>original: "iaspis"</note> for childbirth; and agate <note>original: "achates"</note> for eloquence. In the same way, naphtha draws fire to itself and leaps toward it from wherever it is seen. Similarly, the root of the herb *aproxis* <note>A mythical plant mentioned by ancient naturalists like Pliny, said to catch fire from a distance.</note> attracts fire from afar, just like naphtha. There is a similar inclination between the male and female palm tree; when the branch of one touches the branch of the other, they fold themselves into a mutual embrace; the female does not bear fruit without the male. A solitary almond tree is also less fertile. Vines love the elm and the maple <note>original: "oppium"</note>; and the olive and myrtle mutually delight in each other; similarly the olive and the fig. Among animals, there is friendship between the blackbird <note>original: "merula"</note>...

<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

...and the thrush, the crow, and the heron are found among peacocks and pigeons, turtledoves and parrots. Whence Sappho writes to Phaon:

> And white pigeons are often joined with various birds,
> And the black turtledove is loved by the green bird.
> <note>original: "Et uariis albæ iunguntur ſæpe columbæ, / Et niger à uiridi turtur amatur aue." This poetic excerpt illustrates that natural attraction can bridge even the most striking physical differences.</note>

<margin>The friendship of animals with other things</margin>
Furthermore, the mouse and the whale are friends. Nor is friendship found only among animals themselves, but also with other things, such as with metals, stones, and plants. Thus the feline or cat delights in the herb catnip <note>original: "nepeta"</note>, by the rubbing of which she is said to conceive and to supply the lack of a male. In Cappadocia, mares expose themselves to the blast of the wind, and from its breath and inhalation they conceive. <note>This was a common belief in antiquity, recorded by authors like Pliny the Elder, suggesting the air itself held a generative power.</note> So too frogs, toads, serpents, and all manner of venomous creeping things delight in the plant called "laughter-parsley" <note>original: "apium risus," likely the Celery-leaved buttercup, which was thought to cause fatal contractions of the facial muscles resembling a grin.</note>, of which physicians say that if anyone eats it, they die laughing. Again, when the tortoise is hunted by a serpent, it eats oregano and is strengthened by it; and the stork, when feeding on serpents, seeks safety for itself with oregano. The weasel, when about to fight against a basilisk <term>regulus|Literally "little king," this refers to the basilisk, a mythical serpent whose gaze or breath was thought to be deadly.</term>, eats rue; from this we know that oregano and rue possess power against poisons. Thus in certain animals there is a natural skill and an innate medicinal art: for the toad, when wounded by the bite and poison of another, is accustomed to go to rue or sage and rub the place of the wound, and so free itself from the danger of the venom.

<margin>What things humans have learned from animals.</margin>
In this way, humans have been taught a great many remedies for diseases and the virtues of things by "brute" animals. Swallows showed us that celandine <term>chelidonia|The name is derived from the Greek "chelidōn" (swallow). It was believed that swallows used the plant's caustic yellow sap to heal the eyes of their young.</term> is a herb healthy for the sight, as they heal the eyes of their chicks with it. The magpie, when it is sick, places a laurel leaf in its nest and so recovers its health. Similarly, wood-pigeons, jays, partridges, and blackbirds purge their annual loss of appetite with laurel leaves, with which crows also extinguish the poison of the chameleon. The lion, if it suffers from fever, recovers by devouring a monkey. The hoopoe, having been harmed by eating grapes, heals itself with maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianto"</note>. Deer taught that the herb dittany <term>dictamnum|A famous medicinal plant from Crete, legendary for its ability to cause arrows to fall out of the bodies of wounded animals.</term> is useful for extracting arrows; for when they are struck by a weapon, they eject it by feeding on this herb. The goats of Crete do the same. Furthermore, does, shortly before giving birth, purge themselves with a certain herb called seseli. Similarly, those touched by a venomous spider <note>original: "phalangio"</note> seek safety by eating crabs. Pigs, when harmed by serpents, heal themselves with the same food. Crows, when they feel themselves poisoned by "Gallic toxicum," seek the oak—or as others say, the *coruatia*—for a remedy. Elephants, after devouring a chameleon, help themselves with the wild olive. Bears, harmed by mandrake, escape by devouring ants. Geese, ducks, and other aquatic birds heal themselves with the herb ironwort <note>original: "ſideritide"</note>. Pigeons, turtledoves, and chickens use pellitory <note>original: "helxine"</note>; cranes use the rush. Panthers heal themselves against aconite <note>A highly poisonous plant, also known as monkshood or wolfsbane.</note> with human dung. Boars use ivy; deer use the artichoke <note>original: "cinnare"</note>.

...rhubarb has an inclination against bile; theriac <note>original: "theriaca"; an ancient "wonder-drug" used as a universal antidote to poison</note> against venom; sapphire against carbuncles <note>original: "anthracem"; inflammatory boils</note>, feverish heats, and diseases of the eyes; amethyst against drunkenness; jasper against the flow of blood and harmful phantasms; emerald and the chaste tree <note>original: "agnus castus"; a plant traditionally used to suppress sexual desire</note> against lust; agate against poisons; peony against the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>; coral against the illusions of black bile <note>melancholy</note> and pains of the stomach; topaz against spiritual fires, such as those of avarice, luxury, and all excesses of love. Similar is the inclination of ants against the herb oregano, and against the wing of a bat, and the heart of a hoopoe, from whose presence they flee. Oregano is also contrary to those things that flee the sun, and it resists salamanders. It disagrees with cabbage with such a persistent hatred that they destroy each other in turn. Cucumbers so hate oil that they curl themselves into a hook so as not to touch it. And it is said that the gall of a raven puts to flight and terrifies men from the place where it has been hidden along with certain other things. Likewise, the diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note> is so at odds with the magnet that, when placed nearby, it does not allow iron to be drawn away. Sheep flee from frog-parsley <note>original: "apium raninum"; likely a species of Ranunculus or Cursed Crowfoot</note> as if it were deadly; and what is more wonderful, nature has painted the sign of this death in the livers of sheep, in which the figure of frog-parsley appears naturally described. Similarly, goats so hate basil that they consider nothing more pestilential to themselves. Again, among animals, mice and weasels disagree; hence they say that if the brain of a weasel is added to the rennet, the cheese will not be touched by mice, nor will it be corrupted by age. Likewise, the star-lizard <note>original: "stellio"</note> is so contrary to scorpions that its very sight brings them terror, and the numbness of a cold sweat; therefore, they rot in oil and kill scorpions by anointing the stings with it. There is also an enmity between scorpions and mice; wherefore even a mouse placed over the sting of a scorpion is said to cure it. Enmity also exists between the scorpion and the *stalabores* <note>possibly a type of spider or lizard</note>, asps and ichneumons <note>the Egyptian mongoose</note>. It is also said that nothing is as opposed to serpents as crabs, and that pigs, when struck by a serpent, heal themselves with this food. It is also said that when the Sun is in the sign of Cancer <note>the Crab</note>, serpents are tormented. Furthermore, the scorpion and the crocodile kill each other; and if anyone touches a crocodile with the feather of an ibis, he renders it immobile. The bustard bird flies away at the sight of a horse, and a slave flees at the sight of a ram; he also flees at the sight of a viper. The elephant fears the grunting of pigs, and lions are terrified at the sight of a cock; and panthers do not touch those anointed with the broth of hens, especially if garlic has been cooked in it. There is also an enmity between foxes, swans, bulls, and crows. Among birds, a perpetual war is waged by crows and owls, the kite and the raven, the *pitalles* and turtledoves, the *bicuthus* and the *pagrus*, the *clorius* and the turtledove, sea-eagles and eagles, stags and dragons. Among aquatic creatures there are also enemies: dolphins and whales, the mullet and the wolf-fish, the moray eel and the conger eel. Likewise, the spiny lobster <note>original: "locusta"</note> is so terrified of the octopus that if it sees it nearby, it dies instantly. The conger eels tear at the lobster, and in turn, the octopuses tear at the conger eels. The hyena is said to be in such fear of panthers that it does not even attempt to resist, nor to touch anything of their skin; and if the skins of both are hung opposite each other, they say the hair of the panther falls out. And Horapollo <note>original: "Orus Apollo"; the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> says in his *Hieroglyphics* that if someone, girded with a hyena’s skin, is carried into the midst of enemies, he is harmed by no one and passes through intrepidly. Similarly, the lamb has enmities and harm toward the wolf...

## How the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested, which are in them from their whole species, or are innate to a thing by the particular gift of the individual. Chapter XIX.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'I' with floral scrolling patterns.</image-desc>
<margin>Virtues exist in things in two ways.</margin>
In addition, you ought to consider that the virtues of things are in some according to their species: such as boldness and high-spiritedness in the lion and the rooster, timidity in the hare and the lamb, rapacity or voracity in the wolf, craftiness and fraudulence in the fox, fawning in the dog, avarice in the crow and the jackdaw, pride in the horse, anger in the tiger and the boar, sadness and melancholy in the cat, lust in the sparrow, and so with similar things. For the greatest part of natural virtues follows the species. Some, however, are in things according to the individual, just as there are certain men who vehemently abhor the sight of a cat, so that they cannot look upon it without the gravest horror; which horror indeed is not in them according to the human species, as is manifest. And Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> tells that in his own time there lived a man whom all venomous things fled, and all things died that by chance had seized him with a bite, while he himself remained entirely unharmed. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century German Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> reports that he saw in Cologne <note>original: "Agrippina Colonia"</note> a girl who hunted spiders for food, and being delighted by that kind of food, she was remarkably nourished. Thus there is boldness in the harlot and timidity in the thief. And in this way philosophers say that a certain individual who has never suffered from sickness confers help to every sickness; therefore they say that the bone of a dead man who never had fevers, suspended over a patient, frees them from quartan fever <note>A fever occurring every third day, typically associated with malaria.</note>. There are also many singular virtues in individuals, infused by the celestial bodies, which we have shown above.

<header>OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY</header>

# That natural virtues are present in some things through their entire substance, but in others only in certain small parts or members.
## Chapter XX.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'R' featuring a seated figure and classical architectural motifs.</image-desc>
Again, you must consider that the virtues of things reside in some according to the whole—that is, according to their entire substance or all their parts. For example, that little fish, the remora <note>original: "echeneis"; a suckerfish believed in antiquity to be able to stop a ship in full sail simply by attaching to it</note>, which is said to stop a ship by its touch alone, does not do this through any one specific part, but through its entire substance. Likewise, the hyena possesses a quality throughout its whole substance such that dogs struck by its shadow are struck dumb. Similarly, celandine <note>original: "chelidonia"; a flowering plant in the poppy family</note> benefits the eyesight not through any one part, but through all its parts: no less in the root than in the leaves and seed; and so it is with similar things. 

However, certain virtues are present in things only according to specific parts—perhaps only in the tongue, or the eyes, or other specific members or sections. Thus, in the eyes of the basilisk <note>a legendary serpent king</note> and the catablepas <note>a mythical Ethiopian beast with a heavy head and a lethal gaze</note> there is a most violent power of killing men as soon as they are seen. A similar power exists in the eyes of the hyena: whatever animal it gazes upon, it instantly stays fixed, becomes stunned, and cannot move. A similar power is in the eyes of certain wolves; if they see a person first, that person becomes stunned and grows so hoarse that, should they wish to cry out, they find no use of their voice. Virgil mentions this where he sings:

->The voice itself now flees Moeris,<-
>the wolves saw Moeris first. <note>original: "Vox quoque Moerim / Iam fugit ipsa, lupi Moerim uidere priores." From Virgil’s Eclogues, 9.53-54.</note>

<margin>Why those who cast spells use eyes rather than other parts</margin>
So too there were certain women in Scythia, and among the Illyrians and Triballi, who were said to kill anyone they looked upon in anger. Similarly, we read of the Telchines <note>mythical sorcerers and metalworkers</note>, a people of Rhodes, who changed everything for the worse with their gaze, for which reason they were drowned by Jupiter. For this reason, practitioners of fascination <note>the "evil eye" or the power to influence others by a look</note> use the eyes of such animals in eye-salves to produce similar effects through their spells. 

In a similar way, ants flee from the heart of a hoopoe bird, but not from its head, foot, or eyes. So also the gall of lizards rubbed in water is said to gather weasels, but not the tail or the head. The gall of goats, enclosed in a bronze vessel in the earth, gathers frogs; and a goat’s liver is hostile to all butterflies and moths. Dogs flee from one who carries the heart of a dog; and foxes do not touch poultry who have eaten a fox's liver. Thus, many things have diverse virtues dispersed in different ways through their various parts, just as they are infused from the heavens according to the diversity of what can receive them. Just as in the human body, the bones receive nothing but life, while the eyes receive sight, and the ears hearing. 

And there is in the human body a certain very small bone, which the Hebrews call the Luz <term>Luz: in Jewish folklore, an indestructible bone (possibly the coccyx or a bone in the skull) that serves as the "seed" from which the body is reconstructed at the resurrection.</term>, the size of a peeled chickpea, which is subject to no corruption and cannot even be overcome by fire, but is always preserved unharmed. From this (as they say), like a plant from a seed, our animal body will sprout again in the resurrection of the dead. And these virtues are not revealed by reason, but by experience.

# Of the virtues of things which are in them only during life, and which things remain in them even after death.
## Chap. XXI.

<sig>A</sig>

Page XXVII.

<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'S' featuring two figures, likely classical or biblical, in a landscape setting within a square frame.</image-desc>

Furthermore, it will be necessary to know that certain properties exist in things only during life, while others remain even after death. Thus, the remora <note>original: "echeneis"; a suckerfish believed to have the power to stop ships</note> stops ships, and the basilisk <note>original: "regulus"; literally "little king," a mythical serpent</note> and the catablepas <note>a legendary Ethiopian beast with a lethal gaze</note> kill with their gaze while they are living; yet after death, they perform no such thing. Similarly, they say that in cases of colic <note>original: "torminibus"; severe abdominal pain</note>, if a living duck is placed against the belly, the disease passes into the duck and it dies. Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum (c. 428–347 BCE), a Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician</note> says something similar: if the heart is taken, recently extracted from an animal and still warm and beating, and is hung over a patient suffering from a quartan fever <note>a fever, often malarial, that recurs every four days</note>, it drives the fever away. Likewise, if anyone swallows the heart of a hoopoe, a swallow, a weasel, or a mole while it is still alive and palpitating, it grants them memory, recollection, intellect, and the power of divination.

<margin>Things to be collected from animals must be taken while they are living.</margin>
From this has arisen a general precept: namely, that whatever things are to be collected from animals—whether they be stones, limbs, or excrements such as hair, dung, or hooves—these ought to be taken from the animals while they are still living, and even, if possible, in such a way that the animals remain alive afterward. Therefore, they command that when you collect the tongue of a frog, you should return the frog alive to the water; if you collect the tooth or the eye of a wolf, you should not kill the wolf; and so it is with similar cases. Thus Democritus <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) was a Greek philosopher; in the Renaissance, many magical works were attributed to him</note> relates that if one extracts the tongue from a living sea-frog <note>original: "ranę marinę"; likely the anglerfish or a similar sea creature</note>, with no other part of the body adhering to it, and after letting the frog back into the sea, places that tongue over the heartbeat of a sleeping woman, she will answer truly to whatever she is asked. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs, tied to a patient before sunrise in such a way that the frogs are released blind into the water, will drive away tertian fevers <note>fevers that recur every three days</note>. They also say that these same eyes, when tied on with the flesh of a nightingale in a deer skin, drive away sleep and provide wakefulness. Similarly, the spine of a stingray <note>original: "pastinace radius"</note> tied to the navel is said to make for easy childbirth, provided it was taken while the creature was alive and then returned to the sea. So also they say the right eye of a serpent tied on is useful against watery eyes <note>original: "epiphoras"; inflammation or excessive tearing</note>, if the serpent is let go alive. And there is a certain fish, or rather a very large serpent, called the *myrus*, from which if an eye is plucked and tied to the forehead of a patient, it is said to cure ophthalmia <note>inflammation of the eye</note>; they say the eye grows back on the fish, but that the person who did not release it alive will be captured by another light <note>likely meaning they will be blinded or lose their own sight as a consequence</note>. Likewise, the teeth of all serpents, when taken while they are alive and hung over a patient, are said to cure quartan fever. Similarly, the tooth of a living mole being extracted and the mole released, toothaches are cured. Furthermore, dogs do not bark at those who carry the tail of a weasel that has been set free. And Democritus tells that the tongue of a chameleon, if torn out while it is living, is powerful for the outcome of legal trials, and the same is healthy for women in labor around the house; yet one must be careful not to bring it *into* the house, for that would be most destructive.

<margin>Which powers remain after death.</margin>
There are still properties that remain after death. Regarding these, the Platonists <note>followers of Plato who emphasized the spiritual "Ideas" behind physical objects</note> say that in those things where the Idea of matter <note>the spiritual blueprint or essence that gives matter its form</note> is less deeply submerged, that which is immortal does not cease to work wonders even after the things have died and passed away. Thus in herbs and plants, even when plucked and dried, that very virtue once infused by the Idea still flourishes and works. For this reason, just as the eagle in its life surpasses and conquers all birds, so even when it is dead, its feathers destroy and consume the feathers and plumage of all other birds. By the same logic, the skin of a lion [destroys] all other skins...

...consumes it; and the skin of a hyena destroys the skins of a panther; and the skin of a wolf corrodes the skin of a lamb. And these things do not act only through bodily contact, but sometimes <margin>Different effects of drums made from different skins</margin> through vocal harmony. Thus, a drum made from the skin of an *adib*—that is, a wolf—causes a drum made of lambskin to fall silent. In a similar way, a drum made from the skin of a sea-urchin <note>original: "Ericii marini"; likely referring to the rough-skinned "sea hedgehog" or a type of shark/ray skin used for its abrasive or resonant qualities</note> puts all reptiles to flight, from whatever distance the sound is heard. It is also well known that strings made from the intestines of a wolf, if they are stretched upon a lyre or lute along with strings made from sheep, can produce no harmony whatsoever.

### How lower things are subject to celestial bodies, and how the human body, as well as the activities and manners of men, are distributed among the stars and signs. Chapter XXII.

It is manifest that all lower things are subject to higher things, and in a certain way (as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 CE) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who taught that everything in the universe is interconnected through a chain of "participation."</note> says) they exist within one another: namely, the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest. Thus, in the heavens there are earthly things, but in a causal and celestial manner; and on earth there are celestial things, but in a terrestrial manner—that is, according to their effects. Thus we say there are here certain "solar" beings and certain "lunar" ones, in which the Sun and Moon cause something of their own power to reside. Hence such things receive many operations and properties similar to the operations of the stars and the celestial figures <note>astrological constellations or signs</note> to which they are subject. 

In this way, we know that solar things relate to the heart and the head, because Leo <note>The Lion</note> is the house of the Sun, and Aries <note>The Ram</note> is the Sun’s "exaltation" <note>a position in the zodiac where a planet's influence is most powerful</note>. Similarly, "Martial" things <note>governed by Mars</note> contribute to the head and the testicles because of Aries and Scorpio. Hence, for those whose senses reel and whose heads ache from being drunk with wine, it is an immediate remedy to plunge the testicles into cold water or dilute vinegar. 

But regarding these matters, it is necessary to know how the human body is distributed among the planets and signs. You should know, therefore, that according to the tradition of the Arabs, the Sun presides over the brain, the heart, the thighs, the marrow, the right eye, and the spirit of life. Mercury, moreover, presides over the tongue, the mouth, and the rest of the instruments or organs of the senses (both interior and exterior), as well as the hands, feet, legs, nerves, and the "fantastic" faculty <note>the faculty of imagination or forming mental images</note>. Saturn rules the spleen, the liver, the stomach, the bladder, the womb, the right ear, and the receptive faculty itself. Jupiter rules the liver and the fleshier part of the stomach, <margin>Why the image of a navel was in the temple of Jupiter Ammon.</margin> as well as the belly and the navel; for this reason, antiquity records that an image of a navel was placed in the temple of Jupiter Ammon <note>An ancient Libyan and Egyptian deity later equated with the Greek Zeus; his oracle at the Siwa Oasis was world-famous.</note>. 

There are some, furthermore, who also attribute the ribs, the pubic area, the intestines, the blood, the arms and right hand, the left ear, and the "natural faculty" <note>the biological force governing growth and nutrition</note> to Jupiter. To Mars, they assign the blood, the veins, the kidneys, the gallbladder, the nostrils, the back, the flow of sperm, and the "irascible" faculty <note>the part of the soul associated with anger and courage</note>. Again, they assign to Venus the kidneys and testicles, the vulva and womb, the genital seed, and the "concupiscible" faculty <note>the part of the soul associated with desire and love</note>; furthermore, the flesh and fat, the belly, the pubic area, the navel, and all such parts that serve the "Venereal work" <note>procreation and sexual activity</note>, such as the sacrum, the spine, and the loins. In addition, she is said to preside over the head and the mouth, where the kiss is given as a pledge of love. The Moon, although she claims the whole body and individual limbs for herself according to the variety of the signs, nevertheless specifically claims the brain, the lungs, the marrow of the spine, and the stomach...

<margin>The parts of the human body and which planets and zodiac signs they are subject to.</margin>
...and monsters, and all excrements, as well as the left eye with the power of growth. <note>This sentence completes a list of things ruled by the Moon from the previous page.</note> Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage and father of Hermeticism, to whom many foundational texts on astrology and alchemy were attributed.</note> himself says that there are seven openings in the head of a living creature, distributed among the seven planets: namely, the right ear to Saturn; the left to Jupiter; the right nostril to Mars; the left to Venus; the right eye to the Sun; the left to the Moon; and the mouth to Mercury. Likewise, the individual signs of the zodiac care for their own limbs: thus Aries rules the head and face; Taurus, the neck; Gemini, the arms and shoulders; Cancer presides over the breast, lungs, stomach, and muscles; Leo presides over the heart, stomach, liver, and back; Virgo looks to the intestines and the bottom of the stomach; Libra governs the kidneys, thighs, and buttocks; Scorpio the genitals, vulva, and womb; Sagittarius rules the thighs and the area beneath the groin; Capricorn rules the knees; Aquarius the legs and shins; and Pisces rules the feet. And just as the triplicities <note>In astrology, a "triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> of these signs correspond to one another and agree in the heavens, so they also agree in the limbs. This is well established by experience, since from cold feet the belly and chest often ache, as these limbs correspond to the same triplicity <note>Pisces (feet) and Cancer (chest/stomach) are both Water signs.</note>. Hence, a remedy applied to one benefits the other: for instance, when the feet are warmed, the pain of the belly ceases. 

Mindful of this order, you should know that things subject to any of the planets have a particular "aspect" or inclination toward the limbs attributed to that same planet—especially within its own houses and its exaltation. The other dignities, such as triplicities, terms, and faces, have little influence in this regard. For this reason, Peony, lemon balm, cloves, citron peels, marjoram, dorycnium <note>A medicinal plant, likely Canary Clover or a type of bindweed.</note>, cinnamon, saffron, aloe wood, frankincense, amber, musk, and partly myrrh, heal the head and the heart because of the Sun, Aries, and Leo. Likewise, plantain <note>original: "arnoglossa"; literally "lamb's tongue," a common healing herb.</note>, which is an herb of Mars, heals the head and the testicles because of Aries and Scorpio; and so it is for the rest. Furthermore, Saturnine things contribute to sadness and melancholy; Jovial things to joy and dignity; Martial things to boldness, strife, and anger; Solar things to glory, victory, and courage; Venereal things to love, lust, and desire; Mercurial things to eloquence; and Lunar things to common life. 

<margin>The manners and occupations of men are subject to the planets.</margin>
The very activities and manners of men are distributed according to the planets: for Saturn rules old men, monks, and melancholics, as well as hidden treasures and things acquired through long journeys and great difficulty. Jupiter, however, holds the religious, prelates, kings, and leaders, as well as gains lawfully acquired. Mars rules barbers, surgeons, doctors, executioners, butchers, bakers, and soldiers, who are everywhere called "Mavortians" <note>original: "Mauortii"; a term for those born under the influence of Mars, derived from Mavors, an archaic name for the god of war.</note>. Similarly, the remaining stars signify their own activities, as these are described in the books of the astrologers.

### How it is to be known which stars natural things are subject to, and which things are solar. Chapter XXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial V featuring floral scrollwork and classical motifs.</image-desc>
But to know which thing is subject to which star or sign is very difficult; nevertheless, they are known by the imitation of the rays, or the motion, or the figure of the higher things. Some are also known by their colors and odors, and some by the effects of their operations upon certain things...

...consonant with the stars. Thus, solar things among the elements include fire and bright flame; among the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine health and temperament.</note>, the purer blood and the spirit of life; among flavors, those which are sharp mixed with sweetness. Among metals, gold is solar because of its brilliance; it receives from the Sun the power to strengthen the heart. Among stones, those are solar that imitate the Sun’s rays with golden specks, such as the eagle-stone <note>original: *aëtites*; a hollow geode believed to be found in eagles' nests</note>, which, imitating the Sun with its golden specks, has power against the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and against poisons. Likewise, the stone called the Eye of the Sun, having a shape like the pupil of an eye from whose center a ray shines out, strengthens the brain and aids the sight. Likewise the carbuncle <note>a generic term for red gemstones like rubies or garnets</note>, which glows at night, has power against every airy and vaporous poison.

<margin>The chrysolite stone.</margin>
Thus the chrysolite <note>often identified as peridot</note>, a stone having a thin and bright green color in which a golden star shines when it is held against the Sun, strengthens the vital spirits and helps those with asthma. When it is bored through, filled with the hairs of a donkey, and tied to the left arm, it puts to flight phantasms and melancholic terrors, and drives away foolishness.

<margin>The Iris stone.</margin>
Likewise, the Iris stone, which is similar in color to crystal and is frequently found in a hexagonal shape; when a part of it is placed under a roof facing the Sun's rays while the other part is kept in shadow, it gathers the solar rays within itself and reflects them, making a rainbow <note>original: *Irim*</note> appear on the opposite wall. Also, the heliotrope <note>bloodstone</note>, a green stone like jasper or emerald speckled with red drops, makes the wearer constant, glorious, and of good reputation, and contributes to a long life. Its power over solar rays is marvelous: it is said to turn them into blood—that is, to make them appear blood-red as if the sun were suffering an eclipse—specifically when it is smeared with the juice of the herb of the same name and placed in a vessel full of water. It has another even more wonderful power over the eyes of men, whose sight it so dazzles and blinds that it does not allow the wearer to be seen; however, it does not do this without the help of the herb of the same name, which is also called heliotrope, that is, "sun-follower" <note>original: *folsequium*</note>. Both Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath</note> and William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, Bishop of Paris, who wrote extensively on magic and nature</note> confirm these virtues in their writings.

<margin>The virtues of the Hyacinth.</margin>
The Hyacinth <note>likely a sapphire or zircon in this period</note> also has power from the Sun against poisons and pestilential vapors; it makes the wearer safe and pleasing, contributes to wealth and wit, and strengthens the heart. Held in the mouth, it vehemently cheers the spirit.

<margin>The Fire-lover.</margin>
Likewise the *pyrophilos* <note>literally "fire-loving"</note>, a mixed reddish stone. Concerning this, according to the testimony of Albertus, Aesculapius reports in one of his letters to Octavian Augustus that there is a certain poison of such great coldness that it preserves the heart of a slain man from being burned, so that if it is placed in fire for some time, it is turned into a stone; and this is that which is called *pyrophilos* from the fire. It has a marvelous power against poisons and makes the wearer glorious and formidable to adversaries. But above all, the solar stone is that which Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous ancient philosopher and miracle-worker</note> is said to have found, named the *pantaura*, which attracts other stones to itself just as a magnet attracts iron. It is most effective against all poisons and is called the *pantherus* by others because it resembles the spotted animal, the panther; for this reason, it is also called *pantochras* because it contains all colors. Aaron <note>likely referring to a traditional authority on gems</note> calls it the *euanthum*. Furthermore, the topaz, chrysoprase, ruby, and balas ruby are solar. Likewise, orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*; a golden-yellow arsenic mineral</note> and golden colors...

Among plants and trees, those are solar which turn toward the sun, such as the heliotrope <note>The "sun-turner," likely the common heliotrope or the sunflower</note>, and those which fold their leaves as the Sun departs and gradually unfold them as it rises: such as the lotus, which some testify is a solar shrub based on the shape of its fruit and leaves. The wolf is also sacred to Apollo and Latona. Furthermore, the baboon <note>original: *cynocephalus*, literally "dog-head"</note> is solar; it barks twelve times a day, once every hour, and during the equinox it urinates twelve times every hour; it does the same at night, which is why the Egyptians used to carve its image on water-clocks <note>original: *hydrologiis*; devices used to measure time by the flow of water</note>. 

<margin>Why the Egyptians depicted the baboon on water-clocks.</margin>

Among birds, solar ones include the phoenix (the only one of its kind) and the eagle, queen of birds; likewise the vulture, the swan, and those that applaud the rising sun with a kind of hymn and call out to it, such as the rooster and the crow. The hawk is also numbered among the solar creatures by Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> because in Egyptian theology it is a symbol of spirit and light. Furthermore, solar things include whatever collect a likeness of the Sun’s works, such as glow-worms that shine at night, and also the scarab beetle, which they call *sele* <note>possibly a corruption of a name for the Sun</note>. It is of a shining form and is also called a *cantharus*; it rolls little balls of dung, sits upon them, and generates others. In the interpretation of Apion <note>A grammarian and commentator on Egyptian customs</note>, the scarab is judged to be solar because it collects a likeness of the Sun’s works, and its eyes are known to change according to the course of the sun. Among small fish, the most solar is the sea-calf <note>the seal</note>, which resists lightning; likewise the date-shell and the sea-lung, which shine at night; and the Star-fish <note>original: *Stella*</note>, because of its burning heat. Similarly, the *strombi* <note>conch shells</note> follow a king, as do those that produce pearls; when dried into stone, they harden into a golden color.

->Which things are subject to the Moon. Chapter XXIV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter L depicting a male figure sitting beneath a tree in a landscape.</image-desc>

**L**unar things among the elements are first the earth, then water—both of the sea and of rivers—and all moist things: the juices of trees and of animals, especially those that are white, such as the whites of eggs, fats, sweat, phlegm <note>original: *pituitæ*</note>, and the bodily superfluities. Among flavors, the salty and the tasteless. Among metals, silver. Among stones, those belonging to the Moon are crystal, silver marcasite <note>a brittle, metallic mineral often confused with pyrite</note>, and all white and green stones. Likewise the stone selenite—that is, the moon-stone—which is translucent white with a honey-like glow; it imitates the lunar movement, containing the shape of the moon within itself and reflecting it daily as it increases or decreases in number. # XXXII.
