<margin>Lunar trees and plants.</margin>
...and the beryl. Among lunar plants and trees are the <term>selenotropion</term> <note>original: *selenotropion*; literally "moon-turner," a plant believed to follow the moon's path across the sky just as the heliotrope follows the sun</note> which turns toward the moon, just as the heliotrope turns toward the sun, and the palm tree, which sends out a single branch at each rising of the moon. Also hyssop, a species of rosemary, the smallest of trees and greatest of plants, sharing in the nature of both. Also lunar are the <term>agnus castus</term> <note>original: *hagnus castus*; the Vitex or "Chaste Tree," historically used to preserve virginity</note>, or the chaste tree, and the olive. Similarly, the herb <term>chinostates</term> <note>original: *chinostates*; a legendary herb said to grow and shrink in physical size along with the lunar phases</note>, which increases and decreases with the moon: specifically in its substance and the number of its leaves, not only in its moisture and power. This is a trait that every plant shares in some way, except for <term>Martian onions</term> <note>original: *cepas Martias*; onions traditionally associated with the planet Mars, which were thought to behave contrary to the moon</note>, which alone have the contrary power of shrinking and growing against the moon’s waxing and waning; just as among the birds of Saturnian origin, there is a bird that is most hostile to both the moon and the sun.

<margin>Lunar animals.</margin>
Lunar animals are those that delight in human company, and those that equally excel in the various natural loves and hates, such as dogs of every kind. Also lunar is the chameleon, which always takes on a color similar to the object it faces: just as the moon varies its nature according to the sign in which it is found. Likewise, lunar animals include sows, does, goats, and any animals that observe and imitate the lunar motion: such as the <term>cynocephalus</term> <note>original: *cynocephalus*; the baboon, often depicted in Egyptian art as a lunar observer</note> and the panther. For it is said that the panther has a moon-like spot on its shoulder that grows into a circle and curves its horns in a similar way. Cats are also lunar, for their eyes become larger or smaller according to the phases of the moon; and so are things of this kind, such as menstrual blood, with which magicians perform many wonderful and monstrous deeds. Also the hyena, which changes its sex and is susceptible to various sorceries, and all animals called amphibious—those that live on land and in water together, such as beavers and otters, and those that hunt fish. Furthermore, all monstrous animals and those generated without manifest seeds or <term>equivocally</term> <note>Equivocal generation refers to the old belief in spontaneous generation, where life arises from non-living matter</note>, such as mice born from mating and from the earth through decay.

<margin>Lunar birds.</margin>
Among lunar birds are geese, ducks, divers, and all aquatic birds and hunters of fish, such as herons; also those produced equivocally, such as wasps from the carcasses of horses, bees from the decay of cows, gnats from spoiled wine, and beetles from the flesh of donkeys. Most lunar of all, however, is the two-horned beetle, which they call "bull-formed." After burying its ball of dung, it leaves it for twenty-eight days—the time in which the moon travels through the entire zodiac; on the twenty-ninth day, when it believes the conjunction of the luminaries <note>The new moon, when the sun and moon meet</note> will occur, it opens the ball and throws it into the water, from which the beetles then emerge.

<margin>Lunar fish.</margin>
Among lunar fish are the <term>aelurus</term> <note>original: *ælurus*; likely referring to a species of catfish whose eyes were thought to change with the moon</note>, whose eyes vary with the phases of the moon, and all those that observe the moon’s motion, such as the torpedo <note>the cramp-fish or electric ray</note>, the <term>echeneis</term> <note>original: *echeneis*; the remora, or "ship-holder," believed to have the power to stop vessels</note>, the crab, the oyster, shellfish, and frogs.

Such examples include the black fig, the pine, and the **cypress**, which is a funeral tree; it does not sprout again from its base, bears grim berries, has a bitter taste, a violent smell, an unpleasant shade, and very harsh pitch. Its fruit is useless, yet its wood is incorruptible by time. Furthermore, it is a mournful tree and sacred to <term>Dis</term> <note>original: *Diti*; a name for Pluto or the god of the Underworld</note>, much like **celery** <note>original: *apium*; often translated as celery or wild parsley</note>. In ancient times, people used to strew celery over the linings of tombs before placing the bodies of the dead inside them; for this reason, while it was lawful to weave garlands for festive banquets from all kinds of herbs and flowers, celery was forbidden because it is a plant of mourning and does not suit a joyful occasion. **Reptiles** and other animals are also categorized here: those that are solitary, nocturnal, sad, contemplative, or entirely brutish, as well as the greedy, timid, melancholic, those of much labor and slow movement, those of unclean diet, and those that devour their own young. From these come the mole, donkey, wolf, hare, mule, cat, camel, bear, pig, ape, dragon, basilisk, toad, and all creeping and crawling things, scorpions, ants, and those things born from rot in the earth, in the waters, or in the ruins of buildings, such as mice and various kinds of worms. Among **birds**, those belonging to Saturn are those with long necks and heavy voices, such as cranes, ostriches, and peacocks, which are sacred to Saturn and Juno. Likewise the owl, the screech-owl, the bat, the hoopoe, the raven, and the <term>origis</term> <note>original: *origis auis*; likely referring to a species of lapwing or a bird of ill omen</note>, a most envious bird. Among **fish**, the eel lives apart from other fish, as do the lamprey and the dogfish, which swallow their own young. Likewise turtles, oysters, shellfish, sea sponges, and things of that kind.

### Chapter XXVI. Regarding Jovial things <note>original: *Iouialia*; things belonging to or influenced by the planet Jupiter</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap 'I' featuring two figures, likely a satyr and a child, entangled in stylized foliage.</image-desc>

Among tastes, those that are sweet and pleasant. Among **metals**, tin, silver, and gold, because of their temperate nature. Among **stones**, the hyacinth, beryl, sapphire, <term>tutty</term> <note>original: *tuthia*; a medicinal zinc oxide found in furnace chimneys</note>, emerald, green jasper, and all stones with perpetual green or airy colors. Furthermore, grains like wheat, barley, and spelt, along with raisins, liquorice, sugar, and all things whose sweetness is manifest and subtle, sharing something of a binding and sharp flavor—such as walnuts, almonds, pine nuts, hazelnuts, pistachios, peony roots, <term>myrobalans</term> <note>original: *myrobalani*; plum-like fruits used in medicine</note>, rhubarb, and manna. Orpheus also attributes <term>storax</term> <note>original: *styracem*; a fragrant resin</note> to Jupiter. Among **animals** are those that exhibit a certain dignity and wisdom, and those that are mild, well-trained, and of good character, such as the deer, the bull, and the elephant, as well as all gentle creatures like the sheep and the lamb. Among **birds**, those that are of a temperate constitution, such as hens and the yolks of eggs. Likewise the partridge, pheasant, swallow, and pelican. ### Things which relate to Mars. Chapter XXVII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter M featuring scrolled foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Martial things among the elements include **Fire**, and in a similar way, all things that are burnt or sharp. Among the humors, Mars rules **yellow bile** <note>original: *cholera*; one of the four medieval humors, associated with a hot and dry temperament</note>. Tastes that are **bitter, sharp, and stinging to the tongue**, as well as those called **lachrymose** <note>meaning they cause the eyes to water, like onions</note>, belong to him. Among metals, he rules **iron** and **red brass** <note>original: *æs rubeum*; likely copper or a reddish bronze</note>, and everything fiery, red, and sulfurous. Among stones, his are the **diamond, loadstone, bloodstone, various types of jasper, and amethyst**. Among plants and trees, he claims **hellebore, garlic, euphorbium, cartabana, ammoniac, radish, spurge laurel, monkshood, scammony**, and all things poisonous through an overabundance of heat. Also included are those plants protected by stinging thorns or those that burn, prick, or blister the skin upon contact, such as the **thistle, nettle, and spearwort**. Furthermore, those things which, when eaten, force out tears—such as **shallots, leeks, mustard, and castor-oil** <note>original: *castoreū*; while often referring to beaver musk, here it likely refers to the stinging or medicinal properties of the plant or substance in a Martial context</note>—are his, along with all thorny trees and the **cornel tree**, which is sacred to Mars. Among animals, those that are warlike, predatory, bold, and of a keen imagination are Martial, such as the **horse, mule, he-goat, kid, wolf, leopard, and wild donkey**. Likewise, **serpents** and **dragons** that are dangerous with venom belong to him, as well as anything troublesome to humans, such as **fleas, flies, and the baboon** <note>original: *cynocephalus*; literally "dog-head," referring to the baboon</note>, on account of its irascibility. All birds of prey, meat-eaters, and bone-breakers are his, such as the **eagle, falcon, hawk, and vulture**; also birds considered dire and ill-omened, like **owls, screech-owls, kestrels, and kites**. He rules those birds that are always hungry and most predatory, and those that gulp their food and emit a voice like someone strangling, such as **ravens and crows**; the **woodpecker** above all others is sacred to Mars. Among fish, he possesses the **pike, mullet, stingray, ram-fish, goat-fish, wolf-fish, and the Glaucus**, all of which are both voracious and predatory.

Likewise, the **bull** on account of its pride, and the **calf** on account of its playfulness, are Venereal. ### Things which follow Mercury. Chapter XXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring ornate scrolling foliate and floral motifs.</image-desc>
Among the elements, **water** is Mercurial, although Mercury moves all things without distinction. Similarly, he rules the humors, especially when they are mixed together. Also included are **hermaphroditic animals** and those which change their sex back and forth, such as the **hare** and the **hyena**, and similar creatures. Among birds, those which are naturally clever, melodious, musical, and versatile are Mercurial, such as the **goldfinch, fig-eater, blackbird, thrush, lark, nightingale, calandra lark, parrot, magpie, ibis, purple swamphen**, and the **unicorn beetle** <note>original: "scarabeus unicornis"; likely the rhinoceros beetle, though grouped here with birds/flying things</note>. ### That the whole sublunary world, and all things in it, are distributed
### among the planets. Chapter XXX.

Furthermore, whatever is found in the whole world is affected by the domains of the planets and receives power from them. Thus, in fire, the life-giving **light** is attributed to the **Sun**; the **heat** to **Mars**. In the earth, the varied **surface** belongs to the **Moon** and **Mercury** and the **starry heavens**, but the **entire mass** itself is dedicated to **Saturn**. In the middle elements, where moisture rules, the **airy part** is subject to **Jupiter**, the **watery part** to the **Moon**, while the **mixed part** obeys **Mercury** and **Venus**. By a similar logic, in nature, the **acting causes** <note>the forces that make things happen</note> follow the **Sun**, while the **matter** follows the **Moon**. The **fertility of the acting causes** follows **Jupiter**, and the **fertility of the matter** follows **Venus**. **Swift movement** toward an effect follows **Mars** and **Mercury**—the former because of his intensity, the latter because of his dexterity and multifaceted power. However, the **permanent continuation** of all things is dedicated to **Saturn**. Moreover, in the number of vegetables, every fruit...

->How provinces and kingdoms are distributed to the planets.<-

### Chapter XXXI.

The globe of the earth itself, through its kingdoms and provinces, is distributed among the planets and the signs of the zodiac. For to **Saturn** with **Capricorn** are subjected Macedonia, Thrace, Illyria, India, Ariane, and Gordyene—many of which regions are in Asia Minor. With **Aquarius**, however, there are subject to him the Sauromatic region, Oxiana, Sogdiana, Arabia, Phazania, Media, and Ethiopia; these regions for the most part belong to inner Asia.

To **Jupiter** with **Sagittarius** are subjected Tuscany, the Celtic lands <note>original: "Celtica," referring generally to Gaul</note>, Spain, and Arabia Felix <note>The "Happy" or fertile part of the southern Arabian Peninsula</note>. With **Pisces** belong Lycia, Lydia, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Paphlagonia, Nasamonia, and Garamantica.

**Mars** rules with **Aries**: Britain, Gaul, Germany, Bastarnia, the hollows of Syria <note>original: "concaua Syriae," likely referring to Coele-Syria</note>, Idumea, and Judea. With **Scorpio**, however: Syria, Commagene, Cappadocia, Metagonitis, Mauritania, and Getulia.

To the **Sun** with his **Leo** are subjected Italy, Apulia, Sicily, the Phoenicians, Chaldeans, and the Orsenians (or Orchenians).

**Venus** with **Taurus** holds the Cyclades, the maritime regions of Asia Minor, Cyprus, Parthia, Media, and Persia. With **Libra**, she commands the Bactrians, Caspians, Serica <note>The ancient name for Northern China, the "Land of Silk"</note>, the Thebaid, the Oasis, and the Troglodytes <note>An ancient term for "cave-dwellers" in various regions, often the Red Sea coast</note>.

**Mercury** with **Gemini** holds Hyrcania, Armenia, Matiana, Cyrenaica, Marmarica, and lower Egypt. With **Virgo**, he holds Greece, Achaia, Crete, Babylon, Mesopotamia, Assyria, and Elam—from which they are called "Elamites" in the Scriptures.

Following the **Moon** with **Cancer** are Bithynia, Phrygia, Colchis, Numidia, Africa, Carthage, and all of Carchedonia <note>The territory surrounding ancient Carthage</note>.

We have gathered these things from the opinion of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose *Tetrabiblos* defined these geographical-astrological links</note>; to which many other things could be added according to the writings of other astrologers. Truly, whoever knows how to compare these divisions of provinces—beyond this celestial distribution—with the ministries of the ruling intelligences <note>The angelic spirits that govern the planets</note>, the blessings of the Israelite tribes, the lots of the apostles, and the <term>typical seals</term> <note>Mystical symbols or archetypes found in sacred texts</note> of the Holy Scriptures, will be able to elicit great and even prophetic oracles of future events concerning every region.

<page-num>XXXVII.</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>
<sig>d</sig>

<image-desc>A decorative capital 'S' featuring a woodcut of two scholars in long academic robes standing beside a large, ornate celestial globe mounted on a tripod. One scholar gestures toward the stars on the globe, while the other observes intently, symbolizing the study of cosmography and astrology.</image-desc>

The logic regarding the forms of the fixed stars is to be understood as similar in all respects: thus, they maintain that the terrestrial ram is subject to the celestial **Ram** <note>Aries</note>, and the terrestrial bull and ox to the celestial **Bull** <note>Taurus</note>. Likewise, they say crabs are subject to **the Crab** <note>Cancer</note>, lions to **the Lion** <note>Leo</note>, virgins to **the Virgin** <note>Virgo</note>, and that **the Scorpion** presides over scorpions, **the Horned Goat** <note>Capricorn</note> over goats, **the Archer** <note>Sagittarius</note> over horses, and that fish are under the sign of **the Fishes** <note>Pisces</note>. Similarly, the celestial **She-Bear** <note>Ursa Major</note> presides over bears, the **Water-Serpent** <note>Hydra</note> over snakes, and dogs are under the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius</note>; and so it is for each individual thing. 

Indeed, Apuleius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a famous 4th-century herbal</note> distributed certain principal herbs to the signs and planets as if they were their own property. Specifically: to the **Ram**, sage <note>original: "elelisphacon"</note>; to the **Bull**, upright vervain <note>original: "peristereona orthion"</note>; to the **Twins**, prostrate vervain <note>original: "peristereona hyption"</note>; to the **Crab**, comfrey <note>original: "symphyton"</note>; to the **Lion**, cyclamen <note>original: "cyclaminū"</note>; to the **Virgin**, calamint <note>original: "calamynthū"</note>; to the **Scales**, scorpion-grass <note>original: "scorpiuron"</note>; to the **Scorpion**, mugwort <note>original: "arthemesiā"</note>; to the **Archer**, pimpernel <note>original: "anagallidē"</note>; to the **Horned Goat**, sorrel <note>original: "lapathū"</note>; to the **Water-Bearer**, dragon-wort <note>original: "draconteā"</note>; and to the **Fishes**, birthwort <note>original: "aristolochiā"</note>. 

For the planets: to **Saturn**, houseleek <note>original: "semperuiuum"</note>; to **Jupiter**, agrimony <note>original: "eupatorium"</note>; to **Mars**, hog's fennel <note>original: "peucedanum"</note>; to **the Sun**, heliotrope <note>original: "heliotropium"</note>; to **Venus**, panacea or maidenhair <note>original: "callitrichum"</note>; to **Mercury**, mullein <note>original: "phlomum"</note>; and to **the Moon**, peony <note>original: "agloophotim"</note>.

Musk and sandalwood are dedicated to the Sun with Venus; coriander is dedicated to Venus with Saturn. Among animals, the seal <note>original: "uitulus marinus," or "sea-calf"</note> is under the Sun and Jupiter. Foxes and monkeys belong to Saturn and Mercury, and domestic dogs belong to Mercury and the Moon; and we have already taught more concerning these things in the previous sections.

### On the signs and characters of natural things. Chapter XXXIII.

<margin>Every thing has its own character.</margin>
All stars have their own unique natures, properties, and conditions; they project the signs and characters of these through their rays even into these lower things—into elements, stones, plants, animals, and their various parts. Wherefore every single thing, by its harmonic arrangement and by its own star shining upon it, is allotted a certain special sign or "character" impressed upon it. This mark is significant of that star or harmony, and contains within itself a special <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to an inherent occult power or efficacy</term> that differs from others in genus, species, or the number of the underlying matter. Thus, every thing has its own character for some peculiar effect impressed upon it by its star, especially by that star which holds the primary rule over it. These characters contain and retain the specific natures, virtues, and roots of their stars, and they produce similar operations in other things upon which they are reflected. They call forth and assist the influences of their stars—whether they be planets, fixed stars, images, or celestial signs—whenever they are crafted in the proper material, at the proper time, and with the required ceremonies. Considering this, the ancient sages, who labored greatly to investigate the occult conditions of things, sought out the images, figures, signs, seals, and characters of the stars...

# BOOK ONE.
### 39.

...they have noted those signs which nature itself has painted by the rays of the stars in these lower realms—some in stones, others in plants and in the joints and knots of branches, and others in various members of animals. For the laurel, the lotus, and the heliotrope <note>original: "heliotropium"; plants traditionally associated with the Sun because they turn to face it</note>—all solar plants—reveal the **characters** <note>original: "characteres"; mystical marks or signatures that reveal a thing's hidden nature</note> of the Sun in their roots and cut nodes. 
<margin>The origin of **Spatularia**.</margin>
The same is true in the bones and shoulder blades of animals: from this emerged the species of divination known as **Spatularia** <note>original: "Spatularia"; also called scapulimancy, this is the practice of reading signs in the shoulder blades (scapulae) of animals</note>. Likewise, in stones and quarries, the characters and images of celestial things are not infrequently found. But since in such a great diversity of things, science cannot be handed down except in those few instances that human wisdom can perceive, we shall for now leave aside those things which can be investigated in plants, stones, and other things, or in the limbs of many animals. Instead, let us stop our progress at human nature alone. Since humanity is the most complete image of the entire universe, containing within itself every celestial harmony, 
<margin>Marks of celestial influences are found in abundance within human nature.</margin>
we undoubtedly find in the human form an abundance of the signs and characters of all the stars and celestial influences. These are all the more effective because they are less removed from the celestial nature itself. Truly, just as the number of the stars is known to God alone, so too are their effects and signs regarding these lower things; therefore, no human intellect can ascend to the knowledge of them all. Thus, only a very few have become known, which the ancient Philosophers and **Chiromancers** <note>original: "Chiromantici"; practitioners of palmistry or hand-reading</note> attained partly through reason and partly through experience, while many still lie hidden, locked away in the treasuries of nature. Therefore, we shall note here a few signs or characters of the planets, which the ancient Chiromancers recognized in the hands of men. Julian <note>likely referring to Julian the Apostate or a contemporary mystical source</note> calls these "sacred" or "divine letters," since, according to the word of Holy Scripture, the life of men is written in their hands through them. These signs are always the same and similar to one another among all nations and languages, and they are permanent. To these, both ancient and more recent Chiromancers later added many others; whoever wishes to know them should seek out their volumes. It is enough here to have shown from where the characters of nature derive their origin, and in what things they are to be sought.

## How through natural things and their virtues, we can entice and attract the influences and virtues of celestial bodies. Chapter XXXIIII.

Now, if you desire to receive virtue <note>original: "virtutem"; in this context, it refers to a spiritual power or inherent property rather than moral goodness</note> from some part of the world or from a star, you must apply those things that belong to that star. By doing so, you come under its specific influence—just as wood, when prepared with sulfur, pitch, and oil, is ready to catch fire. Furthermore, when you properly apply many different things to a specific species or individual—things which are scattered but conform to the same "Idea" and star—a singular gift is soon infused from that Idea through the mediation of the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "anima mundi"; a Neoplatonic concept of a spiritual force that connects the divine realm to the physical world</note>. I say "properly prepared," meaning under a harmony similar to the very harmony that originally infused that virtue into the matter.

<margin>An analogy.</margin>
For although things possess certain virtues, as we have said, those virtues are often so hidden that they rarely produce a perfect work on their own. But just as crushing a mustard seed awakens its latent sharpness; and just as the heat of fire brings into view letters written in onion juice or milk which were previously hidden; and just as letters inscribed on a stone with goat's fat—though entirely invisible—come to light and stand out as if carved when the stone is submerged in vinegar; and just as the touch of a broom or a strawberry tree <note>original: "arbuti"; the Arbutus unedo, which in ancient lore was sometimes associated with causing or curing mental agitation</note> stirs up a sleeping madness, so does celestial harmony itself bring forth, awaken, strengthen, and make manifest the virtue latent in matter. It brings it, so to speak, from potentiality into action, provided the things are properly exposed to that harmony under the right celestial opportunity. For example: if you wish to attract virtue from the Sun, seek out those things which are solar—among vegetables, plants, metals, stones, and animals.

### On the mixtures of natural things with one another, and their
### usefulness. Chapter XXXV.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'C' containing a figure in classical robes within a circular medallion, flanked by architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>We have found in lower nature that the gifts of the higher bodies <note>i.e., the planets and stars</note> are not found contained within any single thing. Instead, many species are dispersed among us, just as there are many solar things, yet each one of them does not embrace all the virtues <note>powers or qualities</note> of the Sun; rather, one has certain properties from the sun, and another has others. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary in magical operations to make mixtures. If a hundred or a thousand solar virtues were scattered through as many plants, animals, and similar things, we can melt these together and reduce them into a single form, in which we will see all those mentioned virtues now united and contained. <margin>A twofold power in mixture.</margin>There is, however, a twofold power in such a mixture: one, namely, which was previously inherent in its individual parts and is celestial; the other is acquired through a certain and skillful blending of many things mixed together according to specific proportions, such as agree with the heavens under a specific astrological constellation. This power descends through a certain likeness and relationship of things to one another and to the higher realms, insofar as subsequent virtues correspond step by step to preceding ones, especially where the "patient" <note>the material being acted upon</note> is adapted to its "agent" <note>the celestial force</note>. Thus, from a specific composition of herbs, vapors, and similar things—prepared both physically and astronomically—there results a certain common form, endowed with several gifts of the stars. This is just like the honey of bees, which is extracted from the juices of innumerable flowers and reduced into one form; it contains the virtue of them all by the nearly divine and wonderful skill of the "flies" <note>Agrippa uses "muscarum" (flies) here to refer to bees, a common classical categorization</note>. Yet no less wonderful is what Eudoxus of Cnidus <note>a Greek astronomer and student of Plato</note> relates about artificial honey, which a certain race of giants in Libya knew how to make from flowers so skillfully that it seemed to differ very little from the honey of bees. Furthermore, every mixture composed of many parts is most perfect when it is so bonded from its parts that it becomes one, consistent with itself everywhere, and not easily separated. We sometimes see stones and diverse bodies bonded and united by a certain natural force so that they seem completely one: such as two trees joined by grafting, or oysters joined with stones by some hidden force of nature. Animals have even been seen turned into stones, and thus united with the substance of the stone, so that they seemed now to produce one body of a single kind. Thus ebony, in the category of trees, is sometimes wood and sometimes stone. Therefore, when someone crafts a mixture from many materials under celestial influences, the variety of celestial actions on one hand, and the gathered power of natural things on the other, produces certain wonders through ointments, eye-washes <note>term: "collyria" (medical or magical preparations for the eyes)</note>, fumigations <note>magical incense</note>, and similar preparations. Such things are read in the books of Chiramis, Archytas, Democritus, and Hermes—specifically the book titled *Alchorat*—and many others.

### On the union of mixed things, and the introduction of a more noble form and of sensible life. Chapter XXXVI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting two figures in a landscape, possibly a scholar and a companion, within a square frame.</image-desc>It should be known that the more noble the form of a thing is, the more ready and inclined the thing itself is to receive, and also the more powerful it is to act. Therefore, the incomprehensible wonders of things are produced when, for instance, materials are mixed together and prepared at appropriate times, and then set out to be vivified <note>given life</note> by reconciling to them a life from the stars and a sensible soul <note>original: "animam sensibilem"; in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the level of soul responsible for perception and movement, found in animals</note> as a more noble form. For there is such great power in prepared materials, which we see then acquire life, when a perfect mixture of qualities seems to have broken the prior opposition <note>the conflict between the four elements—earth, air, fire, and water—that exists in unrefined matter</note>. They have truly attained life's perfection insofar as there is a capacity within that life and sensible soul to conceive more noble and sublime virtues <note>powers or properties</note>. Furthermore, celestial power lies dormant elsewhere, like sulfur removed from a flame; but in living bodies, it often blazes up like ignited sulfur, and then it fills all neighboring things with its vapor. Thus, certain marvelous works are brought forth, such as are read of in the book *Nemith*, which is also titled the *Laws of Pluto* <note>a reference to a medieval magical text, possibly related to the "Liber Vaccae" or "Book of the Cow," which describes experiments in spontaneous generation</note>, because such generations are monstrous and are not produced according to the ordinary laws of nature.

<margin>Various procreations of different animals.</margin>For we know that gnats are generated from worms, wasps from a horse, bees from a calf or ox, and a scorpion is generated from a crab when its legs are removed and it is buried. From a duck roasted until it is ground into powder and then thrown into water, frogs are generated; if, however, it is cooked in a pastry and cut into pieces and left in a damp, underground place, toads are generated. From the herb basil <note>original: "basilicone"</note> crushed between two stones, scorpions are generated; and from the hairs of a menstruating woman placed under <margin><note>Handwritten marginalia in ink</note>the true mandrake</margin> dung, serpents are made; and a hair from a horse's tail thrown into water acquires life and turns into a harmful worm. And there is a craft by which, in an egg being hatched by a hen, a form similar to a human is generated—such as I have seen and know how to compose—which the magi claim is effective for marvelous virtues, and they call this the "true mandrake" <term>mandrake: while usually a plant root, Agrippa here refers to a "homunculus" or artificially created being shaped like a human</term>. It is necessary, therefore, to know which and what kind of materials—whether begun or perfected by nature or art, or assembled from many things—are able to receive celestial influences. For the suitability of natural things to celestial ones is sufficient for us to draw influence from them; because, since nothing prevents the celestial bodies from diffusing their light to lower things, they allow no material to be devoid of their power. Therefore, however much of the material is perfect and pure, it is not unfit for celestial influence. For such <margin>The binding of materials to the soul of the world.</margin> is the binding and continuity of matter to the <term>soul of the world: the "anima mundi," a spiritual force believed to permeate all nature and connect the physical world to the divine</term>, which daily flows over natural things and over all that nature has prepared, so that it is impossible for life or some more noble form not to flow into prepared matter.

XLIII.

->BOOK ONE<-

### How by certain natural and artificial preparations, we draw down celestial and vital gifts from above. Chapter XXXVII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing scrollwork and geometric patterns.</image-desc>

The Academics, along with Hermes Trismegistus <note>a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom, magic, and the "Hermetic" tradition</note>, and Iarchas the Brahmin <note>a legendary Indian sage</note>, as well as the Kabbalists of the Hebrews <note>original: "Mecubales"</note>, all confess that everything under the lunar sphere in this lower world is subject to generation and corruption. They also state that these same things exist in the celestial world, but in a celestial manner; then also in the intellectual world <note>the realm of pure thought or divine ideas</note>, but in a much more perfect and superior state; and finally, in the most perfect state in the archetype <note>the original model in the mind of God</note>. By this sequence, every lower thing corresponds to its superior, and through this to the highest, according to its kind. From the heavens, these things receive that celestial power which is called the quintessence <note>literally "fifth essence," a subtle substance distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, or the spirit of the world, or the middle nature. From the intellectual world, they receive a spiritual and living vigor, which transcends all qualitative power. Finally, from the archetype, through these intermediaries, they receive the original power of all perfection according to their degree. Thus, from these lower things one can properly trace back to the stars, from those to their intelligences <note>spiritual beings or angels governing the planets</note>, and from there to the archetype.

<margin>Where magic flows from.</margin>

From this whole sequence flows magic and all occult philosophy. For daily something natural is drawn through art, and daily something divine is drawn through nature. Observing this, the Egyptians called nature a "magician" <note>original: "naturam magam"</note>—that is, the very magical power found in the attraction of likes by likes, and fitting things by fitting things. This kind of attraction, arising from the mutual agreement of things with one another—the superior with the inferior—the Greeks called sympathy <note>original: συμπάθειαν (sympatheian)</note>. Thus, water agrees with earth in its coldness, air with water in its moisture, fire with air in its heat, and fire agrees with heaven in its matter. Fire does not mix with water except through the mediation of air, nor does air mix with earth except through water. Likewise, the soul is not joined to the body except through the spirit, nor is the intellect joined to the spirit except through the soul. 

Thus we see that when nature has formed the body of a fetus, by this very preparation it immediately draws down a spirit from the universe. This spirit is the fuel <note>original: "fomes"</note> within the spirit and body for attaining divine understanding and mind—just as dryness in wood is prepared to receive oil, and the oil soaked into it is the food for fire, and the fire itself is the vehicle for light. By these examples, we see how by certain natural and artificial preparations, we can receive certain celestial gifts from above. For stones and metals agree with herbs, and these with animals, these indeed with the heavens, and these with the intelligences, and those with divine properties and attributes, and with God himself, in whose likeness and image all things were created. 

The first image is the world; the image of the world is man; the image of man is the animal; the image of the animal is the zoophyte <note>a "plant-animal," like coral or sponges, which were thought to bridge the two kingdoms</note>; the image of that is the plant; the image of the plant is metals; and the images of these are stones. Again, in spiritual things, the plant agrees with the beast in vegetation <note>the power of growth and nutrition</note>, the beast with man in sense, man with the spirit <note>original: "daemone"; referring here to a celestial being or genius, not a malevolent demon</note> in intellect, and these with God in immortality.

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic "Chain of Being," arguing that all levels of reality—from stones and plants to celestial intelligences and God—are linked by "sympathy" and can be influenced through specific preparations.</summary>
<keywords>Chain of Being, sympathy, quintessence, Hermes Trismegistus, Kabbalah, spirit of the world, astrology, alchemy, intellectual world</keywords>

XLIIII.

DE OCCULTA PHILOSOPHIA

<margin>Nature’s wondrous binding.</margin>
...immortality. Divinity is joined to the mind, the mind to the intellect; the intellect to intention, intention to the imagination; imagination to sensation, sensation to the senses, and these finally to physical things. For such is the binding and continuity of nature that every superior power, by distributing its rays in a long and continuous series through each inferior thing, flows all the way to the lowest; and inferior things reach the highest through each of their superiors. For in this way, inferior things are connected to superiors in turn, so that the influence from their head—the First Cause <note>In Agrippa’s philosophy, the "First Cause" refers to God as the source of all existence.</note>—proceeds all the way to the lowest things like a stretched string. If one end of this string is touched, the whole thing suddenly trembles, and such a touch resonates all the way to the other end; and when one inferior thing is moved, the superior thing to which it corresponds is also moved, just like the strings on a well-tuned lyre <note>original: "cythara"</note>.

### How we can receive from above not only celestial and vital gifts, but also certain intellectual and divine ones. Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>The mage attracts hidden things through manifest things.</margin>
The Magi teach that through inferior things that conform to superior ones, celestial gifts can be drawn down by favorable celestial influences. In this way, through these celestial means, celestial spirits <note>original: "dæmones." In this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or planetary intelligences.</note>—insofar as they are the attendants of the stars—can be won over and instilled within us. Therefore, when certain materials possessing the natural power of divinity—that is, those which are naturally in harmony with the higher powers—are properly collected and combined, partly through physical means and partly through astronomy <note>meaning the timing of celestial alignments</note>, one can receive from above not only celestial or life-giving gifts, but even certain intellectual, spiritual, and divine ones. Iamblichus, Proclus, and Synesius <note>key philosophers of the Neoplatonic school who blended logic with mysticism</note>, along with the entire school of Platonists, confirm this. Furthermore, Hermes Trismegistus writes that a statue properly fashioned from specific things corresponding to a particular spirit is immediately animated by that appropriate spirit. St. Augustine also mentions this in the eighth book of *The City of God*. For such is the harmony of the world that even supercelestial things are drawn by celestial ones, and supernatural things are harmonized and drawn by natural ones. This is because a single creative power and a participation in the "Forms" <note>the ideal versions of things in the divine mind</note> is diffused through all things. Just as this creative power produces manifest things from hidden reasons, so the mage takes up manifest things in order to attract hidden ones—for example, through the rays of the stars, through incense <note>original: "suffumigationes"</note>, through lights, through sounds, and through natural objects harmonious with the heavens. Within these, beyond their physical qualities, there also exist incorporeal and divine ratios, senses, numbers, and measures. 

Thus we read that the ancients were often accustomed to receive something divine and marvelous by means of certain natural things. For instance, the stone that grows in the pupil of a hyena’s eye, when held under the tongue, is said to grant the power of prophecy. The moonstone, or selenite, is said to do the same. Likewise, they say the *anchitide* stone summons images of the gods, and the *synochitide* stone holds the shadows of the dead that have been summoned. The herb *aglaoptis*—also called *marmoritides* because it grows in the marble of Arabia—produces similar effects on the Persian side; as Pliny relates, the Magi use it when they wish to summon gods. There is also an herb called *theangelis*, which the Magi drink to prophesy. Furthermore, there are certain herbs by which the dead may be called back to life, as the historian Xanthus tells of an herb called *bali*...

XLV

BOOK ONE.

...a slain dragon hatchling was restored to life by its parent, and that the same parent revived a certain Tillo <note>A reference to a story in Pliny the Elder or Xanthus regarding a man killed by a dragon.</note>, whom the dragon had killed. Juba <note>King Juba II of Numidia, a noted scholar-king of the 1st century BCE.</note> also reports that in Arabia, a certain herb recalled a man to life. Whether such things can truly be done by the power of herbs or any other natural thing in humans, we shall discuss in the following pages; however, that this can happen in other living creatures is certain and manifest. For instance, if submerged flies are placed in warm ashes, they revive; and bees submerged in water similarly recover their life in the juice of catnip <note>original: "nepetæ"</note>. Likewise, eels that have died from a lack of water will, if their bodies remain intact and they are placed in vinegar under dung with the addition of vulture's blood, recover their life after a few days. They say that if one cuts a remora <note>original: "Echeneim," a legendary fish believed to stop ships.</note> into pieces and throws them into the sea, the parts will shortly come back together and revive. We also know that the pelican recalls its killed chicks to life with its own blood <note>A common medieval allegory for Christ, though here treated as a natural phenomenon.</note>.

### That we can attract worldly deities, and the spirits who serve them, by using certain worldly materials. Chapter XXXIX.

No one is ignorant of the fact that evil spirits <note>original: "dæmones." Agrippa uses this term for intermediate spirits, which can be good, evil, or neutral.</note> can be attracted by evil and profane arts, just as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine philosopher who wrote extensively on demonology.</note> relates that the Gnostic magi were accustomed to do. Among them, cursed and abominable outrages were performed, such as those once seen in the rites of Priapus <note>The Greek god of fertility, often depicted with permanent arousal.</note> and in the service of the idol called Peor <note>original: "Panor," referring to Baal-Peor, a Moabite god associated with license.</note>, to whom sacrifices were made with the private parts uncovered. Not unlike these—if indeed it is truth and not a fable—is what is read concerning the detestable heresy of the Templars; similar things are well-known regarding malevolent women <note>Referring to the contemporary belief in witches.</note>, for such "old-wives' madness" is often found to stray into these types of outrages. By these and similar means, evil spirits are attracted and conspire together. Just as the malignant spirit said to John concerning the mage Cynops <note>A sorcerer from the apocryphal *Acts of John* who challenged the Apostle.</note>: "Every power of Satan," he said, "dwells there, and enters into a conspiracy with all the principalities, and we ourselves are with him; Cynops obeys us, and we in turn obey him." On the other hand, no one is ignorant that by good works, a pure mind, mystical prayers, devout supplications, and the like, the super-celestial angels are won over to us. Therefore, let no one doubt that in a similar way, worldly deities can also be attracted by certain worldly materials—or at least the spirits <note>original: "dæmones"</note> who are the ministers or followers of these deities. As Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermeticism.</note> says, these are aerial spirits, not super-celestial ones, let alone the higher beings. Thus we read that the ancient priests made statues and images that predicted the future, and infused the spirits of the stars into them. These spirits were not so much "trapped" by the specific materials as they were "delighting" in them; for as they recognize these materials as being congruent to themselves, they dwell in them always and willingly. Through these objects, they speak and perform wonders, just as spirits are accustomed to do when they occupy human bodies.

Likewise, there is the binding of thieves and robbers, so that in a certain place...

...so that they cannot steal; the binding of merchants, so that they are unable to buy or sell in a certain place; the binding of an army, so that it cannot cross a certain boundary; the binding of ships, so that they are unable to leave port by any force of the winds, even with infinite sails stretched by the breeze. Likewise, the binding of a mill, so that it cannot be turned by any force; the binding of a cistern or a well, so that water cannot be drawn from it; the binding of a field, so that crops cannot be produced in it; the binding of a certain place, so that nothing can be built upon it; the binding of fire, so that it cannot be lit in a certain place, and so that a combustible material will not burn even when placed in the strongest fire. Likewise, the binding of lightning and storms, so that they cannot cause harm. Also, the binding of dogs, so that they cannot bark; the binding of birds and wild beasts, so that they are unable to fly or flee; and similar things, hardly credible, which nonetheless have often been known through experience. <margin>How bindings are performed</margin> Such bindings are performed through sorcerous potions <note>original: "veneficia"</note>, through eye-washes <note>original: "collyria"</note>, ointments, love-potions <note>original: "philtra"</note>, through tying and hanging items, through rings, through fascinations <note>bewitchment by sight or word</note>, through strong imaginations and ecstasies of the mind, through images and characters, through incantations and imprecations, through lights, through sounds, through numbers, through words and names, invocations, sacrifices, adjurations, exorcisms, consecrations, devotions, and through various superstitions and observations, and things related to these.

### On sorcerous potions, and their power. Chapter XLI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring scrolling foliate patterns and classical architectural motifs within a square border.</image-desc>The power of sorcerous potions <note>original: "veneficiorum"</note> is said to be so great that they are believed to be able to subvert all lower things, and to make them waste away and change, just as Virgil sings:

> These herbs, and these poisons gathered for me in Pontus,

Likewise, elsewhere regarding the companions of Ulysses:

> Whom the cruel goddess Circe, with powerful herbs,
> Had stripped of human face and clothed in the features and backs of wild beasts.

And a little later:

> Picus, the tamer of horses, whom his wife Circe, captured by desire,
> Struck with her golden wand and transformed with potions
> Into a bird, and sprinkled his wings with colors.

There are also types of such sorcerous potions like those recounted by Lucan regarding that Thessalian witch <note>Referring to Erictho, a legendary sorceress of Thessaly</note> who summoned the spirits of the dead, saying:

> Hither is mixed whatever nature has brought forth with a sinister birth;
> The foam of dogs who fear the water <note>original: "spuma canum, quibus unda timori est" – a reference to rabies</note> was not lacking,
> Nor the entrails of a lynx, nor the knot of the tough hyena <note>Likely referring to the stiff neck or joints of the hyena</note>,
> Nor the marrow of a stag fed on a serpent.
> Nor the remora <note>original: "echeneis"</note> that holds back a ship in the midst of the waters
> While the East wind stretches the ropes, nor the eyes of dragons.

XLVII.

# BOOK ONE

And consider the kinds of things Apuleius tells of that sorceress Pamphila, who worked for the sake of love: her maid Fotis brought her goat hairs shorn from inflated wine-skins, instead of the hair of a Boeotian youth. Pamphila, whose mind was now driven mad, climbed the shingled roof which—being stripped of its tiles on one side and open to the winds—she used in secret, as it was well-suited for her arts because it was open to the eastern and all other vistas. She first arranged her deadly laboratory <note>original: "feralem officinā"</note> with its usual equipment: every kind of spice, mysterious inscribed plates <note>original: "laminis literatis," likely referring to lead curse tablets</note>, and nails saved from ill-fated ships, as well as many limbs of corpses that had been mourned and buried. Here were noses and fingers; there, the fleshy bits of those who had been hanged; elsewhere, the preserved blood of the murdered, and skulls snatched from the teeth of wild beasts. Then, having chanted over the breathing entrails, she made an offering with various liquids—now with spring water, now with cow's milk, now with mountain honey and honey-wine <note>original: "mulsa"</note>. Then she placed those hairs, entwined and knotted together, upon living coals to be burned with many perfumes. Immediately, through the irresistible power of the magical discipline and the blind violence of the compelled spirits, those bodies whose hairs were hissing and smoking took on a human spirit; they felt, they heard, and they walked. Following the scent of their own shorn skins, they came to the place and, longing for entry, leaped against the doors in place of that Boeotian youth.

<margin>Men suddenly turned into beasts of burden.</margin>
Augustine also claims that he heard in Italy of certain women who were sorceresses, so steeped in these arts that, upon giving a piece of cheese, they would immediately turn men into beasts of burden to carry necessary goods; once the work was finished, they would restore them to being men again.

### On the Admirable Powers of Certain Sorceries. Chapter XLII.

<note>The woodcut initial 'N' begins the next section.</note>
Now, however, I shall recount certain sorceries <note>original: "ueneficia," which in this context refers to the occult properties of natural substances</note> so that, by these examples, a path may be prepared for this entire investigation. Among these is menstrual blood; let us see what great powers it possesses in sorcery. For as they say, new wine <note>original: "musta"</note> turns sour at its approach; a young vine <margin>The powers of menstrual blood.</margin> is permanently harmed by its touch; crops that are touched become sterile; grafted plants die; the buds in gardens are scorched, and the fruit falls from the trees. The brightness of mirrors is dimmed by its very gaze; the edge of steel in barbers' razors is dulled, and the luster of ivory is tarnished. Even iron is immediately corrupted by rust. Brass, when touched, takes on a heavy, foul-smelling poison and turns green with rust. Dogs go mad upon tasting it, and their bite is filled with an incurable poison. Hives of bees die and the bees flee when the hives are touched. Linen turns black when it is boiled. Mares, if they are pregnant, suffer a miscarriage if they touch it; it also causes a miscarriage if applied to pregnant women. Female donkeys do not conceive for as many years as the number of grains of barley they eat that have been touched by it. Moreover, the ash of menstrual cloths, if one sprinkles it on clothes being washed, changes the purple color and takes away the hue of flowers. They say that tertian and quartan fevers <note>Periodic fevers often associated with malaria</note> are driven away by menstrual blood enclosed in a silver bracelet with the wool of a black ram. Furthermore, it is said to be most effective for these fevers if the soles of the patient's feet are smeared with it—and it is much more effective if done by the woman herself, even without the patient knowing. In this way, they say that even the fits of the "falling sickness" <note>original: "comitiales impetus," referring to epilepsy</note> and other diseases are cured. However, all agree that if...

XLVIII

### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>Remedy for hydrophobia.</margin> If water or drink is feared because of a dog’s bite <note>This refers to rabies, historically called hydrophobia—the "fear of water"—a symptom of the disease</note>, they say that if a rag dipped in menstrual blood is simply placed under the cup, that fear is immediately dispelled. Furthermore, they report that if women uncover themselves and walk around a field of grain during their period, caterpillars and little worms, beetles, and every harmful thing will fall away. However, caution must be taken that they do not do this at sunrise, for the seeds would then wither. Similarly, it is said to drive away hailstorms and whirlwinds, and to be useful against lightning; Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, an ancient Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* is a primary source for these folk beliefs</note> himself recounts many of these things. You should know that the "venom" is more potent if it occurs during the waning moon, but its power is greatest if it happens during the silent moon <note>original: "silente luna," referring to the new moon when it is invisible</note>. If it occurs during an eclipse of the moon or sun, it becomes incurable. Its strength is of the greatest and most powerful vigor when the purgation first happens in the early years of puberty; it is also particularly potent then for this reason: if the doorposts of a house are touched with it, every evil spell <note>original: "maleficium"</note> in that house is rendered void. Furthermore, they say that the threads of a garment touched by it cannot be overcome even by fire, and if thrown into a blaze, the fire will spread no further. It is also said that if the root of a peony is given to a patient with castoreum <note>A secretion from beaver scent glands used in early medicine</note> and scrapings from menstrual cloths, the falling sickness <note>original: "morbum comitialem," a historical term for epilepsy</note> is healed. Moreover, if you burn or roast the stomach of a stag and add rags stained with menstrual blood, the smoke from it will cause ballistas <note>original: "balistas," here referring to crossbows or hunting engines</note> to be useless for hunting. It is even said that the hair of a menstruating woman, if placed under dung, generates serpents; and if burned, the smell drives serpents away—so great is the power of this "poison" that it acts as a poison even to poisonous creatures.

<margin>Hippomanes.</margin> There is also the *hippomanes* <note>A legendary substance used in ancient Greek and Roman love magic</note>, a small piece of flesh quite famous among magical materials, the size of a dried fig and black in color, which appears on the forehead of a newborn foal. Unless the mother swallows it immediately, she will feel a deep aversion to her offspring and will not suckle it. Because of this, they say it has the greatest power to incite love when it is turned into a powder and drunk in cups mixed with a lover’s blood. There is another magical substance they call by the same name, *hippomanes*: the fluid that flows from the loins of mares when they are driven into a frenzy of desire. Virgil mentions this when he sings:

> From this, finally, comes the "hippomanes," as the
> shepherds truly call it: a thick slime dripping from the groin;
> Hippomanes, which wicked stepmothers have often gathered,
> mixing herbs and non-innocent words. <note>From Virgil's *Georgics*, Book III</note>

Of this, Juvenal the Satirist also says:

> I shall speak of the "hippomanes," the spell, and the boiled
> poison given to a stepson. <note>From Juvenal’s *Satires*, VI</note>

Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the *Argonautica*</note> relates in his *Argonautica* of the "Plant of Prometheus," which he says was born from the gore and blood dripping onto the earth while the vulture tore and fed upon the liver of Prometheus on Mount Caucasus. Its flower, he says, is like saffron, of a Corycian color, with a twin stem growing to the measure of a cubit; the root beneath the earth is like recently cut flesh, emitting a dark juice like that of a beech-tree. If someone performs a sacrifice to Proserpina <note>Goddess of the Underworld</note> and then smears their body with this, he reports that they cannot be harmed by iron or fire. And Saxo Grammaticus <note>A medieval Danish historian</note> writes that a certain Froto <note>King Frotho III, a legendary Danish king</note> had a garment which, when worn, prevented him from being harmed by the point of any weapon. The Hyena also, by many poisons...

XLIX.

# BOOK ONE

<sig>e</sig>

<margin>The magical workings of the Hyena</margin> is infected with charms: for, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*, whose work served as an encyclopedia of wonders for Renaissance magicians</note> relates, if the doorposts are touched with its blood, the arts of deception and magic <note>original: "praestigiorum... artes"</note> are said to be driven away, so that the gods cannot be summoned nor spoken with, no matter how one tries. Likewise, if the ankle-bone <note>original: "talo," referring to the astragalus or hucklebone often used in divination</note> from its left side is boiled with the blood of a weasel and used as an ointment, it causes the person to be hated by everyone. They say the same happens if the eye is boiled. Furthermore, the very end of the intestine is said to be effective against the power of injustices, and to possess great influence for the success of petitions and the outcomes of trials and lawsuits, if one carries even a small amount of it. Also, if a piece of its hide <note>original: "cauerna," likely referring to a cavity or strip of skin</note> is bound to the left arm and one looks at a woman, it acts as a love charm so immediate that she follows at once; however, the skin from its forehead resists fascinations <note>the "evil eye" or magical gazing</note>. <margin>The magical workings of the Basilisk and its blood</margin> They also say that the blood of a Basilisk <note>a mythical serpent king said to kill with its gaze</note>, which they also call the "Blood of Saturn" <note>original: "Saturni sanguinem"</note>, has such great strength in magic that it grants the one carrying it success in petitions to those in power, as well as success in prayers to the gods, remedies for diseases, and the granting of favors. They also say that a tick <note>original: "ricinum"</note>, if it is plucked from the left ear of a dog that is entirely black in color, possesses great power in the divination of life: for if a sick person answers the one who brought the tick (while they stand at the feet and ask about the illness), there is certain hope of life; but if they do not answer, they will die. They also say that a stone bitten by a rabid dog possesses the power of discord if it is placed in a drink; and that one will not be barked at by a dog if a dog’s tongue is placed in the shoe beneath the big toe, especially if it is joined with the herb of the same name, namely houndstongue <note>original: "cynoglossa," a plant whose leaves were thought to resemble a dog's tongue</note>. The same effect is achieved by the membrane from a dog’s afterbirth; moreover, dogs will flee from anyone carrying a dog's heart. And Pliny relates that there are toads called "bramble toads" <note>original: "rubetarum," referring to the Bufo spinosus which lives in thickets</note> which live only among briars and are full of magical properties, and that wondrous things are done with them. For if the small bone from the left side is cast into cold water, it immediately begins to boil; it can also restrain the attacks of dogs and stir up love and quarrels when added to a potion; and if tied on, it stimulates lust. Conversely, with the bone from the right side, boiling water is cooled and will not boil again unless the bone is removed; it cures quartan fevers <note>a recurring fever, often malarial, that peaks every four days</note> when tied on in a fresh snakeskin, and other fevers, as well as inhibiting love and lust. Pliny records that the spleen and the heart from these same toads act as effective remedies against the very poisons made from them. It is also said that iron with which a person has been killed has a wondrous power among magical workings: for if a horse's bit and spurs are made from it, they say any horse, even the most ferocious, is most easily ruled and mastered. And if horseshoes were made from such iron, they say the horse becomes the swiftest and never tires from any labor. Furthermore, they claim that certain characters <note>magical symbols or sigils</note> and names ought to be inscribed upon them. They also say that if someone dips a sword with which men are beheaded into wine, anyone sick who drinks from it is cured of quartan fever. They say as well that a cup prepared from a bear's brain, or drunk from its skull, induces a "bear-fury" <note>original: "ursinam rabiem"</note> so that the man who drinks thinks himself transformed into a bear, and judges everything he sees as being in the form of bears; and he continues in that madness until the power of the cup is dissolved, without any other harm being felt in his temperament.

### On fumigations, and their reasoning and power.

**S**uffumigations <note>The practice of burning incense or herbs to create smoke for ritual purposes.</note> also, when adapted to certain stars, are extremely powerful, in so far as they strongly affect the air and the spirit <note>In Renaissance thought, the *spiritus* was a subtle substance in the body that linked the physical soul to the physical world.</note> so as to opportunely seize celestial gifts under the rays of the stars: for our own spirit is greatly transformed by vapors of this kind, since both are a type of vapor and are similar to one another. The air is also very easily affected by the qualities of lower and celestial things through these vapors; by continuously and suddenly penetrating the chest <note>original: "praecordia," referring to the area around the heart and diaphragm, considered the seat of the spirit.</note>, it wonderfully brings us into a state of similar qualities. Therefore, fumigations are usually employed for one who is about to prophesy in order to affect the imagination; these, being agreeable to certain divinities <note>original: "numinibus," referring to divine powers or spirits associated with specific stars.</note>, adapt us for receiving divine inspiration. 
<margin>Incense conducive to prophecy.</margin>
Thus they say that incense made from flax seed, psyllium seed, and the roots of violet and parsley <note>original: "apii," which can mean celery or parsley, often associated with the dead in antiquity.</note> makes one see future things and contributes to prophecy. Indeed, no one should wonder how much fumigations can do in the air, who agrees with Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of spirits.</note> that by certain vapors exhaling from their proper fumigations, aerial spirits <note>original: "daemones," which in this context refers to spirits of the air, not necessarily evil beings.</note> are immediately attracted and enter in, and that thunder and lightning are induced, and similar things: just as it is known that the liver of a chameleon burnt on the highest roof tiles incites rain and lightning; similarly, the head and throat, if set on fire with oak wood, produce the shocks of rain and thunder. Fumigations are also made under the opportune influences of the stars, causing phantoms of spirits to appear immediately in the air or elsewhere. So they say, if a fumigation is made from coriander and parsley, or henbane with hemlock, 
<margin>Herbs of the spirits.</margin>
spirits are immediately gathered; hence they call those the "herbs of the spirits." Similarly they say, if a preparation is made from the root of the giant fennel <note>original: "cannae ferulae"</note> with the juice of hemlock and henbane, and mullein <note>original: "tassi barbassi"</note>, and red sandalwood and black poppy, and a fumigation is made, it causes spirits and strange figures to appear; and if parsley is added to these, it puts spirits to flight from every place and destroys their phantoms. In a similar way, incense made from calamint, peony, mint, and castor oil plant <note>original: "palma Christi"</note> drives away all evil spirits and harmful phantasms. Furthermore, they report that by certain fumigations, certain animals are gathered or put to flight, just as Pliny reports that when the *liparis* <note>A legendary stone or plant mentioned by Pliny the Elder.</note> is burnt, all beasts are summoned; so by the burnt bones from the top of the throat of a stag, serpents are gathered, but by burnt stag horn they are put to flight. Burnt peacock feathers do the same. Similarly, by burning the lung of a donkey, all poisonous things flee; the hoof of a horse burnt in a house puts mice to flight. The same happens from the hoof of a mule. Flies are also put to flight by it, if the hoof was from the left foot. And they say that if a house or some place is fumigated with the gall of a cuttlefish, prepared with incense <note>original: "thymiamate," an aromatic burning substance.</note>, roses, and aloe wood, and if then some sea water or blood is thrown in that place, the whole house will seem full of water or blood; and if plowed earth is thrown there, the earth will seem to tremble. Moreover, it should be understood that vapors of this kind affect a body and infuse it with power that lasts for a very long time, no differently than a contagious or poisonous vapor of pestilence—which, even kept for over two years in the wall of a house, infects the inhabitants—or as the calamity of epidemic or leprosy lurking in a garment infects the wearer long afterward. Therefore, for images...

For rings and similar magical instruments, and for hidden treasures, certain suffumigations <note>The act of burning substances to produce smoke for ritual or medicinal purposes.</note> are applied, which Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on magic and the soul.</note> testifies are of no small benefit. Thus they say that if someone buries gold or silver or any precious thing when the Moon is conjoined with the Sun at the bottom of the sky <note>original: "in imo caeli," referring to the Fourth House in astrology, the point associated with hidden things and the earth.</note>, and perfumes the place with incense made of coriander, saffron, henbane, parsley, and black poppy—all crushed in equal weights and mixed with the juice of hemlock—that which is so hidden can never be found or taken away, and demons will always guard it. If anyone tries to take anything from there, they will be harassed by those demons and fall into a frenzy <note>original: "phrenesim," a state of delirium or mental disturbance.</note>. 

And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermetic philosophy.</note> says that spermaceti <note>original: "sperma ceti." In this context, it likely refers to ambergris, a highly prized aromatic substance from the sperm whale, rather than the oil.</note> used in incense has no equal for attracting demons. Therefore, if an incense is made from it along with aloeswood, costus, musk, saffron, and aromatics, mixed with the blood of a hoopoe <note>A bird often associated with magical properties in medieval and Renaissance lore.</note>, it very quickly gathers the spirits of the air. If one perfumes the area around the tombs of the dead with it, it gathers the spirits <note>original: "manes," the ancestral spirits or souls of the deceased.</note> and shadows of the dead. 

Thus, whenever we direct a work toward the Sun, we use solar incenses; if toward the Moon, lunar ones, and they did the same for the others. It should be known that just as there is opposition and enmity among the stars and spirits, so too is there among their incenses. For instance, aloeswood and sulfur are contrary to one another, as are frankincense and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury.</note>. Spirits brought in by the smoke of aloeswood flee when sulfur is lit. Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> gives the example of a spirit that used to appear in the form of a lion; when a cock <note>A rooster.</note> was presented, the spirit immediately vanished because the cock is contrary to the lion. One must consider and practice similar things.

### The Composition of Certain Incenses Adapted to the Planets. Chapter XLIV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure amidst scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

**S**o we compose a suffumigation for the **Sun** from saffron, ambergris, musk, aloeswood, balsam wood, and laurel fruit, with cloves, myrrh, and frankincense. All of these are crushed and mixed in a certain proportion—namely, one that yields a sweeter odor—and are incorporated with the brain of an eagle or the blood of a white cock, shaped into the form of little pills or troches <note>original: "trochiscorum," small medicinal lozenges or pellets.</note>.

A **Lunar** suffumigation we compose from the dried head of a frog, the eyes of a bull, and the seeds of white poppy, with frankincense and camphor, which are incorporated with menstrual blood or the blood of a goose.

For **Saturn**, one takes the seeds of black poppy, the seeds of henbane, mandrake root, lodestone <note>original: "lapis magnes," a naturally magnetized mineral.</note>, and myrrh; these are prepared with the brain of a cat or the blood of a bat.

For **Jupiter**, one takes ash tree seeds, aloeswood, storax <note>A fragrant resin.</note>, benzoin gum, lapis lazuli <note>A deep-blue metamorphic rock used as a semi-precious stone.</note>, and the tips of peacock feathers; these are incorporated with the blood of a stork, or a swallow, or the brain of a deer.

For **Mars**, we take euphorbium <note>A resin from the spurge plant.</note>, bdellium <note>A semi-transparent resin.</note>, gum ammoniac, the roots of both types of hellebore <note>Black and white hellebore were distinguished in ancient pharmacology.</note>, lodestone, and a little sulfur; all are incorporated with the brain of a crow, human blood, and the blood of a black cat.

For **Venus**, we compose an incense from musk, ambergris, aloeswood, red roses, and red coral; these are prepared with the brains of sparrows and the blood of pigeons.

For Mercury, a fumigation <note>The act of burning aromatic substances to produce smoke for ritual or medicinal purposes.</note> is made from mastic, frankincense, cloves, and the herb cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphyllo," a five-leaved plant often used in traditional medicine and folklore.</note>, and the stone agate; and they are all incorporated with the brain of a fox or a weasel, and with the blood of a magpie.

There are, furthermore, the perfumes of Saturn: all odoriferous roots, such as costus <note>An aromatic root from the ginger family used in ancient perfumes and incense.</note>, and the herbs of frankincense. The perfumes of Jupiter: every odoriferous fruit, such as nutmeg and cloves. Of Mars: all odoriferous wood, such as sandalwood, cypress, balsam, and aloeswood. Of the Sun: every gum—frankincense, mastic, benzoin, storax, laudanum, as well as amber and musk. Of Venus: flowers—roses, violets, saffron, and the like. Of Mercury: all barks of woods and fruits, such as cinnamon, cassia <note>A spice similar to cinnamon but stronger.</note>, mace, rinds of citron, laurel berries, and every odoriferous seed. The Moon has for its perfume the leaves of all vegetables, such as the Indian leaf <note>original: "folium Indum," likely referring to malabathrum, a type of cinnamon leaf prized in antiquity.</note>, and the leaves of myrtle and laurel. Know furthermore, according to the opinions of the Magi, that in every good work—such as love, benevolence, and similar things—the fumigation must be good, fragrant, and precious. In a bad work, however—such as hatred, anger, calamity, and the like—the fumigation must be foul-smelling and vile. The twelve signs of the Zodiac also have their own perfumes: Aries has myrrh; Taurus, costus; Gemini, mastic; Cancer, camphor; Leo, frankincense; Virgo, sandalwood; Libra, galbanum; Scorpio, opopanax <note>A heavy, sweet-smelling resin from the herb "Hercules-all-heal."</note>; Sagittarius, aloeswood; Capricorn, asafoetida <note>original: "asam." A pungent resin used in both medicine and magic to repel or ground energies.</note>; Aquarius, euphorbium; Pisces, incense <note>original: "thymiana," a general term for incense or a specific aromatic blend.</note>. The most powerful of perfumes is described by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism.</note>, composed of seven aromatics according to the powers of the seven planets: for it receives costus from Saturn, nutmeg from Jupiter, aloeswood from Mars, mastic from the Sun, saffron from Venus, cinnamon from Mercury, and myrtle from the Moon.

->On Eye-Salves <note>original: "Collyriis," medical or magical preparations applied to the eyes.</note>, ointments, love potions, and their powers. Chapter XLV.<-

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'C' containing two figures, possibly Mercury and another figure, in a classical setting.</image-desc>
Eye-salves and ointments, harmonizing the powers of natural and celestial things around our spirit, can multiply, transmute, transfigure, and transform it in various ways. Indeed, they can also induce a transposition of those powers which reside within it, so that it can now act not only on its own body, but also on what is nearby—and this through visual rays, through fascinations <note>The concept of "spell-binding" or influencing another through the gaze or presence.</note>, and through contacts by affecting it with a certain similar quality. Our spirit, however—because it is a subtle, pure, bright, airy, and oily vapor of the blood—is best served by making eye-salves from similar vapors. These agree more in substance with our spirit and, because of that similarity, they allure, attract, and transform the spirit more effectively. Certain ointments and other concoctions possess similar virtues: hence, through contact, diseases, enchantments <note>original: "veneficia," which can refer to poisoning, potions, or sorcery.</note>, or loves are sometimes induced by certain things smeared on the hands or clothes. Similarly, through kisses, by certain things held in the mouth, loves are induced, as we read in Virgil that Venus prayed to Cupid:

> So that when Dido, most joyful, receives you in her lap

<page-num>LIII.</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>
