-> You breathe in a hidden fire, and deceive with poison. <-
<note>original: "Occultum inspires ignem, fallasque veneno." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (1.688), referring to Cupid inflaming Dido’s heart.</note>

<margin>Sight is purer than hearing.</margin>
Sight, because it is purer and perceives more clearly than the other senses—and because it impresses the marks of things more sharply and deeply upon us—agrees most closely and more than any other sense with the phantastic spirit <note>In Renaissance psychology, the 'phantastic spirit' was the subtle vapor that mediated between the physical senses and the soul's power of imagination.</note>. This is evident in dreams, where we more often encounter sights than sounds or other sensations. Therefore, when eye-salves <note>original: "collyria," medicinal or magical washes for the eyes.</note> transform the visual spirits, that spirit easily affects the imagination. The imagination, once affected by various species and forms, transmits them through the same spirit to the outward sense of sight. In this case, a sensation of such forms and images is caused within the eye in its own way, just as if it were being moved by external objects. Consequently, a person thinks they see terrifying images, demons, and similar things. This is how eye-salves are made which cause us to immediately behold shadows of demons in the air or elsewhere, such as I have known to be prepared from the gall of a man and the eyes of a black cat, along with certain other things. A similar preparation is also made from the blood of a hoopoe <note>A bird frequently used in ancient and medieval magic, often associated with secrets and the underworld.</note>, or of a bat and a goat. And they say that if a steel mirror is anointed with the juice of mugwort <note>original: "arthemissiæ," a plant sacred to Artemis/Diana and widely used in divination.</note> and then fumigated, it causes one to see invoked spirits within it. Likewise, certain fumigations or ointments are made which cause those who are sleeping to speak, walk, and perform the works of those who are awake—and sometimes even things that those who are awake would hardly be able or dare to do. Certain ones make us hear horrendous sounds, or delightful ones nowhere present, and other such things.

<margin>The source of the afflictions of maniacs and melancholics.</margin>
This is the same reason why maniacs and melancholics believe they see or hear from the outside those things which the imagination phantasticizes <note>Constructs or creates internally.</note> only within. Hence, they fear things not to be feared and fall into marvelous and most false suspicions; they flee when no one pursues, they grow angry and struggle when no one is present, and they fear where there is no fear. Magical concoctions can also induce such passions through fumigations, eye-salves, ointments, potions, sorceries, lamps and lights, mirrors, images, incantations and songs, and through sounds and harmonies made from the sinews of certain animals tuned to a specific harmony. They may even be induced through various rites, observations, ceremonies, religious acts, and superstitions, as these shall be treated in their proper places. Nor are such passions, apparitions, and imaginings induced only by these artifices, but the things themselves and even men are truly changed and transfigured into various forms. Just so do the poets tell of Proteus, Periclymenus, Achelous, and Mestra, the daughter of Erisichthon. Thus did Circe change the companions of Ulysses; and once, in the sacrifices of Lycaean Jove, after tasting the entrails of the sacrifices, men were turned into wolves—which Pliny says happened to a certain Demarchus, and Augustine thinks the same. Augustine also relates that while he was in Italy, he heard of certain women who, by giving a sorcerous substance in cheese to travelers, turned them into beasts of burden; and when they had carried whatever loads the women wished, they restored them to men, and that this happened at that time to the father of a certain man named Prestantius. Even the Sacred Scriptures testify that the magicians of Pharaoh changed their rods into serpents, and water into blood, and other such things.

**As** the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Anima mundi"; the vital spirit or "world-soul" believed by Neoplatonists to connect the divine realm to the physical world.</note>—whenever through its own power it fertilizes all things, whether naturally generated or artificially made—infuses into them celestial properties to produce certain miraculous effects, then these things themselves exert their power upon us. This occurs not only when they are applied through **fumigations**, or **eye-salves**, or **ointments**, or **potions**, or any other such methods, but also when they are properly wrapped and bound to the body, or suspended from the neck, or placed underneath a person in any way, or even approached with the lightest touch. Through these **bindings**, **hangings**, **wrappings**, **placements**, and **contacts**, the conditions of the body and the soul are changed: from sickness to health, or toward boldness, fear, sadness, joy, and the like. They render those who wear them either gracious or terrifying, accepted or rejected, honored and beloved, or hated and abominable.

It is believed that such passions are infused through the aforementioned methods in the same way that is evident in the **grafting of trees**. In that process, the vital power is transferred from the trunk into a shoot grafted into it, even if they are held together by a binding other than direct contact.
<margin>
The inclination of the **female palm** toward the male.
</margin>
So it is with the **female palm tree**: when she is near the male, her branches lean toward him and bend. Seeing this, gardeners tie ropes from the male to the female; she then returns to an upright position, as if she had already attained the virtue of the male through the continuity of the rope. In a similar way, we see that the
<margin>
The **torpedo** fish induces numbness.
</margin>
**crampfish** <note>original: "torpedo marina"; an electric ray. Ancient writers were fascinated by how its "numbing" power could travel through a fisherman's rod or spear.</note>, even when touched from a distance through a very long rod, suddenly numbs the hand of the one touching it. Furthermore, if anyone touches a **sea hare** <note>original: "lepus marinus"; a type of large sea slug, considered highly toxic and magically dangerous in Roman natural history.</note> with either a hand or a stick while it is dying, they will suffer a fainting of the spirit. Similarly, they say that **starfish**, when smeared with fox blood and fixed to a door with a copper nail, prevent harmful medicines <note>original: "mala medicamenta"; often implying poisons or malevolent magic.</note> from doing any damage. It is also said that if a woman takes a needle, coats it in dung, wraps it in mud in which a human corpse has been buried, and carries it with her in a small cloth that was used in a funeral, no man will be able to have intercourse with her for as long as she has it with her. By these examples, we see how we can receive certain powers through the specific **binding** or **hanging** of certain things, or through simple contact, or through the continuity of a single thread.

However, one must know the specific law and method for binding and
<margin>
How **bindings** and **wrappings** ought to be made.
</margin>
hanging that is appropriate for this art. Specifically, they must be done under a certain and harmonious **constellation**. The aforementioned bindings and hangings should be made with threads of metal, or silk, or from the hair, sinews, or bristles of certain animals. **Wrappings**, on the other hand, should be made in the leaves of herbs, or the skins of animals, or specific types of cloth and similar materials, so that the things agree with one another. For example, if you wish to obtain the **solar virtue** <note>The "virtue" or spiritual influence associated with the Sun, linked to success, health, and authority.</note> of a thing, you should hang it from your neck wrapped in a **laurel leaf** or a **lion’s skin**, using a **gold thread** or yellow silk, while the Sun is reigning in the figure of the heavens. In this way, you can master the solar power of that object. But if you desire the virtue of a **saturnine** <note>The influence of Saturn, associated with gravity, sorrow, time, and hidden knowledge.</note> thing, you should wrap it in a similar way—while **Saturn** is dominant—in the skin of a **donkey** or a **funeral cloth** (especially if intended for an operation of sadness) and hang it with a **black thread**. A similar approach should be taken regarding all other things.

### Concerning rings and their compositions. Chapter XLVII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring intricate floral and scrolling foliage designs.</image-desc>

**Rings** also, which antiquity has always held in high esteem, exert their own power within us when they are fashioned at the opportune moment. In this way, they affect the wearer and their spirit, making them joyful or sad, mild or terrifying, bold or timid, lovable or hateful. They also fortify us against diseases, poisons, enemies, **evil spirits** <note>original: "cacodæmones"; in Renaissance magic, these were specifically malevolent spirits or demons believed to cause harm.</note>, and against any other harmful things, or they may even bind us to the same.

<margin>The composition of rings.</margin>
The method of constructing such rings is as follows: specifically, when some **fortunate star** <note>A planet in a favorable astrological position, such as Jupiter or Venus, which were considered "benefics."</note> is ascending and is favorably aspected by the Moon or joined to it, we must take the stone and the herb subject to that star and fashion a ring from the metal that corresponds to the same star. One should then fix the small stone into it, with the herb or root placed underneath. Finally, one must not omit the inscriptions of **images, names, and characters** <note>Magical symbols or sigils believed to capture the essence of celestial spirits.</note>, nor the proper **fumigations** <note>The practice of burning specific incenses to consecrate the object.</note>. However, we shall discuss these matters elsewhere, where we will treat images and characters. Thus we read in Philostratus that Iarchas, the prince of the Indian sages, gave seven rings—made according to this law and marked with the virtues and names of the seven planets—to **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>. He wore one each day, alternating them according to the names of the days. By the benefit of these rings, he lived beyond his one hundred and thirtieth year, moreover always retaining the glow of youth. In a similar manner, **Moses**, the lawgiver and prince of the Hebrews, having been steeped in the magic of Egypt, is recorded by **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian.</note> to have fashioned rings of love and oblivion. There was also, as Aristotle recounts, the ring of Battus among the Cyreneans, which carried the power of gratitude and honor. We read, furthermore, that a certain philosopher named Eudamus made rings against the bites of serpents, fascinations <note>Magical charms or the "evil eye."</note>, and demons. Josephus relates the same of Solomon. Indeed, we even read in Plato that **Gyges**, King of the Lydians, possessed a ring of wonderful and unusual virtue. When he turned its seal toward his palm, he was seen by no one, though he himself saw all things. Relying on the opportunity provided by this ring, he committed adultery with the queen, murdered the king his master, and slew whomever he thought stood in his way; in these crimes, no one could see him, and finally, by the benefit of that ring, he became the King of Lydia.

### Concerning the virtues of places, and which places correspond to each of the stars. Chapter XLVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' containing a pastoral or field scene with several human figures, one of whom holds a harvesting tool.</image-desc>

**There** are also wonderful virtues in places, either accompanying them because of the things located there, or from the influences of the stars, or arriving in some other way. For, as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic "Natural History."</note> reports concerning the **cuckoo** <note>original: "cuculo"</note>: in whatever place a person first hears that bird, if the right foot is traced around and that footprint (that is, the earth) is dug up, fleas will not be produced wherever that dust is scattered. Thus they say that dust collected from the tracks of snakes, if bees are sprinkled with it, causes them to return to the hive. Similarly, the dust in which a mule has rolled, when sprinkled on the body, mitigates the fires of love. However, the dust in which a hawk has rolled, if tied in a small reddish linen cloth, they say is a remedy for **quartan fevers** <note>A form of malaria where paroxysms occur every fourth day.</note>. So too, a small stone collected from the nest of swallows is said to immediately restore those suffering from **the falling sickness** <note>original: "comitiales"; an old term for epilepsy.</note>, and if bound to them, to protect them forever, especially—

Regarding the places which are appropriated to the stars: to **Saturn** correspond all places that are foul, dark, underground, religious and mournful, such as cemeteries, tombs, and dwellings deserted by men and falling into ruin with age; dark and horrific places, solitary caves, caverns, and wells. To the **Sun** belong bright places, clear air, palaces of kings, the courts of princes, pulpits, theaters, thrones, and all royal and magnificent things. **Venus**, however, inhabits pleasant fountains, green meadows, flowering gardens, decorated bedrooms, and **brothels** <note>original: "lupanaria"; in Renaissance thought, even base locations could be "charged" with the energy of a planet</note> and (as **Orpheus** <note>the legendary Greek poet and musician associated with mystical hymns</note> suggests) blue shores, baths, dancing grounds, and all things pertaining to women. **Mercury** possesses workshops, schools, taverns, merchants' marketplaces, and similar places. The **Moon** inhabits deserts, woods, crags, and massive rocks, mountains, groves, fountains, waters, rivers, seas, shores, and ships; she is also said to wander through various groves, and she possesses public roads, granaries, and the like. For this reason, those about to perform works of love are accustomed to bury or hide the instruments of their art—whether rings, images, mirrors, or other things—for a certain time in a brothel, so that from that place they might be affected by a certain **Venereal faculty** <note>the power or quality of the goddess Venus (love/lust)</note>. They believe this happens in the same way that things standing in a foul place become foul, and those in an aromatic place become aromatic

and fragrant. Even the locations of the world itself pertain to this. Hence, those who are to gather a Saturnine, Martial, or Jovial herb are commanded to look toward the East or the South. First, because these planets rejoice to be Oriental from the Sun; second, because their principal domiciles—namely **Aquarius, Scorpio, Sagittarius**—are southern signs; likewise **Capricorn and Pisces**. But those about to gather a thing belonging to Venus, Mercury, or the Moon are commanded to look toward the West, because they rejoice to be Occidental; or toward the North, because their principal domiciles, which are **Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Virgo**, are northern signs. Thus, in a solar work, one must look toward the East or the South—or rather, always toward the solar body and light itself.

LVII.

# BOOK ONE.

[to which stars, houses, and elements they are distributed.]

### Chapter XLIX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or religious figure, within an ornamental square frame with foliage.</image-desc>

**Light** is a quality of a highly formal nature; it is a simple act of the intelligence and an image. First diffused from the Divine Mind into all things, it exists in God the Father himself—who is the **Father of Lights**—as the first true light. Next, it exists in his Son as an illustrating and exuberant splendor; and in the Holy Spirit as a burning brightness, surpassing all understanding, even (as **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian philosopher who wrote extensively on the celestial hierarchy</note> says) that of the **Seraphim** <term>the highest order of angels, associated with light and fire</term>. In the **Angels**, therefore, light is diffused as a shining intelligence and a pouring-forth of joy beyond the limits of all reason, though received in different degrees according to the nature of the receiving intelligence. It descends next into the celestial bodies, where it becomes an abundance of life and effective propagation, as well as a visible splendor. In fire, however, it is a certain natural vigor implanted by the heavens. Finally, in **Humans**, it becomes the lucid discourse of reason and the knowledge of divine things—entirely rational. Yet even this is multifaceted, either due to the disposition of the body (as the **Peripatetics** <term>followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</term> claim) or, as is more true, according to the whim of the Giver, who divides it among individuals as he wills. From there, it passes to the **phantasia** <term>the faculty of imagination that processes sensory images</term>, standing above the senses but only in an imaginable way, and finally to the senses, especially the eyes. In the eye, it becomes visible clarity, extended through alternating transparent bodies, in which color and reflecting beauty are created. In opaque bodies, however, light becomes a certain beneficial and generative power, penetrating even to the center of the earth. There, where its rays are gathered into a narrow space, it becomes a shadowy heat, tormenting and seething; thus, all things perceive the vigor of light according to their capacity. Light connects all things to itself with life-giving heat and, permeating all beings, conducts their qualities and virtues through everything.

For this reason, the **Magi** <note>ancient practitioners of magic and astrology</note> forbid the shadow of any sick person to be cast upon another, or the urine of a sick person to be uncovered toward the Sun or Moon. This is because the penetrating rays of light, carrying morbid qualities from the diseased body, suddenly project them onto whatever is opposite and afflict it with that same bad quality. This is the reason why **fascinators** <note>those who cast the "evil eye" or use hypnotic influence</note> take care to cover the one they fascinate with their own shadow; similarly, the **hyena** makes dogs mute by the touch of its shadow. 

Furthermore, certain artificial lights are made using lamps, oil-burners, candles, and similar devices made from specific things and liquids, chosen opportunely according to the standard of the stars and composed in harmony with them. When these are lit and shine alone, they are accustomed to produce some marvelous and heavenly effects which men often wonder at. For instance, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> recounts from **Anaxilaus** that the "mare’s poison" <note>original: "equarum uirus"; likely referring to hippomanes, a substance used in ancient love philters</note> taken from a mating, when burned in lamps, represents a monstrous sight of horses' heads; a similar thing happens with donkeys. Also, gnats mixed with wax and lit make one see flies; and the skin of a serpent burned in a lamp makes serpents appear to be present. They also say that when grapes are in bloom, if one ties a vial full of oil around them and leaves it until they are ripe, then uses that oil in a lamp, it makes grapes appear to the viewer. The same holds true for other fruits. If **centaury** <term>a medicinal herb named after the centaur Chiron</term> is mixed with honey and the blood of a **hoopoe** <note>a bird often associated with magical properties in medieval lore</note> and placed in a lamp, the bystanders will appear larger than usual; and if it is lit outdoors on a clear night, one will see the stars running about.

# DE OCCULTA PHILOSOPHIA

...mutually. The ink of the cuttlefish <note>Latin: *piscis sepiae*</note> also possesses such power that, if it is added to a lamp, it makes those nearby appear like Ethiopians <note>A common optical illusion described in medieval magic manuals where the oily ink changed the perceived skin tone of those in the room</note>. It is also said that a candle made from certain Saturnine <term>things associated with the planet Saturn, which governs lead, darkness, and death</term> materials, if lit and then extinguished in the mouth of a recently deceased person, will thereafter—whenever it burns alone—bring the greatest sadness and fear to those standing around. Many similar lights and lamps of this kind are described by **Hermes**, **Plato**, the *Cyranides* <note>An ancient Greek collection of lore on the magical properties of animals, plants, and stones</note>, and among more recent authors, **Albertus Magnus**, in a certain treatise on this singular subject. Colors are also forms of light which, when mixed into physical things, tend to expose those things to the influence of the stars and celestial bodies with which they agree. We shall say in later chapters what colors belong to the lights of the planets; according to these, the natures of the fixed stars may also be perceived, which can likewise be applied here to the flames of lamps and lanterns. But in this place, we shall describe how the colors of lower things and mixtures are distributed among the various planets.

<margin>
Colors of the Planets.
</margin>

Indeed, all colors that are black, shining, earthy, leaden, or dark-brown refer to **Saturn**. Colors that are sapphire, airy, perpetually green, clear, purple, somewhat dark, or gold mixed with silver, pertain to **Jupiter**. Those colors that are red, burning, fiery, flaming, violet, purple, blood-red, and iron-gray refer to **Mars**. Gold, saffron, and the more brilliant purples refer to the **Sun**. Finally, all colors that are white, beautiful, varied, green, reddish, and somewhat saffron or purple, refer to **Venus**, **Mercury**, and the **Moon**.

<margin>
Colors of the Houses of Heaven.
</margin>

<margin>
Colors of the Humors.
</margin>

Furthermore, of the twelve houses of heaven <term>the twelve divisions of the sky used in astrology to determine different areas of life</term>, the first and seventh have the color white; the second and twelfth, green; the third and eleventh, saffron; the fourth and tenth, red; the fifth and ninth, honey-colored; and the sixth and eighth, black. The elements also have their own colors, by which physicians judge the temperament <term>the "complexion" or balance of the four humors within a person</term> and the properties of nature. For an earthy color, produced by cold and dryness, is dark and black, and promises black bile <note>Melancholy</note> and a Saturnine nature. A sky-blue color tending toward white denotes phlegm, for cold makes moisture white but makes dry things black. A reddish color indicates blood. A fiery or glowing, flaming color indicates yellow bile <note>Choler</note>. Because yellow bile is so thin and subtle, it is easily mixed with all things, and consequently causes various other colors: for if it is mixed with blood, it thrives with a dominant redness; if the bile dominates, it makes it reddish-brown; if the mixture is equal, it makes a true red. But if the bile is "burnt" <note>Known as "adust" humors, thought to be caused by excessive internal heat</note> and mixed with blood, it turns the color "cannabinous" <term>the grayish-brown color of raw hemp</term>. It appears red when blood dominates, or somewhat reddish when the bile prevails. If it is mixed with the melancholic humor, it is tinged with blackness. However, with melancholy and phlegm in equal portions, it becomes cannabinous; if phlegm overabounds, it becomes yellow; if melancholy wins out, it becomes bluish-gray; but if it is mixed with phlegm alone in equal parts, it becomes citron-yellow; or if there is an excess of either one, it becomes pale or somewhat pale. All colors, however, are more powerful when they appear in silk or metal, or in transparent substances and precious stones, and in those things which most closely imitate celestial likeness—but most of all in living beings.

LIX.

# BOOK ONE

<margin>
What fascination is.
</margin>
<margin>
The instrument of fascination is the spirit.
</margin>
Fascination <note>In this context, fascination is not just "interest," but a literal binding (ligatio) or spell cast by the eyes—the root of the "evil eye" concept.</note> is a binding that proceeds from the spirit of the fascinator, passes through the eyes of the one fascinated, and enters into their very heart. The instrument of fascination is the spirit—specifically, a certain pure, bright, and subtle vapor generated from the heat of the heart out of the purest blood. This spirit constantly sends out rays similar to itself through the eyes. These emitted rays carry the spiritual vapor with them, and that vapor carries blood, as is visible in bloodshot or bleary eyes <note>original: "lippis ac rubentibus oculis"</note>. The ray from such an eye, sent out toward the eyes of a person looking back, carries with it the vapor of the corrupt blood; by this contagion, it forces the eyes of the beholder to suffer a similar disease. Thus, an eye that is open and fixed upon someone with a strong imagination <term>the mental faculty of forming images, which Agrippa believes can physically project energy</term> shoots its rays—which are the vehicles of the spirit—like needles into the eyes of the person opposite. <margin>Rays are the vehicles of the spirit.</margin> This lingering spirit, striking the eyes of the one fascinated and being driven by the heart of the one striking, wounds the heart and infects the vitals of the victim as if it were entering its own home; this foreign spirit corrupts the internal spirit of the victim. Hence **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of *The Golden Ass*</note> says: "Those eyes of yours, slipping through my own eyes into my deepest vitals, stir up a most piercing fire in my very marrow." <margin>How fascination happens.</margin> You should know, therefore, that humans are fascinated most of all when, by a very frequent gaze, they direct their sight line to sight line, eyes staring back into eyes, rays coupling with rays, and lights joining with lights. Then spirit is joined to spirit, and it strikes sparks; thus the strongest bindings and the most piercing loves are kindled by the rays of the eyes alone, even by a sudden glance, like a dart or a blow penetrating the whole body. From this, the spirit and the blood of the lover, having been כך wounded, are carried toward the beloved and fascinator in the same way that the blood and spirit of a murdered man are said to flow toward the one who struck him. Thus **Lucretius** <note>The Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher</note> sang of these amorous fascinations:

> The mind seeks that body from which it was wounded by love;
> For all usually fall toward the wound, and the blood 
> Springs out toward that part where we are struck by the blow,
> And if the foe is near, a red moisture covers him.

Such is the power of fascination, especially when the vapors of the eyes serve the emotions. For this reason, those who fascinate use eye-salves <note>original: "collyriis"</note>, ointments, amulets, and such things to affect and strengthen the spirit in one way or another. For example, to induce love, they use "Venereal" eye-salves made from *hippomanes* <note>A legendary substance from a mare or a foal's forehead, used as an aphrodisiac</note>, the blood of doves or sparrows, and similar things. To induce fear, they use "Martial" <term>associated with Mars, the god of war</term> eye-salves, such as those made from the eyes of wolves or hyenas. For calamity or sickness, they use "Saturnine" mixtures. A similar logic must be applied to each specific goal.

...the spirit itself is thus released into the water. And Pliny relates that the nail clippings from the hands and feet of a sick person, mixed with wax, are said to become a remedy for quartan, tertian, or daily fevers <note>These are types of malaria or recurring fevers characterized by the number of days between "paroxysms" or spikes in temperature.</note> if they are fixed to another person's door before sunrise; this will provide a cure for these diseases. In a similar way, they command that if all nail clippings are thrown into an ant hill, the first ant that begins to drag one should be caught and tied around the patient's neck, and thus the disease is shaken off. They also say that some disease is drawn away by using wood struck by lightning, thrown behind the back with the hands; and for quartan fevers, they tie a fragment of a nail from a cross <note>original: "claui è cruce" — referring to a nail used in a crucifixion, which was a potent magical object in antiquity.</note> wrapped in wool around the neck, or a rope from a cross, and once the person is freed, they hide it in a cavern where the sun does not reach. Likewise, they affirm that scrofula <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, often called the "King's Evil."</note> and swellings of the parotid glands are healed when the throat is touched by the hand of one snatched away by an untimely death.

They also say that difficult births are immediately resolved when someone throws over the bed in which the pregnant woman lies a stone or projectile that has killed three animals in single strikes: namely, a man, a boar, and a bear. They say a skirmisher's spear performs the same effect if pulled from a human body—provided it has not touched the ground; also, arrows pulled from a body and placed beneath those lying down are said to be a love charm, if they have not touched the ground. They say even epilepsy <term>original: "comitiales morbos"—literally "the election-day disease," so named because an occurrence would cancel public assemblies</term> is cured by food made from the flesh of a wild beast killed with the same iron with which a man was slain. It is denied that defects of the eyes occur, or that those who wash their feet with water and then touch their eyes three times with it ever suffer from bleary eyes. Some heal groin ailments by taking a thread from a loom and tying it with nine or seven knots, naming a certain widow at each knot. 

Likewise, the spleen of a beast is stretched over the spleen of the person in pain, while the healer says he is making a remedy for the spleen; after this, they command the spleen itself to be enclosed in the wall of the bedroom or the roof and sealed with a ring, while a charm is spoken twenty-seven times <note>original: "ter noniesque" — literally "three times nine."</note>. The urine of a green lizard frees one from the same defect if suspended in a pot before the bedroom door of the one being healed, so that the sick person touches it with their hand when going out and returning. Likewise, they say the "Venus" <note>Sexual desire or potency.</note> of the one who does it is inhibited by a lizard killed in the urine of a calf; but he who pours his own into a dog's urine is said to become slower toward Love and to feel a numbness in the loins. On the contrary, they say one's own urine, dropped onto the foot in the morning hours, helps against all evil medicines <note>original: "mala medicamenta" — poisoned potions or hostile spells.</note>. 

<margin>The efficacy of spit or saliva.</margin>
There is a small frog that climbs trees; if one spits into its mouth and lets it go, it is said to cure a cough. It is also wonderful, but easily tested by experiment, what the same Pliny tells: if someone regrets a blow struck from far or near, and immediately spits into the middle of the hand that struck, the person struck is instantly relieved of pain. This is proven with a pack animal; if its gait is corrected immediately by such a remedy, the animal's movement is restored. Some even increase the force of their blows before the attempt <note>By spitting on their hands before striking.</note>. In a similar way, when saliva is applied to the hand, it is good to spit similarly into the shoe of the right foot before it is put on, when one passes a place in which some danger was encountered. We also spit to repel epilepsy and contagions, reflecting them back. Some even seek forgiveness from the gods for a somewhat bold hope by spitting into their own laps.

...blood should be sprinkled around the borders of the field, and the blood itself should be buried in that place where it first began to be drawn. The people of Methana <note>A town in the Argolid region of Greece.</note>, neighbors of the Troezenians, found a most certain remedy against the injury of the South Wind <note>original: "Noti" — the hot, damp south wind which was often destructive to crops.</note> to preserve their vines, which they always found reliable through experience. If, while the wind was still blowing, two men would tear a white rooster <note>original: "gallum gallinaceum album"</note> in half by pulling it in opposite directions; then each, holding his own part, would walk around the vineyards until, having completed the circuit, they both met at the place from which they started, and there they would bury the pieces of the rooster. They also relate that if someone holds a viper over steam <note>or perhaps smoke</note> with a staff, it foretells the future; likewise, a staff with which a frog was knocked away from a snake is said to help women in labor. Pliny himself relates these things. They also command that in gathering roots and herbs, one should first draw three circles around them with a sword before digging them up, and furthermore, one should beware of the wind blowing against them.

Likewise, it is said that if someone measures a dead man with a rope—first from the elbow to the longest finger, then from the shoulder to the same finger, and then from head to feet, performing all these measurements three times—if another person is later measured with that same rope in a similar way, they say that person will become unsuccessful and unfortunate, and fall into calamity and sadness. And Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a famous 13th-century scholar and theologian.</note> recounts from the *Kyranides* <note>An ancient Greek book of magical and medicinal lore.</note> that if any woman has bound you with spells to love her, take her shirt, and through the hood and through her right sleeve, urinate outward, and the spell will be dissolved. And Pliny relates that sitting near pregnant women, or when a remedy is being applied to someone, with the fingers interlaced like a comb <note>This "locking" of the fingers was believed to "bind" the magic or the birth process, preventing it from finishing.</note> is a type of witchcraft; this was discovered when Alcmene <note>In Greek mythology, the mother of Hercules; Hera attempted to stop his birth by having a goddess sit with her legs and fingers crossed.</note> was giving birth to Hercules. It is said to be even worse if this is done around one or both knees. Similarly, placing one’s hams <note>The back of the thighs or knees.</note> over alternating knees is witchcraft; therefore, this was forbidden in the councils of leaders and powers, as it hinders all actions. It is also said that if someone standing before a door calls by name a man lying with a woman, and he answers, if the caller then fixes either a knife or a needle into the door and breaks it, leaving the blade behind, the man will not be able to have intercourse with her as long as those objects remain there.

->On the face, gesture, and habit and figure of the body, and how these correspond to the stars; from which physiognomy, metoposcopy, and chiromancy—the arts of divination—take their foundations.<-

### Chapter LII.

<margin>How much the face and gesture affect the imagination</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' containing a scene of a man seated outdoors under a tree.</image-desc>
The face indeed, as well as gesture, the motion and posture of the body, and the figures we take on, are conducive to receiving celestial gifts; they expose us to the powers above and produce certain effects in us. This is not unlike how, when gathering the herb hellebore <note>A plant used in ancient medicine to purge the body of "black bile."</note>, whether one pulls the leaf upward or downward, this very motion causes the humors <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to control health and temperament.</note> of the person to be drawn upward or downward. No one is ignorant of how much the face and gesture affect the sight, the imagination, and the animal spirit. Thus, those coupling for offspring often imprint upon the children to be born the faces that they themselves then either make or imagine. Thus, the mild and joyful face of a prince in a city gladdens the people; a fierce or sad one suddenly terrifies them. Thus, the gesture and figure of a mourner easily moves one to mercy; thus, the face of a lovely person easily excites love.

However, you must know that gestures and <term>figures</term><note>Here meaning "postures" or "bodily forms."</note> of this kind, as <term>harmonies</term><note>In Renaissance thought, "harmonies" were the proportional relationships that allowed the human body to resonate with the stars.</note> of the body, expose it to the celestial powers no differently than odors and medicines expose the <term>spirit</term><note>The "spiritus," an ethereal substance believed to bridge the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>, and internal passions expose the soul. For just as medicines and the passions of the mind unite with certain dispositions of the heavens, so also the gestures and movements of the body obtain efficacy from certain celestial <term>influences</term><note>Literally "influxes," the flowing down of power from the stars to the earth.</note>. 
<margin>Which gestures represent which planets.</margin>
There are, moreover, gestures representing **Saturn**, which are sad and mournful, such as wailing and striking the head; likewise religious ones, such as kneeling with the gaze fixed downward like a supplicant; striking the breast and similar expressions, both austere and characteristic of a "Saturnine" man, such as the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Persius, Satire 3, lines 78-82.</note> describes:

> With head bowed, and fixing his eyes on the ground,
> When he gnaws his murmurs to himself and mad silences,
> And weighs his words with an outstretched lip.
> <note>original: "Obstipo capite, & figentem lumina terra, / Murmura cum secum, & rabiosa silentia rodit, / Atq; exporrecto trutinatur uerba labello."</note>

Moreover, cheerful and honest faces, honorable gestures, the joining of hands as if applauding or praising, and likewise kneeling with the head lifted upward as if adoring, represent **Jupiter**. Representing **Mars** are sharp, fierce, cruel, angry, and grim gestures and similar facial expressions. **Solar** gestures are high-spirited, honorable, and similar expressions; likewise, walking about and kneeling on a single knee, as if honoring a king. Representing **Venus** are such things as dances, embraces, laughter, and lovely and joyful faces. **Mercurial** gestures are inconstant, energetic, slippery, and the like, with similar expressions. **Lunar** gestures are changeable, sorcerous <note>original: "uenefici," which can mean poisoning or magical/bewitching.</note>, childish, and the like. And just as we have spoken of gestures, so also the physical 
<margin>Figures which correspond to the planets.</margin>
figures of men are distinct: for **Saturn** indicates a man with a color between black and yellow, thin, hunched, with rough skin, prominent veins, a hairy body, small eyes, joined eyebrows, a sparse beard, thick lips, a gaze cast down to the ground, a heavy gait, rubbing his feet while walking, cunning, ingenious, a seducer, and a killer. **Jupiter**, however, signifies a man of a white color suffused with redness, of a beautiful body, good stature, bald, having somewhat large eyes (not entirely black), a wide pupil, short and unequal nostrils, somewhat large front teeth, a curly beard, of good spirit and good morals. **Mars** makes a man red, with reddish hair, a round face, yellow eyes, a horrible and sharp gaze, bold, cheerful, proud, and cunning. The **Sun** signifies a man of a dusky color, between yellow and black, suffused with redness, of a shorter stature yet a beautiful body, with a bald and curly head, yellow eyes, wise, faithful, and desirous of praise. **Venus** signifies a man who is white, tending toward blackness, yet more white, and adorned with redness, with a beautiful body, a beautiful and round face, beautiful hair, and beautiful eyes whose blackness is quite intense, of good morals, a good lover, benevolent, patient, and pleasant. **Mercury** signifies by his figures a man who is not very white nor black, with an oblong face, a high forehead, beautiful eyes (not entirely black), a straight and somewhat long nose, a sparse beard, and having long fingers, ingenious, a subtle inquirer, a turncoat <note>original: "uersipellem," literally "one who changes skin," implying a shifty or versatile nature.</note>, and varied...

The **Moon** truly signifies a person of white color mixed with redness, of a beautiful stature, with a round face that is often <term>marked</term><note>Likely referring to freckles, moles, or "pockmarks."</note>, eyes that are not entirely black, and eyebrows that meet in the middle; such a person is benevolent, easy-going, and sociable. From these figures and gestures, finally, the arts of divination—<term>physiognomonia</term><note>Physiognomy: the practice of judging character from physical features, especially the face.</note> and <term>metoposcopia</term><note>Metoposcopy: a form of divination that predicts character or fate by reading the lines on a person's forehead.</note>—depend. So too does <term>chiromantia</term><note>Chiromancy: palmistry or palm reading.</note> itself, which predicts future events not as direct causes, but as signs through similar effects produced by the same celestial cause. And although these types of divination seem to prophesy through inferior and weaker signs, their judgments are nevertheless not to be despised or condemned when they forecast not from superstition, but from the <term>harmonic correspondence</term><note>The Renaissance belief that every part of the human body (the microcosm) reflects the order of the universe (the macrocosm).</note> of all parts of the body. Whoever now, by nature, study, action, motion, gesture, countenance, the passions of the mind, and the opportunity of time, better imitates the celestial things, he—as if more similar to those higher beings—is able to receive more ample gifts from them.

### On the divination of auspices and auguries. Chapter 53.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting two figures, possibly scholars or clerics, in conversation.</image-desc>There are certain other types of divination depending on natural causes, the art and experience of which are established in various matters: by which physicians, farmers, shepherds, and sailors each forecast from probable signs. Aristotle handed down many of these in his book *On Times*. Among these types of divination, <term>auspices</term><note>Divination from the behavior of animals or natural phenomena.</note> and <term>auguries</term><note>Specifically divination from the flight, song, or feeding of birds.</note> hold the primary place. These were formerly held in such high esteem among the Romans <margin>The Romans did nothing without taking auspices.</margin> that they completed nothing pertaining to public or private business without an auspice. Cicero, in his book *On Divination*, copiously declares that the Etruscan people especially excelled in this craft. <margin>Species of auspices.</margin> There are indeed several species of auspices: for some are called "pedestrian," which are taken from four-footed animals; some are "auguries," which are from birds; some are "celestial," which are from thunder and lightning; some are "falling" [caduca], such as when something had fallen in a temple or elsewhere; and some are "sacred," which were taken from sacrifices. Some of these were called expiatory and "sad" auspices, such as when a sacrificial victim had fled from the altar, or had let out a lowing cry when struck, or had fallen on a part of the body other than it should have. To these is added "Exauguration," namely when the staff had fallen from the hand of the one performing the augury, with which it was the custom to contemplate and take the auspice. <margin>Twelve types of auguries.</margin> <term>Michael Scot</term><note>A 13th-century mathematician and scholar known as a legendary magician; he was the court astrologer to Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II.</note> recites twelve types of auguries: namely, six on the right, the names of which he says are *fernoua*, *feruetus*, *confert*, *emponethem*, *sonnafarnoua*, and *sonnafaruetus*; and another six on the left, the names of which are *confernoua*, *conferuetus*, *uiaram*, *herrenam*, *scaffarnoua*, and *scaffaruetus*. Then, explaining these names, he says: *Fernoua* is an augury when you have gone out of your house for the sake of doing something, and while going you see a man or a bird, walking or flying, in such a way that it places itself before you on your left side; this is for you a sign of good significance regarding the business. *Feruetus* is an augury when you have gone out of your house for the sake of doing something, and while going you first find or see a bird or a man resting before you on your left side; this is for you a bad sign regarding the business. *Viaram* is...

<term>augury</term><note>The practice of divining the future by observing the flight, songs, or behavior of birds, or the movements of people.</note>, when a person or a bird, on its own path or flight, passes before you, coming from your right side and heading toward the left, and vanishes: this is a good sign for you regarding your business. **New Confer** is an augury when you first find a person or bird going or flying, and it pauses before you on the right while you are watching: this is a good sign for you regarding your business. **Old Confer** is an augury when you first find or see a person or bird reclining on your right while you are watching: it is a bad sign for you regarding your business. **New Scimasar** is an augury when a person or bird follows behind your back and passes you, but before it reaches you (or you it), it pauses somewhere on your right while you are watching: it is a good sign for you. **Old Scimasar** is an augury when you see a person or bird behind you pausing on the right side: it is a bad sign for you. **New Scassar** is when you see a person or bird behind you, but before it reaches you (or you it), it pauses in a place while you are watching: it is a good sign for you. **Old Scassar** is when you see a person or bird passing by and pausing in a place on the left side: it is a bad sign for you. **Emponenthem** is when a person or bird coming from the left and passing to the right vanishes from your sight without you seeing it pause again: it is a good sign for you. **Hartenam** is an augury if a person or bird coming from the right, passing behind your back to the left, and you see it pausing somewhere: this is a bad sign. Thus far <term>Scotus</term><note>Michael Scot (c. 1175–1232), a mathematician and scholar who served as the court astrologer to Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. His works on astrology and physiognomy were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>. The ancients also divined from <term>sneezes</term>, which <term>Homer</term> also mentions in the seventeenth book of the *Odyssey*, because he thought they proceeded from a sacred place—namely, the head, in which the intellect flourishes and operates. For this reason, it is said that whatever speech unexpectedly comes into the mouth or mind of one rising in the morning possesses a certain presage and augury.

## On certain various animals, and other things, and what significance they have in auguries. Chapter 54.

<margin>Which birds are <term>ominal</term><note>Birds that provide omens or portents.</note>.</margin>
All initial <term>auspices</term><note>Signs or tokens used to predict the future, specifically those observed at the start of a venture.</note> must be observed at the beginning of any work. For example, if at the start of a task you notice your garment has been gnawed by <term>mice</term><note>The original text says "foricibus" (shears/scissors), but in classical omen literature—such as Cicero's *De Divinatione*—the gnawing of clothes by "soricibus" (mice) is the standard bad omen. This is likely a printer's error in the Latin.</note>, cease from what you have begun. If as you go out you stumble on the threshold, or trip your foot on the road, halt your journey. If any bad omen occurs to you at the beginning of your business, delay what you have started, lest either your whole intention be frustrated or completed uselessly; instead, wait until you seize a favorable hour for action with a better omen. We see many animals that are deceptive and prophetic by a certain power implanted in them by nature. Does not the rooster most skillfully indicate the hours by his song, and by the clapping of his wings put the lion to flight? Many birds announce rain by their song and chatter, as do flies with their sharp stinging; and dolphins precede storms by their frequent leaps above the waters. It would be a long task to recount all the presages that the Phrygians, Cilicians, Arabs, Umbrians, Tuscans, and other peoples who followed auguries have learned from birds and animals—things which have been proven by them through many experiments and examples. For in all things there are hidden oracles of the future; but birds will announce the greatest ominal signs to you. These are the ones whom the poets report were transformed from humans into birds. Therefore, listen carefully to what the <term>crow</term><note>original: "cornix"</note> says, and its position while sitting or flying on the right...

...whether from the left, whether talkative, noisy, or silent, whether it goes before or follows, whether it waits for the arrival of the passer-by or flees, or to where it departs—attend to all these things diligently. Horapollo <note>original: "Orus Apollo"; a legendary author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs which was popular in the Renaissance</note> says in his *Hieroglyphics*: a pair of crows signifies marriage, because this animal lays two eggs from which a male and a female must be born. If, however—which happens very rarely—two males or two females are born, the males, when mated with females, do not mix with other crows; likewise, the females do not mix with other males, but live alone in isolation. Therefore, those who encounter a single crow divine that they must live a widowed life. A black dove portends the same thing, for after the death of its mate, it always lives alone. 

You shall observe ravens with no less diligence, for they say these are preferred for greater matters and take precedence over the crow. Epictetus the Stoic philosopher, a grave authority, felt that if a raven croaked at someone, it portended adversity either to the body, to fortune, to honor, to the wife, or to the children. 

Next, you shall consider swans, who foreknow the secrets of the waters; for their cheerfulness presages happy outcomes not only for sailors but for all other travelers, unless a stronger bird intervenes—for instance, the eagle. The eagle, by the most powerful majesty of its rule, nullifies the testimony of all other birds if it speaks against them. Indeed, it flies higher than all birds and sees more deeply, and is never excluded from the secret counsel of Jupiter himself <note>The eagle was the sacred bird of the Roman god Jupiter</note>. It portends height and victory, but through blood, because it drinks blood rather than water. 

When the Locrians were fighting against the Crotoniates, an eagle flying over them brought victory. To Hiero <note>Hiero I or II, Tyrants of Syracuse</note>, as he went out to the first stages of war, an eagle unexpectedly settling on his shield foretold that he would be king. At the birth of Alexander the Macedonian, two eagles sitting above the house all day portended the omen of a double empire over Asia and Europe. Likewise for Lucius Tarquinius Priscus <note>The fifth king of Rome</note>, the son of Demaratus the Corinthian, who was a fugitive from home due to sedition; as he headed toward Etruria and sought Rome, an eagle snatched his cap and, flying high, placed it back on his head, portending the Roman kingship for him. 

<margin>Auguries to be taken from the greater birds.</margin>

Furthermore, vultures signify difficulty, harshness, and greed, which was verified by experience at the origin of the city’s founding <note>A reference to the contest between Romulus and Remus over the founding of Rome</note>. They also show the locations of future slaughter, arriving seven days in advance; and since they look toward that side where the lower part will be defeated—as if gaping for the greater number of those to be killed—ancient kings used to send out scouts to report which way the vultures turned their gaze. 

The Phoenix, however, promises the success of singular happiness; when it was seen, "New Rome" <note>Constantinople</note> was founded under better auspices. The Pelican, because it undergoes danger for the sake of its children, signifies a man who will undergo a crisis for the sake of his friendship or piety. The "Painted Bird" <note>The woodpecker or *picus*</note> gave its name to the city of the Pictones <note>Poitiers, France</note>, and prefigured the gentleness of the people by its color and voice. The Heron <note>Latin: *Ardea*</note> is an omen of arduous <note>Latin: *arduarum*; a pun on the bird's name</note> matters. The Stork, the bird of concord, brings about harmony. Cranes <note>Latin: *Grues*</note> are named from the old word *gruere*, as if to "congruere" <note>to agree or come together</note>; they always bring what is expedient and cause one to beware the snares of enemies. The hippopotamus <note>original: "popotamus"; here described as a "parricide," reflecting a medieval belief that the young hippopotamus kills its father</note>, a parricide, announces ingratitude for favors and injustice. announces guests. The hen harrier <note>original: "albanellus"; a type of small hawk</note> flying past, if it is carried from the left to the right, indicates the cheerfulness of hospitality; if the opposite, it indicates the opposite. The screech owl [stryx] is always an unlucky bird, as is the little owl [noctua]; because it attacks chicks by surprise at night, just as death comes unexpectedly, it is therefore said to foretell death. Sometimes, however, because it is not blinded by the shadows of the night, it signifies a person’s diligence and vigilance, which was proven when one perched upon Hiero’s spear <note>Hiero II, the King of Syracuse, who saw this as a sign of his future power</note>. Indeed, Dido felt the horned owl [bubo] to be unlucky while she was involved with Aeneas, as the Poet <note>referring to Virgil</note> sang:

> And the solitary owl often complained on the rooftops with a deathly song,
> Drawing out its long cries into wailing.

And elsewhere:

> The sluggish owl, a dire omen for mortals. <note>original: "Ignauus bubo dirum mortalibus omen"; a line from Ovid's Metamorphoses</note>

The same bird sang on the Capitol when Roman affairs were failing at Numantia, and when Fregellae was destroyed because of a conspiracy made against the Romans. Almadel <note>a name associated with a medieval grimoire, the *Ars Almadel*, often cited as an authority on ritual and natural magic</note> says that when horned owls and night-ravens [nycticoraces] turn toward unusual regions and dwellings, it is a judgment that the people of those same regions and houses are about to die; this is because those birds delight in corpses and sense them beforehand. Those who are about to die are already, in power, corpses. But also of the hawk, the herald of strife, Naso <note>Ovid</note> sings:

> We hate the hawk, because it always lives in arms.

Lælius, the legate of Pompey in Spain, was killed among the foragers; a hawk flying over his head is said to have foretold that fate to him. And Almadel says that birds of the same species fighting among themselves signify a change in the kingdom; but if birds of different species wage war against each other, or if birds gather that have not been seen for a long time, they portend a new fortune for that region. Even tiny birds, by their arrival or departure, portend that a family will increase or decrease; indeed, the more serene their flight, the more praiseworthy it is. Thus Melampus the augur <note>a legendary Greek seer who could understand the language of birds</note> conjectured the slaughter of the Greeks from the flight of small birds, when he said: "You see how no bird moves in serene paths." Swallows, because they prepare hiding places for their chicks when they are dying, portend an ample inheritance or a legacy from the dead. A bat encountered by one who is fleeing signifies escape; for although it has no feathers, it nevertheless flies. A sparrow, however, is a bad omen for a fugitive, for in fleeing the hawk it runs to the owl, where it is equally endangered; yet in matters of love, it is a good sign, since it is moved by such lust that it copulates seven times in an hour. Bees are good omens for kings, for they show an obedient people; but flies signify persistence and impudence, because after they have been

A pig indeed is ruinous, for such is its nature; therefore it signifies ruinous men. The horse has the character of quarrels and battles: whence in Virgil, upon seeing white horses, Anchises exclaims:

However, when they are met joined to a chariot, because they pull with a harmonious yoke, they signify that peace is to be hoped for. The donkey is useless: yet it profited Marius <note>Gaius Marius (c. 157–86 BC), a Roman general and statesman. While fleeing from his rival Sulla, he interpreted a donkey's behavior as a sign to escape by sea.</note>, who when declared an enemy of the fatherland, saw a donkey spurning offered fodder and rushing to water. Thinking by this augury that the way of safety was shown to him, he begged a crowd of auxiliary friends to provide this one kind of help and lead him to the sea. Having obtained this, placed upon a small boat, he escaped the hands of the victor Sulla. However, whenever a little donkey occurs in an augury, it always signifies labor, patience, and obstacles. A wolf met on the way is a good messenger, whose efficacy was seen in Hiero of Sicily <note>Hiero II, King of Syracuse</note>, for whom a wolf snatching a tablet in a grammar school confirmed his success in the kingdom; yet it shuts out the voice of the one it has seen first <note>A common ancient belief, found in Virgil and Pliny, that if a wolf sees a man before the man sees the wolf, the man is struck dumb.</note>. During the consulship of P. Africanus and C. Fulvius at Minturnae, a wolf mangled a sentry when the Roman army in Sicily was being overcome by fugitives. Furthermore, it signifies treacherous and bad-faith men, which is known in the progeny of Romulus: for the faith which they once sucked from the mother wolf and kept for each other from the beginning, flowed to their descendants as if by a law of nature. To meet a lion—since this animal is the strongest among the rest, striking terror into all—is good; but for a woman to meet a lioness is bad, because it hinders conception, for a lioness does not give birth a second time <note>A medieval bestiary tradition claiming that the lioness's claws destroy her womb during her first birth, making her forever sterile afterward.</note>. It is good to meet sheep and goats. It is also read in the *Etruscan Book of Prodigies* <note>original: "Oſtentario Tuſcorum"</note> that if this animal [the sheep] is clothed in an unusual color, it portends for the ruler an abundance of all things with happiness. Whence Virgil sings to Pollio:

> But the ram himself in the meadows will change his fleece,
> Now with sweetly blushing purple, now with saffron-yellow. <note>original: "Ipſe ſed in pratis aries iam ſuaue rubenti / Murice, iam croceo mutabit uellera luto." From Virgil's *Eclogue* 4, describing a Golden Age where sheep naturally grow colored wool.</note>

It is also good to meet oxen threshing, but better when plowing, who although they delay the journey by blocking the way, nevertheless compensate for this delay by the grace of hospitality. A dog on a journey is auspicious, because Cyrus, abandoned in the woods, was nursed by a dog for the kingdom; and the angel, the companion of Tobias <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit in the Apocrypha, where a dog accompanies the youth Tobias and the angel Raphael.</note>, did not spurn the dog as a companion. The beaver <note>original: "Caſtor"</note>, because it bites off its own testicles and leaves them behind for hunters, is of bad omen and portends that a man will bring harm upon himself. ...of a dog; conversely, cicadas encourage a journey and announce a good outcome of affairs. A spider <note>original: "Aranea"</note> drawing a thread from above is said to announce the hope of coming money. Similarly, ants <note>original: "formicę"</note>, because they know how to provide for themselves and prepare safe hiding places, therefore portend security and riches, and signify the multitude of an army. Hence, when ants devoured the tame dragon of Tiberius Caesar <note>Tiberius (42 BC–37 AD) was the second Roman emperor. This event was interpreted as a warning of a popular uprising.</note>, the response of the augurs was that he should beware the tumult of the multitude. If a snake <note>original: "anguis"</note> should cross your path, beware of a backbiting enemy; for this animal is powerful in no other limb but its mouth. A snake crawling into the palace prophesied his fall to Tarquinius <note>Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the legendary final king of Rome.</note>. Two snakes were found in the bed of Sempronius Gracchus <note>Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus (c. 210–150 BC), a Roman consul. The story of his sacrifice for his wife Cornelia was a famous example of Roman devotion.</note>; he was told by the soothsayer <term>haruspice<gloss>a priest in ancient Rome who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</gloss></term> that if he released the male or the female, either he or his wife must shortly die. Preferring his wife’s life to his own, he killed the male and released the female, and departed from life a few days later. Thus, the viper signifies wicked women and criminal sons, and the eel signifies a man hostile to everyone, for it lives apart from other fish and is never found joined with others.

<margin>
The most effective omen is from man.
</margin>
Among all auspices and omens, however, none is more effective than man, none more powerful, and none which more clearly exposes the truth. Therefore, when meeting one, you shall diligently note and investigate his condition, age, sex, profession, location, gesture, movement, occupation, complexion, clothing, name, words, and speech. For since so many lights of presage are present in other animals, there is no doubt that these are infused much more effectively and clearly into the human soul; as Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> himself testifies, saying that there is naturally within human minds a certain omen of their own eternity, for the purpose of knowing all series of things and causes. In the foundations of the city of Rome, a man’s head with an intact face was found, which foretold the greatness of the empire and gave the name to the Capitoline Hill <note>The name "Capitol" was traditionally derived from *caput* (head).</note>. The soldiers of Brutus, about to fight against Octavian and Mark Antony, encountered an Ethiopian at the gate of the camp; although they slaughtered him immediately as an omen of an adverse thing, the battle was fought unsuccessfully, and both leaders, Brutus and Cassius, perished. Even the meeting of monks is commonly held to be ominous, especially if it occurs in the morning; because that kind of men live mostly from the business of the dead, just as vultures live from carcasses.

->How auspices are verified through the light of the sense of nature, and concerning<-
->some rules for testing it. Chapter LV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial A with floral and foliage motifs in a woodcut style frame.</image-desc>
Auspices and auguries, which foretell the future from living things and birds, we read were first shown by that theologian Orpheus, which were afterwards held in great esteem among all nations. They are verified through the luminosity of the sense of nature, as if from this source certain lights of divination descend upon four-footed beasts, birds, and other living creatures, through which they have the power to presage human events for us. This is also what Virgil seems to feel when he sings:
> Indeed I do not believe it is because they have a more divine spirit, 
> or a greater foresight of things by fate. <note>original: "Haud equidem credo, quia ſit diuinius illis / Ingenium, aut rerum fato prudentia maior." From Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 1, lines 415-416, discussing the behavior of crows.</note>

<margin>The loftiness of the natural sense</margin>
Moreover, such a sense of nature <note>original: "sensus naturae"</note>, as William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris, a philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul and the natural world.</note> says, is itself loftier than all human apprehension, and is very close and strongly similar to prophecy. From this sense, a certain wonderful splendor of divination is naturally bestowed upon some animals. This is clearly apparent in certain dogs, who, by this kind of sense, recognize, find, track, and seize thieves and hidden men—even those entirely unknown to themselves or their masters—rushing upon them with jaws and teeth. By a similar sense, vultures foresee future slaughter from battles and gather in places where they will occur, as if they foresee the future meal of corpses for themselves. By the same sense, partridges recognize their mother, whom they have never seen, and leave the partridge that steals the mother's eggs to hatch them. By this same sense, certain harmful and terrifying things are felt while the human soul is entirely unaware, which is why terror and horror often seize men who are neither feeling nor thinking about such things. Thus a thief lurking in a house, even when his presence is entirely unknown or unthought of, strikes horror, fear, and restlessness of heart into the inhabitants of that house—perhaps not into everyone, because this kind of splendor <note>Agrippa uses "splendor" to mean a refined spiritual clarity or intuitive light.</note> is not in all men, but in a few. Thus a prostitute hidden in a very large house is sometimes sensed by someone who is entirely unaware she is there. It is recorded in histories that a certain Heraiscus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher from Egypt, said to possess the ability to perceive the spiritual purity of others.</note> of Egypt, a man of a divine nature, recognized "unclean" women not only by sight, but by hearing their voices from a distance, and he was immediately affected by a significant headache because of it. William of Paris also reports that in his own time, a certain woman sensed the approach of a man she loved by this kind of sense from two miles away. He also relates that in his time, a certain stork was convicted of adultery by the male's sense of smell; the male gathered a multitude of storks, and when he revealed the crime of the female, she was judged guilty by the judgment of all, plucked of her feathers, and torn apart. He also recounts a story of a certain horse that, having unknowingly mated with its mother, and later discovering it, tore off its own genitals with its teeth as if avenging the incest upon itself. Aristotle, Varro, and Pliny <note>Three of the most influential natural historians of antiquity: Aristotle (Greek), Varro (Roman), and Pliny the Elder (Roman).</note> recount similar things about horses. Pliny himself tells a similar story of a certain asp in Egypt that was fed daily at a man's table; after giving birth to young, one of which killed the host's son, the mother returned, recognized the fault, killed the offspring, and never returned to that roof again. Now, by these examples, we see how certain lights of presage can descend upon living creatures, established like signs of things in their gestures, movement, voice, flight, gait, food, color, and the like. For according to the doctrine of the Platonists, there is a certain power implanted in lower things through which they largely correspond with superior things. Whence also the silent agreements of animals are seen to harmonize with divine bodies, and their bodies and emotions are affected by these powers, in whose name they are ascribed to their own deities. One must therefore consider which animals are Saturnine <note>original: "Saturnalia"; related to the planet Saturn, often signifying gravity, age, or hidden things.</note>, which refer to Jupiter <note>original: "Iovem"</note>, which to Mars <note>original: "Martem"</note>, and so on for each...

<summary>Agrippa discusses the "natural sense"—a form of animal intuition similar to prophecy—that allows creatures to sense danger, recognize kin, and even enforce moral behavior. He argues that these instincts are a result of the hidden connection between earthly creatures and celestial powers.</summary>

...to elicit the properties of presages. Thus, those birds which relate to Saturn and Mars are all called dire and ill-omened <note>original: "ferales," referring to the dead or funerals</note>: such as the little owl, the screech owl, and the others we have listed above. The horned owl <note>original: "bubo"</note> also, because it is a Saturnine bird, solitary and nocturnal, is said to be of the most unlucky omen, of which the poet says:

> The foul bird, a messenger of coming grief,
> The sluggish owl, a dire omen to mortals.
> <note>original: "Fœda q; sic uolucris uenturi nuncia luctus / Ignauus bubo, dirum mortalibus omen." (Ovid, Metamorphoses, 5.550).</note>

The swan, however, a delightful bird sacred to Venus and even to Apollo <note>original: "Phœbo"</note>, is said to be of the most happy presage, especially in the omens of sailors, because it is not submerged by water; hence Ovid sings:

-> The swan is always the most joyful bird in auguries. <-
<note>original: "Cygnus in auspiciis semper lætissimus ales."</note>

<margin>Singing birds</margin>
There are, moreover, singing birds <note>term: "Oscinæ aues," birds that provide omens through their cries or songs rather than their flight.</note> which make an omen by their mouth and song: such as the raven, the woodpecker, and the crow, regarding which Virgil says:

-> Often the ill-omened crow foretold it from the hollow oak. <-
<note>original: "Sæpe sinistra caua prædixit ab ilice cornix." (Virgil, Eclogues, 1.18). The word "sinistra" literally means "on the left," which in Roman augury often signified an ill omen.</note>

<margin>What must be considered in the flight of birds.</margin>
The birds that portend the future by flight are those such as buzzards, ospreys <note>original: "sanqualæ"</note>, eagles, vultures, cranes, swans, and the like. For in their flight, one considers whether they fly slowly or hurriedly, whether they fly to the right or to the left, and how many fly together at once. In this way, when cranes fly hurriedly, they signify a storm; when they fly silently, they signify fair weather. Likewise, when two birds fly together and they are of the ill-omened kind, they are said to portend evil, because the number two represents division and confusion. In a similar way, you will investigate the reasoning for other birds by applying the logic of numbers here. Furthermore, observing the resemblance in these conjectures is a masterly skill, just as Venus herself, in disguise, taught her son Aeneas with these verses:

> Unless my parents taught me the art of augury in vain,
> Behold twelve swans rejoicing in a flock,
> Whom the bird of Jove <note>The eagle.</note>, gliding from the ethereal region,
> Was scattering in the open sky; now in a long line they seem
> Either to take their ground, or to look down upon the ground already taken.
> Just as they, returning, play with whirring wings,
> And have encircled the pole in a company, and given forth their songs:
> Not otherwise do your ships and the youth of your people
> Either hold the harbor, or enter its mouth with full sail.
> <note>original: Virgil, Aeneid, 1.391-400. Venus uses the behavior of swans to reassure Aeneas that his lost ships are safe.</note>

The most wonderful kind of augury, however, is that of those who hear and understand the speeches of animals, as was the case among the ancients with Melampus, Tiresias, and Thales, and in which Apollonius of Tyana is read to have excelled, who is said to have known the language of birds. Concerning him, Philostratus and Porphyry <note>Two biographers of Apollonius, a 1st-century Pythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker.</note> relate that once, when Apollonius sat in a gathering of friends, looking at sparrows resting in a tree, one little sparrow came from elsewhere, chirping and making a noise with its voice; when all the others followed it and flew away, he said to his companions that the sparrow had announced to the rest that a donkey loaded with wheat had fallen in a narrow lane near the city, and the wheat was scattered on the ground. Moved by these words, many people went to see, and so...
