<margin>The voices of animals are signifiers of the passions of the soul.</margin>
...they found that it had happened just as Apollonius had said, to their great wonder. Porphyry the Platonist <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on vegetarianism and the souls of animals.</note>, in his third book *On Sacrifices*, says that this animal was a swallow. For it is certain that every voice of any animal is a signifier of some passion of its soul, whether an affection of joy, or sadness, or anger; it is not so very wonderful that these voices can be understood by men who have practiced in these matters. Indeed, Democritus himself handed down this art, as Pliny says, naming certain birds from whose mixed blood a serpent is produced; whoever eats this serpent will understand the conversations of birds. And Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy and alchemy.</note> says: if anyone goes out to hunt on a certain day of the Calends of November <note>November 1st.</note> and cooks the first bird he catches along with the heart of a fox, all who eat of this will understand the voices of birds and other animals. The Arabs also handed down that those who have eaten the heart or liver of dragons <note>In this context, "dragons" often referred to large serpents or legendary reptiles.</note> are skilled in the meanings of brute animals; and Proclus the Platonist believed and recorded that the heart of a mole contributes to presages. There were also divinations and auspices taken from the entrails <note>term: "exta," the internal organs of a sacrificial animal, specifically the heart, lungs, and liver.</note> and the fibers of sacrifices, the inventor of which was Tages, of whom Lucan sang:

> And let there be no faith in the fibers, but let Tages, 
> The founder of the art, have fashioned those things.
> <note>original: "Et fibris sit nulla fides, sed conditor artis / Finxerit illa Tages." (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, 1.637-638). Tages was a mythical Etruscan child-prophet who was said to have been plowed up from the earth.</note>

<margin>The liver is the head of the entrails.</margin>
Roman religion considered the liver to be the "head" of the entrails. Hence the soothsayers <note>term: "haruspices," priests in ancient Rome who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>, searching for the future in the organs, would first inspect the liver. They identified two "heads" or lobes within it: one they named for the citizen, the other for the enemy. By comparing these heads, they would pronounce victory for one side or the other, just as we read in Lucan that the entrails signified the slaughter of Pompey’s followers and the victory of Caesar’s men in these verses:

> And what omen appeared that did not go unpunished through the entrails,
> Behold, he saw a mass grow on the head of the fibers;
> One part of the head hangs sick and withered,
> The other part shines, and with a swift pulse wickedly moves the veins.
> <note>original: "Quodq́; nefas nullis impune apparuit extis... Pars micat, & celeri uenas mouet improba pulsu." (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, 1.621-625).</note>

Then, having finished with the vital organs, they would seek the heart. If the victim was found without a heart, or if the "head" was missing from the liver, these were considered deadly omens and were called "piacular" <note>Expiatory or requiring atonement; signs of great divine wrath.</note>. Similarly, it was an omen if the victim fled from the altar, or let out a lowing sound when struck, or fell upon a part of the body other than what was proper. Regarding these things, we read that on the day Julius Caesar went out in purple robes and sat in his golden chair, the heart was twice missing from the entrails while he was sacrificing. And for Gaius Marius, when he was sacrificing at Utica, the liver was missing from the entrails. Likewise, for the Emperor Gaius <note>Caligula.</note> and for Marcus Marcellus: when the consuls Gaius Claudius and Lucius Petellius sacrificed victims, the liver suddenly withered away; not long after, the former died of disease, and the latter fell in battle against the Ligurians, just as the entrails had predicted. This is surely thought to happen either by the power of the gods or the work of demons. Hence, it was always held of the greatest importance among the ancients whenever anything unusual appeared in the entrails: just as when Sulla was sacrificing at Laurentum, the likeness of a crown appeared on the head of the liver. Posthumius the soothsayer interpreted this as portending victory and royal power for him, and for that reason, he advised that Sulla alone should eat of those entrails. Even the color of the entrails has its own significance. Lucan mentions these things:

So great was once the veneration for these arts that all the most powerful and wise men followed them; indeed, the senate and kings did nothing without taking auspices. But today, all these things have been abolished, partly through the negligence of men and partly by the authority of the Church Fathers.

### Chapter LVI. On the divination of lightning and thunderbolts, and how portents and prodigies are to be interpreted. ###

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a seated figure, possibly a classical deity or winged figure, within a circular frame surrounded by floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
Furthermore, in the augury of lightning, thunderbolts, and omens—and in the matter of how portents and prodigies are to be interpreted—the Etruscan seers <note>original: "Hetrusci uates." The Etruscans were famous in the ancient world for their "Etruscan Discipline," a complex system of interpreting lightning and entrails.</note> and priests handed down the knowledge. For they established sixteen regions of the sky, with their own specific deities assigned to each. Moreover, they identified eleven types of lightning and nine gods who would hurl them, passing down accounts of what they signified based on which part of the sky they appeared in. Indeed, whenever portents, prodigies, and omens occur, it is certain that they always foretell something of great importance.

<margin>What kind of interpreter of prodigies one ought to be.</margin>
The interpreter of these things must be an excellent judge of similarities as well as a diligent investigator of the affairs of the princes and provinces of that time. For the care of the heavens is directed toward princes, peoples, and provinces, so that they, above all others, are prefigured and warned through the stars, planets, portents, and prodigies. If the same or something similar appeared in past centuries, it will also be necessary to consider that event and what followed from it. Based on these, one should predict either the same or similar outcomes, because the same signs point to the same things, and similar signs to similar things.

Thus, prodigies preceded many excellent men and kings at their birth or death. As Cicero reports concerning the boy Midas: while he was sleeping, ants dropped grains of wheat into his mouth, which was an omen of great wealth. Likewise, when bees settled on the mouth of the infant Plato as he slept in his cradle, it foretold the sweetness of his future eloquence. To Hecuba, when she was about to give birth to Paris, it seemed in a vision that she gave birth to a burning torch that would set Troy and all of Asia on fire. The mother of Phalaris <note>Phalaris was the infamous tyrant of Acragas known for his cruelty and the "brazen bull."</note> saw a vision of a statue of Mercury pouring blood onto the ground, flooding the entire house. The mother of Dionysius dreamed she gave birth to a little satyr; these prodigious dreams were followed and confirmed by the actual events. The wife of Tarquinius Priscus, seeing a flame lick the head of Servius Tullius, predicted the kingship for him. In a similar way, after the fall of Troy, while Aeneas was debating his flight with his father Anchises, a flame appeared licking the crown of Ascanius's head without causing him any harm; because this portended kingship for Ascanius, it persuaded them all to depart.

All great and notable disasters have been preceded by portents and prodigies. Thus we read in Pliny that in the consulship of Marcus Attilius and Gaius Portius, it rained milk and blood, which foretold that a powerful plague would invade Rome the following year. Likewise, in Lucania, it rained iron that looked very much like sponges the year before Marcus Crassus was slain by the Parthians.

<summary>This page discusses the ancient Etruscan science of interpreting lightning and atmospheric omens, arguing that celestial signs specifically warn of the fates of rulers and nations. It provides numerous historical examples where physical "prodigies" (like fire, insects, or strange rain) accurately predicted the rise or fall of famous figures.</summary>

The same author, regarding the Second Punic War, reports that water mixed with blood descended from the sky like rain at the time Hannibal was ravaging Italy. ### Chapter LVII. On Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy—the four divinations of the elements. ###

<image-desc>Ornamental historiated initial 'E' depicting a seated figure in scholarly attire, possibly a philosopher or teacher, gesturing with one hand.</image-desc>
The elements themselves also teach us of fated events, from which those four famous kinds of divination—Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy—received their names. Concerning these, that sorceress in Lucan seemed to boast of herself when she said:

> Earth, air, ether, chaos, the seas, the fields, and the rocks of Rhodope shall speak the truth. <note>original: "Ad uerum tellus, aërq́;, ætherq́;, chaosq́;, / Equoraq́;, & campi, Rhodopeiaq́; saxa loquentur." This quote is from Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, Book VI, 622–623, spoken by the witch Erichtho.</note>

<margin>Geomancy.</margin>
First, therefore, Geomancy foretells the future from earthquakes, rumblings, swellings, tremors, fissures, chasms, exhalations, and its other impressions; the Arab Almadel <note>A reference to the *Ars Almadel*, a medieval Solomonic grimoire or its purported author.</note> handed down this art. But there is also another kind of Geomancy which divines through points inscribed by some force or by chance upon the earth, which is not part of the present investigation, but we shall speak of it among lots <note>original: "inter fortes." Referring to the practice of cleromancy or divination by casting lots.</note> in the following sections. Hydromancy, however, provides prophecies through watery impressions—their ebbs and flows, rises and falls, storms, colors, and the like—to which are also joined visions that occur in the water. This is a kind of divination discovered by the Persians, such as Varro reports a boy saw: an image of Mercury in the water, which foretold the entire outcome of the Mithridatic war in one hundred and fifty verses. We also read that Numa Pompilius practiced hydromancy; for he drew out images of the gods in water and learned the future from them. Pythagoras also practiced this art long after Numa. Among the Assyrians, a type of hydromancy called Lecanomancy <note>From the Greek *lekane* (basin) and *manteia* (divination).</note> 
<margin>
Lecanomancy, a species of Hydromancy.
</margin>
was also held in great esteem, named from a basin full of water into which they placed gold and silver plates and precious stones inscribed with certain images, names, and characters. To this can also be referred the art by which, through molten lead or wax cast into water, they express the thing we desire to know through clear signs of images. There were also once prophetic springs, such as the spring of Patras in Achaea...

...which was called the water of Juno at Epidaurus; more will be said concerning these in the following sections where we shall speak of oracles. Truly, one might also refer here to <margin><unclear>Fish Divination</unclear></margin> **Fish Divination** <note>original: "Aruspicina piscium"</note>, such as was once practiced among the Lycians in a place called Dina near the sea. In a sacred grove of Apollo, a pit was excavated in the dry sand, into which the person seeking to consult about future events would lower roasted meats. Suddenly, that place would be filled with water, and a great multitude of fish of wondrous shapes, unknown to men, would appear; from their forms, the prophet would foretell what was to come. Athenaeus reports these things at greater length from Polycharmus in his histories of the Lycians. In a <margin><unclear>Aeromancy</unclear></margin> similar way, **Aeromancy** <note>Divination by observing the air and atmospheric phenomena.</note> provides prognostications through atmospheric impressions: through the blowing of the winds, through rainbows, through halos, through mists and clouds, and through shapes imagined in the clouds and visions in the air. So also <margin><unclear>Pyromancy</unclear></margin> **Pyromancy** <note>Divination by fire.</note> divines through fiery impressions: through comets <note>original: "stellas caudatas," literally "tailed stars."</note>, through fiery colors, and through visions and imaginings in the fire. In this way, <margin><unclear>Cicero's wife</unclear></margin> **Cicero's wife** <note>Terentia, who was said to have seen a lucky omen in the sacrificial fires during the Catiline conspiracy.</note> predicted that he would be consul the following year, because when she wished to see something in the ashes after a sacrifice had been completed, a flame suddenly leaped forth. Of this kind are the things that <margin><unclear>Pliny on fires</unclear></margin> **Pliny** says: that earthly fires which are pale and murmuring are perceived as heralds of storms; rain is also signaled if "fungi" <note>The carbonized growths or "snuffs" on a lamp wick.</note> appear on the lamps; if the flame flies in a winding way, it portends wind; and when the lights spit out flames or are difficult to kindle. Likewise, when sparks are gathered hanging from a lamp, or when coal sticks to the bottom of pots when they are lifted, or when a steady fire shakes off embers or emits a spark, or when ash clumps together on the hearth, and when a coal shines intensely. To these is added <margin><unclear>Capnomancy</unclear></margin> **Capnomancy**, so named from smoke <note>From the Greek "kapnos" (smoke) and "manteia" (divination).</note>, because it scrutinizes the flame and smoke, and their colors, sounds, and movements: whether it stretches out straight, or is carried obliquely, or rolls in a circle, just as one reads concerning these in <margin><unclear>Statius</unclear></margin> **Statius** in these verses:

> Let piety be overcome; come, maiden, place the altars,
> Let us seek the gods; she, with her keen sight, observes
> The blood-red tips of the flames, and the fire born 
> Through the air, and yet the clear peaks of light 
> Rising in the midst; she teaches how it then rolls 
> In the empty likeness of a serpent in a double-sided 
> Circle, and breaks with a reddish glow.

Indeed, even in the craters of Etna and in the Nymphaean fields among the Apolloniates, auguries were taken from fire and flames—favorable if they seized what had been cast in, but grim if they rejected them. And we shall also speak of these among the responses of the oracles in later sections.

### Chapter LVIII. On the revival of the dead, on long-lasting sleep and fasting.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral scrollwork and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
<margin><unclear>Magi on the effect of the soul</unclear></margin> The Arab philosophers <note>Likely referring to thinkers such as Avicenna (Ibn Sina) or Al-Ghazali, whose works on the soul's power were influential in the West.</note> agree that some men can elevate themselves above the powers of the body and above the sensory powers; having overcome these by the perfection of heaven and the intelligences, they receive a divine vigor into themselves. Since, therefore, the souls of all men are eternal, and all spirits obey perfected souls, the Magi think that perfected men, through the powers of their own soul, [can influence] other inferior souls already in some way separated...

...thought they could restore [life] to their dying bodies and breathe it back into them, not unlike how a killed weasel is called back to life by the breath and voice of its parent, or how lions bring life to their lifeless offspring by breathing upon them. Since, as they say, all similar things applied to similar things result in a similar nature, and every passive thing that receives the action of an agent also takes on and shares in the nature of that agent, they believe that certain herbs and magical concoctions contribute significantly to this revivification. Such mixtures are said to be made from the ashes of the Phoenix and the shed skins of serpents. This might seem fabulous or even impossible to many, were it not proven by historical record. For we read that many who were submerged in water, others cast into fires and placed upon funeral pyres, others killed in war, and others otherwise rendered lifeless, revived even after several days. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist, who recorded several cases of "apparent death" in his Natural History.</note> testifies to this regarding Aviola, a man of consular rank, as well as Lucius Lamia, Caelius Tubero, Corfidius, Gabienus, and many others. Similarly, we read that Aesop the storyteller, Tyndareus, Hercules, and the Palici <note>Ancient Sicilian deities, often described as twin sons of Zeus/Jupiter and the nymph Thalia.</note> (the sons of Jupiter and Thalia) lived again after death. Many others were recalled to life by mages and physicians, as history records of Asclepius, and as we have narrated above from Juba, Xanthus, and Philostratus, regarding Tillus, a certain Arab, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker of the 1st century AD.</note>. We also read of a certain Glaucus who died, but whom they say was restored to life—contrary to everyone's expectation—by doctors running to him with a herb they call "dragon" <note>original: "draconem"</note>. Others say he revived after tasting a honeyed medicine, which gave rise to the proverb: *Glaucus rose after drinking honey* <note>original: "Glaucus poto melle resurrexit"</note>. Apuleius <note>Author of "The Golden Ass"; this specific scene describes a necromantic rite performed by an Egyptian priest.</note> also refers to the rite of such recalls when speaking of the Egyptian prophet Zachlas: "The prophet, thus appeased, places a certain small herb over the mouth of the body and another upon its chest. Then, turning to the East, having silently prayed to the rising of the august sun, he directed the attention of the onlookers to such a great miracle; already the chest was swelling with a surge, already a healthy pulse was beating, already the body was filled with breath, and the corpse rose up, and the young man spoke out."

<margin>Note</margin>
If these things are to be believed as true, it must be that dying souls sometimes hide within their bodies, overwhelmed by powerful ecstasies <note>Here "ecstasy" (extasis) refers to a state where the soul is "standing outside" its normal function, a deep trance or state of suspended animation.</note> and freed from all bodily action. In this state, life, sense, and motion desert the whole body, yet the person is not yet truly dead, but lies lifeless and as if dead, even for a long period of time. This has very often been discovered during times of pestilence, where many who were being carried out to be buried as dead revived in their graves. 

<margin>Wonderful examples of suffocation and ecstasy.</margin>
We read that this has also occurred many times to women suffering from "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: "suffocatione matricis." In historical medicine, this was a condition where the uterus was thought to migrate or put pressure on other organs, causing fainting or apparent death; it is the root of the term "hysteria."</note>. Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides, the influential Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> recounts from a book of Galen <note>The preeminent Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, translated by the Patriarch, that a suffocation happened to a man which lasted for six days; he neither ate nor drank, and his arteries became hard. He said in the same book that a "repletion" <note>An excess of bodily fluids or "humors."</note> can happen to a man from which the pulse of the whole body is lost, the heart does not move, and he lies as if dead. He also says that from a fall from a high place, or a great shout, or from staying a long time under water, a syncope <note>A sudden loss of consciousness or fainting.</note> can occur lasting forty-eight hours, and the man lies as if dead.

That such states of <term>ecstasy</term> <note>In this context, "extases" refers to a state where the soul seems to stand outside the body, or a deep trance resembling death.</note> can last for a long time without a person being truly dead should be judged no differently than the behavior of dormice, crocodiles, and many serpents, which sleep through the entire winter; they are so expired in sleep that they can scarcely be revived by fire. I myself have often seen a dissected dormouse remain motionless as if dead until it was cooked, at which point the dissected limbs first showed signs of life in the boiling water. <margin>Examples of long sleep.</margin>
to believe, we nonetheless read in the works of esteemed historians that certain men have slept a continuous "long-age" sleep for many years, during which time, until they woke up, they did not age at all. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder.</note> himself testifies to this regarding a certain boy who, exhausted by the heat and his journey, is said to have slept in a cave for fifty-seven years. We also read that **Epimenides of Gnossus** <note>A semi-mythical Greek seer and philosopher-poet.</note> slept for fifty-seven years in a cavern. From this arose the proverb: *To sleep longer than Epimenides.* **M. This opinion is confirmed by ecclesiastical histories regarding the **Seven Sleepers**, who are said to have slept for one hundred and ninety-six years. In Norway, beneath a high cliff, there is a cave where, as **Paulus Diaconus** and **Methodius the Martyr** write, seven men lay sleeping, lulled for a long time without any decay; they say that people who entered to harm them were immediately struck with paralysis <note>original: "contractos," meaning their limbs were drawn up or seized.</note>, so that the local inhabitants, cautioned by this immediate punishment, ceased from bothering them. Furthermore, **Xenocrates**, a philosopher of no small reputation, thought that this long-duration sleep <note>original: "indormitationē"</note> was a kind of natural punishment ordained from eternity for certain demerits of the soul. **M. Damascenus** himself proves by many reasons that this is possible and entirely natural; he does not think it absurd that what is granted to other living creatures—to be able to sleep for many months without food or drink, without excretion, and without wasting away or decaying—could also happen to a human being. Whether it happens through a poisonous potion, a sleep-inducing illness, a fearful slumber, or similar causes, it can last for many days, months, or years, according to the intensity or relaxation of the powers and passions of one's soul. And physicians describe antidotes of which, if one eats even a tiny portion, he can thereafter endure a long period of fasting <note>original: "inedia," a state of not eating.</note>, just as **Elijah** <note>The biblical prophet.</note>, having been fed a certain food by an angel, [traveled for forty days].

## On divination, which happens through dreams. Chapter LIX.

<margin>Dream.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap E featuring a woodcut illustration of a figure in a countryside landscape.</image-desc>THERE is also a species of divination which occurs during sleep, namely of dreams, which is proven by the traditions of philosophers, the authority of theologians, the examples of histories, and daily experience. However, I call it a "dream" here not because it is a phantom or an <term>insomnium</term> <note>original: "infomnium," referring to a non-prophetic dream caused by physical distress or waking thoughts.</note>: for these are vain and hold no power of divination, but rather arise from the remnants of waking thoughts or disturbances of the body. For as often as the body is oppressed by either good or bad fortune, then the same kind of thoughts that fatigued the mind while awake force themselves upon the sleeper—or sometimes the opposite occurs, as in a deceptive dream. Therefore, I call it a "dream" here because it is caused in the <term>phantastic spirit</term> <note>The "phantastic spirit" refers to the faculty of imagination which, in Renaissance psychology, was thought to be the bridge between the physical senses and the higher intellect.</note>, when the mind and body are well-disposed, by the influence of the heavens. A rule for interpreting these is found among the astrologers, in that section titled "on questions," but it is nevertheless insufficient, because dreams of this kind happen to different people in different ways, according to the diverse quality and disposition of the imaginative spirit. For this reason, one common rule for interpreting dreams cannot be applied to everyone. Instead, according to the opinion of Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who wrote a famous treatise "On Dreams."</note>, since the same accidents belong to the same things, and likes to likes, so he who falls into the same or a similar vision many times should designate for himself the same or a similar meaning, passion, fortune, action, and final outcome. Just as Aristotle says, memory is confirmed by the senses, and from memory frequently obtained of the same thing, <term>experience</term> <note>original: "peritia," specialized skill or practical knowledge.</note> is born; from many experiences, art and science are gradually accumulated. By a similar reasoning, one must proceed regarding dreams. Hence Synesius commands that everyone observe their own dreams and the events following them—namely, which visions resulted in which outcomes—and to commit such rules (the visions and the accidents) to the memory of both the dream and the waking state. Through diligent observation, one should accumulate many such rules within oneself; from this accumulation, a certain divinatory art and a way of interpreting one's own dreams gradually arises, provided that nothing slips from the memory. Furthermore, dreams are more effective when...

### On frenzy and the divinations that occur while awake, and on the power of the melancholic humor, by which even demons are sometimes lured into human bodies. Chapter LX.

<margin>Frenzy is a type of divination.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'C' containing a woodcut scene of two figures in a landscape.</image-desc>
It happens also that not only those who are sleeping, but also those who are awake sometimes divine when their soul is set free and driven by its own impulses; Aristotle calls this divination frenzy <note>original: "furorem," often translated as "divine madness" or "ecstatic frenzy"</note>, and teaches that it proceeds from the melancholic humor, saying in his treatise on divination:

> The melancholic, because of their intensity, guess long and well, and quickly imagine a state, most easily receiving the impression of the celestial bodies. And in his *Problems* he says: The Sibyls <note>Prophetic women of ancient Greece and Rome who uttered oracles in a state of trance.</note>, the Bacchides <note>Inspired followers of Bacchus/Dionysus known for ecstatic worship.</note>, Niceratus of Syracuse, and Amon were diviners and poets due to a natural melancholic temperament. The cause of this frenzy, if it resides within the human body, is the melancholic humor; not indeed that which is called black bile <note>original: "atra bilis"</note>, which is such a corrupt and horrible thing that its force is said by physicists and doctors to go beyond the mania it induces, even luring evil demons to obsess human bodies. Therefore, we understand here the melancholic humor that is called natural and white bile. For when this is ignited and burns, it incites a frenzy that leads us to knowledge and divination, especially if it is aided by some celestial influence, particularly that of Saturn. Saturn, being cold and dry like the melancholic humor, flows into it daily, increasing and preserving it. Furthermore, since he is the author of secret contemplation, a stranger to all public business, and the highest of the planets, he always recalls the soul from external duties to its innermost depths, making it ascend from lower things by drawing it to the highest, and bestowing knowledge and the foretelling of future events. This is what Aristotle intends in the book of *Problems*, saying: From melancholy, some have become like divine beings foretelling the future, and some have become poets. He says further that all men outstanding in any science have mostly been melancholic; to which Democritus and Plato also attest, asserting that some melancholic people so excel in genius that they seem divine rather than human.

<margin>The melancholic excel in talent.</margin>
Thus, many melancholic people who were at first unrefined, inept, or insane—as they say Hesiod, Ion, Tynnichus of Chalcis, Homer, and Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, a Roman poet whose "On the Nature of Things" was foundational to Epicureanism; legends claimed he wrote during intervals of insanity.</note> were—are often suddenly seized by frenzy and emerge as poets, singing wonderful and divine things that they themselves can scarcely understand. Hence, the divine Plato says in the *Ion*: "Most prophets, after the impulse of frenzy has subsided, do not sufficiently understand what they have written, though they treated each art correctly while in that frenzy, as the individual practitioners of those arts judge when reading them." Furthermore, they say that the melancholic hu...

### BOOK ONE.

...the power of the [melancholic] humor is such that by its own force it sometimes draws even celestial spirits <note>original: "dæmones." In this context, these are not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense of evil entities, but rather intermediary spirits or "daemons" who act as messengers between the divine and human realms.</note> into human bodies.
<margin>The power of the melancholic humor.</margin>
By their presence and impulse, all of antiquity testifies that men rave and utter many wonders. They believe this happens in three different ways, according to the three levels of the soul's perception: namely the **imaginative**, the **rational**, and the **mental**. They say, therefore, that when the soul is driven by the melancholic humor and—with nothing holding it back—it lets go of the reins of the body and transcends the bonds of the limbs, it is entirely transferred into the **imagination**. It suddenly becomes a dwelling place for lower spirits, from whom it often receives wondrous methods for the manual arts. Thus we see some very unrefined man suddenly turn out to be an excellent painter or architect, or a master of any other art. But when spirits of this kind portend the future to us, they show those things pertaining to disturbances of the elements and shifts in the seasons, such as future rain, storms, floods, earthquakes, plagues, famine, slaughter, and the like. Just as we read in the works of Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," a collection of miscellaneous notes on history and philosophy.</note> that the priest Cornelius—at the time when Caesar and Pompey were clashing in Thessaly—was seized by a frenzy in Padua and foretold the time, the sequence, and the outcome of the battle. When, however, the soul is entirely turned toward **reason**, it becomes the home of "middle spirits"; from here it acquires knowledge and wisdom of natural and human things. Thus we see some man suddenly turn out to be an excellent philosopher, physician, or orator, or predict from future events those things that pertain to the changes of kingdoms and the restoration of ages—just as the Sibyl <note>Prophetic women in the ancient world whose oracles were often collected and consulted by the Roman state.</note> did for the Romans. But when the soul has risen entirely into the **mind** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "Mind" (mens) refers to the highest, most divine part of the soul, above mere logic or reason.</note>, then having been made a receptacle for higher spirits, it learns from them the secrets of divine things—for instance, the law of God, the orders of angels, and those things which pertain to the knowledge of eternal things and the salvation of souls. Concerning future things, it foresees those which lie within divine providence, such as future portents or miracles, a future prophet, or a change in the law. Thus the Sibyls prophesied about Christ a long time before his coming. Thus Virgil, understanding that Christ was already about to be born in the near future, and remembering the Cumaean Sibyl, sang to Pollio:

> The final age of the Cumaean song has now arrived;
> The great order of the ages is born anew.
> Now the Virgin also returns, the reign of Saturn returns;
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven. <note>From Virgil's "Fourth Eclogue," which many Renaissance scholars interpreted as a pagan prophecy of the birth of Jesus.</note>

And a little later, hinting that original sin would be wiped away, he says:

> With you as leader, if any traces of our crime remain,
> Being wiped away, they shall free the lands from perpetual fear.

And he adds:

> He shall receive the life of the gods, and shall see
> Heroes mingled with gods, and he himself shall be seen by them,
> And he shall rule a world at peace through his father's virtues.

And he thereafter adds the fall of the serpent, and that the poison of the tree of death—or the tree of knowledge of good and evil—shall be laid to rest, saying:

> The serpent too shall die, and the deceitful herb of poison. <note>From Virgil’s Eclogue 4, often interpreted by Renaissance scholars as a pagan prophecy of the coming of Christ.</note>

Yet he implies that the fuel of original sin shall remain, when he says:

> Yet a few traces of ancient deceit shall remain.

Finally, acclaiming this progeny as the offspring of a god with the greatest possible hyperbole, he worships him with these words:

There are also certain prognostications that stand midway between the boundaries of natural and supernatural divination, such as in those who are close to death or weakened by old age, who sometimes foresee future things. This is because, as Plato says in the *Republic*, those whose senses are less hindered understand more acutely; and because they are closer to the place to which they are about to migrate, and—as if their bonds were already somewhat loosened—they are no longer entirely subject to the body, they easily perceive the lights of divine revelation.

### On the formation of man, on the external and internal senses and the mind: on the triple appetite of the soul, and the passions of the will. Chapter LXI.

IT IS the opinion of certain theologians that God himself did not create the body of the first man immediately, but composed and formed it from the elements with the help of the celestial beings. This opinion is also supported by Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher whose "Handbook of Platonism" was a major source for Renaissance thinkers.</note> based on the dogma of Plato, who thought that the highest God is the creator of the whole world, the gods, and the <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, and that these are therefore immortal. However, he believed that the "junior gods" <note>Lesser celestial deities or planetary spirits in the Platonic hierarchy.</note> created the other types of mortal living beings at the command of the highest God. For if He had produced these as well, they would have been born immortal. Thus, the gods took certain portions from earth, fire, air, and water, exchanging and binding them together to fashion one body from them all. They subjected this body to the service of the soul, assigning individual provinces within it to each of the soul's powers. They assigned the lower seats to the lower powers: specifically, the <term>precordia</term> <note>The region around the heart; historically considered the seat of emotions like anger.</note> to wrath, and the womb to desire; but the nobler senses they placed in the head, as if in the citadel of the whole body. Then, they formed the various organs of speech.

<margin>To which elements the external senses correspond.</margin>
They divide the senses into the external and internal. The external senses are further divided into the five best known to everyone, to which are attributed five organs or subjects as foundations. These are arranged so that those located in the higher parts of the body also hold a higher order of purity. For the eyes, placed in the highest position, are the purest and are related to the nature of fire and light. Next, the ears, holding the second rank of both place and purity, are compared to air. The nostrils possess the third place, maintaining a middle ground between air and water. After that is the organ of tasting, which is thicker and most similar to a watery nature. Finally, in the last grade, is touch, which is diffused through the whole body and is assigned to the thickness of earth.

LXXXI.

# BOOK ONE

<note>original: "tur." — this is the end of a word from the previous page, likely 'percipiuntur' (are perceived).</note> The senses which are purer are those that perceive sensible objects from a distance without approaching them, such as sight and hearing. Next is smell, which also perceives through the medium of the air without the object drawing close. Taste, however, only senses what is near. Touch operates in both ways: it feels bodies that are close, and just as sight sees through the medium of the air, touch also senses hard, soft, and wet things through a medium such as a rod or a staff. Indeed, touch alone among the senses is common to every animal.

<margin>In taste and touch, man excels the rest of the animals.</margin>

Man possesses this sense most accurately; for in this and in taste he surpasses the rest of the animals, but in the other three senses he is surpassed by certain creatures. For example, a dog sees, hears, and smells more acutely than a man; similarly, lynxes and eagles see more sharply than many other living creatures and man himself. The internal senses, however, as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational for Renaissance psychology.</note> maintains, are divided into four parts. The first of these is called the **common sense** <note>The 'sensus communis', the faculty that unifies data from all five external senses into a single perception.</note>, because it is the first to gather and perfect all the images drawn in through the external senses.

<margin>1</margin>
The second is the **imaginative power**, whose duty—since it perceives nothing itself—is to retain the images received from the earlier senses.

<margin>2</margin>
These it offers to the third nature of sensing, which is **phantasy** <note>In Renaissance thought, 'phantasia' was the faculty that allowed the mind to manipulate, combine, or judge the images stored in memory.</note>—the power of estimating and thinking.

<margin>3</margin>
The work of this power is to perceive and judge, once the images are received, what or of what sort the thing is to which those images belong. Those things which it has thus distinguished, joined, perceived, and judged, it commends to the preservation of the fourth power, which we call **memory**.

<margin>4</margin>
For within that general category are the virtues of discourse, arrangement, pursuit and avoidance, and the incitements to action. In the specific category of the intellectual powers, there are the understandings, virtues, the reasoning of disciplines, counsel, and choice. It is this faculty which shows us future things through dreams; hence phantasy is sometimes called the **phantastic intellect**. It is the final trace of intelligence which, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's ability to connect with the divine.</note> says, being innate to all the powers of the soul, shapes all figures, the likenesses of forms, and operations. It transmits visions or the impressions of powers from one to another: those which shine from the senses, it stirs into opinion; those which come from the intellect, it offers in the second place to opinion. Yet from itself, it receives images from all things and, through its own property and according to a specific likeness, it designates them. It shapes all actions of the soul, accommodates external things to internal ones, and even stamps impressions upon the body.

<margin>The organs of the senses are in the head.</margin>

These senses have their organs in the head. The common sense, along with the imagination, possesses the forward cells of the brain—although **Aristotle** placed the organ of the common sense in the heart. The cogitative power <note>The faculty of thought or reasoning.</note> occupies the highest and middle part of the head, and then memory occupies the back. Furthermore, the organs of voice and speech are many: the muscles between the ribs of the internal chest, the thorax, the lungs, the **trachea** <term>windpipe</term>, the artery, the throat—and most especially that which is cartilaginous, following the recurrent nerves—the **plectrum** <note>Latin: "striker" or "pick"; here referring to the tongue's role in "striking" sounds.</note> of the tongue, and all these small parts and muscles which are organs of breathing out. But the proper organ of speech is the mouth, in which words and speech are molded, formed, and shaped. The tongue and the **uvula** <note>original: "gurgulione"</note> take the place of the plectrum in that organ, and the palate creates the sound by the opening of the teeth and mouth—just as in a lyre—while the nose carries the resemblance of the strings,

LXXXII.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

...moreover contributing to a good or bad resonance. <margin>The dual nature of the mind.</margin> Above the sensible soul, which explains its powers through the organs of the body, the highest place is occupied by the incorporeal mind itself, and this has a dual nature: One nature searches into the causes, properties, and progressions of those things contained in the order of nature, and is satisfied in the contemplation of truth; for this reason, they call it the **contemplative intellect**. The other nature or power of the mind discerns what is to be done and what is to be avoided through deliberation; it is entirely engaged in consultation and action, and for this reason, they call it the **active intellect**. Therefore, nature established this order of powers in man so that through the exterior senses we might know physical things; through the interior senses, we might know the likenesses of bodies beyond that; and further, through the mind or intellect, we might know abstract things which are neither bodies nor similar to them.

<margin>The triple appetite in the soul.</margin> And according to this triple order of the soul's powers, three appetites <note>In this context, "appetite" refers to a natural drive or inclination toward something, not just hunger for food.</note> arise in the soul: The first is **natural**, which is a certain inclination of nature toward its own end (such as a stone falling downward), which exists in all things. The second is **animal**, which follows the senses and is divided into the <term>irascible</term> <note>The spirited part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and overcoming obstacles.</note> and the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>The part of the soul associated with desire, longing, and the pursuit of pleasure.</note>. The third is **intellectual**, which is called the **will**. This differs from the sensitive appetite in that the sensitive is concerned only with those things that can be presented to the senses, desiring nothing unless it is perceived in some way. The **will**, however, even though it is concerned with all possible things, can also be concerned with impossible things because it is free by its very essence—such as it was in the demon who desired to be equal to God. Thus, the soul is continuously altered and corrupted by pleasure and pain while it gives its assent to the lower powers.

Whence four passions <note>The "passions" were seen as movements of the soul that could affect the physical body, roughly equivalent to what we call "emotions" or "affects" today.</note> arise in it from its corrupted appetite, by which the body is likewise sometimes affected. The first of these is called **delight**, which is a certain softness and assent of the mind or will, by which it most willingly consents to, obeys, and complies with the sweetness that the sense offers; they therefore define it as an inclination of the soul toward softening pleasure. The second is called **effusion**, which is a loosening or dissolution of virtue—specifically when, beyond mere delight, the entire power and intention of the mind melts and flows away in the sweetness of a present good, and completely pours itself out and is carried away in enjoying it. The third is called **vaunting** <note>original: "iactantia"</note>, which is a leaping-upward or elation, believing that it has attained some greatest good; by the possession of this, it carries itself out quite insolently, exulting and glorying in vain. The fourth and last is **malevolence**, a certain pleasure derived from the misfortune of another without any benefit to oneself. It is said to be "without benefit to oneself" because if someone should rejoice in another's misfortune for the sake of their own utility, this would be out of benevolence toward oneself rather than malevolence toward others.

And just as these four passions are born from a corrupted appetite for pleasure, so too does **pain** generate just as many contrary passions: namely, **horror**, **sadness**, **fear**, and **envy**, which is pain felt at the good of another without any detriment to oneself. That is, envy is sadness in the face of another's blessings, just as **mercy** is a certain sadness in the face of another's misfortunes.

BOOK ONE. LXXXIII,

The passions of the soul <note>original: "passiones animi"; in this context, "passions" refers to any emotion or internal movement of the mind, from the Latin *pati*, meaning to undergo or be affected by something.</note> are nothing other than certain movements or inclinations arising from the perception of something as either good or bad, suitable or unsuitable. Now, these perceptions are threefold: namely, sensual, rational, and mental. And according to this threefold division, there are passions in the soul. For sometimes they follow sensitive perception, and then they regard a temporal good or evil—seen as a convenience or inconvenience, a delight or an offense—and these are called **natural** or **animal passions**. Sometimes they follow rational perception, and thus they regard good or evil in terms of virtue and vice, praise and blame, the useful and the useless, the honorable and the base; these are called **rational** or **voluntary passions**. Finally, they sometimes follow mental perception and regard good and evil in terms of the just and the unjust, the true and the false, and then they are called **intellectual passions**, or <term>synderesis</term> <note>Synderesis is a philosophical term for the innate "spark of conscience" or the natural capacity of the human mind to understand basic moral principles.</note>.

The subject of these passions of the soul is the "concupiscitive" power of the soul itself, and it is divided into the **concupiscible** <note>The faculty of desire or longing for what is perceived as good.</note> and the **irascible** <note>The faculty of the soul that deals with obstacles, anger, and the struggle to achieve a goal.</note>, and both regard good and evil, but in different ways. For the concupiscible power sometimes regards good and evil absolutely, and thus **love** <note>original: "amor seu libido"</note> is caused, and conversely, **hate**. Or, it regards good as something absent, and thus **longing** or **desire** is caused; or evil as absent but imminent, and thus **horror**, **flight**, and **abomination** are caused. Or, it regards good and evil as present and attained, and thus from the former arises **delight**, **joy**, and **pleasure**, while from the latter arises **sadness**, **anguish**, and **pain**.

The irascible power, however, regards good and evil in terms of the difficulty of attaining, obtaining, avoiding, or repelling them. And this happens sometimes with confidence: and thus on one hand **hope** is caused, and on the other, **audacity**. Sometimes it happens with a lack of confidence, and thus **despair** and **dread** or **fear** arise. Sometimes this irascible power rises up for revenge, and this happens only regarding a past evil, such as an inflicted injury or harm, and **anger** is caused. And so we find eleven passions in the soul itself, which are: **love, hate, desire, horror, joy, pain, hope, despair, audacity, fear,** and **anger.**

### How the passions of the soul change one's own body by altering the accidents and moving the spirit. Chapter LXIII.

When the passions of the soul follow a sensual perception, the phantasy <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty of imagination that processes sensory data.</note> or imaginative power holds the governing force. For by its power, according to the diversity of the passions, it first alters and transforms one’s own body in various ways through sensible change—by changing the "accidents" <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color, temperature, or moisture levels.</note> in the body, and by moving the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum"; refers to the "vital spirits," a subtle, vapor-like substance thought to circulate through the nerves and arteries, acting as the bridge between the soul and the physical body.</note> upward or downward, outward or inward, and producing different qualities in the limbs.

Thus, in **joy**, the spirits are driven outward; in **fear**, they are pulled back; in **shame**, they are moved toward the brain. Likewise, in **joy**, the heart is dilated outward gradually; in **sadness**, it is constricted inward gradually. It happens in a similar way in **anger** or **fear**, but suddenly. Furthermore, anger or the desire for revenge produces heat, redness, a bitter taste, and a flow of the bowels. Fear induces cold, a trembling of the heart...

Compassion <note>original: "misericordia"</note>, which is itself a kind of sadness, often affects the body of the one who feels it so poorly that they seem to suffer exactly as the other person does. It is also well known among certain lovers that the bond of love is so strong that whatever one of them suffers, the other suffers as well. Anxiety also brings about dryness and a blackened complexion. Furthermore, physicians know how much heat the desire of love stirs up in the liver and in the pulse; they use this judgment to detect the name of the beloved in cases of **heroic passion** <term>heroic passion</term> <note>Also known as "amor hereos" or "lovesickness," this was considered a clinical medical condition in the Middle Ages and Renaissance where intense desire caused physical illness.</note>. 

<margin>Passions of the soul sometimes bring about death.</margin>
Thus did Nausistratus <note>Often identified in other texts as the physician Erasistratus.</note> recognize that Antiochus was captured by a love for Stratonice. It is, moreover, manifest that passions of this kind, when they are most vehement, can bring about death. It is common knowledge among the public that people sometimes die from excessive joy, sadness, love, or hatred, and are often even relieved of a disease by them. Thus we read that both Sophocles and Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, died suddenly upon receiving news of a victory in a tragic competition. Likewise, a mother died instantly upon seeing her son returning from the Battle of Cannae <note>A major battle of the Second Punic War (216 BC) where the Romans suffered a catastrophic defeat; the mother had presumed her son dead.</note>. What sadness can do is known to everyone. We even know that dogs have often died from excessive sadness over the death of their masters. 

Sometimes, long-lasting illnesses follow these kinds of passions, and occasionally they are cured by them. Thus, some people looking down from a height tremble with excessive fear, grow dizzy, become weak, and sometimes lose their senses. In this way, hiccups, fevers, and **comitial diseases** <term>comitial disease</term> <note>An old term for epilepsy, so called because the Roman assemblies (*comitia*) would be dissolved if anyone present had a seizure.</note> sometimes follow, while at other times they actually recede. Occasionally, certain miraculous effects occur, as with the son of Croesus; though his mother had brought him forth mute, a vehement fear and intense desire forced out a voice which nature had long denied him. Thus, by some sudden event affecting them, life, sense, and movement often suddenly desert the limbs and often return just as quickly. 

Even the great Alexander himself showed how much vehement anger, joined with high-minded boldness, can do; for during a battle in India, when he was surrounded, he was seen to pour out light and fire from himself. It is read that the father of Theodoric <note>Theodemir, king of the Ostrogoths.</note> poured out sparks of fire from his whole body, so that glittering flames leaped out here and there, even with a sound. And things similar to these sometimes appear even in beasts, as was reported of the horse of Tiberius, which breathed flame from its mouth.

And William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), a philosopher and Bishop of Paris who wrote extensively on the soul.</note> relates that he saw a man who was moved by the mere sight of medicine whenever there was a need for a purgative effect; even though neither the substance of the medicine, nor its taste or smell had reached him, the simple mental image <note>original: "similitudo," meaning a likeness or mental representation.</note> was grasped. By this same reasoning, those dreaming that they are burning or are in a fire are sometimes tortured intolerably, as if they were truly burning, even though the reality and substance of fire is not with them, but only the likeness grasped through the <margin>The wonderful power of the imagination.</margin> imagination. Not infrequently, human bodies themselves are transformed, transfigured, and transported, often indeed in dreams, and sometimes even while awake. Thus Cyppus <note>Genucius Cipus, a Roman praetor mentioned by Ovid and Valerius Maximus.</note>, who was later elected King of Italy, while he was meditating with intense admiration on a bullfight and victory, fell asleep that night in the midst of his care; in the morning he was found with horns, for no other reason than that his **vegetative power** <term>vegetative power</term> <note>In Aristotelian biology, the part of the soul responsible for physical growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note> was stimulated by a vehement imagination, raising "horn-bearing" humors into his head and producing horns. For a vehement thought, while it powerfully moves the mental species, paints the figure of the thing thought of within them; they in turn fashion this in the blood, and the blood imprints it upon the members it nourishes—both one's own members and sometimes even those of another. Just so, the imagination of a pregnant woman imprints the mark of a desired object upon the fetus, and the imagination of one bitten by a mad dog imprints images of dogs in the urine. Thus many people suddenly turn gray; another, from being a boy, grew into a full-grown man in the dream of a single night. To this power many also wish to attribute the scars of King Dagobert <note>A Frankish king who, according to legend, bore physical marks of a spiritual trial.</note> and the **stigmata** <term>stigmata</term> <note>Physical wounds appearing on the body corresponding to the crucifixion wounds of Jesus.</note> of Francis, while the former vehemently feared punishment and the latter more vehemently contemplated the wounds of Christ. Thus many are even transported from place to place, crossing rivers, fires, and inaccessible locations: namely, when the mental species of some vehement desire, fear, or audacity are impressed upon the spirits, mixed with vapors, and move the organ of touch at its origin, together with the **phantasy** <term>phantasy</term> <note>The "phantasia" or internal imagination which directs physical movement in sleepwalking.</note>, which is the beginning of local motion. From this, the limbs and organs of motion are stirred to move, and they are moved without error to the imagined place, not indeed by sight, but by the interior phantasy. Such is the power of the soul over the body that wherever it imagines and dreams itself to be, it lifts up and carries the body along with it. We read many other examples by which the power of the soul over the body is explained with wonder, such as that which Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note> writes of a certain man who, when he wished, could strike his own body with paralysis. It is told of Gallus Vibius <note>A Roman orator who reportedly went mad after trying to understand madness for a speech.</note> that this happened to him alone: that he fell into insanity not by chance, but punished by his own judgment; for while he imitated the insane, thinking his madness was a trick of his talent, he reduced the insanity he was feigning into the real thing. And Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo in "The City of God," Book 14.</note> reports some who could move their ears at will, and some who, without moving their heads, could bring their whole scalp down to their forehead and recall it when they wished; and another who was accustomed to sweat whenever he wished. It is also known that some weep when they want to and pour out tears abundantly; some have even been found who could bring up various things they had swallowed, little by little as if from a bag, whatever pleased them. And today we still see many who so imitate and express the voices of birds, cattle, dogs, and any men, that they cannot be distinguished at all. Indeed, Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder.</note> relates with many examples that women have been changed into males; and Pontanus <note>Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503), an Italian humanist.</note> testifies that similar things happened in his own time regarding a certain woman of Gaeta...

Now, how much the imagination itself can do to the soul, no one is ignorant: for it is closer to the substance of the soul than the senses, and therefore acts more upon the soul than the senses do. Thus a woman, through strong imaginations, dreams, and suggestions introduced by certain magical artifices, is very often bound in the most tight bond of love for someone. Thus they say that Medea, from a dream alone, caught fire with love for Jason. Thus the soul is sometimes entirely withdrawn from the body through vehement imagination or contemplation, just as Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – c. 50 AD), a Roman medical writer.</note> tells of a certain priest who, as often as he pleased, would withdraw himself from his senses and lie as if dead, so that when he was pricked or burned, he felt no pain, and lay motionless and without breath; yet he afterwards reported that he heard the voices of people, if they shouted loudly, as if from far away. Truly, we shall discuss these abstractions more extensively in the following books.

### How the passions of the soul also work outside themselves upon another’s body. Chapter LXV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'P' containing a figure seated in a classical landscape with architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc>
**P**assions of the soul that follow the phantasy <term>phantasy</term> <note>In Renaissance psychology, the 'phantasy' was the mental faculty that processed sensory images and presented them to the intellect.</note>, when they are most vehement, can not only change their own body, but can even transcend to act upon another’s body, so that certain wonderful impressions are produced from it in the elements and external things, and could even remove or inflict certain diseases of the mind or body. For the passions of the soul are the most powerful cause of the temperament <note>The 'temperament' refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determine health and personality.</note> of one's own body. Thus a soul strongly elevated and inflamed by a vehement imagination sends health or sickness, not only into its own body, but also into foreign bodies. Thus Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), an influential Persian physician and philosopher.</note> believes that a camel may fall by the imagination of someone. Thus, in one bitten by a rabid dog who falls into madness, the shapes of dogs appear in his urine. Thus the craving of a pregnant woman acts upon another's body when it stains the fetus in the womb with the mark of the desired object. Thus many monstrous births come from the monstrous imaginations of pregnant women, such as the one Marcus Damascenus mentions in the town of Pietrasanta <note>original: "Petrā sanctā," a town in Tuscany.</note> located in the Pisan borders: a girl was presented to Charles, King of Bohemia and Emperor <note>Charles IV (1316–1378), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, who was hairy and shaggy over her whole body like a wild beast; her mother, while conceiving her, had been affected by a certain religious awe toward an image of Saint John the Baptist <note>St. John the Baptist was traditionally depicted in a garment of camel's hair, appearing "hairy."</note> which was near her bed, and subsequently gave birth to such a child. And we see this happen not only in humans, but also in brute animals. Thus we read that the patriarch Jacob, by throwing rods into the water, caused Laban’s sheep to change color <note>A reference to Genesis 30:37-43, where Jacob uses visual stimuli to influence the breeding of livestock.</note>.

And now it is clear from these examples how the affects of the phantasy, when they intend themselves more vehemently, affect not only one’s own body, but also another’s. LXXXVII.

->**BOOK ONE.**<-

is, for a body to be most easily infected by the vapor of another diseased body, which we plainly see in the plague and leprosy. Furthermore, so great is the power in the vapors of the eyes that they can fascinate <term>fascinate</term> <note>In this context, 'fascinate' refers to the 'evil eye' or the ability to cast a spell through sight.</note> and infect those nearby, just as the basilisk <note>original: "regulus"</note> and the catoblepas <note>original: "catabepla" — a legendary Ethiopian creature said to kill with its gaze.</note> kill men with their sight. And certain women in Scythia, among the Illyrians and Triballians <note>Ancient Thracian tribes known in classical literature for their supposed magical powers.</note>, used to kill anyone they looked upon in anger. Let no one wonder, then, that the body and soul of one person can be similarly affected by the mind of another, since the mind is far more powerful, stronger, more fervent, and more vigorous in motion than the vapors exhaling from bodies; nor are there lacking media through which it may work. Furthermore, the body is no less subject to another's mind than to another's body. In this way, they say a person acts upon another by emotion and habit alone. Therefore, the philosophers command that the company of evil and unfortunate men must be fled far away, for the souls of these men are full of noxious rays, infecting those nearby with a calamitous contagion. On the contrary, they command that the company of good and fortunate men should be sought, because by their proximity they benefit us much. For just as an odor leaps from asafoetida <note>A pungent resin used in ancient medicine and folk magic to ward off evil.</note> or musk, so from an evil man something evil, and from a good man something good, leaps into those nearby, and sometimes remains infused there for a long time.

<margin>Reason is more excellent than phantasy.</margin>
Now truly, if the aforementioned passions have such great power in the phantasy <term>phantasy</term> <note>The mental faculty that receives and retains sensory images.</note>, they certainly have greater power in the reason, insofar as reason itself is more excellent than phantasy. Finally, they have much greater power in the mind <note>original: "mens" — referring to the highest part of the soul, the intellective or divine spark.</note>; for when this mind is fixed upon the heavens with the whole intention of the soul toward a particular benefit, it often affects both its own body and the bodies of others toward which it is directed by some divine gift. In this way, we read that miracles were performed by Apollonius, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Philolaus <note>Ancient Greek philosophers and wonder-workers.</note>, and many prophets, and also the saints of our own religion. Concerning these matters, it will be more clearly revealed below, where we shall discuss religion.

### That the passions of the soul are greatly aided by celestial opportunity: and how necessary constancy of the soul is in every work. Chapter LXVI.

<image-desc>Decorative initial P featuring a figure and foliage within a double-lined square border.</image-desc>
**P**assions of the soul are greatly aided by and do aid the heavens, and they become most powerful when they agree with the heavens, either by a certain natural pact or by voluntary choice and free will. For, as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the foundational astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> says, he who chooses that which is better seems to differ in no way from him who has this by nature. It is therefore most helpful in any work, for the sake of receiving the benefits of heaven, if we also present ourselves as harmonious with heaven in our thoughts, affections, imaginations, choices, deliberations, contemplations, and the like. For passions of this kind vehemently agitate our spirit <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, 'spirit' was a subtle fluid that linked the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> into their own likeness, and suddenly expose us and our affairs to the celestial beings that signify such passions. Furthermore, because of their dignity and proximity to higher things, passions receive celestial influences much more and more fully than any material things can. For our soul can, through imagination or reason by a certain imitation, be so conformed to a particular star that it is suddenly filled with the gifts of that same star, as if it were the proper receptacle for its influence.

LXXXVIII.

**ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY**

The contemplative mind <note>original: "mens contemplatrix"</note>, however—insofar as it withdraws itself from all sensation, imagination, and the deliberations of nature, and recalls itself to separate things <note>This refers to "separated substances," a philosophical term for spiritual beings like angels or intelligences that exist apart from physical matter.</note>—does not belong to this present investigation, unless it exposes itself to Saturn <note>In the Western esoteric tradition, Saturn governs the highest intellectual reaches and deep, often melancholy, contemplation.</note>. For our mind performs many things through faith, which is a firm adherence, a fixed intention, and a powerful application of the one performing or receiving an action. This applies to any matter where one cooperates with the giver of power for the work we intend to do, so much so that there is formed within us, in a sense, an image <note>original: "idolum"</note> of the power to be received, or of the thing to be done by us or within us. We must, therefore, in every work and application of things, vehemently desire, imagine, hope, and most firmly believe, for this will be of the greatest assistance. It is verified among physicians that firm belief, indubitable hope, and love toward the physician and the medicine contribute greatly to health, sometimes even more than the medicine itself. For alongside the power and effective force of the medicine, the strong soul of the physician also works, being capable of changing the qualities in the body of the sick person, especially when the patient, by placing faith in the physician, disposes themselves to receive the power of the healer and the medicine. Therefore, the one operating in magic must possess constant belief, be confident, and in no way doubt or hesitate in mind regarding the achievement of the effect. For just as a firm and persistent belief works wonders even sometimes in "false" works <note>The author suggests that the psychological power of belief can produce results even if the ritual itself is theoretically flawed.</note>, so too does distrust and hesitation dissipate and break the power of the operator's soul, which is the medium between the two extremes. Hence it happens that the desired influence from the higher spheres is frustrated and lost, for it cannot be joined or united to our affairs and works without the stable and solid power of our own soul.

### How the human soul can be joined with the souls and intelligences of the heavens, and together with them, impress certain marvelous virtues upon inferior things.

### Chapter LXVII.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'D' at the beginning of the second section, decorated with scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

Philosophers say, especially the Arabs <note>Referring to medieval Islamic thinkers like Al-Kindi and Avicenna, whose theories on the "rays" of the soul and stellar influence were foundational to Renaissance magic.</note>, that when the human soul is most intent upon some work through its passions and effects, it is joined with the souls of the stars and even with the intelligences. Being thus joined, it becomes the cause by which a certain marvelous power is infused into our works and things. This occurs both because there is in the soul the perception and power of all things, and because all things have a natural obedience to it and a necessary efficacy, moving toward that which the soul desires with strong longing. According to this, the craft of characters <term>characters</term> <note>Magical sigils or symbols believed to capture the influence of specific spirits or planets.</note>, images, incantations, and certain words—as well as many other marvelous experiments—is verified for every matter the soul desires. In this way, whatever the soul of a vehement lover dictates has the power to cause love; and whatever the soul of a powerful hater dictates has the power to harm and destroy. It is similar in all other things that the soul desires with strong longing. For everything it then acts upon or dictates—whether by characters, figures, words, speeches, gestures, and the like—all serve to assist the soul's appetite and acquire certain marvelous virtues, both from the soul of the operator in that hour when such an appetite most possesses it, and from the opportunity and celestial influence then moving the soul in such a way.

LXXXIX.

BOOK ONE.

For our mind <note>original: "animus"</note>, when it is carried into some great excess of any passion or virtue, very often seizes from itself a stronger, better, and more suitable hour or opportunity. This is something that Thomas Aquinas also admits in the third book of *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra Gentiles"; Aquinas was a major medieval theologian whose work was often cited by Renaissance magicians to provide a veneer of Christian orthodoxy to their theories.</note>. Thus, many wonderful virtues are caused by, and follow from, marvelous operations through the great affections in those things which the soul dictates at that hour. But you should know that such things contribute nothing, or at least very little, except to their author and to those who are already inclined toward them as if they were already their author; and this is the way through which their efficacy is found. And there is a general rule in these matters: that every mind <margin>General rule.</margin> which is more excellent in its desire and affection, makes things of this kind more fit and effective for what it craves. Therefore, whoever wishes to work in magic must know and recognize the property, virtue, measure, order, and degree of their own soul within the power of the universe itself.

# How our mind can transform and bind lower things
# to that which it desires.
## Chapter LXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' depicting a person sitting in a room or landscape, marking the beginning of the chapter.</image-desc> There is also in the minds of men a certain power of changing, attracting, hindering, and binding <term>binding: "ligatio," a magical technique used to restrict the actions or will of another</term> things and people to that which the mind desires; and all things obey it when it is carried into a great excess of any passion or virtue, so much so that it overcomes those whom it binds. For that which is superior binds that which is lower and turns it toward itself, and the lower, by the same logic, is turned toward the superior, or is otherwise affected or stirred. For this reason, things that hold a superior rank of a certain star bind, attract, or hinder things that hold a lower rank, according to how they agree or disagree among themselves. Hence, the rooster is feared by the lion <note>A common belief in ancient and medieval natural history, based on the idea that the rooster possesses a "Solar" spirit that overwhelms the lion's nature.</note>, because the presence of the solar virtue agrees more with the rooster than with the lion. Likewise, the magnet attracts iron because it holds a superior rank in the order of the Celestial Bear <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major, which ancient navigators and astrologers associated with the North Pole and magnetic attraction.</note>. So too the diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note> hinders the magnet, because in the order of Mars it is superior to it. In a similar way, a person who is opportunely exposed to celestial gifts—both through the affections of their mind and through the application of the rites of natural things—if they become stronger in the solar virtue, they bind and draw those who are lower into admiration and obedience. In the lunar order, they lead them to servitude or weakness; in the Saturnine, to rest or sadness; in the Jovial, to the showing of veneration; in the Martial, to fear or discord; in the Venereal <note>pertaining to Venus</note>, to love or joy; in the Mercurial, to persuasion and compliance, and similar things. <margin>The root of binding.</margin> Indeed, the root of such binding is the vehement and extreme affection of the soul itself, combined with the concurrence of the celestial order. However, the dissolutions or hindrances of this kind of binding are achieved through a contrary affection, and one that is more excellent and stronger; for just as a greater excess of the mind binds, so also does it loosen and hinder. Finally, where you fear Venus, oppose Saturn; where you fear Saturn or Mars, oppose Venus or Jupiter; for astrologers say these are enemies and greatly contrary to one another. Understand this as diverse and contrary affections causing these effects in these lower things; for in heaven, where there is nothing...
