XC.

HEADER: OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

...nothing is lacking; where all things are governed by love, hatred or enmity can hardly exist.

### ->On speech and the virtues of words. Chapter LXIX.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' containing a circular motif with a stylized face or sun.</image-desc> Having now shown that great power resides in the passions of the mind, it must be known further that no less power exists in words and the names of things, and the greatest power of all exists in connected speech and prayers. It is by these that we differ most from the beasts and are called "rational"—not because of the reason belonging to the soul <note>original: "anima"</note>, which they call the seat of the passions, and which Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> says even brute animals share with us to a greater or lesser degree. Rather, we are called rational because of the reason understood through the voice in words and speech, which is called "enunciative reason" <term>enunciative reason: ratio enunciativa, the faculty of expressing mental concepts through structured language</term>. It is in this part that we most exceed all other living creatures; for among the Greeks, the term *logos* <note>original: "λóγος"</note> signifies reason, speech, and word alike. 

Now, the word is twofold: namely, internal and spoken. The internal word is the mental concept and movement of the soul which occurs in the thinking power without a voice—just as when we seem to speak and argue in our dreams, or even when silent while awake, we often run through an entire speech. The spoken word, however, has its action in the voice and the specific character of speech; it is brought forth with the breath of a human, the opening of the mouth, and the movement of the tongue. In this, nature has joined the physical voice and speech to the mind and intellect, making speech the messenger and interpreter of our intellectual concepts to those who hear us. It is about this that we must speak here. 

Words are, therefore, the most suitable medium between the speaker and the listener, carrying with them not only a concept but also transferring the power of the speaker through a certain active energy <note>original: "energia"</note> into the listeners, and even into other bodies and inanimate things. Furthermore, those words are of greater efficacy than others which represent greater things—such as intellectual, <margin>Which words have greater power.</margin> celestial, and supernatural matters—both more clearly and more mysteriously. These are words established by a more worthy language and a more sacred authority. For these, like certain signs, representations, or sacraments of celestial and supernatural things, obtain power both from the virtue of the things they explain (of which they are the vehicles) and from the force instilled in them by the power of the one who established and speaks them.

### ->On the power of proper names. Chapter LXX.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring intricate floral and foliate patterns within and around the letterform.</image-desc> Almost all writers testify that the proper names of things are highly necessary for magical operations. For since the natural power of things proceeds first from objects to the senses, then from these to the imagination, and finally from that to the mind (in which it is first conceived), it is then expressed through voices and words. Therefore, the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who believed that language and names were not arbitrary but held an essential connection to the nature of reality.</note> say that in this very voice, or word, or name—once formed into its distinct parts—the very power of the thing lies hidden under the form of its meaning, like a kind of life. It is first conceived by the mind itself as if through the "seeds" of things, then brought forth through voices or words as if by birth, and finally preserved in writing. Hence the Magi say that the proper names of things are certain "rays" of things, always present everywhere, preserving the power of the things, insofar as the essence of the thing signified is [contained] in...

BOOK ONE.

Proper names of things are certain rays.

...rules over and distinguishes them, and things are recognized through these names as if through their own proper and living images. For just as the Supreme Architect <note>God, viewed here as the master craftsman of the universe.</note> produces diverse species and particular things from the influences of the heavens and elements along with the virtues of the planets, so too do the proper names of things result from the properties of those same influxes and influences. These names were imposed by Him who counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names <note>original: "qui numerat multitudinem stellarum omnibus eis nomina vocans," a reference to Psalm 147:4.</note>; of these names, Christ says elsewhere: "your names are written in the heavens." Therefore, the First-Formed <note>protoplastes: a common term for Adam, the first human.</note>, recognizing these celestial influences and the properties of individual things, imposed names upon things according to their essences <term>essences: quiditates, the "what-ness" or fundamental nature of a thing</term>, just as it is written in Genesis: that God brought all that He had created before Adam that he might name them. And just as he called a thing, so was its name; these names certainly contain within themselves the wonderful powers of the things signified. Thus, every meaningful voice signifies first through the influence of celestial harmony, and secondarily through the naming imposed by man—although more frequently it happens in various ways through one or the other. However, when both significations concur in any voice or name—those from celestial harmony and those imposed by men—then that name is rendered most effective for action with a doubled virtue, namely natural and voluntary. This occurs whenever it is uttered in the proper places and times, with solemnity and exact intention, upon matter that is properly prepared and naturally susceptible to it. So we read in the works of Philostratus <note>A 3rd-century Greek scholar who wrote a famous biography of Apollonius.</note> that when a certain girl in Rome died on her wedding day and was brought to Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker.</note>, having touched the maiden, he inquired accurately after her name; once he knew it, he pronounced something secret, by which the girl revived. There was also a custom among the Romans in their sacred rites that when they besieged a city, they would diligently seek out its proper name and the name of the deity under whose protection that city was. Having learned these, they would then call out the guardian gods of that city with a certain chant <term>chant: carmen, which can mean a poem, song, or a magical incantation</term>, and devote the city itself and its inhabitants to destruction; thus, with the gods at last absent, they would conquer, just as Virgil sings:

> All the gods have departed, leaving their shrines and altars,
> they through whom this empire stood.
> <note>original: "Excessere omnes, adytis arisq; relictis, / Dii quibus imperium hoc steterat." From Virgil's Aeneid, Book 2.</note>

Truly, he who wishes to know the chant by which the deities were called out and the enemies devoted when a city was surrounded by siege should seek it in the writings of Livy <note>A Roman historian.</note> and Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and writer.</note>; but Serenus Sammonicus <note>A Roman physician and author of a medical poem.</note> also relates more of them in his books of hidden things.

XCII.

## ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

One must consider the virtues, effects, and operations that each star contains within itself, and insert these into chants <term>carminibus: literally "songs" or "poems," but here referring to rhythmic incantations used in ritual</term> by praising, extolling, amplifying, and adorning those qualities which such a star is accustomed to bring and influence. Conversely, one should diminish and reprove those things which the star is accustomed to destroy and hinder, supplicating and entreating for that which we desire to obtain, and accusing and detesting that which we wish to be destroyed and hindered. By this method, one composes a chant that is ornate, elegant, and duly divided into parts according to certain fitting numbers and proportions. The magi <note>practitioners of "natural magic," which used the hidden properties of nature rather than demonic pacts</note> further command that one should invoke and pray by the names of that same star or deity to which such a chant belongs, and by its wonders or miracles, by its courses and paths within its sphere, by its light, by the nobility of its kingdom, by the grace and brightness within it, by its strong and wonderful virtues, and similar things. Just as in Apuleius, Psyche prays to Ceres:

> I beseech you, she says, by your fruitful right hand, I constantly pray by the joy-bringing ceremonies of the harvest, by the silent secrets of the chests <note>cistarum: sacred baskets used to hold ritual objects in the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, by the winged chariots of your servant dragons, and the furrows of Sicilian soil, and the grasping chariot <note>a reference to the abduction of Proserpina by Pluto</note>, and the clinging earth, and the descents <note>original: "demeacula," the path down to the underworld</note> into the dark nuptials of Proserpina, and the return <note>original: "remeacula," the path back to the light</note> of your daughter's light-bearing discoveries, and the other things which Eleusis, the sanctuary of Attica, rules in silence.

Furthermore, along with the many names of the stars, they command us to invoke also by the names of the Intelligences <term>Intelligences: celestial spirits or angelic beings thought to govern the movement and influence of the planets</term> presiding over those stars, about which we shall speak more extensively in the proper place. Whoever desires more examples of these should examine the hymns of Orpheus <note>a collection of ancient Greek poems addressed to various deities, highly valued by Renaissance occultists</note>, for nothing in natural magic is more effective than these, provided that the proper harmony is applied with full attention, along with the other circumstances known to the wise. 

But let us return to our purpose. Chants of this kind, therefore, being aptly and rightly composed according to the rule of the stars, full of intellect and meaning, and pronounced at the right time with vehement emotion—both according to the number and proportion of their parts and the form resulting from those parts—together with the impulse of the imagination, conspire toward a great power within the one incanting. They then immediately transfer that power into the thing being enchanted, in order to bind or direct it toward the goal intended by the emotions and words of the practitioner.

<margin>The spirit of the incanter is the instrument</margin>
The actual instrument of those incanting is a certain most pure harmonic spirit: warm, breathing, living, carrying motion, emotion, and meaning with it, composed of its own parts, endowed with sense, and finally conceived by reason. Therefore, through the quality of this spirit and through its celestial likeness—in addition to what has been said and through the opportunity of timing—chants conceive the most excellent virtues from heaven. These are indeed much more sublime and effective than the spirits and vapors exhaling from vegetable life, such as herbs, roots, gums, spices, fumigations, and similar things. And for this reason, the Magi, when incanting, are accustomed to breathe upon things and "inhale" the words of the chant <note>original: "afflare, & uerba carminis inhalare," implying a physical and spiritual transfer of power via the breath</note>, or to "inspire" the virtue by the spirit itself, so that the entire power of the soul may be directed into the enchanted thing, which has been disposed to receive the said virtue. ### On the wonderful power of incantations. Chapter LXXII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'I' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
The power of incantations or songs <term>carminum: though usually meaning "songs" or "poems," in this context it refers to rhythmic, chanted magical formulas</term> is said to be so great that they are believed to be able to subvert almost all of nature. As Apuleius <note>a 2nd-century Roman novelist and philosopher, often associated with magic</note> says: "By magical whispering, swift rivers are turned back, the sluggish sea is bound, winds expire in unison, the sun is inhibited, the moon is drawn down like foam, stars are plucked out, the day is removed, and the night is held." <note>original: "Magico susurramine amnes agiles reuerti, mare pigrum colligari, uẽtos unanimes expirari, solem inhiberi, lunam despumari, stellas euelli, diem tolli, noctem teneri."</note> And Lucan <note>a Roman poet known for his epic on the civil war, which includes vivid scenes of witchcraft</note> sings of the same:
> The cycles of things ceased, and the day, stretched out,
> Clung to a long night; the upper air did not obey its law.
> The world grew numb, and headlong [was checked] upon hearing the song.
> <margin>and a little before:</margin> The song of the Thessalian women flowed into hardened hearts,
> Love not sufficiently forced. <note>original: "Carmen Thessalidum dura in præcordia fluxit, Non satis adductus amor." This refers to the legendary witches of Thessaly.</note>
> <margin>and elsewhere:</margin> A mind polluted by no blood of swallowed poison 
> Perishes by enchantment.

Likewise, Virgil in *Damon*:
> Songs are even able to draw the moon down from heaven.
> By songs, Circe changed the companions of Ulysses.
> The cold snake in the meadows is burst by chanting,
> <margin>and:</margin> And I saw the sown crops moved to another place. <note>original: "Atq; satas aliò uidi traducere messes." This refers to a common ancient belief that a witch could magically transport a neighbor’s harvest to her own field.</note>

**And** Ovid says in *Without a Title* <note>the *Amores*</note>:
> By a song, Ceres [the grain] is harmed and vanishes into sterile grass,
> The waters of a spring fail, harmed by a song.
> Acorns from the oaks and the chanted grape from the vines 
> Fall, and apples drop though no one shakes them.

If these things were not true, the penalty would not have been so strictly established by laws against those who enchanted the crops. <note>A reference to the Roman Law of the Twelve Tables, which explicitly forbade "singing away" another person's harvest.</note> And Tibullus <note>a Latin elegiac poet</note> says of a certain enchantress:
> I have seen her drawing the stars down from heaven;
> She turns the course of a rapid river with a song.
> She splits the ground with her chant, coaxes spirits from their tombs,
> And calls down bones from the warm pyre.
> When she pleases, she drives clouds from the gloomy sky;
> When she pleases, she calls for snows in the summer heat.

**Regarding** all of these, that sorceress <note>Medea, the famous witch of Greek mythology</note> seems to boast much in Ovid when she says:
> When I wished, with the banks themselves marvelling,
> I sent the rivers back to their own sources; I still the shaken seas,
> And shake the calm seas with my song; I drive away clouds
> And bring them on; I drive away the winds and call them;
> I burst the jaws of vipers with my words and song.

CCLXXII.
ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

> Living rocks and oaks torn from the earth,
> And forests I move, and I command mountains to tremble,
> And the ground to bellow, and the spirits to depart their tombs,
> You too, O moon, I draw down. <note>original: "Viuaq́; saxa sua conuulsaq́; robora terra, Et syluas moueo, iubeoq́; tremiscere montes, Et mugire solum, manesq́; exire sepulchris, Te quoque; luna traho." These lines are from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, describing the powers of the witch Medea.</note>

Furthermore, all poets sing, and philosophers do not deny, that many marvelous things can be achieved through songs <term>carminibus: rhythmic chants or incantations</term>: such as that crops may be moved, thunderbolts may be forced or obtained, diseases cured, and other things of this kind. For even Cato <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (the Elder), a Roman statesman who wrote a famous manual on agriculture</note> used certain songs in his rural affairs against the diseases of cattle, which still survive in his writings. Josephus <note>a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> also testifies that Solomon <note>the biblical King Solomon, who in the Renaissance was widely believed to have been a master of exorcism and magic</note> was skilled in such incantations. Celsus Africanus <note>likely referring to a philosophical or medical source cited in late antiquity</note> also relates, according to the doctrine of the Egyptians, that the human body is cured through as many as thirty-six demons, corresponding to the number of the signs and faces of the zodiac; each of these takes up and guards a specific part of the body. They call upon these demons by their names in their native tongue, and by invoking them with their incantations, they restore the afflicted parts of the body to health.

### On the virtue of writing, and on the making of imprecations and inscriptions. Chapter LXXIII.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial "O" depicting a bearded figure, possibly a prophet or saint, seated in a landscape with a halo around his head. In the background are trees and a gabled building.</image-desc>

The duty of words and speech is to announce the inner parts of the mind, to bring forth secrets from the inner recesses of thought, and to reveal the will of the speaker. Writing itself is the ultimate expression of the mind, the number, collection, state, end, containment, and repetition of speech and voice, forming a habit that is not perfected by the act of a single voice. Whatever is in the mind, in the voice, in the word, in the oration, and in speech—all of this is also in writing. And just as nothing conceived in the mind is not expressed by the voice, so nothing expressed is not also written. Therefore, magicians command that in any work, imprecations <term>imprecationes: spoken prayers or curses intended to direct spiritual power</term> and inscriptions should be made, by which the practitioner expresses his intent. For example, if he gathers a herb or a pebble, he should declare for what use he does it; if he fashions an image, he should say and inscribe for what effect it is made. Indeed, Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century polymath and theologian</note> does not disapprove of these imprecations and inscriptions in his *Speculum*; without them, our works would not be led to their effect, since the mere preparation does not cause the effect, but rather the act of the preparation. We find that the same kind of instructions were in use among the ancients, as Vergil himself testifies when he sings:

> First, I surround you with these three threads, distinct with three colors,
> And three times I lead this image around these altars. <note>original: "Terna tibi hęc primum triplici diuersa colore Licia circundo, terq; hæc altaria circum Effigiem duco." From Vergil's *Eclogues* VIII.</note>

->and a little after:<-

> Tie three colors with three knots, Amaryllis;
> Tie them now, Amaryllis, and say: "I tie the chains of Venus." <note>original: "Necte tribus nodis ternos Amarylli colores, Necte Amarylli modo, & Veneris, dic, uincula necto."</note>

->and in the same place:<-

> As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts
> In one and the same fire, so may Daphnis [be affected] by love for me. <note>original: "Limus ut hic durescit, & hęc ut cera liquescit Vno eodemq; igni, sic nostro Daphnis amore."</note>

# BOOK ONE.
XCV.

God gave to man mind and speech, which (as Hermes Trismegistus says) are considered the rewards of the same virtue, power, and immortality. <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus." Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic Corpus is attributed; Agrippa views him as a primary authority on the intersection of the divine and the natural.</note> Indeed, almighty God by his providence divided the speech of men into diverse languages; these languages, according to their diversity, also received their own specific characters of writing. These characters consist of a certain fixed order, number, and shape—not by chance, nor by accident, nor by the fragile whim of men, but were divinely arranged and formed so that they might harmonize with the celestial and divine bodies and virtues themselves.

<margin>The most holy writing of the Hebrews</margin>
Indeed, above all marks of language, the writing of the Hebrews is the most sacred in all its aspects: in the shapes of the characters, the points of the vowels, and the tips of the accents. <note>original: "pūctis uocaliū & apicibus accentuum." This refers to the *Nekudot* (vowel points) and *Tagin* (crowns or decorative strokes) used in Hebrew scrolls.</note> It consists, as it were, of matter, form, and spirit. It was first engraved in the seat of God, which is heaven, by the position of the stars; according to the shape of these stars—as the masters of the Hebrews testify—the letters themselves were formed. These letters are full of celestial mysteries, both through the things signified by their shape and form, and through the numbers signified within them, as well as through the various harmonies of their binding together. Hence the more secret Kabbalists <term>Mecubales: a Latinized form of the Hebrew "Mekubbalim," meaning those who have received the tradition of the Kabbalah</term> of the Hebrews promise to explain all things—how they proceeded from the first cause and how they may be led back to the same—by the shape of those letters, the forms of the characters, and by their signature, simplicity, composition, separation, curvature, straightness, deficiency, abundance, greatness, smallness, crowning, opening, closing, order, transmutation, joining, and the revolution of letters, points, and tips, as well as the calculation of numbers signified by the letters. Furthermore, the Hebrews divide the letters of their alphabet into three parts: namely, twelve simple, seven double, and three mothers. <term>matres: The "mother letters" (Aleph, Mem, Shin) which, in the Sefer Yetzirah, represent the primary elements.</term> They say these signify the characters of things: the twelve signs of the zodiac, the seven planets, and the three elements—namely fire, water, and earth; for they do not consider air an element, but rather the glue and spirit of the elements. They also coordinate the points and tips with these. Therefore, just as all things were and are produced from the aspects of the planets and signs together with the elements through the craftsman spirit and truth, so from these characters of letters and points—which signify those produced things—the names of all things are constituted. These names are like certain sacraments and vehicles of the things explained, carrying the essence and powers of those things with them everywhere. Their profound meanings and sacraments inherent in those characters, their shapes, numbers, position, order, and revolution, led Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria was a prominent early Christian theologian who argued that divine names lost their power when translated out of their original tongue.</note> to believe that those names, if translated into another language, would retain very little of their proper power, because they would not retain their natural significance. For only the primary names that are correctly imposed have natural activity, because they signify naturally. This is not the case for those names that signify by convention; these have no activity as signs, but only as natural things in themselves. If there is any first and causal language whose words have natural significance, it is certain that this is Hebrew. He who holds the order of this language profoundly and radically, and its letters in proportion...

XCVI.
# OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

[...whoever] knows how to revolve these letters three times, will possess the rule and norm for perfectly discovering the essence of any language. Therefore, there are twenty-two letters which are the foundation of the world and of all creatures that exist and are named within it; every word and every created thing arises from them, and through their revolutions, they receive their name, essence, and power. However, the investigator of these matters must range through the individual combinations of letters until the voice of God becomes clear, and the text of the most sacred letters offers itself openly. For this is why voices and words have efficacy in magical works: because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God. But these things are of a higher speculation than should be treated in this book. 

But let us return to the partition of letters. Among the Hebrews, there are three mothers, namely: א (Aleph), מ (Mem), ש (Shin). <note>original: "tres matres." This refers to the *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Formation), which divides the Hebrew alphabet into 3 "Mothers" (elements), 7 "Doubles" (planets), and 12 "Simples" (zodiac signs).</note> Seven are doubles, namely: ב (Bet), ג (Gimel), ד (Dalet), כ (Kaph), פ (Pe), ר (Resh), ת (Tav). The remaining twelve, namely: ה (He), ו (Vav), ז (Zayin), ח (Het), ט (Tet), י (Yod), ל (Lamed), מ (Mem), נ (Nun), ס (Samekh), ע (Ayin), צ (Tzadi), ק (Qoph) are simples. The logic is the same among the Chaldeans <note>referring to Aramaic speakers or Babylonian sages</note>. In imitation of these, the letters of other languages are also distributed among the signs, planets, and elements in their own specific order. 

For among the Greeks, Α (Alpha), Ε (Epsilon), Η (Eta), Ι (Iota), Ο (Omicron), Υ (Upsilon), Ω (Omega) correspond to the seven planets. Β (Beta), Γ (Gamma), Δ (Delta), Ζ (Zeta), Κ (Kappa), Λ (Lambda), Μ (Mu), Ν (Nu), Π (Pi), Ρ (Rho), Σ (Sigma), Τ (Tau) are attributed to the twelve signs of the zodiac. The remaining five—Θ (Theta), Ξ (Xi), Φ (Phi), Χ (Chi), Ψ (Psi)—represent the four elements and the spirit of the world. 

Among the Latins, these same things are signified, but in a different order: for the five vowels A, E, I, O, U, along with I and V as consonants, are ascribed to the seven planets. <note>In Latin of this period, 'I' and 'V' functioned as both vowels and consonants (J and U/V), bringing the total to seven sounds to match the seven known planets.</note> The consonants B, C, D, F, G, L, M, N, P, R, S, T preside over the twelve signs; the others, namely K, Q, X, Z, make up the four elements. The aspiration H represents the spirit of the world. Y, because it is a Greek and not a Latin character, and serving only Greek words, follows the nature of its own language. 

But it must not be ignored that the Hebrew letters have been found by the wise to be the most efficacious of all, because they have the greatest similarity to the celestial bodies and the world. Indeed, the letters of other languages do not have such great efficacy, because they stand at a further distance from them. The following table will explain the arrangements of these. 

Every letter also has double numbers of its order: namely, *extended* numbers, which simply express the value of the letters according to their order; and *collected* numbers, which gather together the numbers of all preceding letters with themselves. Then there are also *integral* numbers, which result from the names of the letters according to various modes of numbering. <note>This refers to Gematria, where the numerical value of a letter's name (e.g., Aleph spelled out as Aleph-Lamed-Pe) is calculated to find deeper meanings.</note> He who knows the powers of these numbers will be able to elicit wonderful mysteries in every language through its letters, and likewise to gather prophecies of both past and future times. There are, moreover, other mysterious marriages of letters with numbers, but having discussed all these things abundantly in the following books, we will here put an end to this first book.

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED

->LORD, THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE HERMANN OF<-
->Wied, Prince-elector, Duke of Westphalia and Angria, Lord and<-
->Arch-prelate of Cologne and Padeborn, his most gracious<-
->Lord, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim sends greetings.<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'E' featuring a classical figure, possibly a faun or satyr, playing a flute or pipe amidst floral scrolls and vines.</image-desc>

BEHOLD NOW (most illustrious Prince and most distinguished prelate) the remaining books of <term>Occult Philosophy</term> <note>original: "Occultioris philosophiæ"</note> or magic, which I recently promised your Magnificence I would publish when I released the first of them. However, the sudden and unexpected death of the Lady Margaret of Austria <note>Margaret of Austria (1480–1530), Governor of the Habsburg Netherlands and Agrippa’s former patron.</note>, my princess, intervened and slowed my zeal for publishing at that time. Afterward, the wickedness of certain "beaked" sycophants <note>A derogatory reference to those wearing the distinctive "beaked" hoods of certain academic or religious orders.</note> and a number of scholastic sophists stood in the way of their publication. These men have raged against me without pause because of my published declamation <term>On the Vanity of the Sciences and the Excellence of the Word of God</term> <note>original: "de Vanitate scientiarū & excellentia uerbi dei"</note>. They struggle against me with a bitter continuation of hatred, envy, spite, and calumny. Some of them, with raised eyebrows and puffed-out cheeks, have used their declamatory voices in temples to brand me with impiety before the common people. Others have filled the ears of the ignorant with my infamy through whispered rumors in every corner and street of every house. Still others, through public and private gatherings, have incited the Popes, the princes, and even Caesar <note>The Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V.</note> himself against me. 

Because of this, I began to hesitate whether I should publish these remaining books at all, fearing that I might subject myself to even greater slanders and, as the saying goes, jump "out of the smoke into the flame" <note>original: "ex fumo in flammā"</note>. A certain "rustic fear" <note>A Latin idiom for a bashful or awkward hesitation.</note> took hold of me, lest by publishing them I might seem more troublesome than helpful to you, and even stir up the envy of those <term>Zoilists</term> <note>Zoilus was a Greek grammarian known for his harsh criticism; the term refers to envious or nitpicking critics.</note> against your Highness, exposing you to the tongues of detractors. While all these things troubled me with a variety of despairs, my fear was shaken off by the clarity of your intelligence, your exacting discretion, your sincerity of judgment, your religion without superstition, and your other most noted virtues—as well as your authority and integrity, which are beyond all exception. Knowing these could easily restrain and even bridle the tongues of backbiters, I have been encouraged to boldly attempt again what I had almost abandoned out of despair. 

Accept now, therefore, most illustrious Prince, with a good heart, this second book of Occult Philosophy, in which we disclose the mysteries of <term>celestial magic</term> <note>original: "cœlestis magiæ"</note>. Here, everything is revealed and demonstrated which the skilled antiquity of things has produced, and which has come to our knowledge. Thus, after the demonstration of natural powers, the secrets of celestial magic (hitherto neglected and understood by posterity with little accuracy) may now be set forth by us under your protection. From these, whoever shall hereafter profit or gather any fruit may return and ascribe thanks to you, who provided the occasion for this edition and granted the faculty by which these things, the doors having been opened, might be released from their chains.

->F A R E W E L L.<-

# THE SECOND BOOK OF HENRY CORNE-
## LIUS AGRIPPA ON OCCULT PHILO-
### sophy, or on Magic.

### On the necessity of Mathematical disciplines, and on many wonderful works which are performed by mathematical arts alone. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring a figure in a classical robe sitting in a landscape with buildings and a bridge in the distance.</image-desc>

MATHEMATICAL DISCIPLINES ARE so necessary and related to magic that anyone who professes the latter without the former would wander entirely off the path, labor in vain, and never achieve the desired effect. For whatever exists and happens in these lower things through natural virtues is all produced and governed by number, weight, measure, harmony, motion, and light. All things we see in these lower realms have their root and foundation in these mathematical principles. Nevertheless, even without natural virtues, works similar to natural ones can be produced by mathematical disciplines alone. As Plato says, these are things not participating in truth or divinity, but certain likenesses akin to themselves, such as bodies that move or speak, yet lack a vital soul. Such were the statues of Daedalus <note>Daedalus was the mythical Greek inventor and craftsman; his statues were said to be so lifelike they had to be tied down to keep them from running away.</note> and those called <term>automata</term> <note>original: "αὐτόματα" — self-moving machines</note> by the ancients. Aristotle mentions the self-moving tripods of Vulcan and Daedalus, which Homer relates came forth of their own accord into the contest. We also read that in the banquet of Iarbas <note>Likely referring to Iarchas, the leader of the Indian "Gymnosophists" or "naked philosophers" described in the life of Apollonius of Tyana.</note> the Gymnosophist, these tripods moved themselves about, and golden statues performed the duties of cup-bearers and carvers for the guests. We also read of statues of Mercury that spoke, and the wooden dove of Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum (4th century BCE) was a mathematician and engineer credited with building the first flying machine, a steam-powered wooden pigeon.</note> which flew. Cassiodorus also recounts the miracles of Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (6th century CE), a philosopher who also designed water clocks and sundials.</note>: a Diomedes in bronze sounding a trumpet, a bronze serpent hissing, and artificial birds emitting the sweetness of song. Of this same kind are whatever wonders of likenesses proceed from Geometry and Optics, which we mentioned previously when speaking of the element of air. Thus mirrors are made—some concave, others columnar—which create likenesses of things in the air; <margin>wonderful craftsmanship of mirrors.</margin> they appear as shadows seen at a distance outside themselves, just as Apollonius and Vitellius <note>Referring to Apollonius of Perga and the medieval scholar Witelo, both experts on the science of light and reflection.</note> taught in their books on Perspective and Mirrors. We also read that Pompey the Great brought a certain mirror among his spoils from the East to Rome, in which armies of armed men could be seen. Furthermore, certain translucent mirrors are made which, when stained with the juices of specific herbs and illuminated by artificial light, fill all the surrounding air with wonderful apparitions. I myself know how to construct two reciprocal mirrors in which, when the sun is shining, everything illuminated by its rays can be seen most clearly across distances of many miles. Hence the magician, skilled in natural philosophy and mathematics, and knowing the "middle sciences" <note>Agrippa refers to the Quadrivium: arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy, which sit between the physical and the metaphysical.</note> arising from both—Arithmetic, Music,

<summary>This page introduces Book Two of Agrippa’s work, arguing that mathematics is the essential foundation for magic. He lists historical examples of "automata" and optical illusions (mirrors) to show how mathematical principles can simulate life and nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the first chapter of Book Two, shifting from the theoretical necessity of mathematics to historical and physical examples of "mathematical magic"—what we would today call advanced engineering and physics. Agrippa argues that many things attributed to demons are actually the result of human ingenuity and mathematical science.</meta>

<header>ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

Geometry, Optics, Astronomy, and those sciences concerned with weights, measures, proportions, joints, and connections, as well as the mechanical arts that result from them—is it any wonder if someone excelling in these through art and wit performs many miracles that even the most prudent and learned greatly admire? Do there not exist to this day traces of ancient works, such as the Pillars of **Hercules** and **Alexander**, the Caspian Gates cast from bronze and barred with iron beams so that they cannot be destroyed by any wit or art? And the pyramid erected by **Julius Caesar** in Rome near the Vatican, and mountains built in the middle of the sea by art, and high masses of stones, such as those I saw in **Britain** gathered with scarcely credible skill. <note>Agrippa is likely referring to Stonehenge or other megalithic structures he observed during his travels to England in 1510.</note> And we read in the works of faithful historians that by similar arts rocks were once cut away, valleys filled, mountains leveled, rocks tunneled through, promontories opened to the sea, the bowels of the earth excavated, rivers diverted, seas joined to seas, waters restrained, the depths of the sea searched, lakes drained, marshes dried up, new islands created, and others restored to the continent. Although all these things seem to fight against nature itself, we nevertheless read that they were done, and to this day we see their traces. The common folk fable that such things were the work of demons, since the arts and the craftsmen themselves have perished from memory, and there are none who care to understand or investigate them. Therefore, seeing some wonderful spectacle and being blind in their intellect, they reject every effect as the work of demons or think them miracles, when they are actually the works of natural or mathematical disciplines. For instance, if someone were ignorant of the power of the magnet and saw heavy iron carried upward or suspended in the air—just as it is read that the iron idol of **Mercury** was once suspended in the middle of a temple in **Trier** by means of magnet stones—attested by this verse:

-> *The iron caduceus-bearer flutters in the mid-air.* <-
<note>original: "Ferreus in mediis volitat caducifer auris." The caduceus-bearer is Mercury (Hermes).</note>

We read of a similar thing done with the idol of the Sun in the temple of **Serapis** in **Egypt**. Would such a person not immediately say it is the work of demons? Yet if he knew the power of the magnet over iron and had experienced it, all his wonder would cease, and no doubt would remain that it is a work of nature. And here it is fitting for you to know that just as we gather natural virtues through natural things, so through abstract, mathematical, and celestial things, we receive celestial virtues—such as motion, life, sense, speech, prophecy, and divination—even in matter that is less disposed to them, as in things fashioned not by nature but by art alone. And thus it is said that speaking images can be made which predict the future, just as **William of Paris** <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris, a philosopher who wrote extensively on "natural magic."</note> tells of a bronze head cast under the rising of **Saturn** which they say spoke with human voices. Truly, he who knows how to choose matter that is well-disposed and most ready to be acted upon, and an agent that is most powerful, will produce certain and more potent effects. For it is the general opinion of the **Pythagoreans** that just as mathematical things are more "formal" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "formal" refers to the "Form" or essential blueprint of a thing, which Agrippa argues is more powerful than the raw physical matter.</note> than physical things, so they are more "actual" (or active); and just as they are less dependent in their being, so they are also less dependent in their operation. Among all things...

mathematics, numbers, as they are more <term>formal|In Renaissance philosophy, "formal" refers to the "form" or essential nature of a thing, which was considered more real and powerful than its physical "matter."</term>, so also are they more actual <note>original: "actualiores." Here, "actual" refers to the state of being in "act," or having the power to cause effects, as opposed to being merely "potential."</note>; to these, not only the pagan philosophers but also the Hebrew and Christian theologians attribute power and effectiveness for both good and evil.

## On numbers and their power and virtue. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated drop cap 'I' featuring a scholar or philosopher seated at a desk with an open book and several others stacked nearby.</image-desc>
**Severinus Boethius** says: everything whatsoever that has been constructed by the primeval nature of things seems to be formed by the reason of numbers; for this was the principal pattern <note>original: "exemplar"</note> in the mind of the Creator. From this is derived the multitude of the elements; from this, the changes of the seasons; from this, the movement of the stars and the turning of the heavens; and the state of all things subsists through the binding together of numbers. Therefore, numbers are powerful in great and sublime virtues. Nor is it a wonder—since there are so many and such great occult virtues in natural things, even though their operations are manifest—that there should be much greater, more hidden, more wonderful, and more effective virtues in the numbers themselves. This is because they are more formal and more perfect, being implanted in the celestial bodies, mingled with the separate substances <note>A term for angels or purely spiritual beings that exist "separate" from matter.</note>, and finally having the greatest and simplest communion with the **Ideas** in the divine mind, from which they receive their proper and most effective powers. For this reason, they are also very powerful for obtaining demonic and divine gifts, just as in natural things the elemental qualities are very powerful in transforming something into an elemental state. <margin>All things consist of certain numbers.</margin> Again, all things that are and that happen subsist by certain numbers and receive their power from them. For time consists of number, as does all motion and action, and everything whatsoever that is subject to time and motion. Harmony and voices also have their power and consist of numbers and their proportion; and proportions arising from numbers, through lines and points, constitute characters and figures. And these are proper to magical works, existing as a middle ground between both <note>Likely referring to the physical and spiritual realms.</note>, suited by their leaning toward the extremes, as in the use of letters. Finally, all species of natural things and those which are above nature are bound by certain numbers. Seeing this, **Pythagoras** said that number is that by which all things consist, and he distributed specific virtues to specific numbers. And **Proclus** says: Number always exists, yet one kind is in the voice, another in their proportion, another in the soul and reason, and another in divine things. **Themistius**, **Boethius**, and **Averroës the Babylonian** <note>original: "Auerrois Babylonius." This refers to the philosopher Ibn Rushd, though "Babylonian" is a common early modern error or poetic descriptor for Eastern thinkers.</note> along with **Plato**, extol numbers so much that they think no one can philosophize rightly without them. However, they speak of rational and formal number, not of material, sensible, or vocal number—the number used by merchants—which the **Pythagoreans**, the **Academics**, and our **Augustine** care nothing for. Instead, they focus on the proportion resulting from it, which they call natural, formal, and rational number. From this, great mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta," used here in the sense of "sacred secrets" or "mysteries."</note> emanate, both in natural and in divine and celestial things. Through it, a path is opened for investigating and understanding all things that can be known. Through it, the closest access to natural prophecy is gained; and the **Abbot Joachim** himself, in his prophecies, proceeded by no other way than through formal numbers.

### How great powers numbers possess in both natural and supernatural <term>transnatural|Things that transcend the physical world or operate above the laws of nature.</term> things. Chapter III.

<margin>The virtues of the Cinquefoil herb.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' containing a seated figure within a square frame with foliage.</image-desc>
THAT a wonderful efficacy and power lies hidden in numbers, for both good and evil, is taught not only by the most brilliant philosophers with one voice, but is also confirmed by the Catholic doctors. Among these, **Jerome**, **Augustine**, **Origen**, **Ambrose**, **Gregory of Nazianzus**, **Athanasius**, **Basil**, **Hilary**, **Rabanus**, **Bede**, and many others agree. Hence, **Hilary**, in his commentaries on the Psalms, testifies that the seventy elders arranged the Psalms in order according to the efficacy of numbers. **Rabanus**, that most distinguished doctor, also composed a singular book on the virtues of numbers. Furthermore, how many virtues numbers possess in nature is evident in the herb called <term>pentaphyllon|From the Greek for 'five leaves'; commonly known as Cinquefoil or Potentilla.</term>, which is called "five-leaf": for by the power of the number five <note>original: "quinarii"</note>, it resists poisons, drives away demons, and assists in purification. If one leaf is taken in wine twice a day, it cures a one-day fever; three leaves cure a tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every 48 hours, often associated with malaria.</note>; four leaves cure a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every 72 hours.</note>. Similarly, four grains of the seeds of the heliotrope taken in a drink are said to help quartans, while three help tertians. In the same way, vervain is said to heal fevers in wine if, for tertians, it is cut at the third joint, and for quartans, at the fourth. If a snake is struck once with a reed, it dies; if struck a second time, it recovers. These and many similar things are read as testified among various authors.

<margin>A wonderful experiment of the number seven.</margin>
The cause for why these things happen is surely the varying proportion of different numbers to one another. There is also a wonderful experiment concerning the number seven <note>original: "septenario"</note>: that every male born as the seventh son without a female intervening has the power of curing <term>scrofula|Also known as the "King's Evil," a swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck.</term> by touch or word alone. Similarly, every seventh daughter born is said to assist in childbirth in a marvelous way; nor is the natural count of the number considered here, but rather the formal reason which is in the number.

<margin>What is to be considered here regarding numbers.</margin>
And let that which we said above be always kept in mind: that these powers are not in vocal and merchant numbers <note>Agrippa distinguishes between "vocal" (spoken) or "merchant" (commercial) numbers used for mundane counting, and "formal" numbers which represent the underlying structure of reality.</note>, but in rational, formal, and natural numbers; these are the distinct and contained sacraments of God and nature. Whoever knows how to join vocal and natural numbers with divine ones, and to temper them into the same harmony, will be able to work wonders and even gain knowledge through numbers. The Pythagoreans also professed to prognosticate many things through the numbers of names. If some great mystery did not lie hidden in these, **John** would not have said in the **Apocalypse**: *Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the name of the beast, which is the number of a man.* This method of calculating is very famous among the Hebrews and <term>Cabalists|Followers of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that uses the numerical values of letters (Gematria) to find hidden meanings in text.</term>, as we shall show below.

<margin>The significance of numbers.</margin>
But it should be known that simple numbers signify divine things; tens signify celestial things; hundreds signify terrestrial things; and thousands signify things of the future age. Furthermore, since the parts of the soul are joined together according to an Arithmetic mean <note>In an Arithmetic mean (e.g., 2, 4, 6), the difference between terms is equal, representing identity and balance.</note>, because of identity or equality of excess; whereas the body—whose parts differ in magnitude—is composed according to a Geometric mean <note>In a Geometric mean (e.g., 2, 4, 8), the ratio between terms is equal, representing proportional growth and physical structure.</note>...

Indeed, because the living being <note>original: "animal"; referring to the composite entity of a human or creature.</note> itself consists of both—namely soul and body—according to that moderation which fits with harmony, this is why numbers operate most effectively upon the soul, shapes upon bodies, and harmony <note>original: "concentus"</note> upon the living being itself.

### On Unity and its Scale. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' containing a landscape scene with a seated figure, trees, and buildings in the distance.</image-desc>Now let us determine specifically concerning numbers. Because number is nothing other than the repetition of unity, let us first consider unity itself. Unity indeed penetrates every number most simply, and is the common measure, fountain, and origin of all numbers. It contains every number uniquely joined within itself, devoid of all multitude, always the same and immutable. Whence also, when multiplied by itself, it produces nothing but itself. It is indivisible and lacks all parts. If one were to imagine it being divided, it is not cut, but rather multiplied—namely, into unities. None of these unities, however, is greater or lesser than the whole unity, in the way a part is usually smaller than the whole. It is multiplied, therefore, not into parts, but into itself.

<margin>The names of Unity.</margin>
For this reason, some have called it "concord," others "piety," and others "friendship," because it is so joined that it cannot be cut into parts. Furthermore, Martianus <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author of an influential encyclopedia of the liberal arts.</note>, following the opinion of Aristotle, asserts it was named "Cupid" <note>The Roman god of love; here representing the desire for the 'One' or the attraction that binds things together.</note>, because it is only one, and always wishes to be sought after, and has nothing beyond itself; rather, being devoid of all relation or bond, it turns its own fires back upon itself. One is therefore the beginning and end of all things, having neither beginning nor end itself. Nothing is before one, and nothing is after one.

<margin>The excellence of Unity.</margin>
One is the beginning of all things, and all things exist up to one, and beyond it there is nothing. All things that exist desire this "one," because all things proceeded from one; and so that they may all be the same, it is necessary to participate in that one. And just as all things proceeded from one into many, so all things that strive to return to that one from which they proceeded must cast off their multitude. Unity, therefore, is referred to the highest God, who, while being one and innumerable himself, nevertheless creates innumerable things from himself and contains them within himself.

<margin>Unique things in nature.</margin>
There is one God, one world for one God, one sun for one world, and also one phoenix in the world, one king among the bees, one leader in the flocks, one ruler in the herds, and cranes follow one leader; many other living things likewise venerate unity. Among the members of the body, there is one principle by which the rest are governed, whether that be the head or (as others wish) the heart. There is one element conquering and penetrating all things: fire. There is one thing created by God, the subject of all wonders which are on earth and in the heavens; it is in action animal, vegetable, and mineral, found everywhere, known by very few, expressed by no one by its own proper name, but veiled by innumerable figures and riddles. Without this, neither Alchemy <note>original: "Alchymia"</note> nor natural magic can reach their complete end. From one man, Adam, all were produced; by that one man, all died; by one man, Jesus Christ, they were born again.

### On duality and its Scale, Chapter V.

<margin>The names of the Binary.</margin>
**T**he Binary <note>The number two.</note> is the first number, because it is the first multitude; it can be measured by no number except by unity alone, which is the common measure of all numbers. It is not composed of numbers, but coordinated from unity alone, one and one. It is not called an "un-composite" number, but more accurately, "not composite." <note>In Pythagorean mathematics, "composite" numbers are those divisible by others; Agrippa is distinguishing two from the formal category of prime numbers (un-composite), noting it is uniquely the "first sprout" of unity.</note> The Ternary <note>The number three.</note> however, is called the first un-composite number. The binary is the first sprout of unity and the first procreation; hence it is called "Genesis," and "Juno," <note>The Roman goddess associated with marriage and childbirth.</note> and the "imaginable embodiment," and the proof of the first movement, and the first form of parity <note>Evenness or equality.</note>. It is the number of first equality, of the extremity and the interval, and therefore peculiar to justice; its proper act is that it rejoices in two things equally weighed. It is called the number of science, and of memory, and of light, and the number of Man, who is called the "other and lesser world." It is also called the number of charity and mutual love, of marriage and society, just as it was said by the Lord: *The two shall be in one flesh.* And Ecclesiastes says: *It is better for two to be together than one, for they have the benefit of their society; if one falls, he shall be supported by the other. Woe to the solitary man, because when he falls, he has no one to lift him up; and if two sleep, they shall keep each other warm, how shall one grow warm alone? And if anyone prevails against one, two resist him.* <note>Quoting Ecclesiastes 4:9-12.</note> It is also called the number of wedlock and of sex, for there are two sexes, masculine and feminine; and doves lay two eggs, from the first of which they hatch a male, and from the second a female. It is also called the "capable middle," and the parts of good and evil...

### Of the Triad and its scale. Chapter VI.

The Ternary <note>The number three.</note> is the first uncomposed number, a sacred number, a number of perfection, and a most powerful number: for there are three persons in God, and there are three theological virtues in religion. From this it follows that this number contributes greatly to the ceremonies of the gods and religion, as it is under its auspice that prayers and libations are repeated three times. Whence Virgil sings:
> God delights in an uneven number. <note>original: "Numero Deus impare gaudet." From Virgil's *Eclogues*.</note>

And the Pythagoreans used it in sanctifications and purifications, whence it is said in Virgil:
> He likewise thrice washed his companions with pure water. <note>original: "Idem ter socios pura circumluit unda." From the *Aeneid*.</note>

And it is also most fit for bindings <note>referring to "ligations" or binding spells</note>, hence that passage of Virgil:
> These three threads, distinct with three different colors, I first wrap around you, and three times I lead this image around these altars.

And a little after:
> Tie three knots, Amaryllis, in three colors; tie them now, Amaryllis, and say: "I tie the bonds of Venus."

And we read of Medea:
> And thrice she spoke words that bring peaceful sleep, which stop the turbulent sea and the rushing rivers.

And in Pliny, it was a custom in all medicine to spit three times with a prayer, and by this the effect was aided. For the Ternary is perfected by a threefold increase: length, breadth, and depth, beyond which no progression of dimension is given; for this reason it is called the first cubic number. <note>In ancient geometry, the number three represents the first "solid" or three-dimensional body.</note> Thus it is said that nothing can be added to a body of three measures and a cubic number. Wherefore Aristotle, at the beginning of his discourses *On the Heavens*, calls it a law, as it were, according to which all things are disposed. <margin>What three things are in matters.</margin> For all bodily and spiritual things consist of three: beginning, middle, and end. By three (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many hermetic treatises are attributed.</note> says) the world is perfected: by Fate <note>original Greek: "Hemarmene"</note>, Necessity, and Order—that is, the agreement of causes with each other, which most call fate, and the execution toward the offspring, and the due distribution of that offspring. The whole measure of time is concluded in the ternary: namely, past, present, and future. Every magnitude is contained in three: line, surface, and body. Every body consists of three intervals: length, breadth, and thickness. Harmony contains three symphonies: the octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>, the fifth <note>original: "hemiolion"</note>, and the fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. There are also three kinds of souls: vegetative, sensitive, and intellectual; and a threefold division distributes this [intellectual soul] into reason, anger, and desire. And now also, according to the prophet, the world is disposed by God in three: number, weight, and measure. <margin>The Ternary is assigned to the ideal forms.</margin> It is assigned to the ideal forms, just as the binary is to procreating matter, and unity to God the Creator. The Magi also distribute three princes of the world: Oromasim, Mitrim, and Araminim <note>Latinized names for the Zoroastrian figures Ahura Mazda (God/Light), Mithra (the Mediator), and Ahriman (Spirit/Darkness).</note>; that is, God, Mind, and Spirit. Through the cubic or solid ternary, three groups of nine [enneads] of produced things are distributed, vi-

Finally, in this ternary cube—that is, the number twenty-seven <note>Three cubed (3x3x3) equals twenty-seven. In Renaissance Neoplatonism, this number was thought to contain the fundamental mathematical ratios of the universe's soul.</note>—all musical proportions are included, as Plato and Proclus discuss at great length. The ternary also possesses the *diapente* <note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> in harmony, which has the grace of the fifth voice. Furthermore, among the intelligences, there are three hierarchies of angelic spirits. There are three powers of intellectual creatures: memory, mind, and will. There are three orders of the blessed: namely, martyrs, confessors, and innocents. There are three sets of four <note>Agrippa refers to the twelve signs of the zodiac divided into three groups of four.</note> celestial signs: namely, the movable, the fixed, and the common; similarly, there are three sets of four astrological houses: namely, the angular, the succedent, and the cadent. > And three-fold Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana. <note>original: "Tergeminamque Hecaten, tria virginis ora Dianae." From Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>

There are three persons in the supersubstantial divinity. There are three periods of time: of nature, of law, and of grace. There are three theological virtues: hope, faith, and charity. For three days Jonah was in the belly of the fish, and for just as many was Christ in the tomb.

## On the Quaternary and its Scale, Chapter VII.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'Q' containing a circular portrait of a bearded man wearing a cap, possibly representing a philosopher or the author.</image-desc>
<margin>Foundations are all square.</margin>
The followers of Pythagoras call the number four the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A mystical symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe.</note>, and they prefer it above all the virtues of numbers because it is the foundation and root of all other numbers. For this reason, all foundations—whether in man-made, natural, or divine things—are square, as we shall show below. It signifies "solidity," which is also demonstrated by the square figure. The quaternary is the first "plane square" <note>A number multiplied by itself; 2x2=4.</note>, which consists of two proportions: the first being one to two, and the second being two to four. It is born from a twofold progression and proportion—namely, one to one and two to two—beginning from unity and ending in the number four. These proportions differ in that, according to arithmetic, they are unequal to each other, but according to geometry, they are equal. Therefore, the "square" is ascribed to God the Father; indeed, it even embraces the mystery of the entire Trinity. For by its simple proportion (the first, of one to one), the unity of the Father's substance is signified, from which the one Son proceeds, equal to Him. By the other progression (also simple, of two to two), the Holy Spirit is noted as the second progression from both, so that the Son is equal to the Father by the first progression, and the Holy Spirit is equal to both by the second progression. From this comes the most exalted name of God and the divine Trinity, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>: namely, <term>Iod, He, and Vau, He</term>. Here, the breathing sound of the letter *He* denotes the progression of the Spirit from both; for the *He* is doubled, ending both syllables and the entire name. It is pronounced as "Iova" <note>An early Latinized version of the name Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>, as some would have it; from this comes the "Jove" of the Gentiles, whom the ancients used to paint with four ears. Hence, the quaternary is the fountain and head of all divinity.

<margin>Which things consist of fours.</margin>
The Pythagoreans also call it the "perpetual fountain of nature." For there are four degrees in the <term>Scale of Nature</term> <note>The "Great Chain of Being," a hierarchy of all existence.</note>: namely, being, living, feeling, and understanding. There are four motions in nature: namely, ascending, descending, moving forward, and circular. There are four cardinal points in the heavens: namely, the rising (East), the setting (West), the mid-heaven (South), and the bottom of heaven (North). There are four elements beneath the heavens: namely, fire, air, water, and earth. According to these, there are four <term>triplicities</term> <note>In astrology, the twelve zodiac signs are divided into four groups of three, each corresponding to an element.</note> in the heavens. There are four primary qualities beneath the heavens: namely, cold, heat, dryness, and moisture. From these come the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Likewise, the year is divided into four parts: which are spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Similarly, the air is divided into the four winds: the East wind, the West wind, the South wind, and the North wind. There are also four rivers of Paradise, and just as many in the underworld. Furthermore, the quaternary fulfills all science: first, it fulfills the entire simple progression of numbers in four terms—namely, one, two, three, and four—which together constitute the <term>denary</term> <note>The number ten (1+2+3+4=10).</note>. It fulfills every difference of numbers, containing within itself the first even and the first odd number. In music, it possesses the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>The musical interval of a fourth.</note>, the grace of the voice...

...of the fourth; likewise the tetrachord and the Pythagorean diagram, by which he first discovered musical harmonies, and which contains all the harmony of music: for the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter <note>A ratio of 3:2, defining the musical fifth.</note>, sesquitertial <note>A ratio of 4:3, defining the musical fourth.</note>, the octave <note>original: *diapason*</note>, the double octave <note>original: *disdiapason*</note>, the fifth <note>original: *diapente*</note>, the fourth <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>, and every consonance is confined within the limits of the quaternary. It also encompasses all mathematics in four terms, namely, the point, line, surface, and depth. It gathers all of nature into four terms: substance, quality, quantity, and motion. It also fills all of physics, in which there are the seminal power of nature, natural sprouting, the growing form, and the composite. It also encompasses metaphysics in four terms: being, essence, power, and action. It encompasses moral philosophy with the four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. It also holds the power of justice: hence the fourfold law, namely that of providence from God, that of fate from the world-soul <note>original: *anima mundi*</note>, that of nature from the heavens, and that of prudence from man. Moreover, there are four judicial powers in existing things: intellect, discipline, opinion, and sense. It also has much and the greatest power in the mysteries: hence the Pythagoreans used the quaternary itself in their oath, as the highest thing upon which faith rests and belief can be strengthened: hence the Pythagorean oath, which is expressed in these verses:

> I swear to you by the holy quaternary, with a pure mind,
> The fountain of eternal nature and the parent of the soul.

<margin>The name of God is almost everywhere a four-letter word <note>original: *tetragrammaton*</note>.</margin>
Likewise, there are four rivers of paradise, and four gospels received by as many evangelists throughout the entire church. The Hebrews received the principal name of God written with four letters; similarly, the Egyptians, Arabs, Persians, Magi, Mohammedans, Greeks, Tuscans, and Latins write the name of God with only four letters: namely *Theut*, *Alla*, *Sire*, *Orsi*, *Abgdi* <note>Agrippa likely refers to the first four letters of the Hebrew alphabet (A-B-G-D) used as a divine name.</note>, *Theos* <note>original: *θεὸς*</note>, *Esar*, and *Deus*. Hence the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> were accustomed to depict the highest Jupiter with four ears. Hence, in Orphic theology, Neptune is said to drive a four-horse chariot. There are also four types of divine frenzy <note>Agrippa uses "furor" in the Platonic sense of divine inspiration or "divine madness."</note> proceeding from individual deities: namely from the Muses, Dionysus, Apollo, and Venus. Likewise, the prophet Ezekiel saw four living creatures by the river Chebar <note>original: *Chobar*</note>, and four Cherubim in four wheels. Likewise in Daniel, four great beasts ascended from the sea, and the four winds fought. Likewise in Revelation <note>original: *Apocalypsi*</note>, four living creatures full of eyes before and behind stood around the throne of God; and four angels, to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, stood upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds so that they should not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree.

### On the number five and its Scale. Chapter VIII.

The number five <note>original: "Quinarius"</note> is of no small power; for it consists of the first even and the first odd number, as if from female and male: for the odd number is male, but the even is female. Whence Arithmeticians call the former the father, and the latter the mother. Therefore the number five is of no small perfection and virtue, which is generated from the mixing of these numbers: and it is, moreover, the most just middle of the universal number, namely ten. For if you take the number ten and divide it around five on both sides—taking nine from one side and one from the other, or eight from one and two from the other, or seven and three, or six and four—each collection constitutes ten, and five is always its perfect middle and equally distant from each. For this reason it is called the "number of marriage" <note>original: "numerus connubii"</note> by the Pythagoreans. 
<margin>Names for the number five.</margin>
It is also called the number of "justice," because it divides the ten in an equal balance. There are five senses in man: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. There are five powers in the soul: the vegetative <note>governing growth</note>, the sensitive <note>governing perception</note>, the concupiscible <note>governing desire</note>, the irascible <note>governing emotions like anger</note>, and the rational. There are five fingers on the hands, and there are five wandering planets in the heavens <note>excluding the Sun and Moon, which were often categorized differently in ancient astronomy</note>, according to which a fivefold...

Among the elements, there are also five kinds of mixtures: namely, stones, metals, plants, zoophytes <note>Organisms like coral or sea sponges that were historically thought to be intermediate between plants and animals.</note>, and animals; and just as many kinds of animals: namely, men, quadrupeds, reptiles, swimming creatures, and flying creatures. There are also five genera by which all things are composed by God: namely, essence, the same, the other, sense, and motion. The swallow hatches no more than five chicks, which she feeds with great fairness, beginning from the one which is the eldest, and thus observing the order of birth for the others. This number also has great power in expiations: for in sacred rites, it drives away evil demons, and in natural things, it drives away poisons. It is also called the number of happiness and grace, and is the seal of the Holy Spirit, the bond that ties all things together, and the number of the cross, distinguished by the five principal wounds of Christ, the scars of which he deigned to keep even in his glorified body. The philosophers of the nations <note>Agrippa refers here to the "Gentile" or Pagan philosophers, such as the Pythagoreans.</note> dedicated this number as sacred to Mercury, and considered its power to be as much more excellent than the quaternary (the number four) as the animate is more excellent than the inanimate. For in this number, father Noah found grace before the Lord and was preserved in the deluge of waters. By the virtue of this number, Abraham, at a hundred years old, fathered a son by Sarah, a ninety-year-old and sterile woman—a feat beyond what is granted by nature—and he grew into a great people. Hence, in the time of Grace, the name of divine omnipotence is invoked with five letters. For in the time of Nature, the name of God was invoked as a three-letter name <note>The "Trigrammaton."</note>, *Shaddai* <note>original: "שדי"</note>; in the time of the Law, the ineffable four-letter name of God, the *Tetragrammaton* <note>original: "יהוה"</note>, in whose place the Hebrews utter *Adonai* <note>original: "אדני"</note>. In the time of Grace, the name of God is the pronounceable five-letter *Pentagrammaton*, *Ihesu* <note>original: "יהשוה"; this refers to the name of Jesus (Yeshua) with the letter "Shin" inserted into the middle of the Tetragrammaton.</note>, which by no less a mystery is also invoked with three letters as *Ishu* <note>original: "ישו"</note>.

# Chapter IX.
## Concerning the number six and its scale.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'S' depicting two figures, likely scholars or philosophers, engaged in a discussion. One figure is seated and gesturing, while the other stands or sits opposite him in a scholarly or pastoral setting.</image-desc>The **senary** <note>The number six.</note> is a number of perfection, because it is the most perfect by its very nature. In the entire sequence of numbers from one to ten, it alone is so perfect that the sum of its parts equals the whole, lacking nothing in deficiency and overflowing in no abundance. For if its parts—namely its half, its third, and its sixth, which are three, two, and one—are gathered together, they perfectly fill the entire body of the six. This is a perfection which other numbers lack. For this reason, it is asserted by the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> to be entirely suited for generation and marriage, and it is called the "seal of the world." For the world was established in the number six, being neither over-full with immoderate abundance nor frustrated and lacking in necessities. It is for this reason that the world was perfected and finished by God on the sixth day; for on the sixth day, God saw all that He had made, and they were very good. Therefore, the heavens and the earth were finished, along with all their adornment. It is also called the **number of man**, because man was created on the sixth day; and it is called the **number of redemption**, for on the sixth day Christ suffered for our redemption; hence it has a great kinship even with the cross. It is also called the number of labor and servitude: hence it was commanded in the Law that work be done for six days, manna be collected for six days, the earth be sown for six years, and that a Hebrew servant should serve his master for six years. For six days the glory of the Lord rested upon Mount Sinai, covering it with a cloud. There are six wings on the **cherubim**, and six circles in the **firmament** <note>The heavens or the sky.</note>: the arctic, the antarctic, the two tropics, the equinoctial, and the ecliptic. There are six wandering planets—Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—which travel across the width of the **Zodiac** <note>The "sign-bearer" or the path of the sun and planets.</note> wandering to and fro from the ecliptic. There are six substance-forming qualities in the elements: namely, sharpness, rarity, motion, and their opposites: bluntness, density, and rest. There are six differences of position: up, down, forward, backward, right, and left. There are six natural offices without which nothing can exist: namely, magnitude, color, shape, interval, state, and motion. Even the solid shape of a square <note>Agrippa refers here to a cube.</note> has six surfaces. In the harmony of the whole, there are six tones: namely, five tones and two semi-tones, which together make one tone, which is the sixth.
