CLV.
### CLVI. ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar</note> testifies to having seen these things himself. And there are things even more wonderful than those: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lute <note>original: "citharam"</note>. At Megara, a certain rock makes the sound of a stringed instrument <note>original: "fidicinat"</note> at every stroke, so great is the power of Music. Music itself soothes the soul, elevates the mind, incites warriors to battle, and consoles the labor and fatigue of individual works. It recalls the fallen and the desperate, and comforts travelers. The Arabs say that camels carrying heavy burdens are comforted by their singing drivers. In a similar way, 
<margin>Praise of song.</margin>
those carrying heavy loads sing, and are thereby enabled and relieved: for song produces delight and capability; it mitigates the wrathful, gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, tempers the madness of the frenzied, and dissipates vain thoughts. It is for this reason that Democritus <note>Greek philosopher known for the atomic theory</note> and Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school</note> affirm that certain diseases of the body and soul can be either cured or induced in this way. Thus we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna, Lesbians and Ionians, healed the sick; and Ismenias the Theban cured very many who were vexed by the gravest diseases through harmonies <note>original: "concentibus"</note>. Furthermore, Orpheus, Amphion, David, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Asclepiades, and Timotheus were accustomed to perform certain wonders with harmonies and sounds: for at times they excited sluggish souls with familiar musical modes, and at other times they restrained the lascivious, the raging, and the angry with heavier tones. Thus David restrained the raging Saul with his lute. Thus Pythagoras called back a luxurious youth from immoderate lust. Thus Timotheus excited King Alexander to fury, and then restrained him again. Saxo Grammaticus <note>Danish historian (c. 1150 – c. 1220)</note> relates in his Danish history a story about a certain musician who boasted that he could, through the modes of sound, draw men into such a spirit of madness that no listener could remain of sound mind. When he was compelled by the King's command to demonstrate the effect, he set about bending the states of their souls with a variety of sounds. By producing a harmony of unusual severity, he at first filled the listeners with a kind of sadness and stupor; then, changing the severity into applause with more vigorous sounds, he bent them toward a more pleasant state of mind and more petulant movements and gestures of the body; finally, with sharper modes, he excited them to such a spirit of madness that their fury proceeded even to rage and recklessness. We also read of those in Apulia <note>A region in Southern Italy</note> who have been touched by a tarantula <note>original: "phalangio," referring to the Mediterranean black widow or wolf spider associated with "Tarantism"</note>, that they fall into a stupor and lie lifeless until they hear a certain sound; upon hearing their own specific sound, each one dances appropriately to the rhythm and recovers, and if they hear a similar sound a long time afterward, they are suddenly moved to dance. And it is believed (on the testimony of Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, Roman author of Attic Nights</note>) that for those suffering from sciatica <note>original: "ischiacos"</note>, the pain is diminished by the melodies of a pipe. The same author relates from Theophrastus that a melody played on a pipe heals the bites of vipers; and Democritus himself confesses that the harmony of pipes has been a medicine for many human diseases.

Furthermore, we shall not deny that there is a power in sound for receiving celestial gifts, if we agree with **Pythagoras** and **Plato** that the heavens consist of a harmonic composition and that they govern and effect all things through harmonic tones and motions. Truly, song is more powerful than the sound of an instrument, in that—beyond harmonic concord—it proceeds from the conception of the mind, the commanding impulse of the imagination, and the affection of the heart. Together with modulated and tempered air, it easily penetrates the airy **spirit** <note>The "spiritus" was viewed in Renaissance philosophy as a thin, vaporous substance that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note> of the listener, which is the bond of the soul and body. By its motion, it transfers the affection and soul of the singer into the listener, moving emotion by emotion, affecting imagination by imagination, and soul by soul. It strikes the heart and enters the inner reaches of the mind, gradually instilling morals. Moreover, it moves or stills the limbs and the humors of the body. Hence, harmony contributes so much to moving the emotions that not only natural harmony, but even artificial and vocal harmony, exert power over souls and bodies.

It is necessary, however, that all harmonies <note>original: "concentus"</note> proceed from compatible foundations, whether they be in strings, in pipes, or in voices, if they are to come together as one. For no one can make the roar of lions, the lowing of oxen, the neighing of horses, the braying of a donkey, or the grunting of a pig harmonize. Nor can strings made from the guts <note>original: "nervus"</note> of a wolf and a lamb be brought into any consonance, because their foundations are discordant. Yet, the various voices of many humans harmonize because they share a single foundation according to their species. Many birds also harmonize because they share a single closely related genus and a symbol from the heavens. Even artificial instruments harmonize with natural voices because there is a likeness in both, either true and expressed, or through a certain analogy.

Every harmony consists of either sounds or voices. Sound is spirit; voice is sound and animated spirit; speech is spirit with sound and voice that expresses a specific meaning, which proceeds from the mouth as spirit with sound and voice. **Chalcidius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato’s Timaeus</note> says that the voice is sent from the depths of the breast and the lap of the heart, with the spirit striving, where a boundary covered with sinews separates the heart from the lungs; by the tongue striking and forming the narrow passage of the throat, and by the other vocal organs, articulate sounds are emitted—the elements of speech—by which interpreter the secret motions of the mind are opened. Truly, **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> says that the nature of the voice is so obscure that it is not understood how it is made, or what it is at all. Finally, all music is placed in voice, sound, and hearing.

<margin>In what things music is placed.</margin>

Sound cannot become audible without air. Although air is so necessary for hearing, yet as air is not audible by itself, it cannot be reached by any sense except by accident. For sight does not see it unless it is colored, nor does hearing perceive it unless it is sounding, nor smell unless it is scented, nor taste unless it is flavorful, nor touch unless it is hot or cold or the like. Therefore, although sound does not occur without air, sound is not of the nature of air, nor is air of the nature of sound; rather, air exists as the body of the life of our sensitive spirit, and it is not of the nature of any sensible object, but of a simpler and higher power. ### Concerning the correspondence of these with the celestial bodies: and which harmony and which sounds respond to each of the stars. Chapter XXVI.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'C' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or musician, surrounded by foliage and a bird.</image-desc>
Furthermore, you should now know that of the seven planets, Saturn, Mars, and the Moon possess more of a "voice" <note>original: "uocis," referring here to a singular vocal quality or pitch rather than a complex musical arrangement</note> than a "harmony" <note>original: "concentus," a concord or musical blending</note>. Indeed, Saturn has sounds that are sad, hoarse, deep, slow, and as if they were sounds compressed toward a center; whereas Mars has harsh, sharp, threatening, fast, and angry sounds. Between these, the Moon maintains a middle ground. However, Jupiter, the Sun, Venus, and Mercury possess true harmonies. Jupiter has harmonies that are deep, constant, intense, sweet, cheerful, and pleasant. The Sun has harmonies that are venerable, intense, pure, and sweet with grace. Venus has lascivious, luxurious, soft, and voluptuous harmonies, which are dissolved and spread out at the edges. Mercury, however, has harmonies that are more relaxed and manifold, yet happy and pleasant with a certain vigor. 

Moreover, from the particular harmonies and proportions, the musical tone <note>original: "tonus"</note> obeys the nine Muses. Jupiter possesses the grace of the eighth and the fifth intervals combined—that is, the <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note> with the <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>. The Sun obtains the melody of the eighth interval, the <term>diapason</term>, and similarly across fifteen tones, the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>a double octave</note>. Venus holds the grace of the fifth interval, the <term>diapente</term>. Mercury has the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note>, which is the grace of the fourth interval. 

The ancients, moreover, content with the number of the four elements, used four strings in a <term>tetrachord</term> <note>a four-stringed scale</note>, which Mercury is said to have invented, as the author Nicomachus testifies. Of these strings, they intended the *hypate* <note>the lowest string in the Greek system</note> to represent Earth; the *parhypate* or *mese* <note>the middle string</note> to represent Water; the *nete* or *diezeugmenon* or *hyperboleos* <note>the highest string</note> to represent Fire; and the *paranete* or *synemmenon* to represent Air. 

Afterward, Terpander of Lesbos discovered the seventh string, making the number equal to that of the planets. Furthermore, those who followed the number of the elements said that four genera of music correspond to them along with the four humors: they believed the **Dorian** mode resonated with water and phlegm; the **Phrygian** with choler and fire; the **Lydian** with blood and air; and the **Mixolydian** with black bile and earth. Others, looking toward the number and power of the heavens, attributed the **Dorian** to the Sun, the **Phrygian** to Mars, the **Lydian** to Jupiter, the **Mixolydian** to Saturn, the **Hypophrygian** to Mercury, the **Hypolydian** to Venus, the **Hypodorian** to the Moon, and the **Hypomixolydian** to the starry firmament. 

Furthermore, they also related the Muses and the strings to the heavens by these modes of harmony, but not in the same order we described among the numbers and souls of the heavens regarding the nine Muses. For they say the Muse **Thalia** has no harmony, ascribing her to silence and the Earth. **Clio**, however, together with the Moon, moves the **Hypodorian** mode and the *proslambanomenos* string. **Calliope** and Mercury possess the **Hypophrygian** mode and the *hypatehypaton* string. **Terpsichore** with Venus moves the **Hypolydian** and the *parhypatehypaton*. **Melpomene** and the Sun are fitted to the **Dorian** and the *lichanos hypaton*. **Erato** with Mars guards the **Phrygian** and the *hypatemesen*. **Euterpe** and Jupiter correspond to the **Lydian** and the *parhypate meson*. **Polymnia** and Saturn keep the **Mixolydian** and the *lichanos meson*. **Urania** and the starry heaven possess the **Hypomixolydian** mode and the me— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "mese," the middle string.</note>

<margin>note</margin>
Some also investigate the harmony of the heavens from their distance from one another: for that space which lies between the Earth and the Moon—namely, one hundred and twenty-six thousand Italian stades <note>A Greek unit of distance; 126,000 stades is roughly 14,500 miles.</note>—makes the interval of a tone. From the Moon to Mercury, half of that space makes a semitone. An equal amount from there to Venus makes another semitone. From there to the Sun, a triple distance—as if a tone and a half—establishes a fifth <note>original: "diapente," a musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. From the Moon to the Sun, it makes a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron," a musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, creating two and a half tones. From the Sun to Mars, the interval is again as much as from the Earth to the Moon, making a tone. From there to Jupiter, half of that makes another semitone. An equal amount from Jupiter to Saturn also constitutes a semitone. From Saturn to the sphere of the stars <note>The "Firmament" or "Octave" of fixed stars.</note>, there lies again the space of a semitone. Therefore, from the Sun to the starry heaven, there is an interval <note>original: "diastema," a Greek term for a musical gap or interval.</note> of a fourth—consisting of two tones and a half—but from the Earth to the heaven, there is a perfect octave <note>original: "diapason," the interval of an octave.</note> of six full tones. 

Furthermore, a most sweet harmony results from the proportion of the movements of the planets to one another and with the eighth heaven. The proportion of the movement of Saturn to Jupiter is two-and-a-half <note>original: "dupla sesquialtera," a ratio of 5:2.</note>; Jupiter to Mars is six-fold <note>original: "sescupla," usually 6:1.</note>; the proportion of Mars to the Sun, Venus, and Mercury—which complete their journey together—is double; the proportion of those to the Moon is twelve-fold; and of Saturn to the star-bearing sphere, it is one thousand two hundred-fold, if it be true what Ptolemy says: that heaven moves against the "First Mover" <note>The outermost sphere that drives the daily rotation of the universe.</note> by one degree in one hundred years. Thus, by its own motion, the movement of the Moon is faster and makes a higher-pitched sound than the starry sphere, which, being the slowest of all, makes the deepest sound. But by the "violent" motion <note>The external force that makes all spheres revolve daily from East to West.</note> of the First Mover, it is the fastest and highest of all; while the lunar motion is the slowest and deepest. This proportion and reciprocity of movements...

The harmony of the elements is also drawn from their bases and angles, which we discussed previously. For instance, since there is a **double proportion** <note>original: "proportio dupla"; a 2:1 ratio, which in music creates an octave or "diapason."</note> in the bases between fire and air, and a **one-and-a-half proportion** <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a 3:2 ratio, which creates a musical fifth or "diapente."</note> in their solid angles, and again a double proportion in their planes, a harmony is born consisting of a double octave and a fifth. Between air and water, the proportion in the bases is **two-and-a-half** <note>original: "dupla sesquialtera"; a 5:2 ratio.</note>, resulting in an octave and a fifth; while in the angles it is double, resulting again in an octave. Between water and earth, there is a **three-and-a-third proportion** <note>original: "tripla sesquitertia"; a 10:3 ratio.</note> in the bases, from which arises an octave, a fifth, and a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"; the musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>; but in the angles it is again one-and-a-half, constituting a fifth. Furthermore, between earth and fire, the proportion in the bases is one-and-a-half, making a fifth; while in the angles it is double, constituting an octave. However, between fire and water, and between air and earth, harmony is somewhat lacking, because there is a total opposition of qualities between them; they agree only through an intermediate element.

### Chapter XXVII: On the Proportion, Measure, and Harmony of the Human Body.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'H' inside a square frame depicting architectural elements or an interior scene.</image-desc>

**H**umanity, because it is the most beautiful and perfect work and image of God, is also a **lesser world** <note>original: "minor mundus"; also known as the "microcosm." Renaissance thinkers believed the human body was a map of the entire universe.</note>. Therefore, by a more perfect composition, a sweeter harmony, and a more sublime dignity, man contains and sustains within himself all numbers, measures, weights, motions, elements, and everything else that composes him. In him, as in a supreme masterpiece, all things achieve a certain ultimate harmony far beyond the common consonance found in other mixtures. Hence, all the ancients used to count with their fingers and indicate numbers with their digits.
<margin>Numbers and measures were discovered from the joints of the human body.</margin>
Indeed, they seem to have proven that all numbers, measures, proportions, and harmonies were discovered from the very joints of the human body. From this measurement of the body, they partitioned temples, houses, dwellings, theaters, and even ships, machines, and every kind of craft. Every part and member of buildings—such as columns, architraves <note>original: "epistylia"; the horizontal beam that rests on the columns.</note>, bases, pilasters <note>original: "antes."</note>, pedestals <note>original: "stilobates."</note>, and all other such things—were deduced from the human body. Moreover, God himself taught Noah to build the Ark according to the measure of the human body, just as He who built the entire machine of the world made it symmetrical to the human body. For this reason, the world is called the "great world" <note>the macrocosm</note> and man the "lesser world." Hence, some students of the microcosm measure the human body by six feet, a foot by ten degrees, and each degree by five minutes. From this, sixty degrees are counted, which make three hundred minutes. To these are equated as many **geometric cubits** <note>A cubit is an ancient unit based on the length of the forearm.</note> as those by which the Ark was described by Moses. For just as the human body is three hundred minutes in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height, so also the length of the Ark was three hundred cubits, its width fifty, and its height thirty. Thus, in both cases, the proportion of length to width is **six-fold** <note>original: "sescupla"; a 6:1 ratio.</note>, to the height it is **ten-fold**, and the width to the height contains **two-thirds more** <note>original: "suppartiens duas tertias"; a 5:3 ratio.</note>. In like manner, the measurements of all the limbs are proportional...

There is also a **square measure** <note>original: "quadrata mensura"; a key concept in Renaissance art and architecture where the human body is used as a standard for geometric perfection, similar to Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man.</note>, a body of the most perfect proportions: for indeed, if a man is stood upright with his arms outstretched and his feet joined together, he forms an equilateral square, the center of which is at the base of the **pubis** <note>original: "pectinis"; literally "the comb," an anatomical term commonly used in the 16th century to refer to the pubic bone or the lower pelvic region.</note>.

But now let us come to the particular measurements. A man’s circumference under the armpits contains half of his length, the midpoint of which is at the base of the groin <term>pecten|the pubic bone or the base of the pelvic region</term>. From there upward to the middle of the chest between both nipples, and from the middle of the chest to the top of the head, each is a fourth part of the total. Likewise, from the base of the groin down to below the knees, and from there to the bottom of the ankles, is a fourth part of the man. The width of the shoulders <note>original: "spatularum"</note> from one end to the other is the same; and the same is the length from the elbow to the tip of the longest finger, and for this reason, this measurement is called a cubit <note>original: "cubitus"; an ancient unit of length based on the forearm</note>. Hence, four cubits constitute the total height of a man. The width at the shoulders is one cubit, while the width at the waist <note>original: "cinctura"</note> is one foot <term>pes|a unit of measure, historically about 12 inches</term>. Furthermore, six palms <term>palmus|the width of the four fingers of the hand</term> constitute a cubit; four palms constitute a foot, and four fingers constitute a palm. Thus, the total height of a man is twenty-four palms, six feet, and ninety-six fingers. From the base of the groin to the top of the chest is a sixth part of the height; from the top of the chest to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair is a seventh part. For a robust and well-proportioned <note>original: "quadrati"; literally "squared," referring to a sturdy, athletic build</note> body, the foot is a sixth part of the height; but for a taller person, it is a seventh. Nor can the human body exceed a height of seven feet, according to the testimony of Varro and Gellius <note>Marcus Terentius Varro and Aulus Gellius were Roman scholars whose works on natural history were standard references in the Renaissance</note>. The larger joint of the thumb <note>original: "pollicis"</note> determines the opening of the mouth: it is also the distance from the bottom of the chin to the top of the lower lip. The smaller joint, however, is equal to the distance from the top of the lower lip to the bottom of the nostrils; and of all the furthest joints, which they call *onychios* <note>from the Greek word for nails</note>, the fingernails occupy exactly half the length. From the space between the eyebrows to the outer corners of the eyes is the same distance as from those corners to the front of the ears. The height of the forehead, the length of the nose, and the width of the mouth across the upper lip are all equal to one another. Similarly, the width of the palm and the width of the sole of the foot are the same. The height from the bottom of the ankle to the top of the foot is equal to the length from the top of the foot to the tip of the nail. From the top of the forehead to the space between the eyes, and from there to the bottom of the nostrils, and then to the bottom of the chin, the parts are equal. The joined eyebrows are equal to the circles of the eyes, and the semicircles of the ears are equal to the mouth when closed. From this, the circles of the eyes, the ears, and the open mouth are equal.

The width of the nose is equal to the length of the eye; thus, in that space between the two outer edges of the eyes, the eyes themselves occupy two parts, while the nose takes up the third part in the middle. From the very top of the crown to the knees, the navel <note>original: "umbilicus"</note> marks the midpoint. From the top of the chest to the bottom of the nostrils, the "knot of the throat" <note>the Adam’s apple</note> marks the midpoint. From the top of the crown to the bottom of the chin, the eyes are located at the midpoint. From the space between the eyes to the bottom of the chin, the bottom of the nostrils marks the midpoint. From the bottom of the nostrils to the bottom of the chin, the edge of the lower lip marks the midpoint; however, one third of that same distance marks the upper lip starting from the bottom of the nostrils.

Furthermore, all these measurements are in harmony with one another through <term>multiple proportions</term> <note>ratios where a larger number contains a smaller number several times exactly</note> and harmonic concords. For the thicker finger, which is called the thumb, compared to the forearm at the pulse and wrist joint in circular measurement, is in a "sub-double-and-a-half" <note>original: "subdupla sesquialtera," a ratio of 5:2</note> proportion; for the wrist contains the thumb measurement twice and a half again, just as five relates to two. But the ratio of the thumb to the arm near the shoulder is "sub-triple" <note>1:3</note>. The size of the leg or shin compared to the arm is a <term>sesquialtera</term> proportion <note>a ratio of 3:2, representing a musical fifth</note>, just as three is to two. A similar proportion exists between the neck and the shin as exists between the shin and the arm. The proportion of the hip to the arm is triple <note>3:1</note>. The proportion of the whole body to the torso is a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>a ratio of 9:8, representing a whole tone in music</note>. From the torso or chest down to the legs and the soles of the feet, it is a <term>sesquitertial</term> proportion <note>a ratio of 4:3, representing a musical fourth</note>. The chest, from the neck to the navel, compared to the loins or belly down to the end of the torso, is double <note>2:1, representing an octave</note>. The width of the flanks to the width of the hip is 3:2. The head to the neck is triple; likewise, the head to the knee is triple; and the same for the calf and the thigh. The length of the forehead between the temples is four times its height. These are the measurements found everywhere, by which the members of the human body—according to their length, width, height, and circumference—agree with each other and with the celestial bodies themselves. All these measurements are divided by multiple, super-particular, or mixed proportions, from which a manifold harmony results. For a double proportion creates three <term>diapasons</term> <note>octaves</note>; a quadruple proportion creates two octaves and a <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>. In the same way, the elements, qualities, temperaments, and humors are proportioned; for in man...

->OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,<-

...in a healthy and well-composed body, these weights of the humors and temperaments <note>original: "complexionum"</note> are assigned: namely, eight parts of blood, four of phlegm, two of choler, and one of melancholy. Thus, in each case, there is a "double proportion" <note>a 2:1 ratio</note> through the series; but the ratio of the first to the third, and the second to the fourth, is "quadruple" <note>4:1 ratio</note>; and the first to the last is "octuple" <note>8:1 ratio</note>. Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist</note> handed down that the human heart in its first year has a weight of two drachms; in the second, four; and from there, following an equal course until the fiftieth year, it reaches a weight of one hundred drachms. From that point, its weight is reckoned to decrease back toward the same equilibrium, so that when the circuit is completed, it returns to the same starting point. He claimed that the span of life does not exceed the decline of that organ, and by this reasoning, he circumscribed the life of man to one hundred years. Pliny <note>the Roman natural historian</note> testifies that this was also a doctrine <note>original: "haeresim"</note> of the Egyptians. 

Furthermore, the very movements of human limbs correspond to celestial movements. Every person has within themselves the movement of their own heart which, responding to the movement of the Sun, is diffused through the arteries into the whole body. It indicates to us the years, months, days, hours, and moments as a most certain rule. Moreover, it has been discovered by anatomists that there is a certain nerve near the nape of the neck <note>original: "micha," likely "nucha" or the spinal marrow</note> which, when pulled, moves all the limbs of a man in such a way that each is moved by its own proper motion. Aristotle believes that the members of the world are moved by God in just such a manner. There are also two veins in the neck, in the throat where they are divided, which go up to the head; if these are gripped firmly from the outside, men immediately collapse, deprived of their senses, until they are released. 

Thus, the eternal Architect of the world himself, being about to send the soul into the body as into a dwelling, first measures out a lodging-place worthy of it, and grants a most noble soul to a beautiful body. Then, the soul itself, conscious of its own divinity, shapes and adorns the body for itself according to its own character. For this reason, the people of Ethiopia who were ruled by the wisdom of the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a sect of ancient sages</note>—as Aristotle testifies—did not choose their kings from those who were the strongest or wealthiest, but only those who were the most beautiful and outstanding in form. Indeed, they believed they could perceive the greatness of souls through the outward appearance of the body. Considering this, many philosophers, both ancient and more recent, who have searched into the secrets of the hidden causes within the majesty of nature, have dared to assert that no defect of the body occurs, and no disproportion exists in the body, which does not also follow a defect or lack of restraint in the soul; for it is certain that the one grows, unites, and works in turn by the function of the other.

### On the composition and 
### harmony of the human soul. Chapter XXVIII.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring a figure in a robe sitting by a bed or a desk within an architectural frame.</image-desc>Just as the consonance of the body consists of the proper measure and proportion of the limbs, so the consonance of the soul consists of the proper temperament and proportion of its virtues and operations. These are the concupiscible <note>the faculty of desire</note>, the irascible <note>the faculty of anger or spirit</note>, and reason, which are thus proportioned to one another: for reason has the proportion of a *diapason* <note>an octave, 2:1 ratio</note> to desire, but the proportion of a *diatessaron* <note>a perfect fourth, 4:3 ratio</note> to anger. The irascible faculty, however, has the proportion of a *diapente* <note>a perfect fifth, 3:2 ratio</note> to the concupiscible. Therefore, when a most proportionate soul is joined to a most proportionate body, it is certain that such a person obtains a most happy lot even in the distribution of gifts, insofar as the soul agrees with the body in its natural disposition...

...converge, which agreement is indeed most hidden, yet has been somewhat outlined by the wise. But hastening toward the harmony of the soul, it is necessary for us to seek it from those intermediate things through which they have passage to us—that is, from the celestial bodies and spheres. Knowing, therefore, which powers of the soul respond to which of the planets from those things said above, we shall easily recognize their harmony <note>original: "concentus," literally a singing together or concord</note> among themselves. For the Moon <note>original: "Luna"</note> governs the powers of waxing and waning; the power of imagination <note>original: "phantastica uis"</note> and genius depends on Mercury; the faculty of desire <note>original: "concupiscibilis uirtus"</note> from Venus; the vital force from the Sun; the impulsive power, which is also called the irascible <note>associated with anger or spiritedness</note>, from Mars; the natural power from Jupiter; and all receptive power from Saturn. The will itself is like the *Primum Mobile* <note>the "First Moved" sphere in Ptolemaic astronomy that imparts motion to all other spheres</note> and the leader of all those powers according to its pleasure; when joined with the higher intellect, it always tends toward the good. This intellect shows the paths to the will, just as light does for the eye; yet it does not move the will itself, for the will remains the mistress of her own operation, which is why it is called "free will." And although it always tends toward the good as its proper object, it is sometimes blinded by error and driven by animal force to choose evil, believing it to be good. Therefore, free will is defined 
<margin>Free will.</margin> 
as the faculty of intellect and will by which good is chosen when grace is present, and evil when it is withdrawn. Thus grace itself, which theologians also call "charity" or "infused love," is in the will like a "first mover," and when it is absent, the entire harmony falls into dissonance. Furthermore, the soul corresponds to the Earth through sense; to Water through imagination; to Air through reason; and to Heaven through intellect. The soul enters into the harmony of these things according to how they are tempered in this mortal body. Therefore, the wise ancients, recognizing the various harmonic dispositions of bodies and souls according to the diversity of human temperaments <note>original: "complexionum"</note>, did not use music and songs in vain, both for preserving the health of the body and restoring it when lost, and also for leading souls toward wholesome morals, until they might attune the human being to celestial harmony and render him entirely heavenly. Moreover, nothing is more effective for striking down evil demons <note>original: "malis daemonibus"</note> than musical harmony; for since they fell from that celestial harmony, they cannot endure any true concord, seeing it as an enemy, and they flee far away—just as David suppressed the evil spirit raging in Saul with his lyre <note>original: "cithara"</note>. For this reason, songs and musical sounds were introduced into sacred offices by the ancient prophets and fathers who understood these harmonic mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta"</note>.

<margin>How the planets are to be observed.</margin>
For the qualities of the angles <note>In astrology, "angles" refer to the four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> are varied, which the rays of the celestial bodies describe upon the figure of a thing, according to which the celestial virtues are infused. Thus, whenever you are about to perform a work pertaining to any planet, it will be necessary for you to place that planet in its **dignities** <note>Essential dignities are positions where a planet is strongest, such as its Home or Exaltation.</note>, making it fortunate and powerful, and dominant in the day, the hour, and the figure of the heavens. Nor will you wait only for the **significator** <note>The planet that represents the specific goal or person of the ritual.</note> of the work to be powerful; you must also observe that the **Moon** is opportunely directed toward it, for you shall perfect nothing without the favor of the Moon. But if you have several "patrons" <note>planetary helpers</note> for the work, observe that they are all powerful and looking upon one each other with a friendly **aspect**. If you are unable to have such
<margin>How the Moon is to be observed.</margin>
aspects, it is suitable for you at least to take the angles. Indeed, you shall observe the Moon when she either looks upon both <note>meaning two planets involved in the work</note>, or is joined to one and looks upon the other, or when she passes from a conjunction or aspect of one to the union or aspect of the other. That also
<margin>Mercury must be diligently observed.</margin>
I believe should by no means be omitted: that you diligently observe **Mercury** in every work. For he is the messenger <note>original: "cōmeator," a traveler or intermediary</note> between both the higher and lower gods; when he joins with good planets, he increases their goodness; when with evil ones, he pours in their malice. Now, we call a sign or planet **unfortunate** by an aspect of **Saturn** or **Mars**, especially the **opposition** or the **square** <note>Aspects of 180 degrees and 90 degrees, traditionally considered challenging or "hostile" in astrology.</note>; for these aspects are of enmity. But the union <note>conjunction</note>, the **trine**, and the **sextile** aspect <note>Aspects of 120 degrees and 60 degrees, considered harmonious.</note> are of friendship; among these, the conjunction is the strongest. However, if a planet is already looking through a trine, and is also "received" <note>an astrological term where one planet is in a sign ruled by the other</note>, it is esteemed as if it were already joined. Truly, all planets fear conjunction with the **Sun**, but they rejoice in its aspect, specifically the trine and sextile.

### When the planets are of more powerful influence. Chapter 30.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'P' featuring a botanical or floral motif within a square frame.</image-desc>
We shall have powerful planets when they are in their **domicile** <note>the zodiac sign they rule</note>, or **exaltation**, or **triplicity**, or **term**, or **face** <note>These are the five classical levels of planetary strength or "essential dignity."</note>, being "direct" <note>moving forward, not retrograde</note> and outside of **combustion** <note>the state of being too close to the Sun, which "burns" up a planet's power</note>, at their **apogee** <note>their highest or farthest point from Earth</note>, and dominating the figure of heaven—namely, when they are in the **angles**, especially the eastern <note>the Ascendant</note> or the tenth <note>the Midheaven</note>, or in the houses immediately following them, or in their own **joys** <note>specific signs or houses where a planet is said to "rejoice" or function best</note>. But care must be taken that they are not in the bounds or under the dominion of Saturn or Mars, nor in the **shadowy degrees**, **wells**, or **void** places <note>Technical terms for specific degrees in the zodiac that were thought to weaken or "trap" a planet's influence.</note>. You shall observe that the angles of the Ascendant, the tenth, and the seventh houses are fortunate, as well as the Lord of the Ascendant, the place of the Sun, the place of the Moon, and the place of the **Part of Fortune** <note>a calculated point in a chart representing prosperity</note> and its Lord, and the Lord of the preceding conjunction or full moon. Truly, let the malevolent planets fall "unfortunate," unless by chance they are the significators of your work, or can be useful to you in any way; or if they have obtained leadership in your own "revolution" <note>yearly solar return chart</note> or "genesis" <note>birth chart</note>, for then they are least of all to be suppressed.
<margin>When the Moon is powerful.</margin>
Indeed, we shall have the Moon powerful if she is in her own domicile, or exaltation, or triplicity, or face, and in a degree suitable for the desired work, and if she obtains a **Mansion** <note>one of the 28 Lunar Mansions, segments of the zodiac based on the Moon's daily travel</note> competent for herself and the work. Let her not be in the **Via Combusta** <note>the "Burnt Path," a section of the zodiac usually considered unlucky</note>, nor slow in her course; let her not be in the **ecliptic** <note>where eclipses occur</note>, nor combust by the Sun (unless by chance she is in unity with the Sun <note>this is called "cazimi," or in the heart of the Sun, considered a position of great strength</note>); let her not descend in southern latitude when she leaves combustion, nor be opposite the Sun, nor be diminished in light, nor be hindered by Mars or Saturn. Concerning these things, I do not wish to prolong the discourse further here, since these and many other necessary things are sufficiently handed down in the volumes of the Astrologers.

<margin>Fixed stars take on the natures of the planets.</margin>
A similar logic must be held by you regarding the **fixed stars** <note>Stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note>. You should know that all fixed stars derive their significance and nature from the seven planets: but some are of the nature of a single planet, while others truly share the nature of two. Hence, whenever any planet is joined with one of the fixed stars of its own nature, the significance of that star is made more powerful, and the nature of the planet is increased. But if it should be a star of two natures, whichever planet is stronger in its company, that planet's nature will prevail in the significance. For example, if a star is of the nature of **Mars** and **Venus**, and Mars is with it, the nature of Mars will prevail; but if Venus is with it, the nature of Venus will overcome.

<margin>How the natures of the fixed stars are discerned.</margin>
<margin>The colors of the planets.</margin>
Furthermore, the natures of the fixed stars are discerned from their colors, according to how they match certain planets and are assigned to them. Indeed, the colors of the planets are: **Saturn’s** is livid or leaden, and with this, a glowing white; **Jupiter’s** is lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinus"</note> bordering on pale, and with this, bright; **Mars’s** is red and fiery; the **Sun’s** is saffron-colored, and when it rises, burning, and thereafter radiating; **Venus’s** is white, but glowing as the morning star and shining as the evening star; **Mercury’s** is radiating, and the **Moon’s** is a pale yellow <note>original: "blondus"</note>.

<margin>The brighter fixed stars.</margin>
You should also know that the larger and brighter the fixed stars are and appear, the greater and stronger is their significance—such as those stars which are called by Astrologers "of the first and second magnitude." From among these, I shall describe to you some of the more powerful ones for this practice: 

The **Navel of Andromeda** <note>The star Mirach</note>, at twenty-two degrees of **Aries**, is of the nature of Venus and Mercury; others say it is of Jupiter and Saturn. **The Head of Algol**, at eighteen degrees of **Taurus**, is of the nature of Saturn and Jupiter. The **Pleiades** <note>The "Seven Sisters" star cluster</note>, at the twenty-second degree of the same sign, is a constellation of a Lunar nature and a Martian complexion. Likewise, in the third degree of **Gemini** is **Aldebaran**, of the nature of Mars and the complexion of Venus—though Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermetic philosophy</note> places this at the twenty-fifth of Aries. In the thirteenth degree of the same Gemini is **The Goat** <note>The star Capella</note>, of the nature of Jupiter and Saturn. 

In the seventh degree of **Cancer** is the **Great Dog** <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the sky</note>, of Venus; in the seventeenth of the same is the **Lesser Dog** <note>Procyon</note>, of a Mercurial nature and Martian complexion. In the twenty-first degree of **Leo** is the "Royal Star" which is called **The Heart of the Lion** <note>Regulus</note>, of the nature of Jupiter and Mars. In the nineteenth degree of **Virgo** is the **Tail of the Great Bear**, of Venus and the Moon. In the seventh degree of **Libra** is the **Right Wing of the Crow**, and in the thirteenth of the same, the **Left Wing**, both of the nature of Saturn and Mars. In the sixteenth degree of the same is **Spica**, of Venus and Mercury; in the seventeenth of the same is **Alcameth** <note>The star Arcturus</note>, of the nature of Mars and Jupiter; but this one favors when in good aspect with a luminary <note>The Sun or Moon</note>, and hinders when in the opposite. 

In the fourth degree of **Scorpio** is **Elepheia** <note>The star Alphecca in the Northern Crown</note>, of the nature of Venus and Mars. In the third degree of **Sagittarius** is the **Heart of the Scorpion** <note>Antares</note>, of the nature of Mars and Jupiter. In the seventh degree of **Capricorn** is the **Falling Vulture** <note>The star Vega</note>, tempered by Mercury and Venus. In the sixteenth degree of **Aquarius** is the **Tail of the Goat** <note>Deneb Algedi</note>, of the nature of Saturn and Mercury. In the third of **Pisces** is the **Shoulder of the Horse** <note>The star Markab</note>, of the nature of Jupiter and Mars. 

And it shall be a general rule for you to hope for the star’s own gifts when it is dominant, but to be hindered when the star is unfortunate or in an opposing state, which was shown above. For celestial bodies, insofar as they are themselves fortunate or unfortu—

### On the Sun and Moon, and their Magical Principles. Chapter XXXII.

<margin>The Sun's excellence.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' containing a scene with a reclining human figure and foliage.</image-desc>
The Sun and the Moon have been allotted the administration of the heavens and of all bodies that are beneath the heavens: the **Sun** is the lord of all elemental virtues, and the **Moon**, by the virtue of the Sun, is the mistress of generation, growth, and decay. Hence, **Albumasar** <note>A famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD) known in the West as Albumasar.</note> says that life is infused into all things through the Sun and Moon, which **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek prophet and musician.</note> therefore calls the "living eyes of heaven." The Sun gives light to all things from itself and bestows it abundantly upon all, not only in the heavens and the air, but also on the earth and in the innermost depths of the abyss; whatever good we have, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</note> says, we have from the Sun—either from the Sun alone, or from it through other things. **Heraclitus** calls the Sun the "fountain of celestial light." Many **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy.</note> placed the **World Soul** <note>original: "mundi animam"; the vital force that animates the entire universe.</note> principally in the Sun; filling the entire globe of the Sun, it pours out its rays everywhere like a spirit through all things, distributing life, sense, and motion to the universe itself.

Hence the ancient natural philosophers called the Sun the very **Heart of Heaven** <note>original: "cor coeli"</note>. The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers/astrologers.</note> placed it in the middle of the planets. The **Egyptians** also placed it in the middle of the world, namely between the two "fives" of the world: for they place five planets above the Sun, and below the Sun they place the Moon and the four elements. The Sun itself, among the rest of the stars, is the image and statue of the Supreme Prince of both worlds, the terrestrial and the celestial; it is the true light and the most exact likeness of God himself, whose essence represents the **Father**, its splendor the **Son**, and its heat the **Holy Spirit** <note>This is a common Renaissance analogy comparing the Sun's physical properties to the Christian Trinity.</note>. Indeed, the Academics <note>Refers to the Platonic Academy.</note> have nothing by which they can more clearly demonstrate the Divine Essence. It corresponds to God with such harmony that **Plato** calls it the "conspicuous son of God," **Iamblichus** calls it the "image of divine intelligence," and our **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic.</note> calls it the "clear statue of God." 

The Sun sits like a king in the center <note>original: "meditullio"</note> of the other planets, excelling all in light, magnitude, and beauty, illuminating them all and distributing virtue to them for the arrangement of all lower things, and regulating and disposing their steps. Thus, their movements are called diurnal or nocturnal, southern or northern, eastern or western, direct or retrograde. And just as the Sun by its light puts to flight the shadows of the night, so it also drives away any powers of darkness, of which we read in **Job**: *As soon as the dawn appears, they consider it the shadow of death* <note>Job 24:17</note>. And the **Psalmist**, speaking of the lion cubs seeking permission from God to devour, adds: *The Sun has risen, and they are gathered together, and shall lie down in their dens*; after they are put to flight, it follows: *Man shall go forth to his work* <note>Psalm 104:22-23</note>. Therefore, since the Sun holds the middle region of the world, and just as the heart itself presides over the whole body in living beings, so the Sun presides over the heaven and the world, having empire over the entire universe and the things within it. It is the author of time, from whom come the day and the year, cold and heat, and the other qualities of the seasons. And, as **Ptolemy** says, when it has come into the place of any star...

it arouses the power which she has in the air: just as she disposes heat with **Mars**, and cold with **Saturn**, as well as the very spirit and soul of man. For this reason, it is said by **Homer**, and confirmed by **Aristotle**, that such movements exist in the mind as the **Sun**, the prince and moderator of the planets, brings about each day. The **Moon**, however, being closest to the Earth, is the receptacle of all celestial influences; by the swiftness of her course, she joins with the Sun and the other planets and stars every month. Having become, as it were, the wife of all the stars and the most fertile of them, she receives the rays and influences of the Sun and the other planets and stars like a fetus. Then, as if in labor, she brings them forth for the lower world which is near to her. For all the stars flow into her as the final recipient, and she then communicates the influences of all the higher bodies to the lower ones and pours them back onto the Earth. More clearly than all others, she disposes these lower things, and her motion is more perceptible due to the familiarity and proximity she has with us; and as a medium <note>A middle-man or bridge.</note> between both the higher and lower things, she communicates with all of them.
<margin>The motion of the Moon must be diligently observed.</margin>
Therefore, her motion is to be observed above all others, as she is the parent of all conceptions, which she unfolds in various ways in these lower realms according to her varying temperament, motion, position, and her different aspects <note>The angular relationships between celestial bodies.</note> to the planets and other stars. Although she receives powers from all the stars, she is most powerfully filled with life-giving virtue by the Sun whenever she is joined to him, and she borrows her temperament according to his gaze. For in the first quarter, as the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> teach, she is hot and moist; in the second, hot and dry; in the third, cold and dry; and in the fourth, cold and moist. Although she is the lowest of the stars, she unfolds all the conceptions of the higher ones: for from her
<margin>The Golden Chain of Plato.</margin>
the series of things begins in the heavens, which **Plato** calls the **Golden Chain** <note>The *Catena Aurea*, representing the hierarchical link between the divine and the material world.</note>, by which each thing or cause is connected to another and depends on a higher one, until it reaches the supreme cause of all, upon which everything depends. Hence it is that without the Moon as an intermediary, we are entirely unable to attract the power of the higher stars. Thus **Thebit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note> commands that, to capture the virtue of any star, one must take the stone and the herb of that star when the Moon either fortunately enters or fortunately gazes upon <note>original: "aspicit," referring to an astrological aspect.</note> that same star.

### On the XXVIII Mansions of the Moon, and their Powers. Chapter XXXIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure seated amidst foliage.</image-desc> And because the Moon measures the entire **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move.</term> in the space of twenty-eight days, the wise men of the **Indians** and the most ancient **Astrologers** granted twenty-eight Mansions to the Moon. These are fixed in the eighth sphere, and from the various constellations and stars contained within them, as **Alpharus** <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Al-Farabi.</note> says, they receive different properties and names. As the Moon travels through these, she acquires different powers and virtues. According to the opinion of **Abraham** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a notable medieval scholar and astrologer.</note>, each of those mansions comprises twelve degrees, fifty-one minutes, and nearly twenty-six seconds. And so, in these seven mansions, one quarter of the heaven is completed; and in a similar order of the number of degrees, minutes, and seconds, the remaining mansions in each of the quarters have their seven beginnings. This is arranged so that in the first sign of that quarter, three mansions take their beginning; in the remaining two signs, two mansions begin in each. Therefore, the seven following mansions begin from the head of **Cancer**, the names of which are Alnaza or Anatrachya, which means "misty" or "cloudy," being the eighth mansion. The eleventh is called Azobra or Ardaf, which is the "Hair of the **Lion**." It is effective for journeys and profit from trade, and for the redemption of captives. ### On the true motion of celestial bodies to be observed in the eighth sphere, and on the method of planetary hours. Chapter XXXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' in a square frame, depicting a seated human figure amidst floral or leafy ornamentation.</image-desc> Whoever intends to work at a celestial opportunity must observe either both or one of two things: namely, the motions of the stars, or the times. Regarding motions, one must observe when they are in their **dignities** <note>original: *dignitatibus*; these are positions in the zodiac where a planet's influence is strongest</note> or **debilities** <note>original: *deiectionibus*; positions where a planet's influence is weakened</note>, whether essential or accidental. By **times**, I mean the days and hours distributed to their lordships: concerning all these things, enough is taught in the books of the astrologers. But two things must be especially weighed and observed by us in this place: one, that we observe the motion of the stars, their ascensions, and the **cardinal points** <note>original: *cardines*; the four most important points in a horoscope: the Rising, Setting, Midheaven, and Lower Midheaven</note>, as they truly are in the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars. Agrippa is warning that because of the "precession of the equinoxes," the physical stars no longer align with the traditional zodiac signs used in many charts.</note>. Due to negligence in this matter when fashioning celestial images, many happen to err and are cheated of the desired effect. 

The other thing to observe concerns the times in determining the **planetary hours** <note>A system where the day and night are each divided into 12 hours, regardless of the season. This means a "day hour" in summer is much longer than a "day hour" in winter.</note>. For almost all astrologers divide the entire space of time from sunrise to sunset into twelve equal parts and call those the twelve hours of the day. Then, the time that follows from sunset to sunrise, divided by a similar ratio into twelve equal portions, they call the twelve hours of the night. They then distribute those individual hours to individual planets according to the order of their succession, always giving the first hour of the day to the **Lord of the Day** <note>For example, the Sun for Sunday, the Moon for Monday, etc.</note>, then to each in order until the end of the twenty-four hours. In this distribution, the **Magi** <note>Wise practitioners of natural and celestial magic.</note> agree with them, but some disagree in the partitioning of the hours, saying that the space between sunrise and sunset should not be divided into [twelve] equal parts. They say that those hours are called **unequal** not because the diurnal hours are unequal to the nocturnal, but because the individual diurnal and nocturnal hours are also unequal among themselves. Therefore, the partition of unequal or planetary hours has another method of measurement observed by the Magi, which is as follows: 

Just as in **artificial hours** <note>Standard 60-minute hours.</note> (which are always equal to each other), the ascension of fifteen degrees on the **equinoctial** <note>The celestial equator.</note> constitutes one artificial hour; so also in planetary hours, the ascension of fifteen degrees on the **ecliptic** <note>The path of the Sun and planets through the zodiac.</note> constitutes one planetary or unequal hour. The measure of these must be sought and found from the tables of **oblique ascensions** <note>A mathematical adjustment used in astrology to account for the Earth's tilt relative to a specific geographical location.</note> for each specific region.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' decorated with foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc> So great is the magnitude, virtue, and power of the celestial bodies that not only natural things, but even artificial ones—when they are properly exposed to the heavens—suddenly undergo an influence from that most powerful agent and wonderful life. This often bestows upon them a marvelous celestial virtue, which **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, the holy doctor, confirms in his book *On Fate*: where he says that even garments, buildings, and whatever works of art there may be, receive a certain quality from the stars. Thus the magi confirm that not only through the mixture and application of natural things, but also through images, seals, rings, mirrors, and various other instruments—provided they are fashioned at the opportune time under a specific constellation—a certain celestial illumination is captured, and something wonderful can be seen. For the rays of the celestial bodies are animated, living, and sensible, carrying with them marvelous gifts and a most vehement power; even in a sudden moment and by a quick touch, they impress wonderful powers into images, even in material that is less than ideal. However, they bestow more effective virtues upon images if they are fashioned not from just any material, but from a specific substance: namely, one whose natural virtue agrees with the specific work intended, and whose shape is similar to the celestial figure. For such an image—both because of a material naturally congruent to the work and the celestial influx, and because of a shape similar to the celestial figure—is most ready to receive the actions and powers of the celestial bodies and figures. It suddenly conceives the celestial gift within itself, then acts continually upon others, and other things incline themselves toward it through obedience. Whence **Ptolemy** says in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms regarding astrology, traditionally attributed to Claudius Ptolemy.</note> that inferior things obey the celestial ones—not only the stars themselves, but even their images. Just as terrestrial scorpions obey the celestial **Scorpio**, so too do they obey the image of that Scorpion which has been fashioned opportunely under its ascent and dominion.

And so much for the images of the faces thus far; beyond these, there are still three hundred and sixty images in the zodiac, according to the number of degrees, the forms of which **Peter of Abano** <note>original: "Petrus de Ebano" — a 13th-century Italian philosopher and astrologer known for his work on image magic.</note> described. Outside the zodiac, there are also general figures which **Hyginus** and **Aratus** <note>Classical authors whose works on stars and myths were foundational to Renaissance astrology.</note> described for us, and many particular ones according to the number of faces and degrees existing there, of all of which it would be too long to speak. From these, however, the more principal ones are held: **Pegasus**, who is effective against the diseases of horses and preserves knights in war; then there is **Andromeda** <note>original: "Andromacha" — the text likely intends Andromeda, the constellation associated with marital themes.</note>, who reconciles love between a husband and wife, so much so that she is even said to reconcile adulterers. **Cassiopeia** restores weak bodies and strengthens the limbs. **Serpentarius** <note>The "Serpent-Bearer," known today as Ophiuchus.</note> puts to flight poisons and cures the bites of venomous creatures. **Hercules** grants victory in war. **Draco** <note>The Dragon constellation.</note> with both the **Bears** <note>Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, the Great and Little Bears.</note> make a man shrewd, ingenious, strong, and pleasing to gods and men...

## ON the images of Saturn.
### Chapter XXXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a seated scholar or deity figure within a square architectural frame.</image-desc>

**FURTHERMORE**, I shall now discuss the images that the ancients attributed to the planets. Although the ancient sages have written very extensive volumes on these matters, so that there is no need to recount them all here, I will nevertheless recite a few of them. For they made, from the materials of Saturn while he was ascending, an image on the stone called a **magnet** <note>lodestone</note> depicting a man with the face of a stag and the feet of a camel, sitting upon a chair or a dragon; he held a sickle in his right hand and an arrow in his left. They hoped this image would be profitable for a long life. Indeed, **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> proves in the book *Sadar* that Saturn contributes to longevity; he also relates there that certain regions of India are subject to Saturn, and the men there are very long-lived, not dying until extreme old age.

They also made another image of Saturn for longevity on a **sapphire**, during the hour of Saturn while he was ascending or fortunately positioned. Its figure was an old man sitting upon a high chair, having his hands raised above his head, and in them holding a fish or a sickle; beneath his feet was a cluster of grapes. His head was covered with a black or dark cloth, and all his garments were black or dark. They also made this same image against **kidney stones** and diseases of the kidneys, specifically during the hour of Saturn when he was ascending in the third face of Aquarius.

They also made an image from the materials of Saturn for the power of growth, with Saturn ascending in Capricorn; its form was an old man leaning on a staff, holding a curved sickle in his hand, and dressed in black clothes. They also made an image cast from **brass** when Saturn was ascending in his rising—that is, in the first degree of Aries, or more truly, in the first degree of Capricorn; they confirm that this image could speak with a human voice.

They also made an image from the materials of both Saturn and Mercury together, cast from metal in the form of a beautiful man, which they promised would predict the future. They made it on the day of Mercury at the third hour (which belongs to Saturn), with the constellation of Gemini ascending (the home of Mercury, which designates prophets), and with Saturn and Mercury joined together in Aquarius in the ninth region of the heaven, which is also called **God** <note>In traditional astrology, the 9th House is the house of religion, philosophy, and divinity.</note>. Furthermore, let Saturn behold the ascendant in a trine aspect, and the Moon likewise, and let the Sun behold the place of the conjunction. Let **Venus**, holding any angle, be powerful and in the west; let Mars from the Su... <note>Text cuts off mid-sentence.</note>

## On the images of Jupiter. Chapter XXXIX.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting two nude figures or putti flanking the letter within a square frame.</image-desc>
**FROM** the works of Jupiter, they used to make an image for longevity during the hour of Jupiter, when he was fortunately rising in his <term>exaltation: a specific sign in the zodiac where a planet's influence is considered most powerful; for Jupiter, this is Cancer</term>, upon a clear and white stone. Its figure was a crowned man dressed in saffron-colored <note>original: "croceis" — yellow or saffron, the color associated with the benevolent influence of Jupiter</note> garments, riding upon an eagle or a dragon, holding an arrow in his right hand as if he were about to shoot it into the head of that same eagle or dragon. They also made another image of Jupiter at the same favorable opportunity in a white and clear stone, especially in crystal: and it was a naked man, crowned, with hands raised and joined together as if praying, sitting in a four-legged chair <note>a throne or ceremonial seat</note> carried by four winged boys. They confirm that this image increases happiness, riches, and honor, and bestows benevolence and prosperity, and frees one from enemies. They made yet another image of Jupiter for a religious and glorious life, as well as for the favor of fortune: its figure was a man having the head of a lion or a ram, and the feet of an eagle, dressed in saffron garments; and he was called the son of Jupiter.

## ON the images of Mars. Chapter XL.

**FROM** the works of Mars, they made an image in the hour of Mars, while he was rising in the second <term>face: a ten-degree division of a zodiac sign, also known as a decan</term> of Aries, in a Martial stone, especially in a diamond <note>original: "adamante" — while this means diamond, in Renaissance magic it often referred to any extremely hard stone or even magnetite</note>. Its form was an armed man riding upon a lion, holding a naked, upright sword in his right hand, and carrying the head of a man in his left. They say such an image makes a man powerful in both good and evil, so that he will be feared by all; and to the one who wears it, they attribute the power of fascination <note>The ability to bind or influence others through a gaze or presence</note>, so that he terrifies people with his look when he is angry, and strikes them into a stupor. They made another image of Mars to bestow boldness, courage, and fortune in wars and quarrels: its form was an armed and crowned soldier, girded with a sword, carrying a long spear in his right hand; and they made it in the hour of Mars, with the first face of Scorpio rising with him.

## ON the images of the Sun. Chapter XLI.

**FROM** the works of the Sun, they made an image in the hour of the Sun, with the first face of Leo rising with the Sun: its form was a crowned king sitting on a throne, having a raven in his lap, and a globe under his feet, dressed in a saffron garment. They say this image makes a man invincible and honored, and brings undertakings to a conclusion, and drives away vain dreams, and is even effective against fevers and the plague. They made this same image in a balas ruby <note>original: "balayo" — a pale red variety of spinel often used in medieval and Renaissance jewelry</note> or a ruby, in the hour of the Sun, when he fortunately rises in his exaltation. They made another image of the Sun in a diamond, in the hour of the Sun, as he rises in his exaltation: its figure was a crowned woman with a dancing and laughing gesture, standing in a chariot drawn by four horses, holding a mirror or a shield in her right hand, and a staff leaning against her breast in her left...

### On the images of Venus. Cap. XLII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' within a rectangular woodcut frame featuring floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
**FROM** the works of Venus, they used to make an image that was suitable for obtaining grace and benevolence during the hour of Venus, while she was rising in Pisces. Its form was the image of a woman having the head of a bird and the feet of an eagle, holding an arrow in her hand. They made another image of Venus for the love of women on a lapis lazuli stone during the hour of Venus while she was rising in Taurus; its figure was a naked girl with flowing hair, holding a mirror in her hand and a chain tied around her neck, and next to her a handsome youth holding her by the chain with his left hand, while with his right hand he arranges her hair. Let them both be looking at each other amiably, and around them let there be a small winged boy <note>a representation of Cupid or an Eros</note> holding a sword or an arrow. They made another image of Venus in the first face of Taurus, or Libra, or Pisces, with Venus rising; its figure was a girl with flowing hair, dressed in long white robes, holding a laurel branch, or an apple, or flowers in her right hand, and a comb in her left. It is said to make a man peaceful, joyful, strong, and cheerful, and to bestow beauty.

### On the images of Mercury. Cap. XLIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' within a rectangular woodcut frame featuring floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
**FROM** the works of Mercury, they used to make an image during the hour of Mercury, while he was rising in Gemini. Its form was a handsome bearded youth having a <term>caduceus: the traditional staff of Mercury/Hermes, featuring two entwined serpents</term> in his left hand—that is, a rod in which a serpent is coiled—and carrying an arrow in his right, with winged feet. They say this image bestows knowledge, eloquence, and skill in merchandise and profit; furthermore, it reconciles peace and harmony, and cures fevers. They made another image of Mercury while he was rising in Virgo, for benevolence, intellect, and memory; its form was a man sitting upon a chair or riding a peacock, having eagle's feet and a crest on his head, and holding a cock or a fire in his left hand.

### On the images of the Moon. Cap. XLIIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' within a rectangular woodcut frame featuring floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
**FROM** the works of the Moon, they used to make an image for travelers against weariness during the hour of the Moon, while she was rising in her <term>exaltation: the zodiac sign where a planet's influence is strongest; for the Moon, this is Taurus</term>. Its figure was a man leaning upon a staff, having a bird on his head and a flowering tree before him. They made another image of the Moon for the increase of the fruits of the earth, and against poisons and the infirmities of children, during the hour of the Moon while she was rising in the first face of Cancer. Its figure was a horned woman riding upon a bull, or a seven-headed dragon, or a crab; she should have an arrow in her right hand and a mirror in her left, dressed in white or green robes, and having two serpents coiled around the horns on her head, one serpent coiled around each arm, and likewise one around each foot. And let these things said concerning the figures of the planets be sufficient.

### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon’s dragon. Chapter 45.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</image-desc>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon <note>original: "capitis & caudæ draconis Lunæ"—referring to the North and South Nodes of the Moon, where its orbit intersects the ecliptic</note>; specifically, the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter theta <note>original: "thita" (Θ). The serpent biting its tail is a common symbol for the Nodes in Renaissance magic.</note>. They made this when Jupiter, along with the Head <note>The North Node, or "Caput Draconis"</note>, held the <term>midheaven: the highest point of the zodiac at the time of the calculation</term>. They affirm that this image contributes greatly to the success of petitions. They intended to represent a good and happy <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or celestial entity, not necessarily an evil "demon"</term> through this image, and they chose to figure it as a serpent. Indeed, the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this animal as divine above all others, noting its divine nature because there exists within it a sharper spirit and a more abundant fire than in other animals. This is shown by its swift movement without any feet or hands or other limbs, and because it periodically renews its age and grows young again by shedding its skin.

However, they made the image of the Tail <note>The South Node, or "Cauda Draconis"</note> in a similar fashion when the Moon was eclipsed in the Tail, or was poorly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made this to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an "evil genius" <note>original: "malum genium"—a malevolent spirit or influence</note>. A certain Hebrew man had enclosed such an image in a golden double-belt which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first King of Spain of that name <note>Peter of Castile, known as "the Cruel" (1334–1369). Historical legend suggests he abandoned his wife Blanche almost immediately, with some accounts blaming a cursed belt.</note> (whether she was aware of it or was ignorant). When he was girded with it, it seemed to him that he was cinched by a serpent. Once the magic power inserted into the belt was discovered, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chapter 46.

They also made images in the individual <term>mansions of the moon: 28 divisions of the zodiac through which the Moon travels daily</term>. 

In the **first** mansion, for the destruction of someone, they made on an iron ring the image of a black man clothed and girded in hair-cloth <note>original: "cilicio"—a coarse garment made of goat's hair, worn for penance</note>, throwing a small spear with his right hand. They sealed this in black wax, smoked it with liquid storax <note>a fragrant resin</note>, and made imprecations. 

In the **second**, against the wrath of a prince and for reconciliation with him, they sealed in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and smoked it with aloeswood. 

In the **third**, they made an image on a silver ring of square measure, the figure of which was a well-dressed woman sitting in a chair, with her right hand raised over her head. They sealed it and smoked it with musk, camphor, and "aromatic claw" <note>original: "ungula aromatica"—likely the operculum of certain sea snails, used in incense</note>. They asserted that this bestowed prosperity of fortune and every good thing. 

In the **fourth**, for revenge, separation, enmity, and ill-will, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and smoked it with red myrrh and storax. 

In the **fifth**, for the favor of kings and officials and for a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and smoked it with sandalwood. 

In the **sixth**, to place love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and smoked them with aloeswood and amber. 

In the **seventh**, to acquire every good thing, they sealed in silver the image of a well-dressed man, with hands stretched toward heaven for...

In the seventeenth <note>Al-Iklil, "The Crown"</note> against thieves and robbers, they engraved with an iron seal the image of an ape, and they fumigated it with the hair of an ape. In the eighteenth <note>Al-Kalb, "The Heart"</note> against fevers and pains of the belly, they engraved on brass the image of a snake holding its tail above its head, and they fumigated it with the horn of a stag; they also carried this same seal to drive away serpents and all poisonous things from the place where it was buried. In the nineteenth <note>Al-Shaulah, "The Sting"</note> for easy childbirth and the provocation of menstruation, they engraved on brass the image of a woman holding her hands over her face, and they fumigated it with liquid <term>storax: a fragrant, balsamic resin</term>. In the twentieth <note>Al-Na'am, "The Ostriches"</note> for hunting, they engraved on tin the image of an archer who is half-man and half-horse, and they fumigated it with the head of a fox. ### On the images of the Behenian fixed stars. Chapter XLVII.

Furthermore, now concerning the operations of the fixed stars, according to the opinion of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many foundational texts of alchemy and astrology were attributed</note>, under the head of Algol <note>the "Demon Star" in the constellation Perseus</note>, they made an image whose figure was the head of a man with a long beard, having a bloody neck. They say it brings about the success of petitions, makes the bearer bold and magnanimous, preserves the limbs of the body unharmed, protects against witchcraft, and reflects evil attempts and malicious incantations back upon the adversary. Under the constellation of the Pleiades <note>The Seven Sisters in Taurus</note>, they made the image of a virgin girl, or the figure of a lamp. It is said to increase the light of the eyes, gather demons, summon winds, and reveal secrets and hidden things. Under Aldebaran <note>the bright red "Eye of the Bull"</note>, they made an image in the likeness of God, or a flying man: it confers riches and honor. Under the Goat <note>original: "hirco," referring to the star Capella in the constellation Auriga</note>, they made an image whose figure was like a man wishing to rejoice with musical instruments. It makes the bearer graceful, honored, and exalted before kings and princes, and provides help against the pain of teeth. Under the Greater Dog <note>the star Sirius, the brightest in the night sky</note>, they made the image of a greyhound, or a virgin girl. It confers honor, benevolence, and the grace of men and aerial spirits: and it gives the power of pacifying and reconciling kings, princes, and other men. Under the Lesser Dog <note>the star Procyon</note>, they made the image of a rooster, or of three girls. It confers the grace of gods, spirits, and men: it gives power against witchcraft, and preserves health. Under the Heart of the Lion <note>the star Regulus</note>, they made the image of a lion, or a cat, or the figure of an honored man sitting in a chair. It makes a man temperate, removes anger, and gives grace. Under the Tail of the Great Bear <note>the star Alkaid</note>, they made the image of a pensive man, or a bull, or the figure of a calf. It is effective against incantations, and makes the bearer secure on journeys. Under the wing of the Crow <note>the star Algorab</note>, they made the image of a crow, or a snake, or
