It gives prosperity and increases wealth. These are the images of certain fixed stars, which they command to be engraved in their respective stones under their influence.

### Concerning geomantic figures, which are intermediate between images and characters, and a table of the same. Chapter 48.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring an ornate border and a scene with two figures conversing in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>

There are yet other figures, constructed through numbers and the positions of the stars, and assigned both to the elements and to the planets and signs. These are called **geomantic** <note>from "geomantia," a form of divination traditionally performed by making marks in the earth or sand</note>, because geomantic diviners reduce the points of their lot—cast through the excess of parity and imparity <note>the counting of "even" or "odd" dots to form a figure</note>—into these figures. When these figures are engraved or impressed under the dominion of their planets and signs, they also take on the virtue and power of images. These figures are, as it were, a middle ground between **images** <note>literal representational pictures</note> and **characters** <note>abstract symbols or sigils</note>. However, anyone who desires to know the natures, qualities, properties, conditions, significations, and <term>astrological outcomes: outcomes or predictions based on the stars; from the Greek "apotelesmata"</term> of these figures precisely should seek them out in the volumes of the geomancers. There are no more than sixteen of them in number, of which

### Concerning images whose form is not in the likeness of any celestial figure, but in the likeness of that which the operator’s mind desires. Chapter 49.

There is yet another way of making images, not according to the likeness of celestial figures, but according to the likeness of that which the operator's mind <note>original: "animus operantis"</note> desires, of which there are effigies and traces. Thus, for love we fashion images embracing one another; for discord, images striking one another; but to bring about calamity, destruction, or hindrance to a person, a house, a city, or any other thing, we fashion images that are distorted and broken in their limbs and parts, according to the likeness and figure of that thing which we wish to destroy or hinder. 

The Mages <note>original: "Magi"</note> command that when casting or carving these images, one should write upon them the name of the desired effect. This should be on the back when the effect is evil, such as destruction, and on the belly when it is good, such as love. Furthermore, on the forehead of the image, one should write the name of the species or the individual whom the image represents, or for whom—or against whom—it was made. Again, on the breast, write the name of the sign or the face <note>A "face" or decan is a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note> of the ascendant and its lord, as well as the characters <term>Characters: Occult symbols or "sigils" believed to represent the signatures of spirits or planets.</term> and the names of their angels. 

They also command that while fashioning the image, the incantation for the intended effect should not be kept silent. Indeed, Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent medieval philosopher and theologian; the *Speculum Astronomiae* mentioned here was a highly influential text on the morality of astrology and magic attributed to him.</note> affirms all these things in his *Mirror of Astronomy*. Once the images are finished according to their various powers, they are used in different ways: sometimes they are hung or bound to the body; sometimes they are buried under the earth or beneath a river; sometimes they are hung in a chimney over smoke, or from a tree to be moved by the wind; sometimes with the head upward, sometimes downward; and sometimes they are cast into boiling water or into fire. 

For they say that in the same way the makers of images affect the image itself, so do they bring similar sufferings upon those to whom the images are assigned, just as the operator's mind dictates. We read that Nectanebus the Mage <note>Nectanebo II, the last native pharaoh of ancient Egypt, who in medieval legend was reimagined as a powerful sorcerer and the secret father of Alexander the Great.</note> made wax images of ships with such skill and artifice that when he submerged the images in water, the ships of his enemies were similarly submerged and endangered in the sea. The celestial configurations <note>original: "constellationes"</note> to be observed for these and similar images are taught to us by that part of astrology which is written concerning elections <term>Elections: The practice of choosing the most astrologically auspicious time to begin a specific action or ritual.</term>.

### Concerning certain celestial observations, and the practice of some of these same images. Chapter 50.

Now I will tell you the observations of the celestial bodies which are required for the practice of some images of this kind. Thus, to make someone fortunate, we fashion an image in which these things are made fortunate: namely, the significator of life, the givers of life, the signs, and the planets. Furthermore, let us fortify the ascendant and the midheaven <note>original: "medium coeli," the highest point of the zodiac at the time of the ritual.</note> and their lords. Likewise, the position of the Sun and the position of the Moon, the Part of Fortune, and the lord of the conjunction or prevention <note>The new or full moon occurring just before the person's birth.</note> made before their birth, while depressing the malevolent planets. If, however, we wish to fashion an image for calamity, we shall do the opposite: and those things which...

Here we place fortunate influences, and in the same way unfortunate influences, by raising malevolent stars. Do the same to bring good fortune to a certain place, a region, a city, or a house. Likewise, for destroying or hindering any of the aforementioned things, let an image be made under the <term>Ascension: The specific zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the ritual.</term> of that thing which you wish to destroy or hinder. You shall then afflict <note>original: "infortunabis"</note> the lord of the house of life <note>The First House in an astrological chart, representing the physical body and existence.</note>, the lord of the ascendant, and the Moon; the lord of the house of the Moon, the lord of the house of the lord of the ascendant, and the tenth house and its lord. 

However, for the improvement of a place, set fortunate planets in its ascendant, and in the first, tenth, second, and eighth houses. You shall favor the lord of the ascendant and the lord of the house of the Moon. To drive away certain animals from specific places, so that they cannot breed, live, or remain there, let an image be made under the ascension of that animal which we wish to drive away, and in its likeness. For example, if we wish to drive away scorpions from a place, let an image of a scorpion be made while the sign of Scorpio is rising, with the Moon. You shall afflict the ascendant, its lord, and the lord of the house of Mars <note>Mars is the planetary ruler of Scorpio.</note>. You shall also afflict the lord of the ascendant in the eighth house <note>The eighth house is associated with death and endings.</note>; and let them be joined by a malevolent aspect, such as an opposition or a square. Let the name of the ascendant, its lord, the name of the Moon, the name of the lord of the day, and the name of the lord of the hour be inscribed upon the image. Then, let a pit be made in the middle of the place from which you wish to expel them; bring into it earth taken from the four corners of that same place, and bury the image there, head downwards, imprecating or pronouncing: "This is the burial of scorpions, so that they may not enter this place." Do the same for similar creatures.

Also, for profit, let an image be made under the ascendant of a person's birth, or under the ascension of that place to which you wish to grant profit. Favor the ascendant and its lord, and make the lord of the second house—which is the house of substance <note>The Second House governs personal wealth and possessions.</note>—joined with the lord of the ascendant in a <term>Trine or Sextile: Harmonious astrological angles of 120 or 60 degrees, believed to facilitate the flow of energy.</term>. Let there be <term>Reception: A condition where two planets are in each other's signs of dignity, indicating mutual support.</term> between them. You shall favor the eleventh house, its lord, and the eighth. If you are able, place the <term>Part of Fortune: A calculated point in a chart representing prosperity and well-being.</term> in the ascendant or the second house. Let the image be buried in that place, or carried by the person to whom we wish to grant profit.

Also, for concord and love, let an image be made on the day of Jupiter <note>Thursday</note>, under the ascendant of the birth of the one you wish to be loved. Favor the ascendant and the tenth house, and hide the evil planets from the ascendant. Have the lords of the tenth and eleventh houses be fortunate planets, joined to the lord of the ascendant by a trine or sextile with reception. Then make another image, specifically for the person you wish to incite to love. Consider if they are a friend or companion of the one you wish to be loved; if so, let the image be made under the ascension of the eleventh house from the ascendant of the first image. If it is a wife or husband, let it be under the ascension of the seventh house. If a brother, sister, or blood relative, let it be under the ascension of the third house; and so for similar cases. Place the <term>Significator: The specific planet chosen to represent a person or thing in a chart.</term> of the ascendant of the second image joined to the significator of the ascendant of the first image. Let there be reception between them, and let other factors be fortunate, as in the first image. Afterward, join both images together in an embrace, or place the face of the second image to the back of the first image. Let them be wrapped in fine linen and carried, or buried.

### Concerning characters which are fashioned according to the norm and imitation of the celestial bodies, and how they are derived from Geomantic figures, with a table of the same.

->Chapter 51.<-

Characters also have their commonality from the rays of the celestial bodies, cast into one another according to a certain number by a certain peculiar property. Just as these celestial bodies conspire toward diverse virtues through the various strikes of their rays falling upon each other in different ways, so also characters—drawn in different ways according to the diverse concurrences of such rays—suddenly obtain diverse operations. These are often much more effective than the properties of purely physical mixtures. But the true characters of the heavens are the very script of the angels, which among the Hebrews is called the script of <term>Malachim: A "celestial alphabet" where the positions of stars are connected to form letters, used for divine communication.</term>, through which all things in heaven are described and signified for anyone who knows how to read. But concerning these, more in later parts. Now, however, they also fashion characters from <term>Geomantic figures: Patterns of dots used in earthly divination which correspond to astrological influences.</term>, binding the points of each together in various ways, and attributing them to those planets and signs according to the logic of the same configurations from which they were formed; the following table will explain their construction.

### Chapter 52. Concerning characters which are drawn from the things themselves by a certain likeness.

<margin>What characters are.</margin>
We have stated above that there is a certain method of creating images, not based on the likeness of celestial forms, but according to the imitation of that which the soul of the practitioner desires. This same reasoning must also be understood regarding certain <term>characters: symbolic marks or glyphs used in magic to represent specific forces.</term> <note>original: "characteribus"</note>. Indeed, characters of this kind are nothing other than "disjointed" images, yet they possess a probable likeness to a celestial image, or to that which the practitioner’s soul desires—whether that likeness is drawn from the whole image or from a specific mark that represents the entire thing. For example, we form the characters of Aries and Taurus from their horns, like so: ♈, ♉. Gemini from an embrace: ♊. Cancer from its forward and backward movement: ♋. Leo, Scorpio, and Capricorn from their tails: ♌, ♏, ♑. Virgo from the ear of grain: ♍. Libra from the scales: ♎. Sagittarius from the arrow: ♐. Aquarius from the waves: ♒. And Pisces from the fish: ♓. By similar reasoning, the character of Saturn is drawn from a scythe: ♄. Jupiter from a scepter: ♃. Mars from a dart: ♂. The Sun from roundness and golden brilliance: ☉. Venus from a mirror: ♀. Mercury from a caduceus: ☿. The Moon from the horns of its waxing and waning: ☽. 

From these, characters are subsequently composed according to the mixtures of signs, stars, and natures. For example, for the <term>fiery triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</term> <note>original: "triplicitatis igneæ"</note> <image-desc>hook-like character</image-desc>. Earthy: <image-desc>coiled character with a tail</image-desc>. Airy: <image-desc>loop and wave character</image-desc>. Watery: <image-desc>multi-limbed linear character</image-desc>. Likewise, according to the one hundred and twenty conjunctions of the planets, just as many complex or composite characters result from multiple figures. For example, Saturn and Jupiter are joined like this: <image-desc>combined glyph of Saturn and Jupiter</image-desc> or this: <image-desc>alternative combined glyph of Saturn and Jupiter</image-desc>. Saturn and Mars: <image-desc>combined glyph of Saturn and Mars</image-desc> or this: <image-desc>alternative combined glyph of Saturn and Mars</image-desc>. Jupiter and Mars: <image-desc>combined glyph of Jupiter and Mars</image-desc> or this: <image-desc>alternative combined glyph of Jupiter and Mars</image-desc>. Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars: <image-desc>combined glyph of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</image-desc> or this: <image-desc>alternative triple combined glyph</image-desc>. 

And just as these examples use two or three planets, characters should also be formed for the others and for larger groups. By the same logic, characters for other celestial images in any "face" or degree of the ascending signs should be drawn as concisely as possible to resemble the image. This follows the path of imitation toward what the practitioner’s soul desires: for love, the figures should be mixed together, embracing and obeying one another; for hatred, conversely, they should be turning away, attacking, mismatched, and dissolved. Finally, we shall not hesitate to display here the characters that <term>Hermes: referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermetic philosophy.</term> assigned to the fixed stars and <term>Behenian stars: a selection of fifteen stars considered especially powerful in medieval magic.</term> <note>original: "beheniis"</note>. CXCVIII.

->OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,<-

# That no divination is perfect without astrology.
## Chapter LIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial L featuring a seated scholar in a robe, holding a book, set within a square frame with floral and architectural ornamentation.</image-desc>

We have spoken in the preceding chapters about various kinds of divinations: but it must be observed that all these require the use and rules of astrology, as a key absolutely necessary for the knowledge of all secrets. All kinds of divinations, whatever they may be, have their roots and foundations in astrology itself, so that without this they seem to bring little or nothing. Yet the astrological dominion itself—insofar as the celestial bodies are the causes and signs of all those things which exist and happen in these lower realms—provides the most certain demonstrations of whatever is hidden or future from the position and motion of the celestial bodies alone. The present place does not require more to be said about this, since immense volumes have been written by the ancients on this science, and they stand openly for everyone. Therefore, whether a <term>physiognomist</term> <note>original: "physionomus"; a practitioner who judges character or destiny from physical features</note> examines the body, or the face, or the forehead, or the hand; or whether an interpreter has scrutinized a dream or an omen; if the judgment is to be correct, the <term>figure of the heavens</term> <note>original: "cœli figura"; a horoscope or astrological chart cast for a specific moment</note> must likewise be scrutinized. From its indications, together with the conjectures of similarities and signs, true opinions of the things signified may be born.

Moreover, if some <term>prodigy</term> <note>original: "prodigium"; an unnatural or omen-like event, such as a comet or a strange birth</note> appears, the figure of the heavens must be erected. Those things that preceded in the revolutions of the years must also be scrutinized, specifically from great conjunctions and eclipses. Then also the nativities, origins, enthronements, foundations, revolutions, progressions, and directions of the princes, nations, kingdoms, and cities where these appeared must be considered, and in which place of the celestial figure each of these has fallen. From all these, we may finally hunt for the reasonable and most probable significance of these things. They claim that the same sequence, though with less labor, must be followed in the interpretations of dreams. Furthermore, those who predict the future while <term>alienated by frenzy</term> <note>original: "furore alienati"; referring to prophetic trances or divine madness</note> do so only when agitated through the stars or their lower instruments; whence their prophecies are finally also to be adapted to the celestial things, just as we read in Lucan concerning the <term>Tuscan Seer</term> <note>Refers to the Etruscan diviner Arruns in Lucan’s epic poem "Pharsalia"</note>:

> Taught the movements of the lightning, and the warm veins
> Of the entrails, and the movements of the wing wandering in the air.
> <note>original: "Fulminis edoctum motus, uenasq́; calentes / Fibrarum, & motus errantis in aere pennæ." (Lucan, Pharsalia 1.587-588)</note>

After the city had been purified, after the victim sacrificed, after the entrails inspected, finally the sentence was pronounced from the dispositions of the celestial stars. Indeed, even <term>geomancy</term> <note>original: "geomātia"; a method of divination using marks on the ground, which Agrippa here links to the sixteen astrological figures</note> itself—the most accurate of lot-castings, which divines through points of the earth or another surface, inscribed either by chance or by some force—first reduces those to celestial figures: namely, to those sixteen which we named above. From their properties and reasons, it forms a judgment in the astrological manner. And to this end belong whatever divining tools of natural lot-castings exist: whose power can come from nowhere else than from heaven and from the mind of the one performing it. For whatever is moved, agitated, or produced in these lower realms by any motion, must necessarily imitate the motions and influences of the higher things, to which

as if to roots, causes, and signs; when the matter has been reduced to these, it then indicates its meaning to us according to astrological rules. Hence, tokens and the <term>Platonic solids</term> <note>These are the five regular polyhedra: the four-sided tetrahedron, the six-sided hexahedron (cube), the eight-sided octahedron, the twelve-sided dodecahedron, and the twenty-sided icosahedron.</note>—the tetrahedron, hexahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron—are fashioned and inscribed with specific numbers, signs, and stars at favorable times under celestial influences. When cast, they possess a wonderful power for divining and predicting, much like those **Praenestine lots** <note>original: "Pręnestinæ tesseræ"; ancient Roman oracle tokens used at the Temple of Fortuna Primigenia in Praeneste</note> in which the fates of the Romans were said to be contained.

->On lots, and when and from where their power of<-
->divination arises. Chapter LIV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a winged putto or spirit within a square frame.</image-desc>
Whatever divinations or predictions of human events are made through **lots** <note>original: "sortem"; the practice of casting lots or sortilege</note>, it is necessary that they have some sublime, hidden, and occult cause beyond mere chance. This will certainly not be an <term>accidental cause</term> <note>original: "causa per accidens"; in Aristotelian philosophy, an incidental or chance occurrence that lacks a direct, purposeful intention</note>, as Aristotle described fortune. Indeed, in the series of causes—since according to the **Platonists** an accidental cause can never be a primary or sufficient cause—it is necessary for us to look higher and find a cause that knows and intends the effect itself. We must place this cause not in corporeal nature, but in immaterial and incorporeal substances which truly administer the lot and dispense it as an indication of truth. These may be in human souls, or separate spirits and **daemons** <note>original: "dæmonibus"; here referring to intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note>, or in celestial intelligences, or in God himself. 

That there can be sufficient power and virtue in the human soul to direct such lots is evident because there resides in our soul a divine power and likeness, as well as the apprehension and power over all things. And as we said in the first book, all things have a natural obedience to the soul; by necessity, they possess motion and efficacy toward that which the soul desires with a strong longing. All virtues and operations of things, both natural and artificial, obey the soul when it is carried into an **excess of desire** <note>original: "excessum sui desiderii"; a state of intense focus or heightened spiritual state where the soul's will influences physical reality</note>. All lots of whatever kind then assist the appetite of such a soul and acquire for themselves wonderful powers of prophecy—both from the soul itself and from the celestial opportunity of that hour in which the excess of desire most strongly invades it. 

This same reasoning is also the root of all **astrological questions** <note>original: "astrologicarum quæstionum"; referring to horary astrology, where a chart is cast for the moment a question is asked</note>. For the soul, elevated into an excess of desire, seizes for itself the most convenient and effective hour and opportunity. When a figure of the heavens is constructed for that moment, the astrologer can judge and clearly know the answer to what the seeker wishes to discover. However, because lots are directed not always by the human soul, but also (as we said) by the ministry of other spirits, and because the mind of the diviner is not always disposed toward that excess of passion we mentioned, it was the custom among the ancients to perform certain sacred rites before casting lots. By these, they called upon divine intelligences and spirits to rightly direct the lot. Therefore, however much prophecy such lots portend, it must not happen by chance or fortune, but by a spiritual cause, by whose power the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note> or the hand of the one casting the lot is moved...

By these verses, his hope of obtaining the empire did not turn out to be in vain. Similarly, among the Hebrews and even among us Christians—with certain theologians not disapproving—lots are taken from the verses of the **Psalms**. There are many other kinds of lots, and there are human lots which possess no power of divination but were observed among the ancients and among us, and even recommended by laws for choosing magistrates to avoid envy. **Cicero** also made mention of these in his oration *Against Verres*; however, those do not fall under our current purpose. Truly, as for those divine and sacred lots that pertain to oracles and religion, we shall discuss them in the following book. For now, let me advise you that however much presage, divination, or guidance lots are found to possess, they do not have it because they are "lots," but through the power of some **sublimer operation** <note>Agrippa suggests the physical tokens are just tools for a higher spiritual or psychological force.</note> joined to them.

### On the soul of the world and of the celestial bodies, according to the traditions of the poets and philosophers. Chapter LV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a human figure, possibly a child or scholar, seated and gesturing within an ornamental frame.</image-desc>
Since the heavens and the celestial bodies possess power, influence, and manifest operation upon these lower things, it is necessary that they be **animated** <note>original: "animata"; meaning "possessed of a soul" or "living."</note>. Indeed, an operation can by no means proceed from a purely physical body. Therefore, all the most noble poets and philosophers affirm that the world itself has a soul, and the celestial bodies likewise, and that this soul is **intelligent**. Hence, **Marcus Manilius**, in his *Astronomica* addressed to Augustus, sings:

<margin>Manilius</margin>
> This work, constructed from the body of the immense world,
> And the members of nature established in diverse forms—
> Of air and fire, of earth and the lying sea—
> A divine power of soul rules; and by a sacred path
> God breathes together with it, and governs it with silent reason.

<margin>Lucan</margin>

For what else do these verses seem to intend, but that the world not only possesses a spirit and a soul, but even participates in the divine mind? They suggest that the origin, power, and vigor of all lower things depend upon the soul of the world itself. This is what all the **Platonists**, the **Pythagoreans**, **Orpheus**, **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note>, **Aristotle**, **Theophrastus**, **Avicenna**, **Al-Ghazali**, and all the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> confess and confirm.

->The same is confirmed by reason.<-

## Chapter LVI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring a landscape with a classical building and a figure, possibly a shepherd or traveler, in the foreground.</image-desc>
The world has a soul; the heavens, the stars, and the elements have a soul, with which they cause a soul in these lower and mixed things. They also possess a spirit, as we said in the first book, which is present in the body by means of its soul. For since the whole body of the world is a certain body whose parts are the bodies of all living beings—and insofar as the whole is more perfect and noble than its parts—the body of the world is more perfect and noble than the body of any individual living creature. It would be absurd if every imperfect little body, every tiny part of the world, and even the most lowly animals, such as flies and little worms, were worthy of life, possessed life, and had a soul, while the world itself, an intact, most perfect, total, and most noble body, neither lived nor had a soul. 

It is no less absurd to think that the heavens, the stars, and the elements, which most generously provide life and soul to individual things, should themselves lack life and soul; and that any plant or tree should be of a nobler condition than the heaven, the stars, and the elements, which are naturally their cause. For who, unless they are devoid of life themselves, would deny that the earth and water live, which of themselves generate, vivify, nourish, and increase innumerable trees, plants, and living beings? This appears most clearly in those things born spontaneously <note>original: "sponte nascentibus"; referring to the pre-modern belief in spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from decaying matter or elemental forces without parents.</note>, and in those where corporal seeds are lacking. For the elements could not generate and nourish living things of this kind if they themselves lacked life and a soul. Perhaps some will say—

...who [argue] that living things of this kind are produced not by the soul of the earth or water, but from the influences of celestial souls. To these the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who emphasized the reality of spiritual forms over material things.</note> respond that an accident <term>accident: a non-essential quality or property of a thing (like its color or heat) that cannot exist on its own without a "substance."</term> cannot generate a substance, unless perhaps it is subjected as an instrument of a proximate substance. They say "proximate substance" because an instrument removed from the craftsman is not moved toward the intended effect of the art. Thus, those celestial influences, since they are certain accidents far removed from their own vital substances or from life itself, will not generate a vital substance in these lower things. 

<margin>In the General Treatise <note>original: "In Trac: de com:"; likely referring to the *Libellus Communis*, a part of the *Corpus Hermeticum* attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note></margin>
And Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of Hermetic philosophy and magic.</note>, in the Treatise which he titled "On Common Things," says: "The whole is in the world; it moves either by growing or decreasing. That which moves, lives for that reason; and since all things move—even the earth, especially by generative and transformative motion—it also lives." 

<margin>Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle, known for his works on botany and metaphysics.</note></margin>
If anyone should doubt that the heavens live, says Theophrastus, he is not considered a philosopher; and he who denies that the heaven is animated, so that its mover is not its form, destroys the foundations of all philosophy. Therefore the world lives, and has a soul and sense; since it gives life to plants which are not born from seed, and provides sense to animals which are not born through copulation <note>Agrippa refers to the historical belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to emerge from decaying matter through the influence of the stars.</note>.

->That the soul of the world and celestial souls are rational,<-
->and participants in the divine mind.<-
### Chapter LVII.

THAT the souls we have mentioned also possess reason is clear from this: for since all the works of the said souls harmonize with one another in a perpetual order, it is necessary that they be governed not by chance but by reason, by which reasons they direct and lead all their operations to certain ends. For it is necessary that the earth possess the "reasons" <note>In the Platonic sense, "reasons" (rationes) are the formative spiritual blueprints or "logoi" that govern how physical things take shape.</note> of earthly things, and water of watery things; similarly in the others, by which individual things are procreated in their own time, place, and order, and often, when damaged, are recreated. Therefore, philosophers do not judge the soul of the earth to be like the lowly soul of just any body, but to be rational, and moreover to understand, and to be a goddess. Furthermore, it would be absurd if, while we possess the reasons for our own works, the celestial souls and the very soul of the universe did not possess the reasons for theirs. 

<margin>Plato in the Timaeus <note>original: "Plato in Ti:"; Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation and structure of the physical world.</note></margin>
But if (as Plato says) the world could be made as good as possible by Good itself, and has been so made, it will certainly be a participant not only in life, sense, and reason, but also in intelligence and mind. Since the soul is the perfection of the body, and that body is more perfect which has a more perfect soul, it is necessary that since celestial bodies are most perfect, they also have the most perfect souls. They are, therefore, participants in intellect and mind, which the Platonists also prove from the perseverance of their order and course: because motion, since it is free by its nature, can easily go astray and wander about in turn, unless it is governed by intellect and mind—and indeed a perfect one, foreseeing the most choice path and the best end from the beginning. This perfect mind, because it is most powerfully present to the soul (such as the soul of the world, and the souls of the celestial bodies and elements), doubtless [leads] most orderly and perfectly toward...

### On the names of celestial souls, and their dominion over this lower world, namely man. Chapter 58.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' showing a scholar or author seated at a desk surrounded by books and writing tools.</image-desc>Now, the names of the celestial souls are quite numerous and diverse, according to their multifaceted power and virtue over these lower things. They have been given various names which the ancients used in their hymns and invocations. Regarding this, it should be noted that every soul of this kind, according to Orphic theology <note>A mystical tradition attributed to the legendary poet Orpheus, emphasizing the divine origin of the soul and the use of music and ritual to connect with the gods.</note>, is said to have a double power: one placed in knowing, and the other situated in giving life to and governing its own body. In this way, in the celestial spheres, Orpheus calls that former power Bacchus, and the latter he calls a Muse. Hence, no one is intoxicated by any Bacchus who has not first been joined to his own Muse. Thus, nine Bacchi are designated around nine Muses.

Therefore, in the ninth sphere <note>The highest celestial sphere in the old model of the universe, often called the Primum Mobile or First Mover.</note>, Orpheus places the Bacchus "the Winnower" <note>original: "Cribronium"</note> and the Muse Calliope. In the starry sky, Bacchus Picionius and the Muse Urania. In the heaven of Saturn, Bacchus Amphietus and the Muse Polyhymnia. In the heaven of Jupiter, Bacchus Sabazius and the Muse Terpsichore. In the heaven of Mars, Bacchus Bassarius and the Muse Clio. In the heaven of the Sun, Bacchus Trietericus and the Muse Melpomene. In the heaven of Venus, Bacchus Lysius and the Muse Erato. In the heaven of Mercury, Bacchus Silenus and the Muse Euterpe. In the heaven of the Moon, Bacchus Lyaeus and the Muse Thalia.

Similarly, in the spheres of the elements, he names the souls in this way: In fire, he places Phaneta and Aurora. In air, Jupiter the Thunderer and Juno. In water, Oceanus and Tethys. In earth, Pluto and Proserpina. The Magi <note>Ancient practitioners of wisdom and magic, particularly from the Persian tradition.</note> call the World Soul (the soul of the whole universe) the Mundane Jove; the World Mind they call Apollo; and the nature of the world, Minerva. Furthermore, in fire, they name Vulcan; in water, Neptune; and they addressed them by various names.

Among the stars of the zodiac, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that numbers and celestial harmonies were the keys to understanding reality.</note> also placed twelve particular gods, or souls, situated in the "hearts" of these signs, and from there governing the entire constellation. Specifically: in the heart of Aries, Pallas; in the heart of Taurus, Venus; of Gemini, Phoebus; of Cancer, Mercury; of Leo, Jupiter; of Virgo, Ceres; of Libra, Vulcan; of Scorpio, Mars; of Sagittarius, Diana; of Capricorn, Vesta; of Aquarius, Juno; and in the heart of Pisces, Neptune. Manilius sings of this in these verses:

<margin>Manilius <note>Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century AD Roman poet and author of the *Astronomica*, a poem on astrology.</note></margin>
> Pallas protects the Wool-bearer [Aries], the Cytherean [Venus] the Bull,
> Fair Phoebus the twins [Gemini], the Cyllenian [Mercury] the Crab,
> Jupiter himself, with the Mother of the Gods, rules the Lion.
> The Virgin [Virgo] belongs to grain-bearing Ceres, and the forged Scales [Libra]...
<note>original: "Lanigerum Pallas, taurum Cytherea tuetur / Formosus Phœbus geminos, Cyllenius cancrum / Iupiter & cum matre deum regit ipse leonem / Spiciferę est uirgo Cereris, fabricataq; libra"</note>

And the most ancient Orpheus himself, writing to Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and disciple of Orpheus in Greek mythology.</note>, enumerates even more of these celestial powers than those mentioned above, assigning to them various names, roles, and duties, and addressing each with their own specific hymns. Therefore, let no one think these are the names of evil and deceiving demons; rather, they are the names of natural and divine virtues, distributed throughout the world by the true God for the service and benefit of humanity—at least for those who know how to use them. Antiquity itself assigned individual members of the human body to each of these powers: for instance, the ear to memory, which Virgil also dedicates to Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, saying: "Cynthius <note>An epithet for Apollo, referring to his birthplace on Mount Cynthus.</note> pulled my ear and warned me." <note>original: "Cynthius aurem Vellit & admonuit," from Virgil's Eclogues.</note> In the same way, Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious rites.</note>, as Livy relates, consecrated the right hand to Faith, as it is the seal of fortitude and the hand by which oaths are sworn. The fingers are under the protection of Minerva, and the knees are given to Mercy. For this reason, people bend their knees when seeking pardon. Some dedicate the navel to Venus as the seat of luxury. Others, who refer all members to the center itself, claim the navel is consecrated to Jupiter. Hence, in the temple of Jupiter Hammon <note>A major deity combining the Greek Zeus/Jupiter and the Egyptian Amun, whose oracle was in the Libyan desert.</note>, the image of a navel was celebrated. The ancients followed many other details, assigning even the smallest members and joints to their own specific powers. If these are understood correctly, and the true presiding powers are recognized, none of these associations are foreign to proper piety; for even the sacred scriptures testify that all our members are ruled by celestial virtues, which we shall discuss more extensively in the following book. Not only members, but all human activities are distributed among their own powers: such as hunting to Diana, war to Pallas [Athena], and agriculture to Ceres. Regarding these, Apollo speaks thus in the oracles found in Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who preserved many ancient oracles.</note>:

He is called **Dionysius** in the night, but **Apollo** in the day, as if he were the one "driving away evils." He is called the Sun <note>original: "Sol"</note> because he contains the light of all the stars; hence he is called *Adad* by the Assyrians, which signifies "alone," and by the Hebrews *Schemesch* <note>original: "שמש", Shemesh</note>, which is interpreted as his proper name. <margin>Venus.</margin> **Venus** is called lady, nourishing, shapely, starry, white, beautiful, placid, multi-powerful, the fruitful lady of love and beauty, the progeny of the ages and the initial parent of humans, who at the first beginnings of <term>things</term> <note>original: "rerum"</note> joined the diversity of the sexes with a doubled love, and daily propagates the kinds of humans and animals with eternal offspring; the queen of all joys, the lady of gladness, the friendly leader, the friend, the merciful and of good reception, always perpetually beneficial to mortals, granting the sweet affection of a mother to the misfortunes of the wretched, the hostess of the human race, letting no moment of time pass without her benefits.

CCVII.

### BOOK SECOND.

<meta>catchword: world</meta>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the text, featuring an engraved landscape scene with a winding path or river leading toward distant hills under a sky with clouds.</image-desc>

Celestial souls <note>original: "aiẽ" / "animae"</note> pour their virtues into celestial bodies, which then transmit them to this sensible world: for from no other cause than the celestial do the virtues of the earthly sphere proceed. Hence the Magus <note>A practitioner of "natural magic," which involves understanding and utilizing the hidden laws of nature and the heavens.</note>, intending to operate through these virtues, uses a skillful invocation of the higher powers, with mysterious words and an ingenious speech, drawing one thing to another. This is done through a natural power and a certain mutual harmony between them, by which things follow of their own accord, or are sometimes drawn against their will. For this reason, Aristotle says in the sixth book of *Mystic Philosophy* <note>Agrippa refers to the *Theology of Aristotle*, a Neoplatonic work falsely attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>: that where anyone, by binding or fascinating <note>In this context, "binding" (ligatio) and "fascination" (fascinatio) refer to the technical magical practice of constraining or influencing a person or object through occult means.</note>, invokes the sun or other stars, praying that they might cooperate in a desired work, it is not the sun or other stars that hear that speech; rather, they are moved in some way by a certain natural connection and mutual sequence, by which the parts of the world are mutually subordinated to one another and have a mutual consensus because of their great union.

Just as in the human body, one member is moved by perceiving the movement of another; and as in a lute <note>original: "cithara"</note>, when one string is moved, another is also moved. Thus, when someone moves one
<margin>"</margin>
part of the world, others are also moved by perceiving the movement brought upon them. Therefore, the knowledge of the depen-
<margin>"</margin>
dency of things following one another is the foundation of every marvelous operation, which is ne-
<margin>"</margin>
cessarily required to exercise the power of attracting superior virtues. Moreover, the words of men are certain natural things: and because the parts of the world naturally draw one another and act mutually upon themselves, therefore the Magus, invoking through words, operates through the fit powers of nature, leading or drawing certain things by the love of one for another because of the sequence of one thing to another; or repelling them, because of the hatred of one for another, arising from the contrariety and difference of things and the multitude of virtues. Although these may be contrary or different, they nevertheless complete one whole; sometimes he even compels things by celestial virtue through a certain dominion, since he is not a stranger to heaven.

Therefore, if a man receives the impression of any binding or fas-
<margin>"</margin>

<margin>"</margin>
suffers according to his animal and sub-worldly part. For they cannot
<margin>"</margin>
draw the soul that knows and understands by reason, but only that part which conceives that impression and impulse through the sense, insofar as the animal spirit <note>term: "spiritus animalis" — In Renaissance physiology, the "animal spirits" were subtle fluids that carried sensations and commands between the brain and the body.</note> of man is affected by the celestial
<margin>"</margin>
influx and the cooperation of worldly things beyond its former or natural disposition. Just as a son moves a father to labors,
<margin>note.</margin>
even against his will, for the sake of preserving someone for whom the father might be weary; and the appetite for ruling moves others to anger and other labors for the sake of obtaining dominion. And the deficiency of nature, and the fear of poverty, move one to desire riches. And the adornment and beauty of a woman is an incitement to lust for her. And the harmony of a most wise musician <note>original: "fici" / "physici"</note> moves the listeners with various passions: some of whom follow the consonance of the art voluntarily, while others even conform themselves by gesture against their will, because their sense is captivated, while reason does not attend to these things.

But the common people do not wonder at these kinds of fascinations and bindings, nor do they detest them, because of their familiarity; however, they wonder at other physical ones because they are ignorant of them and are not accustomed to them. Hence they fall into errors, thinking those things to be above nature or against it, which are actually from nature and according to it. It must be known, therefore, that every supe-
<margin>"</margin>
rior moves its next inferior, in its own degree and order, not only in bodies but also in spirits. Thus the universal soul moves particular souls; and the rational soul acts upon the sensual, and that upon the vegetative: and every part of the world acts upon another, and each is fit to be moved by another; and every part of the world...

CCVIII.

### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

...of this lower world receives influence from the heavens according to its own nature and aptitude, just as one part of a living body receives influence from another. And the superior intellectual world moves all things below itself, since it contains all the same beings, from the first to the last, as the lower worlds. Therefore, celestial bodies move the bodies of the elementary world—those which are composite, capable of being generated, and perceptible to the senses—from the outer edge to the center. They do this through superior, eternal, and spiritual essences that hang from the primary intellect, which is the **active intellect** <term>active intellect: in Neoplatonic philosophy, the "Intellectus Agens" is a cosmic mind that radiates the power of thought and understanding into the human soul</term>. But they also move by a virtue implanted by God through his **Word** <note>original: "verbum," referring to the divine Logos or creative command</note>, which Word the Babylonian sages, the Chaldeans, call the **Cause of Causes** <note>original: "causam causarum"</note>, because all beings are produced from it; even the active intellect itself is secondary to it. This is due to the union of this Word with the first Author, from whom all existing things are truly produced. 

Therefore, that Word is the image of God; the active intellect is the image of the Word; the soul is the image of the intellect; but our own word is the image of the soul, through which it acts upon natural things in a natural way, since nature is the soul's work. And each of these perfects its successor as a father does a son; and no later thing exists without the prior. For they are dependent upon one another in an ordered chain, so that when a later thing is destroyed, it returns to the nearest prior thing, until it reaches the heavens, then the **universal soul** <term>universal soul: the "Anima Mundi," or a spiritual force that permeates and animates the entire universe</term>, then the active intellect—by which all other creatures exist—which itself exists in the principal Author, which is the creating Word, to which finally all things return.

<margin>What must be contemplated by one who wishes to perform a miraculous work.</margin>

Therefore, our soul, if it wishes to perform some miraculous work in these lower regions, must contemplate its own origin, so that it may be strengthened by it, enlightened, and receive the power of acting through each degree from the first Author himself. Effort must therefore be made so that we contemplate the *souls* of the stars more than their *bodies*: and the super-celestial intellectual world more than the celestial bodily world. For the former is more noble, even if the latter is distinguished and serves as a necessary preliminary to it—and without which middle ground, the **influx** <term>influx: the spiritual or astrological flow of power from higher spheres to lower ones</term> of that superior world cannot be attained. 

For example: the Sun, king of the stars and most full of light, receives that light from the intelligible world above all other stars, because its soul is more capable of receiving that intelligible splendor. Wherefore, he who desires to attract the influx of the Sun must contemplate the Sun not only by observing its outer light, but also its inner light. And this no one can do, unless they return to the very soul of the Sun, and become similar to it, and comprehend its intelligible light with intellectual vision, just as one sees sensible light with the physical eye. For such a person will be filled with its splendor and will receive into himself its light, which is a **prototype** <note>original: "hypotypus," an original model or impression</note> impressed from the supreme sphere. Clothed in this enlightenment, truly made equal to the Sun, and aided as if by a spiritual lift, he will attain that supreme clarity and all the forms participating in it according to the desire of his intellect. And when he has drunk the light of the highest degree, then his soul will approach its perfection, and be made like the spirits of the Sun; he will reach the virtues and enlightenments of supernatural power, and enjoy their potency, if he has found faith in the first Author. 

First, therefore, one must implore help and assent from the first Author himself; and that not with the mouth only, but also with religious gesture and a suppliant mind, praying abundantly, incessantly, and with integrity, that He may enlighten the mind and remove the darkness growing over souls because of the body.

# TO THE MOST EXALTED
## LORD, THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, HERMANN VON
### WIED, Prince-Elector, Duke of Westphalia and Angria, Lord
### and Archbishop of Cologne and Paderborn, his
### most gracious Lord, Heinrich Cornelius
### Agrippa von Nettesheim.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a landscape scene with a figure (possibly a traveler or shepherd), a river with a bridge, trees, and buildings with a prominent tower in the background.</image-desc>

IT IS A MOST NOBLE OPINION OF THE ANCIENT MAGI <term>Magi: ancient philosopher-priests of Persia, often associated in the Renaissance with deep wisdom and the study of both nature and the stars</term> (Most Illustrious Prince) that in this life we must labor at nothing more than that we should not degenerate in the least from the nobility of the soul—by which we come closest to God and put on a divine nature—lest at any time the soul, growing sluggish in empty idleness, should be dissolved into the fragility of the earthly body and the vices of the flesh, and we lose it, as if cast away through the dark precipices of perverse desires. Therefore, it is fitting that we so instruct the soul that it, being mindful of its own dignity and nobility, always thinks, does, and works at something worthy of itself. This, however, is solely and most greatly afforded to us by the knowledge of divine science: when, occupied always with divine studies by the remembrance of His majesty, we contemplate divine things through all the moments of the hours with sagacious and ever-watchful inquiry. Thus, ascending through the individual ranks of creatures even to the archetype <term>archetype: the original pattern or "First Cause" in the mind of God from which all things are modeled</term> itself, we draw from Him the inerrable virtue of all things. Those who neglect this, trusting only in natural and worldly things, are often prone to be confounded by various errors and deceptions, and very frequently deceived by evil demons.

The understanding of divine things, however, purges the mind of errors and renders it divine; it affords an infallible power to our works, and drives far away the frauds and obstacles of all evil demons. At the same time, it subjects them to our command and even compels the good angels and all the powers of the world into our service—namely, because the power of our works is drawn from the archetype itself. When we ascend to Him, it is necessary that every creature obey us, and the entire chorus of the heavens follows us. For (as Homer says) *No god would dare remain in his seat when Jove is moved* <note>original: "Nullus deorum ausit in suis sedibus permanere moto Ioue"</note>. And immediately then he rules (as Aristophanes says) through one of the gods, whom it is lawful to take up commands, who then, by his office, may carry out our petitions according to our wish. Since, therefore (Most Illustrious Prince), a divine and immortal soul has been given to you, and since the bounty of divine providence, a favorable fate, and the liberality of nature have so endowed you that you are able—with keenness of mind and soundness of senses—to look upon, scrutinize, contemplate, discern, and judge the pleasant spectacles of natural things, the sublime dwellings of the heavens, and the most difficult inner shrines <note>original: "adytus," referring to the innermost, most sacred part of a temple</note> of divine things: being bound to you by the necessity of your great virtues, I am your debtor, and even...

...erywhere, I have learned the mysteries of divine and ceremonial magic <term>Ceremonial Magic: The branch of magic involving rituals, the summoning of spirits, and the use of sacred names to reach the divine</term> without falsehood, I am communicating them through true definitions of thought without envy, not hiding their understanding. I have gathered what the ancient priests of the Egyptians (the servants of Isis <term>Isis: A major Egyptian goddess associated with magic and motherhood</term>), the ancient seers of the Chaldeans <term>Chaldeans: An ancient people of Mesopotamia famous for their advanced knowledge of astrology and the occult</term>, the divine wise men of the Hebrew Cabalists <term>Cabalists: Practitioners of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that seeks to understand the hidden relationship between the eternal God and the mortal universe</term>, as well as the Orphic, Pythagorean, and Platonic schools—the most profound philosophers of the Greeks—along with the Brahmans of the Indians, the Gymnosophists <term>Gymnosophists: Meaning "naked philosophers," a term used by the Greeks to describe ancient Indian or Ethiopian ascetics who lived in solitude and practiced severe self-discipline</term> of the Ethiopians, and the pure theologians of our own religion have handed down.

I have explained by what power of words, what potency of seals <term>Seals: Also called sigils, these are symbolic diagrams or signatures used in magic to represent and command spiritual forces</term>, what songs of blessings and curses, and what virtue of observations they once performed such astounding and admirable wonders. In this third book of *Occult Philosophy*, I intimate these things to you, bringing to light matters that have lain covered in the filth of antiquity and wrapped in the fog of forgetfulness as if in Cimmerian darkness <term>Cimmerian darkness: A proverbial expression for total darkness, named after the mythical Cimmerians who were said to live in a land of perpetual mist and gloom</term>.

I now return to you the full and complete work of *Occult Philosophy* or *Magic* in these three books, which I have finished with watchful care and with equal labor of mind and body, and with the greatest effort—though the style may be unrefined, the subject matter is clearly most difficult. Therefore, I wish to ask for this one pardon: that you do not look for the grace of oratory or elegance of speech in these books, which I wrote long ago in my youth when my speech was still crude and my oratory unformed. Now, I have only revised the sequence of thoughts, not the flow of the speech; for I have cared less for the elegance of words as the abundance of the material took its place. I believe I have fulfilled my duty well enough if I have performed to the best of my ability what I promised to report concerning the secrets of Magic, and if I have cleared my conscience of the debt I owe to you.

But since I have no doubt that many nosy sophists <term>Sophist: In this context, a person who uses clever but false arguments, specifically those who attack new ideas to preserve their own status</term> will conspire against me—those who boast that they are the "grandsons of God" and full of divinity, and who claim for themselves judgment over the leaves of the Sibyl <note>original: "Sybillæ foliis"; a reference to the Sibylline oracles written on leaves that were easily scattered by the wind, implying the critics' judgments are arbitrary or based on incomplete information</note>—they will attempt to judge and condemn these works of ours with a new fire. This is because the "lettuce does not suit their lips" <note>original: "dissimiles suis labris lactucas"; a Latin proverb meaning that something is not to one's specific taste or is too sophisticated for them</note> and the marjoram is unfamiliar to their nostrils, and also because of the sparks of hatred once conceived against me that lie poorly hidden under the ashes. They will attack even before they have read any of it or understood it correctly at all. 

Therefore (Most Illustrious Prince and wisest Prelate), this work, dedicated to you by the merit of your virtues and now made yours, I further submit to your censorship and commend to your protection. If wicked and treacherous sophists, in the gross insanity of envy and slander, wish to gnaw at it, you may happily protect and defend it with the clarity of your discernment and the fairness of your judgment. Farewell most happily.

For this reason, in the celebration of the sacred rites of the Eleusinian Ceres <note>Ceres: The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture; the Eleusinian Mysteries were the most famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece</note>, only the initiated were admitted, with a herald acting as a guard, who cried out that the profane crowd should stay far away. In the book of Esdras <note>Referring to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra), specifically chapter 14</note>, we read the same precept concerning the hidden secrets of the Hebrew Cabalists <term>Cabalists: Practitioners of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism focused on the esoteric interpretation of the Torah</term>, explained in these words: "Deliver those books to the wise among the people, whose hearts you know are able to grasp and keep these secrets." For this reason, the religious volumes of the Egyptians pertaining to the secrets of their ceremonies were made from hieratic—that is, sacred—paper. In these, they wrote unrecognizable letters, which they called "sacred." Macrobius, Marcellinus, and others record that they were called hieroglyphics <term>hieroglyphics: Agrippa understands these not just as writing, but as a deliberate code to hide spiritual truths from the uneducated</term>, specifically so that such writings could not be understood by the profane. This is also testified by Apuleius in these words: "The sacrifice having been performed," he says, "he brought forth from the hidden part of the sanctuary certain books, marked with unrecognizable letters; some were shapes of animals of this kind, suggesting condensed words of a formulated speech; others were knotted and twisted like a wheel, or crowded together like vine-tendrils, protected from the curiosity of the profane."

Therefore, by remaining silent and concealing the secrets of religion, we shall be worthy disciples of this science. praying greatly to God to know why this had happened to him, he received an answer through a dream: it was because he had defiled divine matters with a kind of lewdness by publishing them to the common people. Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher who sought to link Plato with Pythagoras and even Jewish thought.</note> also, who was quite curious about hidden things, drew the wrath of the divine powers because he had published the sacred rites of the Eleusinian goddess <note>Referring to the Eleusinian Mysteries, the most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> by interpreting them. For he dreamed that the Eleusinian goddesses were standing in the dress of prostitutes before an open brothel; while he wondered at this, they responded angrily that they had been violently dragged by him from the sanctuary of their modesty and prostituted to any passerby. By this he was warned that the ceremonies of the gods must not be made common. Therefore, it was always the labor of the ancients to wrap up the secrets of God and nature and to cover them with various riddles. This law was observed by the Indians, the Brahmans, the Ethiopians, the Persians, and the Egyptians. Hence Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermeticism.</note>, Orpheus, and all the ancients and philosophers—Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Aristoxenus, Ammonius—kept this with inviolable faith. Hence Plotinus and Origen, and the other disciples of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the influential teacher of Neoplatonism.</note>, as Porphyry relates in his book on the education and discipline of Plotinus, swore not to publish the master's doctrines. Because Plotinus violated the oath made to Ammonius and published the secrets, he was consumed as a punishment for his transgression (as some assert) by a <margin>//</margin> horrendous feast of lice <note>A common historical trope where "betrayers" or "heretics" were said to die of phthiriasis, or a lice infestation.</note>. Christ himself, while he yet lived on earth, spoke with such law and reason that only his most secret disciples <margin>//</margin> might understand the mystery of the word of God, while others might perceive only parables; commanding moreover that what is holy should not be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine. Therefore the prophet says: "I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you." <note>original: "Abscondi in corde meo eloquia tua, ut non peccē tibi." From Psalm 119:11.</note> It is not fitting, therefore, to commit to public letters those secrets which are to be communicated only by mouth among a few wise men. For this reason, you will forgive me if I have passed over many and more powerful secret mysteries of ceremonial magic in silence. <margin>//</margin> I believe I shall have done enough if we report those things which are necessary to know, so that you do not leave the reading of this book entirely empty of those mysteries. But let these things be communicated to you under the same law by which Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> binds Timothy: namely, that the secrets should not be exposed by those who understand them to the unworthy, but being gathered among the wise, they should be guarded with the reverence that is fitting. Furthermore, I wish you to be warned at this beginning that, just as the divine powers themselves loathe public and profane things and love secrets, so every magical experiment flees the public eye, seeks to be hidden, is strengthened by silence, but is destroyed by publication; nor does a complete effect follow from it. For all these things suffer loss when they are thrust upon talkative and incredulous minds. It is necessary, therefore, for a magical operator, if he wishes to gain fruit therefrom, to be secret, and to reveal his work, his place, his time, his desire, and <margin>//</margin> his will to no one, except to a teacher or a <margin>//</margin> coadjutor <note>An assistant or partner in the work.</note>, or a companion who must also be faithful, believing, silent, <margin>//</margin> and made worthy by nature or education. Indeed, even the talkativeness, incredulity, and unworthiness of a companion hinders and disturbs the effect in every operation.

<page-num>CCXII,</page-num>
<header>### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY ###</header>

<image-desc>An ornamental historiated woodcut initial 'C' decorated with foliate scrolls and vines.</image-desc>Near the beginning of the first book of this work, we spoke of what kind of person a mage <term>magus; a practitioner who seeks to understand and navigate the hidden laws of nature and the divine</term> ought to be. Now, however, we shall recount a matter that is arcane, necessary, and secret to anyone who strives to work in this art, which is the beginning, the completion, and the key to all magical operations: and this is the **dignification** <term>dignificatio; the process of making oneself worthy or spiritually "dignified" to interact with higher powers</term> of man toward such sublime virtue and power. For this faculty requires a wonderful dignification in a person. For the very intellect that is within us—the highest mind of the soul—is the sole operator of wonders. When it has been submerged in too much commerce with the flesh, and the soul is occupied with the sensory things of the body, it deserves no command over divine substances. Therefore, many pursue this art in vain.

<margin>note</margin>It is necessary, therefore, that we who strive toward such great heights should meditate chiefly on two things. One, clearly, is by what reason we may abandon carnal affections, fleeting senses, and material passions. The other is by what path and in what manner we may ascend to that pure intellect itself, joined to the powers of the gods. Without these, we can never successfully climb to the scrutiny of secret things or to the power of marvelous operations. For in these consists the entire dignification which nature, merit, and a certain religious art provide.

**Natural dignity** is the optimal disposition of the body and its organs, which obscures the soul with no "thickness" <note>original: "crassitudine"; referring to a lack of spiritual clarity or "coarseness" caused by the physical body</note>, nor prevents it by any inner turmoil or humor <term>humore; the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term>. This dignity arises from the position, motion, light, and influence of the celestial bodies and souls which are present at each person's birth—such as those whose **ninth house** <note>In astrology, the ninth house governs philosophy, religion, and higher knowledge.</note> is made fortunate by Saturn, the Sun, and Mercury. Mars, too, in the ninth house, commands spirits. But these matters are treated extensively in the books of the stars. 

Truly, he who is not such by nature must compensate for the defects of nature through education, the best regimen, and the prosperous use of natural things, until he emerges complete in every internal and external perfection. For this reason, such great diligence is observed in the **Mosaic Law** concerning the priest: that he be unpolluted by the dead, by a widowed woman, or by a menstruating woman; that he be free from leprosy, from a flow of blood, or from a hernia; and that he be whole in all his limbs—not blind, nor lame, nor hunchbacked, nor with a deformed nose. 

And **Apuleius** <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), a Platonic philosopher and author known for his defense against charges of magic.</note> in his *Apology* says that a boy to be initiated into divination by a magical song ought to be chosen as healthy, unharmed, talented, handsome, whole, clever in mind, and eloquent in speech, so that the divine power might dwell in him as if in a good house; and that the boy’s mind itself, quickly experienced, might be restored to its own divinity.

**Meritorious dignity**, however, is perfected by two things: namely, by doctrine and by work. The goal of doctrine <note>meaning "learning" or "instruction"</note> is to know the truth. Therefore, as was said near the beginning of the first book, one must be learned and expert in those three faculties <note>The three branches of Agrippa's philosophy: Natural (Book 1), Mathematical/Celestial (Book 2), and Religious/Ceremonial (Book 3).</note>. Then, with impediments removed, one must move the soul itself entirely toward contemplation and turn it inward upon itself. For the apprehension and power of all things reside within ourselves. We are, however, prohibited from enjoying these by the passions standing in our way from our birth, by false imaginations, and by immoderate appetites. Once these are expelled, divine knowledge and power are suddenly present. Furthermore, religious operation obtains no less efficacy than...

<page-num>CCXIII.</page-num>
<header>### BOOK THREE ###</header>

it is often effective on its own for us to acquire <term>god-like virtue; deificam uirtutem—a state of being where the human soul participates in the power of the divine</term>. For so great is the power of sacred works, when performed and presented according to the proper rites, that even if they are not fully understood—provided they are observed piously and with integrity, and believed with a firm faith—they have no less efficacy in decorating us with divine power. 

Indeed, that dignity which is acquired through the art of religion is perfected by certain religious ceremonies, expiations, consecrations, and sacred rites, performed by one whose spirit has been consecrated by public religion: one who possesses the power of the laying on of hands, and of initiating through <term>sacramental virtue; the spiritual power inherent in a religious rite</term>, by which a <term>character; an indelible spiritual mark or seal impressed upon the soul</term> of divine virtue and power is imprinted. This they call the **divine consent**, through which a man, leaning upon the divine nature and made as if a companion to the heavenly beings, carries within himself the innate power of the godhead; and this rite is numbered among the ecclesiastical sacraments. 

If, therefore, you are now a <margin>"</margin>man perfected in mind by sacred religion, one who thinks most piously and constantly regarding religion, <margin>"</margin>and believes without hesitation; and if you are such a person to whom the authority of sacred things and <margin>"</margin>nature have conferred a dignity above others, whom the deities by no means despise, <margin>"</margin>you will be able—by praying, consecrating, sacrificing, and invoking—to attract spiritual <margin>"</margin>and celestial virtues, and to imprint them upon whichever of your affairs you wish, and to enliven every <margin>"</margin>work of magical science with that very power. 

However, whoever presumes to operate in magical works beyond the authority of an office, without the merit of holiness and learning, and without the dignity of nature and education, will labor without fruit; he will deceive both himself and those who believe in him, and will incur the indignation of the deities, not without great peril.

->**Of the two supports of ceremonial Magic,**<-
->**religion and superstition.**<-
->**Chapter IV.**<-

<margin>Note / Note here:</margin>
THERE are two things which govern every operation of ceremonial Magic: namely, **religion** and **superstition**. Religion itself is the constant contemplation of divine things, and the <term>binding; religatio—the root of the word 'religion,' implying a re-connecting of the human to the divine</term> with God and the divine powers through pious works; through this, by means of reverent service, worthy veneration and the sanctification of worship are bestowed upon them, and the ceremonies of divine worship are performed according to the rite. 

Thus, religion is a certain discipline of external sacred acts and ceremonies, through which we are reminded of internal and spiritual things as if by certain signs. This is so deeply implanted in us by nature that we are distinguished from other living creatures more by this than by our capacity for reason. Therefore, whoever neglects these and trusts only <margin>"</margin>in the powers of natural things (as we said above) is very often <margin>"</margin>deceived by evil demons. For this reason, those who are more religiously and holily educated do not <margin>"</margin>plant a tree, nor plant a vineyard, nor undertake even the smallest work without a divine invocation, <margin>"</margin>just as the <note>original: "doctor gentium" — the Teacher of the Gentiles, a traditional title for the Apostle Paul</note> commanded the Colossians, saying: *Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to him and to God the Father through him.* <note>Colossians 3:17</note> Therefore, to add the strengths of religion to physical and mathematical virtues is so far from being a fault that to fail to join them is an impious crime. Hence, in the *Book of Senators*, <note>likely a reference to the 'Sefer Ha-Zekenim' or a similar Hebrew text known to the author via Christian Hebraism</note> **Rabbi Henitia** says: "Whoever makes use of any of the creatures while omitting a blessing, uses it as if by theft and robbery from God and the Church."

<margin>Lactantius.</margin>
For no religion (as **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy and Christianity</note> testifies) is so erroneous that it does not contain some element of wisdom; by which those people can find pardon who have maintained the highest duty of man in their intention, even if not in the actual deed. However, a man cannot arrive at true religion by himself, unless he is taught by God. Therefore, every form of worship that is foreign to true religion is **superstition**; and every veneration that offers more in divine worship than true religion requires is also superstition. Likewise, so is that which offers divine worship either to one whom it should not, or in a manner that it should not. Great care must therefore be taken lest, through some perverse rite of superstition, an injury be done to the most high and almighty God and the sacred powers under Him; for this would be both wicked and most unworthy of philosophers. Therefore, although superstition is foreign to true religion, it is not entirely or in every case rejected, since in many things it is tolerated and even observed by the high priests of religion. I speak especially of that superstition which is a certain imitation of religion; for insofar as it imitates whatever is found in religion—miracles, sacraments, rites, observations, and other such things—it gains no small power from them. It also obtains no less force from the **credulity** of the practitioner.

For how much a constant credulity can achieve was discussed in the first book, and it is publicly known among the common people. Superstition, therefore, requires <term>credulity; credulitas—in this context, an intense, unshakeable psychological belief that bridges the gap between the mind and the spiritual world</term>, just as religion requires faith. Indeed, a constant credulity is so powerful that it may even work miracles in false opinions and operations. For anyone in their own religion—even a false one—provided they most firmly believe it to be true, elevates their spirit by that very principle of credulity until they are made like those spirits who are

the leaders and princes of that religion; and they may perform things that reason and nature do not discern. But hesitation in credulity, and distrust, [destroys] every work...

### Chapter VI. How by these guides the human soul climbs into the divine nature, and is made a performer of miracles.

### That the knowledge of the true God is necessary for the Magician, and what the ancient Magi and philosophers thought about God.
### Chapter VII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring a scholar or figure seated at a desk, surrounded by a circular frame and ornate flourishes.</image-desc> Since the being and operation of all things depend upon the supreme God, the creator of all, and then also upon the other divinities <note>original: "numinibus" — divine powers or spirits.</note> to whom the power of making and creating has been given—not as the primary source, but by way of an <term>instrumental cause</term> <note>A cause that acts as a tool or instrument for a higher power, rather than acting on its own authority.</note> through the power of the first creator (for God is the beginning of all and the **first cause**; and whatever is produced by secondary causes is produced even more so by the first cause, which is the producer of those secondary causes, and which we therefore call "secondary gods")—it is therefore necessary for every magician to know God himself, the producer of all things and the first cause. He must also know the other gods or divinities (which we call **secondary causes**) and must not be ignorant of what worship, what veneration, and what sacred rites—conforming to the condition of each—they are to be honored with. For whoever invokes the gods but does not pursue them with their proper honor, nor distributes to each what is fitting, will not attain their presence or the desired effects. Just as in a musical harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly sounds dissonant. Sometimes, one even incurs danger and punishment, as it is written concerning the **Assyrians** whom **Shalmaneser** <note>Salmanafar V, an Assyrian king mentioned in 2 Kings 17.</note> moved into **Samaria**; because they were ignorant of the laws of the god of that land, the Lord sent lions among them, which killed them because they did not know the ritual of the god of the land. Now, therefore, let us see what the ancient Magi and philosophers thought in agreement regarding God. For we read that when **Nicocreon**, the former tyrant of the Cypriots, once asked who the supreme god might be, the oracle of **Serapis** <note>A syncretic Greco-Egyptian deity.</note> answered him that he should be held as the greatest god whose head was the heaven, whose belly was the seas, whose feet were the earth, whose ears were located in the ether itself, and whose eyes were the light of the shining sun.
