<margin>What God is.</margin>
Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom many occult and philosophical works were attributed in the Renaissance.</note> also, in his sacred history of Persian matters, defines God thus: "God is the first among all things that feel no decay or corruption: unborn, and never to perish, devoid of parts, and most like unto himself, the driver and author of all good things, the father of all things, the best and wisest, the sacred light of justice, the most absolute perfection of nature, and its inventor and wisdom." Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of 'The Golden Ass,' often cited for his Platonic and demonological insights.</note>, however, describes him as the *basileus* <note>Greek for "king" or "ruler."</note>, that is the king, the cause, reason, and initial origin of the entire nature of things, the supreme parent of the soul, eternal, the savior of living beings, a progenitor without propagation, encompassed by neither place nor time, nor any change, and therefore thinkable by few, but speakable by none. Hence, Euripides teaches that the supreme God should be named Jove <note>Jupiter</note>: through whose head Orpheus sang that all things proceeded into the light: but that the other powers should be considered ministers: which are clearly outside of God, and separated from him. Hence these ministers of God themselves are called "separated intelligences" <term>intelligentiae separatae: a philosophical term for spiritual beings like angels or planetary spirits that exist apart from physical matter</term> by the philosophers. Therefore, they say that religious worship is owed to this supreme Jove, and to him alone: but is not owed to the other deities except for his sake.

### What the ancient philosophers thought regarding the divine trinity. Chap. VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a scholar or saint seated at a desk with books in a study or landscape setting.</image-desc>Augustine and Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was often both a source and an adversary for early Christian theologians like Augustine.</note> testify that the Platonists posited three persons in God, the first of which they call the Father of the universe; the second, they call the Son and the first Mind; it is also called this by Macrobius. The third they call the Spirit, or the Soul of the World: which Virgil also, following the opinion of Plato, calls "Spirit" where he sings:
->The spirit nourishes from within, and the mind, infused throughout the limbs,<-
->moves the entire mass.<- <note>A famous quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book VI, often used to explain the concept of the Anima Mundi or World Soul.</note>

Plotinus and Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> teach that the Son of God, the first mind—that is, the divine intellect—flows from God the Father, just as a word comes from a speaker, or as light comes from light. From this, he received the names of both the Word <note>original: "verbum" and "sermo"</note> and the Splendor of God the Father. ### Chapter IX.

The Catholic doctors and the faithful people have decreed that it must be so believed and professed, that there is one sole true God, uncreated, immense, omnipotent, eternal: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; three persons indeed, coeternal and coequal with one another: yet one essence and substance, and a nature altogether simple. This is the Catholic faith, this is the orthodox religion, this is the Christian truth, that we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity: neither confounding the persons, nor dividing the substance <note>Agrippa is here paraphrasing the Athanasian Creed, the standard statement of Trinitarian orthodoxy.</note>. The Father from eternity begot the Son, and gave him his substance; and nevertheless retained it. The Son also, by being born, received the Father's substance: yet he did not take the proper person of the Father, nor did the Father transfer it to the Son: for both are of one and the same substance, but of different persons. This Son also, though he be coeternal with the Father, begotten from the Father's substance before the ages, was nonetheless born in time from the substance of the Virgin, and his name was called Jesus: perfect God, perfect man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh: to whom nothing human was lacking, except sin. It is therefore necessary that we believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is God and man: one person, two natures. ### Chapter 10.

God himself, although he is of a most united essence in a trinity of persons, we nonetheless do not doubt that there are in him many certain divine powers <note>original: "numina." This refers to divine presence or manifestations of power.</note>, like rays emanating from him. These the pagan philosophers call "gods," the masters of the Hebrews call "Numerations" <note>Referring to the <term>Sephiroth</term>, the ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself.</note>, and we call "attributes." Examples include: wisdom, which Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek hero and musician, often regarded as the founder of "Orphic" mysteries.</note> calls Pallas; intelligence, which he calls Mercury; the formation of offspring, which he calls Saturn; the productive force, which he calls Neptune; the secret nature of things, which he calls Juno; love, which he calls Venus; the lucid life, which he calls the Sun or Apollo; the reason of the entire world, which he calls Pan. But the soul, as it generates lower things, contemplates higher things, and withdraws into itself, he celebrates with a triple name: Mars, Neptune, and Ocean. And there are many more of this kind, about which he sings elsewhere:
> Jupiter, and Pluto, Phoebus, Dionysus, are all one. 
> ->But why do we speak twice? One God stands present in all things.<- 
And concerning the same, Valerius Soranus <note>A Roman poet and grammarian of the 1st century BCE.</note> sang: 
> Almighty Jupiter, king of kings, himself both god and 
> Father and mother of the gods, the one god and the all.

<margin>Pliny's opinion on God.</margin>
Thus those most prudent theologians of the nations worshipped one God under various names and powers, and even under different genders. As Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher of the 1st century AD.</note> says, "fragile and laborious mortality has divided him into many parts, mindful of its own weakness, so that each might worship in portions that which he most needed." Thus, those who had need of faith invoked Jupiter; those who needed providence, Apollo; those who needed wisdom, Minerva; and whatever other things people needed, they invoked by other names. Hence arises that manifold variety of divine powers, on account of the manifold and varied distribution of graces; yet God is one, from whom all things come. Whence Apuleius <note>A Roman philosopher and rhetorician, author of *The Golden Ass*.</note> says in his book *On the World* to Faustinus: "Since there is one God, and the same divine power, he is indeed called by many names, on account of the multitude of species, whose diversity makes him multiform." ### On the Divine Names, and Their Power and Virtue. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a mythical beast or dragon intertwined with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

**D**eity itself, although it is most unified, nevertheless receives various names, not because they explain different essences or godheads within Him, but because they represent certain properties emanating from Him. Through these names, many benefits and diverse gifts distill upon us and those things which are created, as if through certain channels. We have described ten of these names above, which **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> also recounts to **Marcella**: **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic and philosopher</note> collects forty-five names, both of God the Father and of Christ. The Hebrew Kabbalists <note>original: "mecubales"</note> derive seventy-two names of both angels and of God from a certain text in Exodus, which they call the name of seventy-two letters, and the **Shem HaMephorash** <note>original: "Schemhamphoras"</note>, that is, the "Explanatory Name." Others, proceeding further, suggest so many divine names from individual passages of scripture that their number and what they signify are almost entirely unknown to us. 

From these, therefore, besides those we mentioned above, is the name of the divine essence **Eheyeh** <note>Hebrew: אהיה, "I Will Be"</note>, which Plato translated as "He who is" <note>Greek: ὤν (on)</note>. Hence some call God "the Being" <note>Greek: τὸ ὄν (to on)</note>, others "He who is" <note>Greek: ὁ ὤν (ho on)</note>. There is another name **Hu** <note>Hebrew: הוא, "He"</note>, revealed to Isaiah, hinting at the abyss of divinity: which the Greeks translated as "The Same" <note>Greek: ταυτὸν (tauton)</note>, and the Latins "The Self-Same" <note>Latin: idem-psum</note>. There is also another name **Esh** <note>Hebrew: אש</note> received from Moses, which sounds like "fire": and there is the name of God **Na** <note>Hebrew: נא</note>, to be invoked in disturbances and troubles. There is also the name **Yah** <note>Hebrew: יה</note>, and the name **Elyon** <note>Hebrew: עליון, "The Most High"</note>, the name **Makom** <note>Hebrew: מקום, "The Place"</note>, the name **Kaphu** <note>Hebrew: כפו</note>, the name **Yinnon** <note>Hebrew: ינון</note>, and the name **Emet** <note>Hebrew: אמת</note> which is interpreted as "truth": and it is the seal of God. 

And two other names, **Tzur** <note>Hebrew: צור</note>, and **Even** <note>Hebrew: אבן</note>, both of which signify a solid rock, and one of them expresses the Father with the Son: and we have placed many other names in the scales of numbers above. And many names of God and of angels are extracted from the sacred scriptures by the Kabbalistic art, the Calculatory art, the Notary art <note>A medieval system of magic (Ars Notoria) focused on memory and rapid learning via divine names</note>, and by **Gematria** <note>original: "Gimetria," a method where words are associated with numerical values</note>: where one name or many words are gathered by retracting certain of their letters; or a single name, dispersed through its individual letters, signifies or restores many things. They are sometimes gathered from the heads of words <note>This refers to an acronym system called Notarikon</note>, like this name **Agla** <note>Hebrew: אגלא</note> from this verse of Holy Scripture: **Atah Gibor Le-olam Adonai** <note>Hebrew: אתּה גבּור לעולם אדני</note>, which is: [Thou art mighty forever, O Lord.]

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter XI regarding the nature of divine names. While the previous page introduced the ten primary names of God (the Sephiroth) as described by Jerome and Dionysius, this page focuses on the specific Kabbalistic methods used to derive new, hidden names from biblical verses.</meta>

CCV.
->OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY<-

Thou art mighty forever, O Lord. <note>original: "Tu es fortis in æternũ deus." This is the Latin expansion of the Hebrew acronym AGLA (Atah Gibor Le-olam Adonai), a common protective formula.</note> Similarly the name **Iaia** <note>Hebrew: יאיא</note> is derived from that verse: *The Lord our God, the Lord is one* <note>Hebrew: יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד; original Latin: "deus deus noster deus unus." This is the Shema, the central declaration of Jewish faith.</note>. Similarly the name **Iaua** <note>Hebrew: יאווא</note> comes from that verse: *Let there be light, and there was light* <note>Hebrew: יהי אור ויהי אור; original Latin: "fiat lux & facta est lux"</note>. Similarly the name **Ararita** <note>Hebrew: אראריתא</note> from this verse: *One principle of his unity, the principle of his singularity, his changing is one* <note>Hebrew: אחד ראש אחדותו ראש ייחודו תמורתו אחד; original Latin: "unum principium unitatis suæ, principium singularitatis suæ, uicissitudo sua unum"</note>. There is also another name, **Hacaba** <note>Hebrew: הקבה</note>, extracted from this verse: *The Holy One, blessed be He* <note>Hebrew: הקדוש ברוך הוא; original Latin: "sanctus benedictus ipse"</note>. Similarly the name **Iesu** <note>Hebrew: ישוּ; Jesus</note> is found in the beginnings of these two verses, namely: *Until Messiah comes* <note>Hebrew: יביא שלוה ולו; original Latin: "Quousq; ueniat Messiah"</note> and the other: *His name shall endure* <note>Hebrew: ינון שמו וית; original Latin: "permanet nomen eius"</note>. Similarly this name **Amen** <note>Hebrew: אמן</note> is from this verse: *The Lord is a faithful King* <note>Hebrew: אדני מלך נאמן; original Latin: "dominus rex fidelis"</note>. 

Sometimes these names are extracted from the ends of words, just as the same name **Amen** comes from this verse: *Not so the wicked* <note>Hebrew: לא כן הרשעים; original Latin: "non sic impii"</note>, but with the letters transposed. Thus in the final letters of this verse: *What is my name? What is it?* <note>Hebrew: לי מה שמו מה; original Latin: "mi hi quid? nomen eius quid?"</note> the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note> is found. In all these methods, a letter is placed for a word, or a letter is extracted from a word—either from the beginning, or from the end, or from anywhere. 

And sometimes these names are extracted from all the letters individually, just as those seventy-two names of God are extracted from those three verses found in **Exodus** <note>Exodus 14:19-21</note>, beginning with these three words: **Vayissa**, **Vayavo**, **Vayet** <note>Hebrew: ויסע ויבא ויט</note>. The first and last verses are written from right to left, but the middle one is written conversely from left to right <note>This refers to the "Boustrophedon" or "ox-turning" style of writing used to generate the 72-fold name of God</note>, as we shall show in later sections. 

And thus sometimes a word is extracted from another word, or a name from a name, through the transposition of letters—just as **Messiah** <note>Hebrew: משיח (Mashiach)</note> is formed from **Ismah** <note>Hebrew: ישמח (Yismach), meaning "he shall rejoice"</note>, and **Michael** <note>Hebrew: מיכאל</note> from **Malachi** <note>Hebrew: מלאכי, meaning "my messenger"</note>. Sometimes, however, it is done through alphabetic substitution, which the Kabbalists call **Ziruph** <note>Hebrew: צירוף (Tziruf), meaning combination or permutation</note>; for instance, from the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>Hebrew: יהוה (YHWH)</note> are elicited the names **Mazpaz** <note>Hebrew: מצפץ</note> and **Kuzu** <note>Hebrew: כוזו</note>. Frequently, names are also exchanged through numerical equality <note>This technique is known as Gematria</note>, as **Matattron** <note>Metatron; Hebrew: מטטרון</note> stands for **Sadai** <note>Shaddai; Hebrew: שדי</note>, for both equal three hundred and fourteen. By the same reasoning, the name **Iiai** <note>Hebrew: יאי</note> is equivalent to the name **El** <note>Hebrew: אל</note> through numerical equality, for both make thirty-one. 

And these are the hidden secrets about which it is difficult to bring judgment or to deliver complete knowledge; nor can they be understood and taught in any other language than Hebrew. Indeed, as **Plato** says in the *Cratylus*, divine names were held by the "barbarians" <note>In this context, referring to the ancient Hebrews as the recipients of divine wisdom</note> who received them from God, without whom no one can at all grasp the true discourses and true names by which God is called. Therefore, we can say nothing else of them except what has been revealed to us from God by His kindness. For they are the sacraments and vehicles of divine omnipotence—not established by men, nor even by angels, but by the highest God himself, in a certain mode, according to the immovable number of their characters and the eternal stability of their form, breathing the harmony of divinity and consecrated by divine assistance. Wherefore those in the heavens fear them, those in the depths tremble at them, angels worship them, demons are terrified, and every creature reveres them, and every religion venerates them: whose religious observation and devoted invocation with fear and trembling...

invocation provides us with great power, a deifying union, and a potency for miraculous works and effects that surpass nature. Therefore, it is never right to change these names for any reason. For this reason, Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar who argued that names have intrinsic power tied to their original languages.</note> instructs that they must be preserved incorruptly in their own characters; and Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom many Renaissance occultists attributed "Chaldean Oracles."</note> also forbids the changing of barbaric and ancient words. For as Plato says in the *Cratylus*: "All divine words or names were produced either by the gods first, or by antiquity (the beginning of which is not easily known), or by the barbarians." <note>original Latin: "barbaris." In this context, "barbaric" refers to non-Greek languages, specifically Hebrew, Egyptian, or Chaldean, which were considered more "primordial."</note> Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who defended the use of ritual and "meaningless" divine names in his work *On the Mysteries*.</note> similarly instructs that they are not to be transferred from their own language into another, for he says names do not preserve the same meaning <note>original Latin: "mentem," literally "mind" or "essence."</note> when interpreted into another tongue. These divine names are therefore the most fit and effective medium for reconciling and uniting man with the gods, just as we read in Exodus: *In every place where there is a memorial of my name, I will come to thee, and I will bless thee.* In the book of Numbers, the Lord says: *They shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.*

<margin>
In what manner divine names are to be venerated.
</margin>

For this reason, the divine Plato in the *Cratylus* and in the *Philebus* commands that divine names be venerated more than temples and divine statues, because a more expressive image and power of God resides in the duty of the mind—especially one divinely inspired—than what is preserved in the works of human hands. Therefore, sacred words do not possess power in magic simply from themselves as words, but from the hidden power of the divine spirits <note>original Latin: "numinum"</note> working through them in the souls of those who cling to them through faith. In these people, the hidden power of God is transmitted through the words, as if through vehicles, into those who have "ears to hear" <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 11:15.</note>—those purified by faith and the most refined character, who through divine invocations have been made a dwelling place of God and are capable of these divine influences. Whoever, therefore, rightly uses these divine words or names with that purity of mind, in that manner, and by that law through which they were handed down, will obtain and perform many marvelous things, just as we read concerning Medea:

> And thrice she spoke the words that bring peaceful sleep,
> Which halt the churning sea and stay the rushing rivers.
<note>These lines are from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book 7, describing the enchantress Medea.</note>

<margin>
Orpheus.
From Philostratus.

The ancient doctors of the Hebrews observed this above all others, being accustomed to performing many wonders through words. The Pythagoreans also demonstrated this, miraculously curing diseases of both the mind and body with certain words. So too we read that Orpheus, when he was one of the Argonauts, averted a most cruel storm with certain words. In a similar way, Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus, author of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.</note> relates that Apollonius, with certain words spoken in secret, resurrected a dead girl in Rome, and with other words summoned the ghost of Achilles. Furthermore, Pausanias reports that in the Lydian cities of Hierocaesarea and Hypepa, there were two temples sacred to the goddess they called the Persian. In each of these, when the divine rite was to be performed, a magician placed dry wood upon the altar and, singing hymns in his native tongue, then pronounced certain barbaric words from a book he held in his hand. Once these were spoken, the wood would soon be seen to burn spontaneously without any fire being applied, catching a most brilliant flame. CCXXXII.

->ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,<-

Nor indeed should anyone lack confidence, or wonder that sacred words—by which the almighty God established the heaven and the earth—possess great power when bound together, since it has been discovered through experiment, as **Costa Ben Luca** <note>Qusta ibn Luqa (820–912), a Melkite Christian physician and translator in Baghdad, known for his works on physical and spiritual effects.</note> says, that many other non-physical things can do much. Experience has proven, for example, that the finger of an aborted fetus suspended from a woman's neck prevents conception for as long as it remains there. Furthermore, in certain sacred words and divine names, there is a great and divine power, which is the operative virtue of a marvelous effect. **Zoroaster, Orpheus, Iamblichus, Synesius, and Al-Kindi**, and all the most illustrious of the philosophers testify to this; even **Artephius** <note>A legendary alchemist and magician, often identified with Apollonius of Tyana.</note>, the mage and philosopher, wrote a singular book on the virtues of words and characters. **Origen**, no inferior to any of the most illustrious philosophers, asserts against **Celsus** <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity.</note> that a wonderful power lies hidden in certain divine words. And in the Book of **Judges**, the Lord says: "My name is **Pele** <note>original: פלא, a Hebrew word meaning 'wonderful' or 'miraculous'; see Judges 13:18.</note>," which is interpreted among us as "the worker of miracles" or "the one who performs wonders."

<margin>But the true name is known to God alone.</margin>
However, the true name of God is known neither to men nor to angels, but to God himself alone; nor will it be published (as the sacred scriptures testify) until the arrangement of God has been fulfilled. Yet, God has other names among the angels, and still others among men. There is no name of God among us (as **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Referring to Maimonides (Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon), the famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> says) that is not taken from His works, signifying Him by participation—except for the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH, considered too holy to be spoken aloud by many traditions.</note> itself. This is the holy name, signifying the substance of the Creator in a pure sense, in which nothing else participates with God the Creator. Therefore, it is called the "separated name," which is written but not read, nor is it expressed among us, but merely named. It signifies according to the heavenly language, which belongs to God, and perhaps also to the angels. In a similar way, there are also names for the angels: some among themselves and in their own idiom—which **Paul** calls the "tongues of angels," of which very little is known to us. All their other names are derived from their offices and works, which are not of such great efficacy. Therefore, the mages summon them by their true names—namely, those celestial names contained in the holy scriptures.

CCXXXIII.

### BOOK THREE.

power, it is right to accommodate it to the same place, time, and species. Whence **Augustine** says in his *Book of Questions*: "Every visible thing in this world has an angelic power set over it." Hence **Origen** <note>A 3rd-century theologian who integrated Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> says in his commentary on the *Book of Numbers*: "The world itself has need of angels who preside over earthly armies, kingdoms, provinces, men, beasts, and the birth and growth of animals, shrubs, plants, and other things, bestowing that virtue <term>virtue: here meaning an inherent spiritual power or efficacy</term> which they say exists in things by an **occult property**." Much more so is there a need for angels who preside over holy works, virtues, and men, so that they—who always behold the face of the highest Father—may, by right guidance, lead men and every single thing, even the smallest, to its proper place, like harmonious members of this world. In this world, God dwells as the chief high priest, disposing all things most sweetly; He is not contained or circumscribed by it, but contains all things. This is as **John** describes in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> regarding that heavenly city, over whose twelve gates twelve angels preside; they flow into those gates, which receive names from the divine name revolved twelve times. And in the foundations of that city are the names of the twelve apostles and of the Lamb. For just as in the Law, the names of the tribes of **Israel** were inscribed on the stones of the breastplate <note>original: *superhumeralis*, the priestly ephod/breastplate</note> and on the foundations of the holy city described by **Ezekiel**, and the **four-letter name** <term>four-letter name: The Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the sacred name of God in Hebrew.</term> ruled over them; so in the Gospel, the names of the apostles are inscribed on the stones of the foundation of the heavenly city. They stand for the tribes of Israel in the church, and upon them flows the name of the Lamb—that is, the name of **Jesus**—in which resides all the power of the four-letter name. Indeed, that four-lettered Father gave all things to Him. Therefore, the heavens receive from the angels that which they pour down; but the angels receive from the great name of God and of Jesus, whose virtue is first in God, and then diffused into those groups of twelve and seven angels. Through these, it is extended into the twelve signs [of the zodiac] and the seven planets, and consequently into all other ministers and instruments of God, penetrating down to the lowest things. <margin>John 14</margin> Hence **Christ** says: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you." <margin>Mark 16</margin> And rising again, He says: "In my name they shall cast out demons," and so forth; so that it is no longer necessary to use the four-letter name, whose entire power has been transferred into the name of Jesus, in which alone wonders are performed. <margin>Acts 4</margin> Nor is there any other name (as **Peter** says) given to men under heaven by which we must be saved, except that one. <margin>Note</margin> However, let us not think that by naming Jesus with a polluted mouth, as if it were merely the name of some man, we can perform miracles by His power. Rather, it is necessary to invoke it in the Holy Spirit, with a purged mind and a fervent soul, so that we may attain those things promised to us in Him—especially with **prior knowledge**, without which there is no hearing [of prayer], <margin>Psalm 90</margin> according to that prophetic saying: "I will hear him, because he has known my name." Hence today, no favor can be drawn from the celestial beings unless the authority, favor, and consent of the name of Jesus intervenes. Because of this, the **Hebrews** and **Kabbalists** <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, though most skilled in divine names, can work nothing in those ancient names after Christ, as their fathers once did. ### Chapter XIII. Of the members of God, and of their influence upon our own members.

<margin>What the members of God are.</margin>
<margin>What the garments of God are.</margin>

We read in various places of Holy Scripture about various members and ornaments of God. By the **members of God**, we understand certain multiple and most simple powers remaining within God himself, distinguished among themselves by the sacred names of God. The **garments** and ornaments of God, however, are like certain paths or relations, or <term>emanations: spiritual "out-flowings" from the Divine source into the created world</term> or channels through which He diffuses Himself. Whenever our mind touches the "fringe" of these garments, a divine power goes out from some member, just as **Jesus** cried out regarding the woman with the hemorrhage: 
<margin>Luke 8</margin>
"Someone touched me: for I perceived power going out from me." <note>original: "Tetigit me aliquis: nam ſenſi de me exire uirtutem."</note> These members in God are therefore similar to ours; but they are the **Ideas** and archetypes of our own members. If we conform our members rightly to them, then, being transformed into that same image, we are made true sons of God and like unto God, acting and performing the works of God. ii

Philosophers have established, as we have shown above, that the heavens and the stars are divine living beings, and that their souls are intelligent, participating in the divine mind. They also established that some separate substances <note>Agrippa refers to "substantiae separatae," which are spiritual beings like angels or intelligences that exist independently of physical matter.</note> preside over them, while others are subordinate to them, acting as rulers and ministers, which they call **Intelligences** and **Daemons**.
<margin>Plato</margin>
But Plato himself also asserted that celestial souls are by no means confined to their bodies in the same way our souls are confined to our bodies. Instead, they are wherever they wish to be, and they simultaneously enjoy the vision of God. Without any labor or anxiety, they rule and move their own bodies, and by moving these, they easily govern the lower things. For this reason, they used to call souls of this kind "gods," and they established divine honors for them, dedicating prayers and sacrifices to them and worshipping them with various cults. And these are the gods to whom all the nations were assigned, about whom Moses commanded in Deuteronomy, saying:
<margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin>
"Lest perhaps, lifting up your eyes to heaven, you see the sun, and the moon, and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived, you adore and worship them, which were assigned to all the nations that are under the whole heaven; but the Lord **Tetragrammaton** <note>The "four-letter" name of God (YHWH), which Agrippa treats as the highest and most sacred name, distinguishing the direct rule of God from the rule of planetary spirits.</note> took you and led you out of the furnace of Egypt, so that he might have a people of inheritance for himself."
<margin>Deuteronomy 17</margin>
And in the seventeenth chapter of the same volume, he calls the sun, the moon, and the stars "gods."
<margin>Genesis 25</margin>
And the teachers of the Hebrews, regarding what is read in Genesis—that Abraham bestowed gifts upon the sons of his concubines, namely *Shemoth* <note>original: "Shemoth steltōia," likely a corruption of "Shemoth zarim," meaning "foreign names" or "alien names."</note> or "alien names," but left Isaac as the heir of all that he possessed—say that the sons of the concubines were not assigned to the God **Tetragrammaton** and the supreme Creator in Abraham's blessing, but rather to alien gods and spirits. Isaac and his seed, however, were assigned to the almighty God **Tetragrammaton** himself, and were in no part assigned to alien spirits.
<margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin>
Hence they are reproached in Deuteronomy because they served alien gods and adored those whom they did not know and to whom they were not assigned.
<margin>Joshua 24</margin>
Furthermore, after leading the people into the promised land, overcoming their enemies, and distributing the lots of the possessions of Israel, Joshua gave the people a choice so that they might choose which spirit they would worship, saying: "The choice is given to you today to choose what pleases you, whom you ought especially to serve—whether the gods your fathers served in Mesopotamia, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell." But when the people responded, "We will serve the Lord **Tetragrammaton**, and he shall be our God," Joshua said to them: "You will not be able to, for the Lord God **Tetragrammaton** is holy, and strong, and a jealous God." <margin>Joshua 24</margin>
And he set up a very large stone, saying: "This stone shall be a witness for you, lest perhaps afterward you wish to deny and lie to the Lord your God." Thus, there were gods to whom the other nations were assigned: the sun and moon, the twelve signs of the zodiac, and the other celestial bodies and divine works. **Albertus** Magnus, in his book *On the Four Co-equals*, and Thomas Aquinas in his books *On Spiritual Creatures*, and John Duns Scotus in his commentary on the second book of the *Sentences* <note>original: "super secundo Sententiarum." But if anyone wishes to oppose these thinkers entirely and hold these to be sacrilegious dogmas, let him listen to Augustine in the *Enchiridion* and in the *Retractations*, and Thomas in the second book of *Against the Gentiles* and in the *Quodlibets*, and Scotus on the *Sentences*, and William of Paris in his *Summa on the Universe*, who respond unanimously: whether celestial bodies are called animate or inanimate is of no consequence to the Catholic faith. Although it may seem ridiculous to many that souls themselves are placed in the spheres and stars, and that each presides over its own regions, cities, tribes, peoples, nations, and languages like the gods of the heathens, it will not seem foreign to those who understand correctly.

# On intelligences and demons, their three-fold kind and various names, and on infernal and subterranean demons.
### Chapter XVI.

<margin>What an intelligence is.</margin>
<note>The woodcut initial 'N' shows a landscape with a tree and a small building.</note> **N**ow, consequently, we must discuss intelligences, spirits, and demons. An **intelligence** is an intelligible substance, free from all mass of a gross and corruptible body, immortal, insensible, present to all things, and influencing all things. And the nature of all intelligences, spirits, and demons is the same.
<margin>Who demons are here and how many kinds there are.</margin>
I speak of **demons** <note>original: "dæmones." From the Greek *daimon*, meaning a spirit or divine power; here the author distinguishes them from "devils."</note> here not as those whom we call devils, but as spirits so named from the proper meaning of the word, as if they were "knowing," "understanding," and "wise" beings. According to the tradition of the Magi, there are three kinds of these. The first they call **super-celestial**, which are minds entirely separated from bodies and are like intellectual spheres; they worship the one God as their firmest and most stable unity or center. For this reason, they are even now called gods, because of a certain participation in divinity, for they are always full of God and intoxicated with divine nectar. These are concerned only with the one God; they do not preside over the bodies of the world, nor are they adapted to the ministry of lower things. Instead, they pour the light received from God into the lower orders and distribute specific offices to each. These are followed in the second order by the **celestial intelligences**, which they call **mundane demons** <note>original: "dæmones mundanos." Spirits of the world or cosmos.</note>. That is, beyond divine worship, they are applied to the spheres of the world and preside over each of the heavens and stars. Hence, they distribute them into as many orders as there are heavens in the world and stars in the heavens. They called some **Saturnians**, who preside over the heaven of Saturn and Saturn itself; others **Jovials**, who preside over the heaven of Jupiter and Jupiter itself; and likewise for the others...

CCXL.

### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHIA

<note>The text continues from the previous page, discussing how authorities classify spirits.</note> ...of the stars, they name various **demons** <note>original: "dæmones." In this context, a demon refers to a *daimon* or intermediary spirit, not necessarily an evil entity.</note> by name as well as by power; and because the ancient astronomers <note>original: "astrologi." In the Renaissance, astrology and astronomy were often used interchangeably as the same discipline.</note> claimed there were fifty-five motions <note>Referring to the Aristotelian model of the nested celestial spheres.</note>, they devised as many **intelligences**, or demons, for them. They also placed demons in the starry heaven to preside over the signs, the **triplicities** <note>Groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note>, the **decans** <note>Ten-degree subdivisions of the zodiac.</note>, the **quinaries** <note>Five-degree subdivisions of the zodiac.</note>, the degrees, and the stars. For although the entire school of philosophers, even the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, assigns only one intelligence to each celestial orb, nevertheless, since every single star and particle of heaven has its own proper and distinct power and influence, it is necessary that they also have their own presiding intelligence to bestow and enact that power.

<margin>The number and duties of demons.</margin> Thus, they established twelve princes of demons to preside over the twelve signs of the zodiac, and thirty-six to preside over as many **decuries** <note>Another term for decans (10-degree segments).</note>, and seventy-two to preside over as many quinaries of the heaven and over the languages and nations of men. They also set four to preside over the triplicities and the elements, and seven governors of the entire world according to the seven planets. To all of these, they gave names and seals, which they call **characters**, and they used them in their invocations, incantations, and carvings, inscribing them on the instruments of their operations: images, plates, seals, rings, charts, waxes, and the like. For instance, if they were working toward the Sun, they would invoke through the names of the Sun and through the names of the solar demons, and so on for the others.

Thirdly, they place demons as ministers to arrange those things that are in the lower regions, whom **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who wrote extensively on the spiritual world.</note> calls certain "invisible powers" to whom the management of things upon the earth has been entrusted. For often, though visible to no one, they direct our journeys and all our business; often they are even present in battles and, through secret aid, provide the desired successes to their friends; indeed, they are said to be able to reconcile prosperties or inflict adversities as they please.

<margin>The classification of demons.</margin> In a similar way, they distribute these into several orders: some are **fiery**, others **watery**, others **airy**, and others **earthy**. These four species of demons are reckoned according to the four powers of the celestial souls: namely, the **Mind**, **Reason**, **Imagination**, and **Nature** (the life-giving and moving force). Hence, the fiery demons follow the *Mind* of the celestial souls, which is why they assist in the contemplation of more sublime things. The airy demons, following *Reason*, favor the rational power, and by separating it in a certain way from the sensual and vegetative, they serve the active life, just as the fiery ones serve the contemplative life. The watery demons, following *Imagination* and sense, serve the life of pleasure. The earthy demons, following *Nature*, favor the vegetative nature. Furthermore, they also distinguish this kind of demon into **Saturnine** and **Jovian** <note>Spirits associated with the planets Saturn and Jupiter.</note>, according to the names of the stars and heavens. Moreover, they say some are of the East, others of the West, others of the South, and others of the North. Finally, no part of the world is left without its own assistance from these demons—not because they are only there, but because they rule there most strongly. For they are everywhere, although some work and exert influence more powerfully in certain places than in others. Nor indeed should these things be understood as if they were subject to the influences of the stars, but rather that they respond to the **supramundane heaven** <note>The spiritual realm existing above the physical celestial spheres.</note>, by which all things are primarily directed, and to which all things must be conformed; hence, just as they are assigned to various stars, so too they are assigned to various places and...

CCXLI.

### BOOK THREE

<meta>The text continues the discussion of how spirits are assigned to govern various parts of the created world.</meta>

...these **demons** <note>original: "dæmones." Referring to intermediary spirits or "daimons," which in classical and occult philosophy could be good, neutral, or evil.</note> are assigned to specific times: not because they are restricted by time or place, any more than they are restricted by the physical bodies over which they are set to preside, but because the order of Wisdom has so decreed. Therefore, they favor and protect those bodies, places, times, and stars more than others. Thus, some have been called diurnal (of the day), others nocturnal (of the night), and others meridian (of the midday). In a similar way, some are called spirits of the woods, others of the mountains, others of the fields, and others of the household. From this come the **Sylvans, Fauns, Satyrs, Panes, Nymphs, Naiads, Nereids, Dryads, Pierides, Hamadryads, Potamides, Hyades, Agaptae, Pales, Pareades, Dodonae, Feniliae, Lavernae, Pareae, Muses, Aonides, Castalides, Heliconides, Pegasides, Maeonides, Phoebiades, Camoenae, Graces, Genii, Lemures,** <note>These are various classes of nature spirits, nymphs, and minor deities from Greek and Roman mythology, categorized here as "demons" or terrestrial spirits.</note> and the like. Some call these the "common folk" of the gods; others call them demigods or goddesses.

Some of these are so close and familiar to men that they are even affected by human disturbances. Plato believes that through the instruction of these spirits, men often perform marvelous illusions, just as through the instruction of men, certain animals that are closer to us—such as apes, dogs, and elephants—
<margin>//</margin>
often perform wonders beyond their own species. And those who have written the history of the Danes and Norwegians testify that various kinds of demons in those regions are subject to the service of men. Furthermore, they claim that some of these spirits are corporeal and mortal, whose bodies are born and perish, though they are very long-lived. This is the opinion of the Egyptians and the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, especially those of late antiquity who integrated magic and theology.</note>, and is especially confirmed by **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of spirits.</note>. **Plutarch** <note>A Greek historian and philosopher.</note>, the philosopher **Demetrius**, and the rhetorician **Aemilianus** affirm the same thing. They testify, based on many wonders of their own time, that the great demon **Pan**, and many others, first wailed aloud and then died.

Therefore, regarding these demons of the third kind, the opinion of the Platonists is that there are as many legions of them as there are stars in heaven. They also say that there are as many demons in each legion as there are stars contained in the heaven itself. However, concerning the number of **good demons** <note>In this context, equivalent to angels.</note>, there are those who (as **Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> records) believe they make up ninety-nine parts of the whole, according to the parable of the hundred sheep <note>Referring to Matthew 18:12-14, where the one lost sheep represents humanity and the ninety-nine represent the heavenly host.</note>. Others think they make up only nine parts, according to the parable of the ten silver coins <note>Referring to Luke 15:8-10.</note>. Others believe the number of angels is equal to the number of men, because it is written: *He set the bounds of the people according to the number of the angels of God* <note>original: "constituit terminos populorum iuxta numerum angelorum dei." A reference to Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Septuagint version.</note>. Many authors have written many things regarding their number.
<margin>7B</margin>
But more recent theologians, following the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note>, **Augustine**, and **Gregory**, easily resolve the matter by saying that the number of good angels transcends all human understanding. To these correspond an equal number of unclean spirits—as many existing in the lower world as there are spirits of the world in the higher world, as some theologians claim to have received from oracles. Beneath these, they place a genus of subterranean or dark demons, whom the Platonists call **deserting angels** <note>original: "desertores angelos." Spirits who abandoned their divine stations; fallen angels.</note>, the punishers of crimes and impiety according to the decree of divine justice. They call them evil demons and wicked spirits because they often harm and injure of their own accord. They count many legions of these as well, distinguishing them in a similar way according to the names of the stars and elements and parts of the world, and they assign to them kings and prin...

### Concerning the same according to the opinions of theologians. Chapter XVII.

<margin>The threefold distinction of angels.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' depicting a bearded male face in profile looking left, integrated into the letter's structure.</image-desc>Our theologians, following **Dionysius** <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian whose work "The Celestial Hierarchy" established the standard ninefold order of angels.</note>, similarly establish a threefold distinction of angels. They divide each of these into three orders, so that there are three distinctions and nine orders. These they call **hierarchies**, and the orders they call **choirs**; **Proclus** <note>A Greek Neoplatonist who influenced Christian angelology.</note> also distinguishes them by the number nine. In the highest hierarchy, they place the **Seraphim, Cherubim,** and **Thrones**, whom they view as super-celestial spirits <note>original: "dæmones," used here in the classical sense of intermediary beings rather than evil "demons."</note> who contemplate the order of divine providence: the first in the goodness of God; the second in the essence of God as the ultimate form; and the third in His wisdom.

In the middle hierarchy, they place **Dominations, Virtues,** and **Powers**, functioning as worldly spirits <note>original: "mundanos dæmones."</note> who join together in the governance of the world. Of these, the first order commands what the others execute; the second order administers the heavens and sometimes works together to perform miracles; and the third order restrains those things that seem able to disturb the divine law.

In the lower hierarchy, they place **Principalities, Archangels,** and **Angels**, whom **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work on theurgy (divine magic).</note> also counts. These descend as ministering spirits to care for lower things. Of these, the first order takes care of public affairs—princes, magistrates, provinces, and kingdoms—each assigned to their own. Thus it is read in **Daniel**: *The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days* <note>Daniel 10:13. In this context, "princes" refer to angelic guardians of nations.</note>; and **Jesus son of Sirach** testifies that a ruling angel is set over every nation. This also seems to be indicated by **Moses** in the Song of Deuteronomy, saying: *When the Most High divided the nations, he established their boundaries according to the number of the angels of God* <note>Deuteronomy 32:8. Agrippa is citing the Septuagint/Greek version of the Old Testament here, which mentions "angels" where the Hebrew text usually says "sons of Israel."</note>. The second order assists in sacred matters, directing divine worship for individual men, and offering the prayers and sacrifices of men before the gods. The third order arranges all minor matters, and they are present as individual guardians to individual people. Among these are also those who provide power to the smallest herbs and stones, and to all lower things; they have much in common with God and much in common with men, serving as mediating ministers.

Indeed, <margin>Athanasius's opinion on angels.</margin> **Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD), a prominent Church Father.</note>—in addition to the Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim who are closest to God, magnifying Him with unceasing hymns and restless praise and praying for our salvation—names seven other orders, which he calls by the common name "the host of heaven." The first of these is the **Doctrinal order**, from which came the one who spoke to Daniel, saying: *I have come to teach you what will happen to your people...*

...to you in the last days. <margin>The Tutelary order.</margin> Next is the **Tutelary** order <term>Tutelary: From the Latin "tuela," meaning protection; these are guardian spirits over nations or individuals.</term>, about which we also read in the Book of **Daniel**: *Behold, Michael, one of the chief Princes, came to help me.* And in the same book: *At that time shall Michael rise up, the great Prince, who stands for the children of your people.* To this same order belonged **Raphael**, who guided the younger **Tobias** on his journey and brought him home again. <margin>The Procuratorial order.</margin> After this is the **Procuratorial** order <term>Procuratorial: Spirits that manage or administer human affairs, like a steward or "procurator."</term>, mention of which is found in the book of **Job**, where it is read: *If there be an angel speaking for him, he shall pray unto the Lord, and he will be favorable unto him.* These are also explained by what is written in the sixteenth chapter of **Ecclesiasticus** near the end: *The works of the Lord are done in judgment from the beginning: and from the time he made them and the institution of men, he assigned them their portions, and their beginnings in their own nations. He garnished their works for ever, and they neither hungered nor labored, and they did not cease from their works. No one shall ever oppress his neighbor.* <margin>The Ministerial order.</margin> Then follows the **Ministerial** order, of which **Paul** says to the Hebrews: *Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?* <margin>The Auxiliary order.</margin> After these is the **Auxiliary** order, about which we read in **Isaiah**: *The angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand.* <margin>The order that Receives Souls.</margin> Following this is the order that **Receives Souls**, of which we read in **Luke**: *The soul of Lazarus was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.* In the same place we are taught to *make for ourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, that they may receive us into everlasting habitations.* <margin>The order of Assistants.</margin> Furthermore, there is the order of **Assistants** <note>original: "Adsistenti um," referring to those who stand in the presence of a monarch.</note>, of whom we read in **Zechariah**: *These are the two sons of oil of splendor, who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.* 

<margin>How the Hebrews number the orders of angels.</margin> The theologians of the **Hebrews**, however, count and name these orders differently. In the highest place are those they call the **Holy Living Creatures** <note>original Hebrew: חיות הקדש (*Hayyot HaKodesh*), often translated as the "Living Creatures" seen in Ezekiel's vision.</note>, or "the Lives," through whom God—as the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: "יהוה" (YHVH), the four-letter name of God.</note>—bestows the gift of being. In the second place follow the **Wheels** <note>original: אופנים (*Ophanim*)</note>, that is, forms or wheels, through whom God—as the **Tetragrammaton**—distinguishes the primal chaos. In the third place are the **Aralim** <note>original: אראלים (*Aralim*), often translated as "The Valiant ones."</note>, great, strong, and robust angels, through whom God—pronounced as **Tetragrammaton-Elohim**, or the Tetragrammaton joined with the letter *He* <note>original: יהוה with "he" conjuncto</note>—administers the form of flowing matter. In the fourth place are the **Brilliant Ones** <note>original: חשמלים (*Hasmalim*), often translated as "Amber" or "Glowing" ones</note>, through whom **El** <note>original: אל</note> the God fashions the images of bodies. The fifth is the order of the **Seraphim** <note>original: שרפים (*Seraphim*), meaning "Burning ones"</note>, through whom God—as **Elohim Gibor** <note>original: אלהים גיבור, "God of Might"</note>—draws forth the elements. The sixth is the **Malachim** <note>original: מלאכים (*Malachim*)</note>, that is, of the angels, through whom God—as **Eloah** <note>original: אלוה</note>—produces metals. The seventh is the **Elohim** <note>original: אלהים</note>, that is, the gods, through whom God—as the **Tetragrammaton Sabaoth** <note>original: יהוה צבאות, "Lord of Hosts"</note>—produces the vegetable kingdom. The eighth is the **Sons of the Gods** <note>original: בני אלהים (*Bne Elohim*)</note>, through whom God—as **Elohim Sabaoth** <note>original: אלהים צבאות</note>—procreates animals. The ninth and lowest are the **Cherubim** <note>original: כרובים (*Cherubim*)</note>, through whom God—as **Shaddai** <note>original: שדי, "Almighty"</note>—cares for the human race. Below these is the animate order, called the **Men** <note>original: אישים (*Issim*), literally "men" or "individuals," but here referring to saintly human-like spirits</note>, that is, heroes, strong and blessed men, through whom God—as **Adonai** <note>original: אדני, "Lord"</note>—bestows the gift of prophecy.

# CCXLIII.
## ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>The first order of demons.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' featuring a figure amidst decorative foliage.</image-desc>
There are also those from the school of theologians who distribute evil demons into nine ranks, as if they were opposing the nine orders of angels. Of these, the **first** are those called **pseudothei**, <term>pseudothei: From the Greek, meaning "false gods."</term> that is, false gods, who, usurping the name of God, wish to be worshipped as gods and demand sacrifices and adorations, just like that demon who said to **Christ**: *If falling on the ground you will adore me, I will give you all these things:* showing him all the kingdoms of the world. And the prince of these is he who said: *I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the most high,* who is therefore called **Beelzebub**, <note>original: "Beelzebub"</note> which means "the ancient god." 

<margin>The second.</margin>
These are followed in the **second** place by the spirits of lies, of the kind that went forth as a lying spirit in the mouth of the prophets of **Ahab**. Their prince is that serpent **Python**, <term>Python: In Greek mythology, the serpent of Delphi; in this context, it refers to spirits that provide false or deceptive prophecies.</term> from whom **Apollo** was called "the Pythian," as was that **Pythonic woman** <note>Refers to the Medium of Endor who summoned the spirit of Samuel.</note> in the book of **Samuel**, and another in the Gospels who had a Python <note>Often interpreted in the New Testament as a "spirit of divination."</note> in her belly. This kind of demon, therefore, mingles itself with oracles, and mocks men with divinations and predictions until it deceives them. 

<margin>The third.</margin>
In the **third** rank are the **vessels of iniquity**, which are also called the **vessels of wrath**. These are the inventors of evils and of all wicked arts, such as that demon **Theutus** <term>Theutus: Also known as Thoth; Plato mentions him in the "Phaedrus" as the inventor of writing, numbers, and games of chance.</term> in **Plato** who taught games and dice. From these, indeed, all crime, malice, and deformity proceed, of whom **Jacob** said in **Genesis** during the blessings of **Simeon** and **Levi**: *Vessels of iniquity are in their habitations; into their counsel let my soul not come.* <margin>Psalm 7.</margin> The **Psalmist** calls them "vessels of death," <margin>Isaiah 13, Jeremiah 50</margin> **Isaiah** calls them "vessels of fury," and **Jeremiah** calls them "vessels of wrath," **Ezekiel** calls them "vessels of slaughter and destruction." Their prince is **Belial**, <term>Belial: A Hebrew term meaning "without a yoke," implying one who is lawless or rebellious.</term> which is interpreted as "without a yoke," or "disobedient," a "transgressor," and an "apostate," of whom **Paul** says to the **Corinthians**: <margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin> *What agreement has Christ with Belial?* 

<margin>The fourth.</margin>
There follow in the **fourth** place the **avengers of crimes**, <margin>The fifth.</margin> and their prince is **Asmodeus**, <term>Asmodeus: A demon known from the Book of Tobit; here described as an executioner of judgment.</term> which is to say "making judgment." After these, in the **fifth** rank, come the **jugglers**, <note>original: "praestigiatores," meaning those who perform deceptions or illusions.</note> who imitate miracles and serve **Cacomagi** <term>Cacomagi: Evil magicians or sorcerers who use their craft for harm.</term> and sorcerers, seducing the people with their miracles just as the serpent seduced **Eve**. Their prince is **Satan**, of whom it is written in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> that he seduces the whole world, performing great signs and making fire descend from heaven to earth in the sight of men, seducing those dwelling on earth because of the <margin>The sixth.</margin> signs which were given to him to perform. In the **sixth** rank, the **aerial powers** present themselves: these mingle with thunder, lightning, and flashes, corrupting the air and bringing in pestilences and other evils. Among their number are those four angels whom the **Apocalypse** describes, to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, holding the four winds from the four corners of the earth. Their prince is called **Meririm**: <term>Meririm: A name likely derived from the Hebrew for "bitterness" or "noon," associated here with the "midday demon."</term> he is the "midday demon," a burning spirit, and a demon raging at noon, whom **Paul** calls in the letter to the **Ephesians** the "prince of the power of this air," and the spirit that works in the <margin>The seventh.</margin> children of disobedience. The **seventh** dwelling is held by the **Furies**, sowers of evils, discords, wars, and devastations. Their prince in the **Apocalypse** is called **Apollyon** in Greek and **Abaddon** in Hebrew, <margin>The eighth.</margin> which is to say "the exterminator" and "the waster." In the **eighth** place stand the **accusers** or **scouts**, whose prin-

CCXLV.
### BOOK THREE. CCXLV.

...the prince **Astaroth**, <note>original: "Astaroth"</note> that is, the explorer; called in Greek the **devil**, <note>original: "diabolus"</note> that is, the accuser or slanderer, who in the **Book of Revelation** <margin>Revelation 12</margin> is called the accuser of our brothers, accusing them before the sight of our God day and night. Furthermore, the last place is held by the tempters or ambushers, who are present individually to every human being, whom we therefore call "evil geniuses," and their prince is **Mammon**, <note>original: "Mammon"</note> which is interpreted as greed or cupidity. Moreover, all agree that evil demons wander in this lower world, hostile to everyone, for which reason they are called "devils." Concerning them, **Augustine** says in the first book of *On the Incarnation of the Word to Januarius*, saying: *Regarding the devil and his angels and the opposing powers, the preaching of the Church has taught that these things indeed exist; but what they are, or how they are, it has not explained clearly enough.* Among many, however, this opinion is held: that this devil was an angel and became an apostate, having persuaded many angels to fall away with him, who even until now are called his "angels." <note>Augustine (354–430 AD) was a foundational Christian theologian; here the author cites his caution regarding the specific nature of demons.</note> Nevertheless, **Greece** does not think that all of these were damned, nor indeed that all of them are evil by purpose, but that from the beginning of time the distribution of things was established by such reason that the execution of punishment for sinful souls was delegated to them. Other theologians say that no demons were created evil, but were cast out and thrown down from the orders of the good spirits from the heavens on account of their transgression. Their fall is taught not only by our theologians and those of the **Hebrews**, but is also confirmed by the doctrines of the **Assyrians**, **Arabs**, **Egyptians**, and **Greeks**. **Pherecydes the Syrian** <note>A 6th-century BC Greek philosopher often credited with the first prose treatment of Greek mythology and the soul.</note> describes the fall of the demons, and **Ophin** <term>Ophin: Derived from the Greek "ophis" (serpent).</term>—that is, the demonic serpent—as the head of the rebelling army. **Trismegistus** in his *Poimandres* and **Homer** in his poems under the name of **Ate** <note>original: "Atarum"</note> sing of this same fall; and **Plutarch**, in his discourse on usury, indicates that **Empedocles** knew of such a lapse of the demons. The demons themselves have also many times confessed their fall. <margin>The various pursuits of demons.</margin> Thus, these spirits, cast down into this valley of misery, partly wander near us in this murky air; others inhabit lakes, rivers, and the seas; others haunt the lands and terrify earthly things, and those who dig wells and mines they attack; they cause openings in the earth and shake the foundations of mountains. Nor do they vex only humans, but also animals. Some, content only with laughter and illusion, strive to weary people rather than harm them. Others, raising themselves up with giant bodies beyond normal height, then lowering themselves to the smallness of pygmies and turning themselves into various figures, disturb men with vain terror. Others apply themselves to lies and blasphemies, such as the one we read about in the **Third Book of Kings**, <margin>1 Kings 22</margin> saying: *I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all the prophets of Ahab.* But the worst kind of demons are those who haunt the roads, rushing upon those passing by, delighting in wars and the shedding of blood, and afflicting men with the cruelest insults. We read of such spirits in **Matthew**, because of the fear of whom no one dared to pass by that way. Now indeed, Scripture mentions nocturnal, diurnal, and midday demons; and describes other spirits of wickedness by various names, such as we read in **Isaiah**: <margin>Isaiah 34</margin> **onocentaurs**, **hedgehogs**, **shaggy ones**, **sirenes**, **lamiae**, **screech owls**, **ostriches**... <note>Isaiah 34:14 contains a list of creatures inhabiting a desolated land; here, they are interpreted as various types of demonic spirits or hybrids.</note>

<margin>The opinion of Origen regarding demons.</margin>
The opinion of **Origen** <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar known for the controversial theory of *apokatastasis*, or the ultimate restoration of all beings to God.</note> regarding demons is this: that demons, who by their own will withdrew from the service of God with their prince the devil, if they begin to repent even a little, are clothed in human flesh. Through this penance, after the resurrection, they may return by the same path through which they came into the flesh to the vision of God, having been restored to their rights, being then still freed from ethereal and aerial bodies. At that time, every knee shall bow to God—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—so that God may be all in all. Furthermore, **Saint Irenaeus** approves the opinion of **Justin Martyr**, who said: **Satan** never dared to speak blasphemy against God before the Lord had arrived on earth, because he did not yet know his own damnation. Moreover, many believe that most of the fallen demons hope for their future salvation, as they are taught by the history of **Paul the Hermit** <note>The first Christian hermit, whose life was recorded by Saint Jerome.</note> written by **Jerome**, and honored by the Church in the canonical hours; and from the legend of **Saint Brendan**. <note>A reference to the "Voyage of Saint Brendan," a medieval tale of a monk searching for the Isle of the Blessed.</note> They also bring forward this argument that their prayers are to be heard: because it is read in the Gospels that **Christ** heard the prayers of the demons and granted them permission to enter the herd of swine. <note>Referring to the Miracle of the Gadarene Swine (Matthew 8:28–34).</note> This is also supported by the seventy-first Psalm according to our numbering (but the seventy-second according to the numbering of the Hebrews), where we read: *Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the earth.* In that place, according to the Hebrew truth, it is read: *Before him the inhabitants of the wilderness shall bend their knees*—that is, the aerial spirits when they shall worship, as the **Kabbalists** <note>Practitioners of Jewish mysticism; Agrippa frequently cites Kabbalah as a source of hidden wisdom.</note> assert—*and his enemies shall lick the dust.* They explain this as referring to **Zazel** <note>Zazel is often identified in occult texts as the spirit or "intelligence" of the planet Saturn.</note> and his army, of whom it is read in **Genesis**: *You shall eat the earth all the days of your life.* And elsewhere the prophet says: *Because the dust of the earth is his bread.*

For this reason, the Kabbalists also think that some demons are to be saved, which it is certain that Origen also felt.

CCXLVII.
### BOOK THREE.

**Regarding the bodies of demons**, there is a great disagreement between modern theologians and philosophers. **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and "Angelic Doctor" of the Church.</note> affirms that all angels are incorporeal <note>original: "incorporeos," meaning having no physical body.</note>, and likewise the evil demons; he suggests they occasionally take on bodies, which they soon cast off. **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian Neoplatonist.</note> also constantly affirms in *On the Divine Names* that angels are incorporeal. **Augustine**, however, in his commentary *On Genesis*, reveals this: "Demons are called aerial and fiery animals, because they thrive in the nature of aerial bodies, and are not dissolved by death, since the element that is more suited to acting than to suffering prevails within them." <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430). The "suffering" here refers to being physically acted upon or broken down.</note> He seems to suggest that all angels had aerial bodies from the beginning of their creation, formed from the purer and higher part of the air, suited for action but not for suffering; and that after the fall, these were preserved for the good angels, but for the wicked ones, they were changed into a thicker quality of air so that they might even be tormented by fire. Furthermore, **Basil the Great** attributes bodies not only to demons but even to pure angels, describing them as certain thin, aerial, and pure spirits. **Gregory Nazianzen** <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the 4th-century church.</note> also agrees with these views. **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of "The Golden Ass."</note> does not think all demons have bodies; for in his book *On the God of Socrates*, he says: "There is another more majestic kind of demons who, being always free from corporeal shackles and bonds, are managed by certain prayers." However, **Psellus**, both a Platonist and a Christian, thinks the nature of demons is not without a body; yet he does not think the angelic and demonic body is the same, for the former is devoid of all matter. The demonic body is, in a way, material, like the bodies of shadows, and subject to passion <note>In this context, "passion" means being subject to external forces or pain.</note>, so that it even feels pain when struck, and can be burned by fire into visible ashes—an event recorded as having once happened in Tuscany. And although it is a spiritual body, it is nonetheless highly sensible and susceptible to touch; even if cut apart, it joins back together and restores itself, just like air and water, though in the meantime it suffers greatly. For this reason, they fear the edge of a blade, and darts, and swords. Hence, in **Virgil**, the Sibyl says to Aeneas:

> And you, set forth upon the path, and draw the sword from its scabbard. <note>A quote from Virgil's "Aeneid," Book 6, line 260. The Sibyl is instructing Aeneas as they enter the underworld.</note>

<margin>Various kinds of demonic bodies</margin>
Upon which **Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> says that he wished Aeneas to have a consecrated sword. **Orpheus** also describes the kinds of demonic bodies. There is indeed one body that consists only of fire, but it does not allow itself to be seen; these Orpheus calls the fiery and celestial demons. Another is tempered by a mixture of fire and air, which are called ethereal and aerial. If a certain watery quality is added to this, a third kind arises, called the aqueous demons, who are sometimes perceived by sight. If something earthy is added to these, though not very thick, they are called terrestrial demons; these are more visible and often encountered by our senses. The bodies of the higher demons or angels are composed of the purest ethereal element, and are not easily visible to any man unless they offer their appearance by divine will. They are woven of threads so splendid and so thin that, by their rarity, they let all the rays of our sight pass through, or by their splendor they strike the sight back, or by their subtleness they frustrate it. Regarding these, **Chalcidius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato's "Timaeus."</note> says: "The ethereal and aerial demons, because their bodies do not have so much fire as to be transparent, nor so...

Their entire structure, bound together from the clarity of the ether and the fluidity of the air, has formed an unbreakable surface. Other demons are neither so virtuous nor so troublesome, nor are they always invisible; sometimes they are seen, changing into different figures. They take on the shadowy forms of bloodless ghosts, dragging with them the filth of a heavy body. They have an excessive fellowship with matter <note>original: *sylva*, literally "forest," but used here in the philosophical sense of *hyle* or prime matter, which ancient writers often associated with a "malignant soul."</note>, and because of their proximity to the earth and water, they are even affected by earthly pleasures and lusts. Of this kind are the lamiae <note>mythological man-eating monsters or witches</note>, and the incubi, and the succubi <note>demons believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping humans</note>. It is perhaps not an absurd guess that Melusina <note>A figure of European folklore, often depicted as a woman who is a serpent or fish from the waist down.</note> belonged to their number. However, the subterranean and dark demons cannot achieve the same variety of shapes as the others because their imaginative faculty is confined within the narrow limits of a thick and sluggish body. Furthermore, those who are watery or inhabit the moist parts of the earth mostly resemble women because of the softness of their element; of this kind are the Naiads <note>water nymphs</note> and Dryads <note>tree nymphs</note>. Those, however, who inhabit waterless and arid places show themselves as males with drier bodies, appearing as Satyrs, or "Onoscelos" with donkey legs, Fauns, Sylvans, and incubi. Regarding these, Augustine relates that many have learned through the mastery of experience that these beings have often been wicked toward women, seeking and performing intercourse with them. He also notes that certain demons, whom the Gauls call "Dusii," constantly attempt this lustful behavior.

->On the infestation of evil demons, and the protection<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a landscape with a building in the background and a figure in the foreground.</image-desc>
IT is the common opinion of theologians that all evil demons are of such a nature that they hate both gods and men equally. Therefore, divine providence has appointed purer demons <note>the author uses "demons" here in the classical sense of "spirits," including what we would call angels.</note> as our nearby overseers, to whom it has commended us as if to shepherds or rulers. These protect us daily, and they ward off, restrain, and bind the evil demons so that they cannot harm us as much as they might wish. This is just as we read in the Book of Tobit, that Raphael seized the demon named Asmodeus and banished him to the desert of Upper Egypt. Concerning these spirits, Hesiod says: "There are thirty thousand immortals living upon the earth, guardians of mortal men appointed by Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>, who observe acts of justice and deeds of mercy, clothed in air and going everywhere over the earth." For no prince and no nobleman would remain safe, no woman would remain uncorrupted, and no man in this valley of ignorance would reach the end appointed for him by God, if good demons did not stand by us for our protection, or if evil demons were permitted to satisfy the wicked wills of men. Therefore, just as a specific guardian is assigned from the good demons to each person to strengthen the spirit of man toward the good, so some enemy is sent forth from the evil ones, presiding over the flesh and its itching desires. The good guardian fights for us on behalf of the spirit against the enemy and the flesh.
