CCXLIX.
### BOOK THREE. CCXLIX.

However, man stands in the middle between these combatants, and being left in the hand of his own counsel, he grants victory to whomsoever he wills. We cannot, therefore, accuse the angels if they do not lead the nations 
<margin>The wickedness of nations is not to be attributed to the angels.</margin>
entrusted to them to the knowledge of the true God, or to true piety and religion, and instead allow them to slip into errors and perverse worship; rather, it must be attributed to those who have turned aside from the right path of their own accord, adhering to spirits of error and giving victory to the devil. For it is in the hand of man to whom he wishes to adhere, and whom he wishes to conquer; and if the enemy demon is once defeated by him, that demon is made his servant, and once conquered, he cannot further attack another, like a wasp that has lost its sting. With this opinion Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for his complex views on the soul and spiritual warfare.</note> also agrees in his book *Periarchon* <note>original: *Periarchon*, Greek for "On First Principles."</note>, concluding that the saints, fighting against evil demons and conquering them, diminish their army, so that it is no longer lawful for him who has been conquered by one person to trouble another thereafter. 

Just as a good spirit is given to every person, so also is a diabolical evil spirit given; both of these seek union with our spirit, and strive to draw it to themselves and to be mixed with it, like wine mixed with water. The good one, indeed, through good works conforming to itself, transforms us by uniting us into angels, just as it is written of John the Baptist in Malachi: "Behold, I send my angel before your face." <note>original: *Ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam.* Malachi 3:1.</note> 
<margin>Malachi 3</margin>
Concerning this transformation and union, it is written elsewhere: "He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him." The evil demon also strives through evil works to make us conformable and united to itself, just as Christ says of Judas: "Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a 
<margin>John 6</margin>
devil?" <note>original: *Nonne ego uos elegi duodecim, & unus ex uobis diabolus est?* John 6:70.</note> And this is what Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the *Hermetica*—a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts—is attributed.</note> says: when a demon flows into a human soul, it scatters the seeds of its own notion, whence such a soul, sprinkled with these seeds and pregnant with fury, brings forth wonders therefrom, and performs whatever are the offices of demons. For when a good demon <note>The author uses "demon" here in the classical sense of *daemon*, meaning a guiding spirit or divine power, which could be either good or bad.</note> flows into a holy soul, it raises it to the light of wisdom; but an evil demon, poured into a depraved soul, incites it to thefts, homicides, lusts, and whatever are the offices of evil demons. 

Good demons (as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine.</note> says) purge souls most perfectly; moreover, some provide us with certain things, while others, being present, give health to the body, virtue to the soul, and security to the mind. They erase what is deadly within us, cherish our natural heat, and make it more effective for life, and they always infuse a light of intelligible harmony into the mind. 

Whether there are many guardians for a man, or only one, theologians contend among themselves; we think there are many, as the prophet says: "He has given his angels charge over you, that they may guard you in all 
<margin>Psalm 90</margin>
your ways" <note>original: *Angelis suis mandauit de te, ut custodiant te in omnibus uiis tuis.* Psalm 91:11 (numbered 90 in the Vulgate).</note>—which, according to Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>, has a place not only in Christ, but in every human being. Therefore, all men are governed by the ministry of diverse spirits, and are led to whatever degree of virtue, merit, and dignity they have shown themselves worthy of. But those who are unworthy are cast down and thrust out by evil demons, and as if abandoned by good spirits, are pushed down to the extreme degree of misery, as their evil merits require. However, whoever is assigned to the more sublime angels is preferred even over other men; for their angels, having care for them, elevate them and [subject others to them...]

Indeed, he fears and reveres that power which the higher angels instill into those above us, and by a certain terror, they lead those who are lower into a fear of presidency. Homer seems to have sensed this when he said that the Muses, born of Jove, assist kings (also born of Jove) as inseparable companions, and through them, these kings are made venerable and august <note>original: "Augustos," referring both to the title of the emperors and the quality of majesty</note>. Thus we read that Mark Antony, once joined in a singular friendship with Octavian Augustus, used to play games with him frequently. But since Augustus always left as the victor, a certain magician warned Mark Antony with this opinion: "What is it to you, O Antony, with that youth? Flee from him and avoid him; for although you are older in years, more excellent in experience, more illustrious in lineage, and as a commander of many you have endured many wars, <margin>Augustus's genius is more excellent than the genius of Mark Antony</margin> nevertheless your genius <note>In Roman belief, the "Genius" was a personal protective spirit that shaped a person's character and luck.</note> dreads the genius of this youth, and your fortune flatters <note>original: "subblanditur," meaning to submit or yield to the charm of another</note> his fortune; unless you flee far away, all your fortune seems destined to fail and pass to him." Is not a prince a man similar to other men? How would other men fear and revere him unless a divine terror elevated him, and by striking fear into the rest, pressed them down so that they might revere him as a prince? Therefore, we must strive so that—having been purified by acting rightly and following sublime things, and even by choosing opportune times and places—we may be committed to the rank of the more sublime and powerful angels, who, by taking care of us, may rightfully prefer us over others.

### On following one's own genius, and investigating its nature.
## Chapter XXI.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' showing a landscape with figures and a building in the background.</image-desc>
Just as every region in the heavens possesses a certain star and celestial image that influences it more than others, so also in the super-celestial realms it obtains a certain Intelligence <note>A term for a high-ranking spiritual being or angel governing a celestial body or sphere.</note> that presides over and protects it, along with infinite other ministering spirits or demons of its own order. These are all called by the common name "Sons of <term>Elohim Sabaoth</term> <note>original: "בני אלהים צבאות" (B'nei Elohim Tzva'ot), meaning "Sons of the God of Hosts."</note>," that is, the sons of the God of hosts. Hence, whenever the Most High deliberates on war, slaughter, the desolation of some kingdom, or the subjection of a people in these lower realms, then—just as these things are to come to pass on earth—a conflict of those spirits in the heavens precedes them. As it is written in Isaiah: "The Lord of hosts shall visit the host of the high ones in the high place, and the kings of the earth upon the earth." We also read in <margin>Daniel 10</margin> Daniel about this conflict of spirits and presidencies: namely, of the prince of the kingdom of the Persians, the prince of the Greeks, and the prince of the people of Israel, and of their mutual conflict. Homer also seems to have once perceived this when he sang:

> Such a great rumor spread through the celestial hall,
> When the gods rushed into savage battles one after another:
> Phoebus Apollo fought against Neptune,
> Pallas Athena strove against Mars,
> Quivered Diana stood against Juno in war.

CCLI.
### BOOK THREE. 251.
x iiii

->The swift Cyllenian <note>An epithet for the god Mercury, who was born on Mount Cyllene.</note> presses Latona <note>The mother of Apollo and Diana; in astrology, her "weapons" often refer to the rays of the Sun and Moon.</note> with his weapons.<-

<margin>The Genius is changed according to the change of place.</margin>
Nevertheless, although spirits and demons of every kind exist in every individual region, those who are of the same order as the presiding ruler of that region are more powerful there than others. Thus, in a solar region, solar spirits flourish above the rest; in a lunar region, lunar spirits; and so it is with the others. From this it arises and follows that when we change locations and provinces, various outcomes of our affairs and business present themselves and follow us—being more fortunate in one place and less so in another. This occurs where our genius <term>daemon</term> <note>Agrippa uses "daemon" in the classical Greek sense of a "daimon" or guiding spirit, not necessarily an evil entity.</note> has obtained greater power, or where we have acquired a more powerful demon of the same order in that place. Thus, solar people, if they move to a solar region or province, will be rendered far more fortunate there because they will have their leaders or genii more powerful and favorable in that location. Under their excellent protection, all their affairs are often led to happy endings, even beyond expectation and the measure of their own strength. Hence it is that the choice of place, region, and time—where one might exercise themselves, live, and frequent according to the nature and instinct of their own genius—contributes greatly to the happiness of life.

<margin>A change of name is sometimes beneficial.</margin>
A change of name is also sometimes beneficial; for since the properties of names are indicators of the things themselves, declaring the conditions of their forms as if in a mirror, it follows that by changing names, the state of affairs often happens to change as well. Hence, Holy Scripture introduces God changing the names of Abram and Jacob when He was about to bless them—calling the former **Abraham** and the latter **Israel**—and not without cause.

<margin>From where the nature of the Genius may be discerned.</margin>
Moreover, the ancient sages teach that the nature of each person's genius can be known from the stars, their influence, and their aspects <note>The angular relationships between planets in a birth chart.</note> which occur in each person's nativity <note>original: "Genesi," referring to the astrological moment of birth.</note>. However, they do so with such diverse and disagreeing systems that it is most difficult to wrest these secrets of the heavens from their hands. For **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> seeks the genius from the star that is the mistress of the birth chart. **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> however, seeks it either from that star or from the planets that have the most dignities there, or from that house which the Moon entered after the house it occupied at the person's birth. The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers.</note> seek the genius only from either the Sun or the Moon. Others, including many of the **Hebrews**, think it should be sought from one of the cardinal points of the heavens, or all of them together. Others seek the good genius from the eleventh house (which they therefore call the "Good Demon") and the evil genius from the sixth house (which they call the "Evil Demon"). Since the inquiry into these matters is laborious and most occult, we shall much more easily investigate the nature of our genius from within ourselves. We should attend to those things which have been suggested by the mind since our earliest age, undistracted by contagions, or those things which the mind suggests when purged of vain cares and sinister affections once impediments are removed—the things which the instinct of nature dictates and to which the heaven inclines us. These are, without doubt, the persuasions of the genius who was given to each person from the beginning of their birth, leading and persuading us toward that which his star inclines us.

<summary>Agrippa explains how a person's fortune is tied to their guiding spirit (Genius), which can be influenced by geographical location, name changes, and astrological configurations. He concludes that internal intuition is often a more reliable guide to one's Genius than complex astrological calculations.</summary>

OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### That every man has a threefold guardian, and from what sources each proceeds. Chapter XXII.

<margin>Sacred spirit <note>original: "Sacer dæmon"</note></margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' depicting a scholar or religious figure seated at a desk, surrounded by books and architectural motifs.</image-desc>Every person has a threefold good spirit <term>daemon</term> <note>Agrippa uses the word "daemon" in the classical sense of a "daimon"—a guiding spirit or intermediary power—rather than the modern concept of an evil "demon."</note> as their own guardian: one is sacred, the second is of birth, and the third is of profession. The sacred spirit, according to the doctrine of the Egyptians, is assigned to the rational soul as it descends—not from the stars or planets, but from a supernal cause, from God himself, the ruler of spirits. This spirit is universal and above nature. It directs the life of the soul and always presents good thoughts to the mind, constantly working to illuminate us, though we do not always notice it. However, when we are purified and live tranquilly, it is then perceived by us; then 
<margin>Note.</margin>
it speaks with us, as it were, and communicates its voice to us—having previously been present in silence—and it continually strives to lead us toward sacred perfection. By the help of this spirit, we are also able to avoid the malice of fate. The Platonists believe that if this spirit is religiously honored by us with integrity and holiness (as we know **Socrates** did), we are wonderfully helped by it, whether through dreams or signs, by turning away evils and anxiously providing good things. For this reason, the Pythagoreans, in harmony with this, were accustomed to pray to **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iouem"</note> that he might either lead them away from evils himself or show them by which of the spirits such a thing could be granted. But the spirit of birth, which is also called the **genius**, descends from the disposition of the world and the circuits of the stars that are active during one's generation.

<margin>Spirit of birth, the genius.</margin>
There are those who believe that the soul, just as it is about to descend into the body, naturally sets apart a guardian for itself from the choir of spirits; they suggest it does not so much choose this leader for itself as it is, in turn, chosen by that spirit for protection. This spirit is the executor and guardian of life; it joins the soul to the body, cares for the soul once it is communicated to the body, and assists the person in that very duty for which the celestial powers designated them at birth. Therefore, whoever has received a fortunate genius is rendered virtuous, effective, strong, and prosperous in their works; for this reason, they are called "well-fortunated" or "well-born" by the Philosophers. <margin>Spirit of profession.</margin> But the spirit of profession is given by the stars to which the particular profession or sect that a person follows is subject. The soul secretly desires this spirit when it begins to use choice within this body and takes on specific habits. This spirit changes when the profession changes; furthermore, according to the dignity of the profession, more worthy and even more sublime professional spirits assist us. They care for a person successively, as one acquires different professional guardians from day to day as they ascend from virtue to virtue. Thus, when a profession agrees with our nature, a 
<margin>//</margin>
professional spirit is present that is similar to us and in harmony with our genius, and life is rendered more tranquil, happy, and prosperous. But when we undertake a profession dissimilar or contrary to our genius, our life is rendered laborious and troubled by the discordant patrons. Thus it happens that someone may profit in a particular science, art, or ministry with little time and labor, while another labors in vain with much sweat and study. And although no science, no art, and no virtue should be despised, nevertheless, so that you may live prosperously and act happily, first acknowledge your genius.

If you have the guardians of your nature and your profession in harmony, you will feel a double progress and increase in both; but if they should be different, follow the better one, for sometimes you will receive better nourishment from an excellent profession than from your birth.

## On the language of angels, and their conversations both among themselves and with us. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>What the speech of angels is.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a landscape with classical architecture and trees.</image-desc>
We might doubt whether angels or demons, since they are pure spirits, use any vocal speech or language among themselves or toward us, were it not that **Paul** says in a certain place: *If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels* <note>original: "Si linguis hominū loquar & angelorū"</note>. But what that speech of theirs is, or what language they use, is still a matter of doubt among many. For most people believe that if they use any idiom, it is **Hebrew**, because this was the first of all languages, it emanated from heaven, and it existed before the confusion of tongues arose in Babylon. In this language, the Law was given by God the Father, the Gospel was preached by Christ the Son, and so many oracles were given through the Holy Spirit in the prophets. And while all other languages have suffered and continually suffer various changes and corruptions, this one alone always remains inviolate. Furthermore, an evident sign of this opinion is that while demons and individual <term>intelligences</term> <note>Agrippa uses "intelligences" to refer to the high-ranking spiritual beings that govern celestial bodies or nations.</note> may use the speech of the specific nations where they dwell, they never speak in any other idiom to those who know the Hebrew language, but in that one alone.

<margin>The speech of angels is hidden from us.</margin>
However, how angels speak is hidden from us, just as they themselves are. For us to speak, a tongue is necessary along with other instruments, which are the jaws, the palate, the lips, the teeth, the throat, the lungs, the windpipe, and the pectoral muscles, which receive the beginning of their motion from the soul. Truly, if someone speaks to another from a distance, he requires a louder shout; thus, one who is near whispers into the listener's ear. And if he could be joined to the listener with a more direct spirit, his speech would require no sound at all, but would glide into the listener without noise, like an image into the eye or a mirror. This is how souls departed from the body speak, and how angels and demons speak. What a man does with a sensible voice, they do by impressing the concept of the speech into those to whom they speak, in a better way than if it were expressed through an audible voice. Thus the **Platonists** say that **Socrates** perceived his own <term>daemon</term> <note>A personal guiding spirit.</note> with a sense, though not of this body, but with the sense of an <term>ethereal body</term> <note>A subtle, light-filled "spirit-body" believed to sit between the physical body and the soul.</note> hiding within this one; for...

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

Likewise, <term>Avicenna<note>A famous Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose philosophical works deeply influenced medieval and Renaissance thought.</note></term> believes that angels are usually seen and heard by prophets through reason. That instrument—whatever that power may be through which a spirit makes known to another spirit, or to a human, the things that bubble up in the mind—is called the "tongue of angels" by the apostle Paul. Most often, however, they also emit a perceptible voice, <margin>Acts 1</margin> as when those crying out at the ascension of the Lord said: *Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?* and in the Old Law, they spoke with many of the Fathers with a perceptible voice. But this occurs only in assumed bodies. However, by what senses the spirits themselves <margin>Note</margin> and demons hear our invocations and prayers, and see our ceremonies, we are utterly ignorant. For the body of demons is spiritual, in large part sensitive everywhere and on all sides by its nature, so that it touches, sees, and hears without a medium, and nothing can be an impediment to them. Yet they do not perceive in the same way we do with distinct organs; but perhaps just as sponges drink up water, so they draw in all perceptible things with their entire body, or in some other way unknown to us. For not all living creatures that we see are equipped with the same sensory organs; for we know many lack ears, yet we know sound is perceived by them, though by what means, we do not know.

### Chapter XXIV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a seated figure within the letter's curves, with another figure standing to the left, possibly in a garden or architectural setting.</image-desc>
SPIRITS, both good and evil, have manifold and diverse names. Their proper and true names, however, just as those of the stars, are known to God alone, who alone counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names. None of these can be known by us except through divine revelation, and very few have been expressed for us in the Sacred Scriptures. Truly, the masters of the Hebrews think that names were imposed upon the spirits by Adam himself, according to that which is written: *God brought all things which He had made to Adam so that he might name them; and whatever he called a thing, that is its name.* From this, the <term>Kabbalists<note>original: "mecubales"; practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note></term> together <margin>Man can impose names on spirits.</margin> with the Magi, think it is within the power of man even to impose names upon spirits. Because, in truth, no human voice can compose a name that can express the nature of divinity and the all-encompassing virtue of the angelic essence, names are most often <margin>From where names are imposed on spirits.</margin> imposed upon spirits based on their works, signifying a certain office or effect, such as is desired from a choir of spirits. These names then—no differently than offerings and sacrifices devoted to the gods—obtain efficacy and virtue for drawing down from the heavens or raising from the depths some spiritual substance that works the desired effect. # OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The four winds and their four angels.</margin>
...liel, Requiel, Abrinaël, Aziel, Tagriel, Alheniel, Amnixiel. There are also four princes of the angels who are set over the four winds and over the four parts of the world, of whom **Michael** is set over the eastern wind; **Raphael** over the western; **Gabriel** over the northern; and **Noriel**—whom others call **Uriel**—over the southern. 

<margin>Angels of the elements.</margin>
They are also assigned to the elements: to air, **Cherub**; to water, **Tharfis**; to earth, **Ariel**; to fire, **Seruph**, or according to Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note>, **Nathaniel**. Each of these spirits is a great prince and possesses much freedom of power in the dominion of their planets and signs, and in their seasons, years, months, days, and hours, and in their elements, parts of the world, and winds. Each of them rules over many legions. By the same reasoning, among the evil spirits, four most powerful kings preside over the others according to the four parts of the world, whose names are called **Urieus**, king of the east; **Amaymon**, king of the south; **Paymon**, king of the west; and **Egyn**, king of the north. The doctors of the Hebrews perhaps more correctly call these **Samaël**, **Azazel**, **Azaël**, and **Mahazaël**. Under these, many other princes of legions and presiding officers hold dominion, as well as countless demons of private duties. 

<margin>The Telchines</margin>
Furthermore, the ancient theologians of the Greeks number six demons whom they call **Telchines** <note>original: "Telchines"; mythical sorcerers and spirits from Greek lore associated with the sea and the island of Rhodes</note>, while others call them **Alastores** <note>original: "Alastores"; avenging spirits or demons of misfortune</note>. These, being malicious toward men, draw the water of the Styx <note>the river of the underworld</note> with their hands and scatter it upon the lands, from which calamities, plagues, and famines follow. These are said to have been **Acteus**, **Megalesius**, **Ormenus**, **Lycus**, **Nicon**, and **Mimon**. For the rest, he who desires to know exactly the distinct names, offices, places, and times of the angels and even the evil demons should seek them in the volume of *Temples* by Rabbi Simon, in the same author's *Book of Lights* <note>original: "libro Luminū"; likely referring to the Zohar or the Sefer HaBahir</note>, in the treatise *On the Magnitude of Stature* <note>original: "de Magnitudine ſtaturæ"; the Shi'ur Qomah, a mystical text describing the "measure" of God's body</note>, in the treatise on *Temples* by Rabbi Ishmael <note>referring to Hekhalot or "Palace" literature</note>, and in almost all commentaries on the *Book of Formation* <note>original: "libri Formationis"; the Sefer Yetzirah</note>, where one will find extensive writings about these things.

### Chapter XXV.

<margin>A general rule.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
There are also other sacred names assigned to individual duties for both good and evil spirits, much more powerful than those previously mentioned. These are extracted from the holy scriptures according to the art handed down by the Hebrew Kabbalists, just as certain names of God are drawn from specific passages. The general rule for these is that wherever something about the divine essence is expressed in holy letters, a divine name can be properly gathered from that place. Truly, wherever a divine name is found expressed in the holy scriptures, consider the ministry that lies beneath that name. 

<margin>Rule for extraction</margin>
Therefore, wherever the scripture speaks of the ministry or work of any good or evil spirit, the name of that same spirit—whether good or evil—can be extracted from that place, provided this unchanging rule is observed: that from good things, the names of the good [spirits are extracted], and from evil things, the names of the evil [spirits]...

CCLXVII.

->BOOK THREE.<-

...words, compacted of joined and alternating letters, though their sound and meaning may be unknown, it is necessary to confess—based on the secret principles of philosophy—that they possess more power in a magical work than names that carry a clear meaning. This is because when the mind is astonished by their enigmas, and the whole edge of the intellect is intent upon them, firmly believing that something divine lies beneath, it reverently sounds these words and names (even if they are not understood) for the glory of the deity, with a spiritual affect of piety, capturing itself in obedience to Him.

### On the calculatory art of such names according to the tradition 
### of the Cabalists. Chapter XXVII.

THERE is yet another artifice for such names which they call the **calculatory art** <term>calculatory art: likely referring to Gematria or Temurah, Kabbalistic methods of deriving new words or numerical values from existing sacred names</term>, and it is performed through the following tables. One enters with a sacred name—whether divine or angelic—into the descending column of letters, taking those letters which you find at the common angles under their respective stars and signs. When these letters are arranged in order, the name of a **good spirit** is constituted, possessing the nature of that star or sign under which you entered. If, however, you enter by the ascending column, taking the common angles above the stars and signs marked in the bottom line, the name of an **evil spirit** is constituted. And these are the names of the spirits ministering from any order or heaven, both good and evil, which according to this method you can multiply into nine names for as many orders; thus, by entering with one name, you can elicit another spirit of a higher order from the same, whether good or evil. 

However, the beginning of this calculation depends upon the names of God; for every voice has power in Magic insofar as it depends upon the voice of God and is formed from it. Thus, we ought to know that every angelic name must proceed from some primary name of God. Therefore, the angels are said to "bear the name of God," according to that which is written: <note>original: "quia est nomē meum in illo"</note> "for my name is in him" <note>A reference to Exodus 23:21, implying the angel acts with divine authority</note>. Therefore, so that the names of good angels may be distinguished from the names of evil ones, it is customary to suffix to them some name of divine omnipotence, such as **El**, or **On**, or **Iah**, or **Iod**, and to pronounce it together with the name. 

Because **Iah** <note>original: "Iah"</note> is a name of beneficence, and **Iod** <note>original: "Iod"</note> is a name of deity, these two names are only attached to the names of angels. However, the name **El** <note>original: "El"</note>, which signifies force and virtue, is therefore added not only to good spirits, but sometimes even to evil spirits. 
<margin>an evil demon's <unclear>me / his dominion</unclear></margin>
For not even evil spirits can subsist or act at all without the power of God. 

Furthermore, it should be known that the common angles of the same star and sign must be taken, unless one has entered with a "mixed name," such as the names of **genii** <term>genii: guardian spirits or tutelary deities associated with a person or place</term>, and those of which we spoke in the preceding chapter, which are composed from the dispositions of heaven according to the harmony of different stars. Whenever the table is entered with these, the common angle must be taken under the star or sign of the entering letter. There are, moreover, those who extend these tables so far as to think that if one enters with the name of a star, or an office, or a desired effect, a demon—both good and evil—may be elicited to serve that office or effect. In a similar way, entering with the proper name of any person, the names of their genii [can be found]...

CCLXVIII.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

...confide that they can extract for themselves, under that star which seems to preside over a specific person—whether they know this from **Physiognomy** <term>Physiognomy: the practice of judging a person's character or fortune from their outward appearance, especially the face</term>, or from the passions and inclinations of the mind, or from their profession and fortune—whether they are **Martial** (of Mars), **Saturnine** (of Saturn), **Solar** (of the Sun), or of the nature of another star. And although these primary names, in terms of their literal meaning, have little or no power, yet the names extracted in this way and derived from them are of the greatest efficacy—just as solar rays collected in a concave mirror burn most strongly, even though the sun itself is only moderately warm. 

The order of letters in these tables under the stars and signs is almost similar to the order of **decans** <term>decans: 36 subdivisions of the zodiac, each spanning 10 degrees</term>, nines, and twelves used by astrologers. **Alfonso the Cypriot** <note>original: "Alfonsus Cyprius"; likely referring to an astrological or Kabbalistic commentator</note> once wrote about this calculatory art, and someone else (I know not who) adapted it for Latin characters. However, since the letters of every language—as we showed in the First Book—have a celestial and divine origin in their number, order, and shape, I would easily concede that this calculation of the names of spirits can be done not only through **Hebrew** letters, but also through **Chaldean**, **Arabic**, **Egyptian**, **Greek**, **Latin**, and any others, provided tables are properly constructed after the pattern of the presiding [celestial powers]. 

But many object here that in these tables it happens that many men of different nature and fortune often obtain the same **genius** <term>genius: a presiding spirit or guardian assigned to a person at birth</term> because of having the same name. Therefore, it should be known that it is not thought absurd that the same **demon** <note>original: "dæmonem"; in this context, a neutral term for a spirit or guiding entity</note> can be distinguished by many souls, and that the same spirit can preside over many people. 

Furthermore, just as different men often share the same name, so spirits of different offices and natures can be noted by one name and one and the same sign or character, yet with respect to different things. For just as the **serpent** sometimes represents Christ and sometimes the devil, so the same names and the same signs are equated now to some order of **evil demons**, now to some order of **good angels**. Finally, the burning intention of the invoker itself—through which our intellect is joined to the **separated intelligences** <term>separated intelligences: spiritual beings, like angels, that exist independently of physical bodies</term>—brings it about that we have now this spirit, now another obeying us, even if invoked under the same name. <margin>everything</margin>

### Chapter XXX.

Among the **Hebrews**, I find several methods of characters. One is very ancient—namely, the old script used by **Moses** and the prophets, the form of which must not be rashly revealed to anyone; for the letters they use today were established by **Ezra** <note>The Hebrew alphabet used today is the "Square Script" (Ashuri), which tradition says Ezra the Scribe brought back from the Babylonian exile to replace the "Old Hebrew" (Paleo-Hebrew) script</note>. There is also a script among them which they call **Celestial**, because they show it placed and shaped among the stars, just as other astrologers derive the images of the zodiac signs from the patterns of the stars. There is also what they call the script of **Malachim** or **Melachim** <note>original: "Malachim uel Melachim"; "Malachim" means messengers or angels, while "Melachim" means kings</note>—that is, the script of angels or the royal script—and there is another they call the **Passing of the River** <note>original: "transitus fluuii"; a mystical alphabet likely named after the crossing of the Euphrates by the Jews returning from Babylon</note>. ### Script of the Crossing of the River.

There is yet another method among the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Jewish mystics who studied the hidden meanings of the Torah and the universe through the Hebrew language</term>, which was once held in great veneration, but today has become so common that it has almost fallen into use among the profane. It is as follows: let the twenty-seven characters of the **Hebrews** <note>This includes the 22 standard letters plus the 5 final forms (Soffit) of certain letters</note> be divided into three classes, each of which contains nine letters.

The **first class**—namely א ב ג ד ה ו ז ח ט <note>Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth, He, Vau, Zain, Cheth, Teth</note>—are the signs of simple numbers <note>the units 1 through 9</note> and of intellectual things, distributed into the nine orders of angels.

The **second class** holds י כ ל מ נ ס ע פ צ <note>Yod, Caph, Lamed, Mem, Nun, Samech, Ayin, Pe, Tzadi</note>, the signs of the tens <note>numbers 10 through 90</note> and of celestial things, within the nine spheres of the heavens.

The **third class** holds the four remaining letters along with the five final forms in order—namely ק ר ש ת ך ם ן ף ץ <note>Qoph, Resh, Shin, Tau, and the final forms of Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, and Tzadi</note>—which are the signs of the hundreds <note>numbers 100 through 900</note> and of inferior things, namely the four simple elements and the five kinds of perfect compounds <note>the "perfect compounds" usually refer to categories of physical existence: stones, metals, plants, animals, and humans</note>.

These three classes they then distribute into **nine chambers**, of which the first is of the three units—namely the intellectual, celestial, and elemental <note>grouping together the characters for 1, 10, and 100</note>. The second is of the "dyads" <note>grouping 2, 20, and 200</note>, the third of the "triads" <note>grouping 3, 30, and 300</note>, and so on for the rest. These chambers are formed from the intersection of four parallel lines, intersecting each other at right angles, just as is expressed in this following figure:

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

There is yet another way of forming characters, common to almost all letters and languages, and quite easy, which is done through the binding together of letters <term>ligature: a character consisting of two or more joined letters</term>. For instance, if the name of the angel **Michael** is given, its characters will be formed as follows:

->Hebrew<- ->Greek<- ->Latin<-

<image-desc>Three composite sigils (ligatures) representing the name Michael in three different scripts. The Hebrew sigil is composed of thick, block-like geometric forms. The Greek sigil is a vertical stack of letters including Chi, Alpha, and Eta. The Latin sigil is a slender vertical ligature combining the letters M, I, C, H, A, E, L.</image-desc>

And this method is most widely accepted among the Arabs, nor is there any script that connects itself as readily and elegantly as Arabic. However, it must be understood that angelic spirits—since they are pure intellects and entirely incorporeal—are not actually compelled by signs, characters, painted figures, or any other human gestures. Rather, because we are ignorant of their essence and quality, we dedicate and consecrate characters, figures, and signs to them based on their names, their works, or otherwise according to our own feelings. We do this not because we can compel them to us in any way, but so that we may rise up toward them. Through these mysterious characters and figures, we first focus our internal and external senses upon them; then, through a certain wonder of our reason, we are led into a religious veneration of them; and from there, we are carried away with our whole mind into ecstatic adoration. It is then—with wonderful faith, infallible hope, and life-giving love—that by invoking them in spirit and in truth with their true names and characters, we obtain the power requested from them.

---

### Yet another way of forming characters, and concerning the signs of spirits which are received by revelation alone. ->Chapter XXXI.<-

There is another kind of character, received by revelation alone, which can be discovered by no other means. The power of these characters comes from the very divinity revealing them; they are certain hidden seals of that divinity, breathing the harmony of some godhead. Or, they are like certain covenants or pacts of an initiated alliance between us and them. Of this kind is the sign shown to **Constantine** <note>Constantine the Great (272–337 AD), the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity.</note>, which many called a cross, inscribed with Latin letters: **BY THIS, CONQUER** <note>original: "IN HOC VINCE"</note>. Another was revealed to **Antiochus**, surnamed **Soter** <note>Antiochus I Soter (324–261 BC), a king of the Seleucid Empire; "Soter" means Savior.</note>, in the figure of a pentagon, which signifies health; for when it is resolved into letters, it spells out the word **HEALTH** <note>original Greek: "ὑγίεια" (Hygeia)</note>. Relying on the confidence and power of these signs, both kings reported a remarkable victory against their enemies. Likewise **Judas**, who for this reason was afterward surnamed **Maccabeus**, when about to fight with the Jews against Antiochus Eupator, received from an angel that noble sign **MKBI** <note>original Hebrew: מכבי (Maccabee)</note>. By its power, they first laid low fourteen thousand men along with a huge number of elephants, and then again thirty-five thousand of the enemy. For this sign is representative of the four-letter name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHVH.</note>, and is a memorable symbol of the name of seventy-two letters through numerical equality <term>gematria: a system where words with the same numerical value are considered connected</term>, and its explanation is: **"Who is like unto thee among the gods, O Lord?"** <note>original Hebrew: מי כמוך באלים יהוה (Mi Chamocha Ba'elim YHVH). The word "Maccabee" is formed from the first letters of this phrase.</note>

### BOOK THREE

Who is like unto thee among the strong, O Four-Lettered Name? <note>original Latin: "Quis sicut tu in fortibus tetragramme." This is a translation of the Hebrew phrase *Mi Kamokha Ba-elim YHVH*, the acronym of which spells "Maccabee."</note> Therefore, the forms of these three aforementioned seals are to be shaped as follows:

->Seal 1<-
**IN THIS CONQUER**
<note>original Latin: "IN HOC VINCE." The seal contains a Chi-Rho (the first two letters of Christ in Greek) combined with a cross or anchor.</note>

->Seal 2<-
**Alpha and Omega**
<note>A pentagram containing the Greek letters Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω), symbolizing the beginning and the end, along with other mystical symbols.</note>

->Seal 3<-
**M-K-B-Y**
<note>A rectangular seal containing the Hebrew letters representing the Maccabean motto, surrounded by stylized celestial or magical characters.</note>

Furthermore, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the nature of spirits.</note> speaks of these seals and characters in his book *On Responses*, saying that the gods themselves indicated those things they delighted in, by which they might be called forth, and what ought to be offered to them. He explains that they showed the very figures of the statues as they should be, as well as the characters and forms, and that he learned these things from the oracle of Proserpina <note>The Roman name for Persephone, queen of the underworld.</note>. Moreover, he says that Hecate <margin>The statue of Hecate, and in what manner sacrifices are to be made to her.</margin> instructed how statues should be established for her: they were to be surrounded with wormwood; house mice were to be painted, which were her most beautiful ornaments and most pleasing to her spirit; and as many mice were to be taken as there were forms of her. Then blood, myrrh, storax <note>A fragrant resin used in incense.</note>, and certain other things were to be burned. If these things were done, she would appear in a dream and give answers to the practitioner. But we shall provide the oracle of Hecate itself, for it speaks thus:

> <margin>The Oracle of Hecate.</margin>
> Pay heed, I shall teach you what sort of image to make for me:
> Choose a thing born in a wild place, and place wormwood
> Around it; then carve the whole and paint mice,
> Those which are accustomed to dwell in houses; let these be
> Most beautiful ornaments and most pleasing to our spirit.
> Then grind together myrrh, frankincense, storax,
> And the blood of the mice themselves; from there,
> Sing sacred words over the sacrifice, and bring as many mice
> And set them back as you see forms of me; then take laurel,
> And from its trunk fashion a sheath, and then pour out
> Pious prayers to the image, and pay your due
> Vows. If you do these things, you shall see me in your sleep.

Such were the secret mysteries of the pagan gods and spirits <term>dæmones: here used in the Greek sense of intermediary spirits, rather than necessarily evil entities</term> in olden times, by which they persuaded men they could be compelled, detained, and bound. Hence, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who specialized in theurgy (ritual magic).</note> and Porphyry teach that it is necessary for one invoking sacred spirits to honor each with its own proper respect, and to distribute to each what is fitting—be it through favors, offerings, gifts, sacrifices, words, or characters suited to their condition and as similar to them as possible. Otherwise, one will by no means achieve the presence of the deities or spirits, nor the desired effect; indeed, those who are invoked may even attempt to do harm, especially to those who have behaved more negligently in that matter. <insert>Recorded from seen <unclear>remi</unclear> <unclear>pernis</unclear> acts</insert>

### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### How good spirits are attracted by us, and how evil spirits are overcome by us.
#### Chapter XXXII.

<margin>How it is necessary to beseech spirits.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring a man standing in a pastoral landscape next to a tree.</image-desc>The effective presence of religion achieves the results of spirits, for no work of any miraculous efficacy can be performed in religion unless some good spirit is present there as the director and fulfiller of the work. Good spirits, however—even if they are attracted by us in various ways—can nevertheless be bound by no chains, or at least hardly at all, but only beseeched by certain sacred things. As we read in Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), a Platonist philosopher and author of *The Golden Ass*, often cited in magical texts regarding the nature of daimons.</note>: "by the celestial stars, by the infernal powers, by the natural elements, by the silences of the night, by the conceived increases of the Nile, by the secrets of Memphis, and the sistrums <note>A sistrum is a musical percussion instrument associated with the worship of the Egyptian goddess Isis.</note> of Pharos." And elsewhere in Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist who wrote extensively on theurgy and the summoning of spirits.</note>: "You who emerged from the linen, who sit in the place, who sail in a ship, who change your form every hour, and are transformed in every sign of the zodiac." Through these and similar symbolic prayers and hymns, because they are signs of divine virtues, spirits would sometimes accommodate themselves to human uses—not because they were compelled by some necessity, but they approach more easily of their own accord, following a certain habit and being overcome by the prayers of those invoking them. Hence, in Porphyry's book *Of Responses*, Hecate <note>A goddess of Greek mythology associated with crossroads, magic, and the underworld; often viewed in Neoplatonism as the "World Soul."</note> says:

->Entreated by your words, I have come here.<-

->And in the same place elsewhere, it says:<-

> Overcome by the prayers of men, the celestial powers
> Are forced to seek the earth, and reveal future events.

<margin>Note: The reason for the assistance of spirits.</margin>
But also, the fellowship of divinity with the human mind brings it about that the good spirits themselves willingly assist us and communicate their power and virtue to us. They help us daily with illuminations, inspirations, oracles, prophecies, dreams, miracles, wonders, divinations, and auguries, working and acting upon our souls as images fellow to themselves. They shape these souls with their influences and make them most like themselves, to such an extent that our soul often performs wonders almost as great as the celestial spirits are accustomed to do. Truly, evil spirits are overcome by us with the help of the good, especially when the petitioner is strong in holiness toward God and chants sacred words and a formidable speech—namely, by conjuring through divine power, through the venerable names and seals of supernatural virtues, through miracles, through sacraments, through sacred mysteries and the like. Malignant spirits fear these conjurations or exorcisms insofar as they are performed in the name of religion and divine virtue. For this reason, even profane men often bind or cast out evil spirits with such sacred conjurations, as the spirits cannot endure such things.

<margin><unclear>True expressions and the truth of things</unclear></margin>
Hence Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and martyr.</note>, in his book *That Idols Are Not Gods*, says: "That spirits, when adjured by the true God, immediately yield to us and confess, and are forced to depart from obsessed bodies; and they either leap out immediately or vanish gradually, according as the faith of the sufferer assists, or the grace of the one swearing inspires." And Athanasius <note>Saint Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), a prominent Church Father known for his defense against Arianism.</note> in his book on...

CCLXXIX.
# BOOK THREE

In *Various Questions* <note>original: "Uariis quæstionibus"; likely referring to the *Quaestiones ad Antiochum ducem* attributed to Athanasius.</note> it is said that there exists no word more terrible or more destructive to the power of demons than the beginning of the sixty-seventh Psalm: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered." <note>Psalm 68:1 in modern numbering. The original Latin provided is: "Exurgat deus, & dissipentur inimici eius."</note> For as soon as this word is spoken, the devil immediately vanishes and disappears with a howl. And Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar.</note>, in his work *Against Celsus*, says that by the naming of the name of Jesus, many have been seen to cast out countless demons from both the souls and bodies of men, and that it has exercised the greatest power over those from whom the demons were driven. Often, even by threats and insults alone, we can restrain or repel evil demons—especially the lesser ones, such as <term>lamiae</term> <note>Mythical female demons or spirits often associated with kidnapping children or seducing men.</note>, <term>incubi</term> <note>Male spirits said to haunt the sleep of women.</note>, and the like—just as we read in Lucan <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet.</note> regarding that witch <note>Referring to Erictho, a powerful Thessalian witch in Lucan's epic poem *Pharsalia*.</note> who says:

> Now I shall call you by your true name,
> And I shall leave the Stygian hounds in the light above;
> I shall follow you through the pyres; as a guardian through funerals
> I shall expel you from the tombs, and drive you from every urn.
> And you, Hecate <note>The Greek goddess of magic, witchcraft, and the night.</note>, who are accustomed to appear to the gods
> With a different face than that which you feign,
> I shall show you in your pale, wasted form,
> And I shall forbid you to change your face from the underworld.

And in Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–247 AD), author of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.</note> we read that when Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker.</note> and his companions were traveling by night under a bright moon, a phantom of a <term>lamia</term> met them, turning itself now into one shape, now into another, and sometimes vanishing suddenly from their sight. Apollonius, recognizing immediately what it was, rebuked it with heavy and insulting words and urged his companions to do the same; for he knew this was the best remedy against such invasions. When his companions obeyed his words, the shrieking phantom fled swiftly like an apparition. Indeed, this kind of demon is so fearful that they are moved, tremble, and are compelled even by feigned terror and false, impossible threats. Hence Chaeremon the sacred scribe <note>A Stoic philosopher and priest of Egypt in the 1st century AD.</note> says that these are the things by which demons are most strongly forced.

There is, moreover, as was said above, a certain kind of demon that is not so harmful, but is close to humans, so that it is even affected by human passions; many of these enjoy the conversation of men and gladly live with them. Some fall in love with women, others with boys; some delight in the company of various domestic or wild animals. Some inhabit the woods and groves; others live around springs and meadows. Thus the **Fauns** and **Lemures** inhabit the fields; the **Naiads**, the springs; the **Potamides**, the rivers; the **Nymphs**, the pools and waters; the **Oreades**, the mountains; the **Humedes**, the meadows; the **Dryads** and **Hamadryads**, the woods—which are also inhabited by **Satyrs** and **Sylvans**. These same spirits delight in trees and turf, just as the **Naptae** and **Agaptae** delight in flowers; the **Dodonae**, in acorns; and the **Paleae** and **Feniliae**, in fodder and the countryside.

Therefore, whoever wishes to invoke these may easily do so in the places where they dwell, by enticing them with fragrant fumigations <note>The practice of burning incense or herbs to create a scented smoke for ritual purposes.</note> and with sweet sounds on strings and musical instruments that are fashioned from the guts and appropriate woods of certain animals; and also by employing chants, songs, and incantations suitable for this purpose: and that

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>
From men, lares, lemures, and larvae are made.
</margin>
Among these things, the most important is simplicity of mind, innocence of soul, firm belief, and constant silence. Therefore, spirits most often appear to children, women, and obscure little men from the lower common folk. However, they flee and tremble before steady and bold spirits who are strangers to fear; they are harmless to the good and pure, but harmful to evil and impure men. To this class also belong the <term>lemures</term> <note>original: "lemures"; in Roman mythology, these were the restless or malevolent spirits of the dead.</note>, <term>lares</term> <note>original: "lares"; guardian deities or spirits of the household.</note>, <term>larvae</term> <note>original: "laruæ"; terrifying ghosts or spirits of the wicked.</note>, and other shadows and terrors of the deceased. Hence Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note> says that the souls of men are sometimes <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmões"; here meaning guiding spirits or entities, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, and that they become <term>lares</term> if they have deserved well—whom the Greeks call <term>Eudaemons</term> <note>original: "Eudęmonas"; literally "good spirits" or "blessed ones."</note>, that is, happy spirits. But they become <term>lemures</term> and <term>larvae</term> if they have deserved poorly, and these are harmful spirits made from men, which the Greeks therefore call <term>Cacodaemons</term> <note>original: "Caco demones"; literally "evil spirits."</note>. They are called <term>Manes</term> <note>Spirits of the dead who are not yet classified as good or evil.</note> when it is uncertain whether they have deserved well or ill. There are many examples of these apparitions, such as the one mentioned by Pliny the Younger <note>Roman author (61–113 AD); the story refers to a haunted house in Athens.</note> regarding the house of Athenodorus of Tarsus the philosopher, in which the image of a ghastly old man was seen with a troublesome noise of rattling chains. And Philostratus <note>Sophist and biographer (c. 170–250 AD).</note> tells a similar story of the <term>Lamia</term> <note>A man-eating monster or succubus in Greek mythology.</note> of Menippus the Lycian philosopher, which turned into a beautiful woman at Corinth, whom Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker (1st century AD).</note> discovered to be a <term>lemur</term>. He also discovered a similar one among the Ephesians under the appearance of a begging old man, who was the cause of a plague; at his command, the man was covered with stones and appeared as a dog like a mastiff, and soon the plague ceased. <margin>Note</margin> This must be known: whoever works intellectually with evil spirits shall bind them through the command of the good; but whoever works only in a worldly manner shall work judgment for himself to <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A term for hell or a place of spiritual punishment.</note>.

### On the bonds of spirits, and their adjurations and banishments. Chapter XXXIII.

---

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'V' with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
The bonds by which spirits are tied, entreated, or banished are threefold. Some of them are taken from the elemental world, such as when we adjure a spirit by lower and natural things that are either related or adverse to it, insofar as we wish to invoke or banish it. This is done by flowers, herbs, animals, snow, ice, the depths <note>original: "tartara"; referring to the underworld or deep places of the earth.</note>, fire, and the like, as these are also often included in divine praises, blessings, and consecrations. This is evident in the *Song of the Three Children* <note>A biblical hymn found in the Book of Daniel, calling on all of creation to praise God.</note>, and in that psalm: "Praise the Lord from the heavens," and in the consecration and blessing of the Paschal candle. For this bond works upon spirits through their power of perception by reason of love or hatred, insofar as these spirits preside over, favor, or abhor certain natural or even supernatural things—just as these things themselves have mutual love or hatred for each other. Hence that saying of Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note>: "Just as the lion fears a rooster, especially a white one, so a spirit appearing in the form of a lion suddenly vanished when a rooster was presented."
<margin>2</margin>
The second bond is taken from the celestial world, namely when we adjure by the heaven, the stars, their movements, rays, light, grace, brightness, nobility, strength, influence, wonders, and such like. And this bond works upon spirits by way of a certain admonition...

It also possesses some degree of command, especially over the ministering spirits and those who are from the lowest orders. <margin>The Third Bond</margin> The third bond itself comes from the intellectual and divine world, which is perfected by religion; for instance, when we adjure by the sacraments, by miracles, by divine names, by sacred seals, and other mysteries of religion. Therefore, this bond is the highest and strongest of all, acting upon spirits through authority and power. <margin>The order to be observed in using the bonds</margin> However, it must be observed that just as universal providence is followed by particular providence, and universal souls are followed by particular souls, so we first invoke through the higher bonds and through the names and virtues that rule over things, and then through the lower ones and the things themselves. <margin>What things are bound by these bonds</margin> It should also be known that through these bonds, not only spirits but all creatures are bound—such as storms, fires, floods, plagues, diseases, the force of arms, and every kind of animal—by employing them either in the manner of an adjuration, or in the manner of a prayer or blessing. For example, in the adjuration of serpents, beyond natural and celestial means, one commemorates from the mysteries and religion the curse of the serpent in the earthly paradise and the lifting up of the serpent in the desert. Furthermore, one employs that verse of the ninety-first <note>The text says "nonagesimi noni" (99th), but the quote "Super aspidem..." is from Psalm 91:13. Medieval and Renaissance numbering often varied or contained errors.</note> Psalm: *You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.* <note>original: "Super aſpidem & baſiliſcum ambulabis, & conculcabis leonem & draconem."</note> <margin>The power of superstition</margin> Superstition also has great power in these matters through the transfer of some sacramental rite to that which we intend to bind or hinder; for instance, applying the rites of excommunication, burial, or funeral services to exterminate diseases, or serpents, mice, or little worms—which we read has been done in many places and is still accustomed to be done.

### Concerning the soul-like order and the heroes. Chapter XXXIV.

After the choirs of blessed spirits, the next is the <term>animastic</term> <note>original: "animaſticus"; pertaining to the soul or spirits derived from human souls.</note> order, which the Hebrew theologians call <term>Issim</term> <note>original: "Iſſim"; in Kabbalistic hierarchy, these are "the souls of the righteous" or "men-spirits."</note>, that is, strong and robust men. The magi of the gentiles call them <term>heroes</term> and <term>demigods</term>, or <term>speaking gods</term> <note>original: "deos ſermones"; likely referring to gods who communicate with humanity.</note>. Fulgentius, an author not to be despised, thinks they are called this either because they are not deemed worthy of heaven due to the poverty of their merit, yet are not considered earthly because of the reverence for their grace—such as <term>Priapus</term>, <term>Hippo</term>, and <term>Vertumnus</term> <note>Roman deities associated with fertility, horses, and seasons respectively.</note> once were—or because they excelled in this life in divine virtues and benefits to the human race, and after stripping off this mortal man, they were translated into the choirs of the blessed gods, perpetually providing for mortals with the same virtues and benefits they once held in this life. Or perhaps it is because they were procreated from the secret seed of the powers above, whom they believe were born from the mingling of gods or <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmonum"; here referring to intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil beings.</note> with humans. Therefore, they were allotted a certain middle nature, as those who are neither angels nor men. This is an opinion which <term>Lactantius</term> <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD).</note> also follows. And there are even today those who have commerce and conjugal mingling with daemons; and it is already believed by everyone that <term>Merlin the Briton</term>, the prophet, was the son of a daemon and born of a virgin. But they also thought that <term>Plato</term>, the prince of wisdom, was born of a virgin birth, fathered by a phantom of <term>Apollo</term>. And it is handed down in histories that certain women of the Goths (whom they call <term>Alrumnas</term> <note>original: "Alrumnas"; a reference to the "Alrunas" or Gothic wise women/prophetesses mentioned by Jordanes.</note>)...

[prophesy] <note>This completes a word from the previous page, likely "vaticinantur," meaning they prophesy or relate.</note> that women remarkable for both their beauty and character, who long ago left the camp of Filimer—or as others say, Idanthresus—the king of the Goths, migrated into the wilderness of Asiatic Scythia across the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov, traditionally considered the boundary between Europe and Asia.</note>. There, embraced by Fauns and Satyrs, they gave birth to the first Huns. Moreover, according to Psellos <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar and philosopher influential in Renaissance magic.</note>, demons sometimes cast seed from which certain small creatures arise. Therefore, the power of these heroes in arranging and ruling these lower things is no less than the power of gods and demons; they have their own distributed duties and protections. For this reason, temples, statues, altars, sacrifices, vows, and other so-called mysteries of religion were dedicated to them just as to the gods themselves. Their invoked names possess divine and magical virtues for performing certain miracles, which Eusebius relates many experienced regarding the name of Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus in antiquity.</note> when invoked. We read many such things about Hercules, Atlas, Aesculapius, and other heroes of the nations among ancient poets, historians, and philosophers. But these are the delusions of the heathens.

Concerning our own holy heroes <note>Here referring to the Christian Saints as the true "heroes."</note>, however, we believe they are empowered by divine authority. Indeed, over all of them (as the theologians of the Hebrews also attest) rules the soul of the Messiah <note>original: *anima Meschihæ*</note>, who is Jesus Christ himself. He administers and distributes the various gifts of his grace in these lower regions through his various saints, like limbs suited for this purpose. 

<margin>
Christ works through the saints as if through instruments.
</margin>

And each saint receives a specific duty of cooperation. Hence, when we implore them through various prayers and invocations, according to the multiform distribution of graces, each most willingly imparts to us their own gifts, benefits, and favors. They do so much more promptly and abundantly than the angelic powers, because they are closer to us and more related to our nature, having once been humans themselves and having endured human feelings and weaknesses. Their names, ranks, and offices are more familiar to us.

From this nearly infinite number of them, there are twelve princes: specifically, the twelve apostles of Christ who (as the Gospel truth says) sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. In the Apocalypse, they are distributed over the twelve foundations at the twelve gates of the heavenly city; they preside over the twelve signs of the zodiac, are marked upon twelve precious stones, and the world is distributed among them.

After those are the seventy-two disciples of Christ, who themselves also preside over as many celestial groups of five <note>Groups of five degrees in the zodiac, known as quinaries or pentads.</note>, and tribes, and peoples, and nations, and tongues: after whom is an innumerable multitude of saints, who themselves also have received various duties, and places, and nations, and peoples into their protection and care, whose most manifest miracles we openly see and confess in response to the prayers of the faithful who invoke them.

## ->On mortal and earthly gods. Chapter XXXV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or ruler, in a classical architectural setting.</image-desc>

After these, the next are the mortal gods, whom we likewise call heroes and earthly gods, or companions of the supernal gods—namely kings, princes, and pontiffs <note>The Latin 'pontifices' refers to high priests or religious leaders, including the Pope.</note>, by whom this world is ruled, and by whose laws it is disposed. We look up to, worship, and venerate them as gods for this reason: because God himself allowed his own name to be shared with them, and confirmed it to them by its proper naming, calling them gods, just as he said to Moses: "I have made you a god to Pharaoh." <note>Exodus 7:1</note> And elsewhere he commanded concerning them, saying: "You shall not revile the gods." <note>Exodus 22:28; 'gods' here often interpreted as judges or rulers.</note> And again: "If the theft be hidden, the master of the house shall be brought to the gods." <note>Exodus 22:8</note> And the Psalmist says: "The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham, for the strong gods of the earth are vehemently exalted." <note>Psalm 47:9</note> And elsewhere: "God stands in the council of the gods, but in the midst he judges the gods." <note>Psalm 82:1</note> And a little after: "I said, you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High." <note>Psalm 82:6</note> Indeed, he even commanded that they be worshipped and venerated, decreeing tithes and firstfruits for them, and granting them the right of the sword <term>gladii ius</term> <note>The legal authority to execute capital punishment or use force.</note>, and forbidding that they be cursed, and commanding that obedience be shown to them, even if they are difficult. Hence all antiquity called its princes "gods," and worshipped them as divine powers, just as Janus testifies <gloss>-ur</gloss> in Ovid, in the first book of the *Fasti*, saying:

> "Then I was reigning, when the earth was powerful with gods,
> And divine powers were mixed in human places."
> <note>Original: "Tunc ego regnabam, potens cum terra deorum / Esset, & humanis numina mixta locis."</note>

And the divine Plato, in the third book of the *Republic*, established that princes, both living and <gloss>and</gloss> dead, should be celebrated with divine honors. This institution has been received among all nations and from the earliest age: namely, to deify princes with divine honors and to consecrate them with eternal memory. Hence they bestowed their names—which would never fail—upon cities, provinces, mountains, rivers, seas, islands, and the ocean. Then they dedicated pyramids, colossi, triumphal arches, trophies, statues, shrines, games, and festivals to them with great pomp; they even called the heavens, stars, days, and months by their names. Hence January is from Janus, July from Julius, August from Augustus; so too Mercury’s day <note>Wednesday</note> from Mercury Trismegistus, Jupiter’s day <note>Thursday</note> from Jove. We read that this custom was observed not only by the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, but also by the furthest barbarians: the Goths, Danes, and Teutons. Hence, on the testimony of Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian.</note>, that which those others call Mercury’s day, these call Odin’s day; that which those call Jupiter’s, these call Thor, after Odin and Thor, who were formerly kings of the Goths and Danes. Nor were the Goths named for any other reason than that [they called] their highest god...

CCLXXXIIII.
# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

[...in their] language they call God <note>Original Latin: *Gotthum*, a Latinization of the German *Gott*.</note>. From this, they are also called Teutons, because they called the god Mars, whom they worshiped, Teutan <note>Likely referring to Toutates, a Celtic deity often equated by the Romans with Mars or Mercury.</note>, by which name the Gauls also called Mercury. Therefore, kings and pontiffs <note>High priests or religious leaders.</note> (provided they are just) are associates of the gods, and are powerful with similar authority. Hence, by touch or word alone, they cure diseases; they sometimes command the seasons and the heavens, just as Virgil sang of Augustus:

> It rains all night, the spectacles return in the morning,
> Caesar holds a shared empire with Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods; original: *Nocte pluit tota, redeunt spectacula mane, Diuisum imperium cum Ioue Caesar habet.*</note>.

And the Scripture testifies concerning Joshua, who, while fighting in Gibeon, commanded the sun and moon, saying: "Sun, do not move against Gibeon, and moon, against the valley of Ajalon." And the sun and moon stood still at his command, nor did the sun set for the space of one day, until he had avenged himself upon his enemies, and the Lord obeyed the voice of a man. Moses also divided the Red Sea, and Joshua divided the Jordan, and they led the people across with dry feet. Alexander the Macedonian did the same while leading his army. Sometimes they even excel in the prophetic spirit, just as we read in the Holy Scripture regarding Caiaphas, that he prophesied because he was the high priest of that year. Since, therefore, it is so—that the Lord willed the kings and pontiffs of the earth to be called gods through the communication of his name and power—it certainly becomes us to deserve well of them, to prefer their judgments to our own, and clearly to obey, supplicate, adore, and honor them with every kind of veneration, and to revere the supreme God himself within them.

### On man, how he was created in the image of God. Chapter XXXVI.

<margin>
Hermes Trismegistus.
</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter E featuring interlaced vines and foliage.</image-desc>
The most excellent God (as Trismegistus says) fashioned two images similar to himself: namely, the world and man. In the first, he might play with certain wondrous operations; in the second, however, he might enjoy delights. Since He himself is one, he created one world. Since He himself is infinite, he created the world round <note>In the Renaissance, the sphere was considered the most "infinite" and perfect shape as it has no beginning or end.</note>. Since He himself is eternal, he created the world incorruptible and everlasting. Since He himself is immense, he created the world the greatest of all things. Since He himself is the supreme life, he also adorned the world with vital seeds, bringing forth all things from itself. And since He himself is omnipotent, by his will alone, and not by any necessity of nature, he created the world—not from pre-existing matter, but from nothing. And since He is the highest goodness, embracing his Word (which is the first Idea of all things) with his best will and essential love, he fabricated this outward world according to the model of the inward world (that is, the Ideal world), yet without sending anything out from the essence of the Idea; rather, he created from nothing that which he held from eternity through the Idea.

<margin>
The image of God is the world; the image of the world is man.
</margin>
God also created man in his own image; for just as the world is the image of God, so man is the image of the world. Because of this, some think it was said that man was not simply created as the image of God, but *according to* the image <note>Latin: *ad imaginem*.</note>, as if he were the image of an image. Therefore, he is called the <term>microcosm<note>From the Greek *mikros kosmos*, meaning "little world."</note></term>, that is, the lesser world. The world is a rational, immortal animal; man is likewise a rational animal, but mortal—that is, dissoluble. For (as Hermes says), since the world itself is immortal, it is impossible for any part of it
