# BOOK THREE.

<margin>The name of death is empty.</margin>
...to perish: therefore the name of death is empty. And just like a vacuum, dying exists nowhere. Therefore, we say of man, when the soul and body are separated, it is not because any part of them perishes or is turned into nothingness. Nevertheless, the true image of God is His word, His wisdom, life, light, and truth, existing through itself; and of this image, the human mind is a reflection. It is because of this that we are said to be made "in the image of God," not in the image of the world or of created things. For just as God can neither be touched, nor perceived by the ears, nor seen with the eyes, so the mind of man can neither be seen, heard, nor touched. And just as God Himself is infinite and can be compelled by no one, so too the human mind is free, and can neither be forced nor measured. Furthermore, just as God manages this entire world and whatever is in it by mind alone, so the human mind encompasses the world in thought; and—which is a quality shared by man alone with God—just as God moves and governs the entire world by a mere nod, so the human mind drives and rules its own body by a mere nod.

It was necessary, therefore, for the mind of man—thus sealed by the word of God—to also clothe the corporeal man according to the most perfect model of the world. Thus, man is called "another world" <note>Original: *alter mundus*, often translated as the "Microcosm" or "little world."</note> and "another image of God," because he has within himself everything that is contained in the greater world, so that nothing is left out which is not also truly and realistically found within the man himself. And all these things within him perform the same functions as they do in the greater world. Within him are the elements, possessing the truest properties of their nature. Within him is an ethereal body <note>Original: *æthereum corpusculum*, a "subtle" or "spirit" body believed in Neoplatonic philosophy to bridge the gap between the physical body and the immortal soul.</note>, the vehicle of the soul, corresponding in proportion to the heavens. Within him are the vegetative life of plants, the senses of animals, a celestial spirit, angelic reason, and a divine mind—and the true joining and divine possession of all these things flowing together into one.

Hence, in the sacred scriptures, man is called "every creature" <note>A reference to Mark 16:15, "Preach the gospel to every creature," which medieval commentators often interpreted as meaning "to man," who contains all levels of creation.</note>. Not only is man made as another world, encompassing all parts of the world within himself, but he even conceives and contains God Himself. For this reason, Sixtus the Pythagorean <note>A philosopher to whom a collection of moral maxims, the *Sentences of Sextus*, was attributed.</note> says that the mind of man is the temple of God, which Paul expressed much more clearly when he said: "You are the temple of God." The sacred scripture testifies to this same thing in many
<margin>Man, the temple of God.</margin>
places. Man is, therefore, the most distinct likeness of God, since man contains within himself all things that are in God. However, God contains all things through a certain eminence, by His power and simply, as the cause and principle of all things; but to man He gave the power to similarly contain all things, though by a certain act and composition, as the connection, bond, and knot of all things <note>Original: *nexus, uinculum atq; nodus*. This is a central theme in Renaissance philosophy, viewing man as the "pivot" of the universe.</note>.

Thus man, and man alone, enjoys this honor: that he has a shared symbol with all things, an operation with all things, and a conversation with all things. He symbolizes with matter in his own subject; with the elements in his fourfold body; with plants in his vegetative power; with animals in his sensory power; with the heavens in his ethereal spirit and the influence of the higher parts upon the lower; with the angels in intellect and wisdom; and with God in the containment of all things. He converses with God and the divine intelligences through faith and wisdom; with the heavens and celestial beings through reason and discourse; and with all lower things through sense and dominion.

### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

[The mind] acts with all things, and has power over all things, even over God Himself, by understanding and loving Him. And just as God knows all things, so too can man know all knowable things, since he possesses as his proper object "being" in its universal sense, or (as others say) "the truth" itself. Nor is anything found in man—no disposition at all—in which some spark of divinity does not shine; nor is there anything in God that is not also represented in man. 

Whoever, therefore, shall know himself, shall know all things in himself. He will know, first and foremost, God, in whose image he was made; he will know the world, whose likeness he carries; he will know all creatures, with whom he shares a common bond. He will understand what sustenance <note>Original: *fomenti*, referring to a kind of spiritual or physical nourishment or vital fuel.</note> he can obtain and entreat from stones, plants, animals, elements, the heavens, demons, angels, and from every single thing. He will know how he can adapt each thing to its specific place, time, order, measure, proportion, and harmony, drawing and leading them to himself no differently than a magnet draws iron. 

Even Geber <note>Original: *Geber*, the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath often regarded as the father of alchemy.</note>, in his *Summary of Alchemy*, teaches that no one can reach the perfection of that art who has not recognized its principles within himself. Indeed, the more anyone knows himself, the greater the power of attraction he attains, and the greater and more wonderful works he performs. He shall ascend to such perfection that he is made a <margin>The perfection and dignity of man.</margin> son of God, and is transformed into that same image which is God, becoming one with Him. This power is granted neither to angels, nor to the world, nor to any other creature, but to man alone: specifically, the ability to become a son of God and to be united with God. 

Once man is united with God, all things that are within man are likewise unified: first the mind, then the spirit and the animal powers <term>animal powers: from the Latin 'anima' (soul), these are the faculties of sensation and movement shared with animals.</term>, the vegetative power <term>vegetative power: the basic biological functions of growth and reproduction shared with plants.</term>, and the elements, down to the very matter itself. This draws the body along with it—since the mind is the body's form—leading it into a better lot and a heavenly nature, until it is glorified into immortality. This, which we have just described, is the peculiar gift of man, whose dignity consists of this divine image proper to himself and shared with no other creature.

There are other theologians, however, who assign the three powers of man—memory, intellect, and will—as the image of the Divine Trinity. There are those who go even further, placing this image not only in those three powers (which they call "primary acts"), but also in "secondary acts." They suggest that just as memory represents the Father, intellect the Son, and will the Holy Spirit, so too the "word" produced by our intellect, the "love" flowing from our will, and the intellect itself (which possesses, presents, and produces its object) denote and teach of that same Son, Spirit, and Father. 

The more "secret theologians" <note>A common reference to mystical or Kabbalistic thinkers.</note> teach that, furthermore, every one of our limbs represents something in God and bears His image. They claim that even in our passions we represent God, albeit through a certain analogy. For in the Sacred Scriptures we read of God’s anger, fury, repentance, complacency, love, hatred, playfulness, delight, pleasures, indignation, and similar things; we have already spoken of the divine members in previous sections that may apply here. 

Hermes Trismegistus <note>Original: *Mercurius Trismegistus*, the legendary "Thrice-Great" sage to whom many foundational texts of Western esotericism are attributed.</note>, having also confessed the Divine Trinity, <margin>Hermes Trismegistus acknowledged the mystery of the Trinity.</margin> describes it as Intellect, Life, and Radiance, which he elsewhere calls Word, Mind, and Spirit. He says that man, being made in the image of God, represents this same Trinity; for within him is an understanding mind, a life-giving word, and a spirit that is like...

287.
### BOOK THREE.

...divine radiance spreading itself everywhere, filling, moving, and connecting all things. However, this is not to be understood as the "natural spirit"—which is the medium through which the soul is united with the flesh and body, through which the body lives and acts, and through which one limb operates upon another (the spirit we discussed in the first book). Instead, we are dealing here with the **rational spirit**. This spirit is also corporeal in a certain sense, though it does not have a thick, tangible, or visible body; rather, it possesses a most subtle body that is easily united with the **mind**—specifically, that higher and divine part of us. Nor should anyone wonder if we say the rational soul is that spirit and something corporeal, or that it has and tastes of something "body-like" while it is in the body and uses it as an instrument—provided you understand what the Platonists mean by that "ethereal little body" <note>This refers to the *ochema* or "astral vehicle," a concept in Neoplatonism where the soul inhabits a subtle, luminous body to navigate between the physical and spiritual realms.</note> which serves as the soul’s vehicle.

<margin>The Platonists posit three parts in man.</margin>
Thus, Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century and founder of Neoplatonism.</note> and all the Platonists, following Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings on magic and philosophy are attributed.</note>, similarly posit three things in man, which they call the **supreme**, the **infimum** (lowest), and the **middle**. The supreme is that divine part which they call the **mind** (*mens*), or the "higher portion," or the "illuminated intellect."

<margin><unclear>The breath of life</unclear></margin>
Moses, in Genesis, calls this the "breath of life" <note>original: *spiraculum vitarum*</note>, breathed into us by God, or by His spirit. The lowest part is the **sensitive soul**, which they also call the "idol" <note>original: *idolon*, meaning an image or reflection of the higher self.</note>; Paul the Apostle calls this the "animal man" <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 2:14; the person governed by physical senses rather than spirit.</note>. The middle part is the **rational spirit**, connecting and binding both extremes—namely, the animal soul with the mind—and sharing in the nature of both ends. Yet it differs from that supreme part, which is called the illuminated intellect, mind, light, and supreme portion. It also differs from the animal soul, from which the Apostle teaches we ought to separate it through the power of the word of God, saying:

> The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of the soul and the spirit. <note>Hebrews 4:12</note>

For just as that supreme portion never sins, never consents to evil, and always resists error and urges us toward the best things; so that lower portion, the animal soul, is always submerged in evil, sin, and lust, and drags us toward the worst things, of which Paul says:

> I see another law in my members, taking me captive in the law of sin. <note>Romans 7:23</note>

<margin>The Mind</margin>
The **Mind**, therefore, the supreme portion, is never condemned; instead, leaving its companions to be punished, it departs unharmed to its origin. But the **Spirit**—which Plotinus calls the "rational soul"—since it is free by its nature, can adhere to either side at will. If it adheres constantly to the higher portion, it is eventually united to it and beatified, until it is taken up into God. If it adheres to the lower soul, it is corrupted and loses its merit, until it becomes an evil demon. But enough regarding the mind and spirit for now; let us now look at the **Speech**, or the **Word**. Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> considers this to be of equal value for attaining immortality.

<margin>Speech, or the Word.</margin>
For it is Speech, or the **Word**, without which nothing was made nor can be made. Indeed, it is the expression of the expresser and the expressed; it is the speaking of the speaker, and that which he speaks is the Speech and the Word. It is the conception of the conceiver, and that which he conceives is the Word. It is the writing of the writer, and that which he writes is the Word. It is the formation of the former, and what he forms is the Word. It is the creation of the creator, and what he creates is the Word. It is the making of the maker, and what is made is the Word. It is the knowledge of the knower, and the thing known is the Word. And everything that can be said is not...

->**OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY. Book 3.**<-

...is nothing but the Word, and it is called "Equality" <note>original: "aequalitas"; in Renaissance Neoplatonism, this refers to the Son or the Word being equal to the Father and acting as the balancing principle of the universe</note>: for it bears itself equally toward all things, since it is no more one thing than another, bestowing equally upon all that they might be what they are, neither more nor less. It makes itself sensible <note>perceptible to the senses</note> and makes all sensible things, just as light makes itself and all visible things visible. For this reason, the Word is called by Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio," referring here to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermetic philosophy</note> the "shining son of the mind." Moreover, the conception by which the mind conceives itself is the internal Word generated by the mind—namely, the knowledge of itself. But the external and vocal word is the birth and showing-forth of that internal Word, and it is a spirit proceeding from the mouth with sound and a voice signifying something. 

Truly, every voice of ours, every word and speech, unless it be formed by the voice of God, is mingled with the air and vanishes; but the spirit and Word of God remain, accompanied by sense and life. Therefore, all our speech, all words, every spirit and voice of ours have no power in magic, except insofar as they are formed by the divine voice. Even Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher</note> himself, in his *Meteorology* and at the end of his *Ethics*, confesses that there is no power, whether natural or moral, except through God. And in his *Secret Teachings* <note>original: "secretis dogmatibus"; likely referring to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a book of advice and occult lore once attributed to Aristotle</note>, he asserts that our good and healthy intellect can do much regarding the secrets of nature, provided that the influence of divine power is present, but otherwise not at all. 

Thus also our words can produce many miracles, provided they are formed by the Word of God, in which also our univocal generation <note>A term from formal logic and philosophy meaning the production of an offspring that is of the same nature as the parent; here, it refers to man "giving birth" to spiritual effects</note> is perfected, just as Isaiah <note>The biblical prophet</note> says: "From thy face, O Lord, we have conceived," <note>original: "A facie tua domine concepimus," a variation on Isaiah 26:18</note> just as women rightly conceive from the face of their husbands, "and we have brought forth the spirit." To this also belongs, in a way, what is passed down among the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by ancient Greeks to describe Indian ascetics and yogis</note> of the Indians, as if by the authority of this opinion, that Buddha <note>original: "Budda"</note>, the prince of their dogma, gave birth to a virgin from his side. And among the Muslims <note>original: "Mahometistas"</note> there is a constant opinion that many, whom they call *Nefesogli* <note>Turkish: *Nefesoğlu*, meaning "Son of the Breath"; a term for those believed to be conceived through a spiritual breath or holy influence</note> in their own language, are born in a certain hidden way of divine dispensation without carnal intercourse. For this reason, their lives are marvelous, impassive, and like that of angels, entirely supernatural. 

But setting aside those trifles, only the King Messiah, the Word of the Father made flesh, Jesus Christ, has revealed this secret, to be more openly manifested in the fullness of time. For this reason, the Creator gave to man a Mind very much like Himself (as Lazzarelli <note>Ludovico Lazzarelli, a 15th-century Italian Hermetic poet and scholar</note> sang in the *Mixing-Bowl of Hermes* <note>original: "Cratere Hermetis," a dialogue inspired by the Hermetic writings</note>):

> And the Father has already given speech to man,
> So that he might bring forth gods like unto the gods,
> With sense instilled from above.
> Exceedingly happy is he who knows the gifts
> Of his own lot, and fulfills them willingly:
> For he is to be numbered among the gods,
> Nor is he lesser than the gods above.
> These men repress every danger of fate,
> And put to flight the destruction of diseases from afar.
> They give prophetic dreams, and bring help
> To the tribulations of men, and give evils to the impious.
> They give noble rewards to the pious, and thus
> They fulfill the command of God the Father.

->**BOOK THREE.**<-

These are the disciples, these are the children of God, who were born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, nor of menstrual blood <note>original: "menstruatæ"; referring to the medieval biological belief that the physical body was formed from menstrual blood, contrasting here with spiritual birth</note>, but of God. And this is the power of the Word, formed by the Mind, into a subject rightly prepared and disposed to receive it—much like a seed into a womb, joined together for generation and birth. I say "prepared and rightly disposed" because not all things become participants of the Word in the same way, but some in one way, and others in another. These are among the most hidden secrets of nature, concerning which no more should be discussed in public.

# On the human soul, and by what means it is joined to the body.
### Chapter XXXVII.

<margin>What the human soul is.</margin>
<image-desc>Large woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring a landscape illustration with a winding river, trees, and distant hills within the frame of the letter.</image-desc>
The human soul is a certain divine light, created after the image of the Word <note>original: "uerbum"; the Logos or divine reason</note>, the cause of causes and the first exemplar; it is a substance of God, shaped by the seal whose character is the eternal Word. Likewise, the human soul is a certain divine substance, indivisible and present as a whole in every part of the body, produced by an incorporeal author in such a way that it depends only upon the power of the agent, not upon the "womb" of matter. The soul is a substantial number <note>following the Pythagorean and Platonic idea that the soul is a self-moving number, representing harmony and proportion</note>, uniform, rational, and capable of turning back upon itself; it surpasses all physical and material bodies by a vast distance. Its division is not according to matter, nor does it proceed from lower or coarser things, but from the efficient cause: for it is not a quantity-based number, but is removed from all physical laws. Therefore, it is neither divided nor multiplied by parts. The soul is thus a certain divine substance emanating from divine fountains, bringing "number" with it—not that divine number by which the Creator disposed all things, but a rational number so that, having proportion with all things, it may be able to understand all things.

Therefore, such a human soul, according to the opinion of the Platonists, proceeding immediately from God, is joined to this coarser body through appropriate intermediaries. Hence, in its very descent, it is first wrapped in a celestial and airy "little body," which they call the **ethereal vehicle** <note>original: "æthereum uehiculū"; in Neoplatonism, this is the "astral body" that carries the soul from the heavens down into the physical shell</note> of the soul, and others call the "chariot" of the soul. By this means, at the command of God (who is the center of the universe), it is first infused into the middle point of the heart, which is the center of the human body. From there, it is diffused through all the parts and limbs of its body, when it joins its "chariot" to the **natural heat** <note>the vital warmth believed to sustain life</note>. Through this heat, it joins to the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritui"; here referring to the "vital spirit," a subtle vapor produced in the heart that acts as a bridge between soul and flesh</note> generated in the heart; through this spirit, it immerses itself into the **humors** <note>the primary fluids of the body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>; through those humors, it clings to the limbs. It becomes equally close to all these things, even though it is poured from one into another: just as the heat of a fire is closely joined to air and water, even if it is carried through the air to reach the water.

Thus it is clear how the immortal soul is enclosed by a coarser and mortal body by means of an immortal "little body"—namely, the ethereal vehicle. But when these intermediaries are dissolved or fail through disease or evil, then the soul itself recollects its being through each intermediary and flows back into the heart, which was the soul's first receptacle. When the spirit of the heart fails and its heat is extinguished, the soul leaves the heart and the man dies. The soul then flies away with this ethereal vehicle, and once it has departed, the guardian spirits and demons...

What divine gifts man receives from above from the individual orders of the heavens and the intelligences <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "Intelligences" were the spiritual beings or angels that governed the movements and influences of the planets.</note>.

# Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>*What man receives from the planets*</margin>
Through the seven planets, as if through instruments from the highest fountain of all good things, all virtues are poured out into men: through Saturn, sublime contemplation, deep intelligence, gravity of judgment, firm speculation, stability, and an unmoving purpose; through Jupiter, unshaken prudence, temperance, kindness, piety, modesty, justice, faith, grace, religion, equity, clemency, and royalty; through Mars, undaunted truth, constant strength and fortitude, the heat of courage and the power of action and practice, and an unchangeable vehemence of mind; through the Sun, nobility of mind, clarity of imagination, the nature of knowing and forming opinions, maturity, counsel, zeal, the light of justice, reason and judgment separating right from wrong, purging the light from the darkness of ignorance, the glory of discovered truth, and charity, the queen of all virtues; through Venus, fervent love, the sweetest hope, the movement of desire, order, longing, beauty, sweetness, the desire for growth, and the propagation of oneself; through Mercury, penetrating faith and belief, clear reasoning, the vigor of interpreting and pronouncing, gravity of eloquence, sharpness of wit, the discourse of reason, and swift mobility of the senses; through the Moon, peaceful harmony, fecundity, the power of generating and increasing, of waxing and waning, and moderate temperance, and a faith which, dealing in things both open and hidden, provides leadership to all, yet also the movement toward earthly things according to the way of living one's life, and providing growth for oneself and others. 

However, these influences are drawn principally from those seven intelligences who stand before the face of God, who prepare the soul as the seat of those virtues. The planets, however, only dispose the body, rendering the complexion <note>original: "complexionem"; refers to the balance of the four "humors" or bodily fluids that were believed to determine a person's physical and mental health</note> manageable and well-proportioned and tempered for all good things; they are like the instruments of the intelligences. God, truly, provides both the influx and the increase as the primary cause along with all the others. Therefore, those who have examined the virtues and various dispositions of souls judge that they obtain various natures according to the diversity of the means through which they pass to us, and that these are joined with the bodies themselves only through the stars that are proportioned to them. Thus, in a body guided by a Jovial <note>relating to the planet Jupiter</note> temperament, they believe a soul is infused that is tempered by the divinity and intelligence of Jupiter, and so on for the rest. According to this disposition, if the soul acts well in this body, once purified and expiated, it returns to the divinity and the mansion from which it descended.

<margin>*What he receives from the angelic orders.*</margin>
And now, man is also strengthened by wonderful virtues from the angelic orders: namely, from the Angels, so that he may be a messenger of the divine will and an interpreter of the divine mind; from the Archangels, so that he may rule over all things over which they are given presidency—the beasts of the earth, the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air; from the Principalities, so that all things may be subject to him, and he...

CCXCI.
->BOOK THREE<-

...embracing strengths, and attracting all things to itself by a most hidden and super-celestial force: from the **Virtues** <note>In the celestial hierarchy, Virtues are angels associated with miracles and the preservation of the natural world.</note>, man receives the power by which he may be strengthened to fight constantly against the enemies of truth and for the prize for which we run the race in this life; from the **Powers**, he receives a defense against the enemies of this human dwelling; from the **Dominions**, he receives help by which we can subject the "domestic enemy" <note>The "domestic enemy" refers to the unruly passions and bodily desires that dwell within a person.</note> whom we always carry with us, and so reach our destined end. From the **Thrones**, we receive the means to be bound together, so that being gathered back into ourselves, we may fix our memory upon those eternal spectacles. From the **Cherubim**, we receive the light of the mind, the power of wisdom, and the transcendent images and figures by which we may contemplate divine things themselves. From the **Seraphim**, we receive the gift of being joined to them at last by a perfect fire of love. 

These are the steps, these are the ladders, through which men easily ascend to every kind of virtue by a natural connection and path. This happens according to the varying disposition of the body and soul, the favor of the stars in shaping the body, and the presidency of the **Intelligences** <note>Spiritual beings or angels believed to govern the movements and influences of the celestial spheres.</note> over them. During the soul's descent, it takes on a nature from these beings, just as light takes on the color of the glass through which it passes. This is further aided by the supreme power of the Creator, from whom all good comes, and without whom nothing good or perfect can be achieved. Therefore, all those labor in vain who, trusting only in the natural course and the favor of lower things, think they can reach divine heights; and those who, while standing only on celestial ground, strive to seize from the heavens those things which ought to be received from God alone. For indeed, these lower things—I mean animals, herbs, stones, and metals—have their power supplied by heaven; heaven receives its power from the Intelligences; and these from the Creator. In the Creator, all things pre-exist with the greatest power, just as in man himself—the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: 'little world'; the idea that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe</term>—there is no part that does not correspond to some element, some planet, some Intelligence, and some measure in the **archetype** <term>archetype: the original divine model or 'blueprint' of the universe in the mind of God</term>, as we have shown above.

## How celestial influences, although good by nature, are corrupted in these lower things and become the causes of evils.

### Chapter XXXIX.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter Q showing a man in a landscape, kneeling in a gesture of prayer or philosophical contemplation while looking up at a radiant, beaming sun.</image-desc>
Since every virtue and power comes from above—from God, the Intelligences, and the stars—who can neither err nor do evil, it is necessary that all evils and everything discordant found in these lower things do not come from a malice in the influence itself, but from the bad disposition of the receiver. This is just as **Chrysippus** <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) who wrote extensively on fate and personal responsibility.</note> rightly sang:

> "How falsely mortals accuse the gods, and foolishly complain: 
> for we ourselves are the cause of our own evils, 
> and each man is harmed by his own folly."
> <note>original Latin: "Quàm falso accusant superos, stultéq; queruntur / Mortales: etenim nostrorum causa malorum / Ipsi nos sumus, & sua quenq; uecordia lędit."</note>

Hence **Jupiter**, remembering the downfall of **Aegisthus** <note>A figure in Greek myth who seduced Clytemnestra and was later killed by her son Orestes.</note> (who was killed by **Orestes**), says in **Homer’s** council of the gods:

> "Oh, what a crime! The mortal race first blames us, the gods, 
> and thinks we are the cause and fountain of the evils 
> that come: but they perish by their own wicked deeds, 
> when they seek troubles for themselves of their own accord, beyond what fate requires."
> <note>original Latin: "O facinus, mortale genus nos numina primum / Incusat, causamq; putat fontemq; malorum / Quæ ueniunt: sua sed pereunt ob facta nefanda, / Cum præter fatum sibi sponte incommoda quærant,"</note>

CCXCII.
# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY #

When, therefore, the perversity of a subject perversely receives an influx <note>original: "influxus"; a term in Neoplatonic and hermetic philosophy referring to the spiritual or astrological power flowing from higher celestial bodies down to the earthly realm.</note>, or when its weakness cannot endure the power of the higher beings, then a discordant, deformed, and evil result arises from that celestial influx—now received into a matter full of discord. Even though the celestial powers themselves always remain good, existing in their own nature and flowing from the "Giver of Lights" <note>A reference to God, derived from James 1:17.</note> through the holy intelligences <note>Angelic beings that govern the celestial spheres.</note> and the heavens until they reach the Moon, their influence remains good, as if in its first degree. However, when it is later received into a baser subject, the influence itself becomes debased. For then, due to the diverse nature of the receiver, it is received in diverse ways; it is altered by the conflicting qualities within that same subject, and suffers along with the suffering subject. Thus, from all things finally contained within the subject, something results that is quite different from what the higher beings originally poured down.

<margin>
What the higher things influence upon the wicked.
</margin>

Therefore, a harmful quality in these lower things is far removed from the celestial influx itself. Just as the calamity of a person with sore eyes should not be blamed on the light, nor a fire on the element of heat, nor wounds on the iron, nor chains and prisons on the judge—but rather on the ill-disposed and the wrongdoers—so too should the blame for evils not be cast upon the celestial influxes. Thus, in those of us who are well-disposed, the influxes of the higher beings "work together for good" <note>A paraphrase of Romans 8:28.</note>; but for the ill-disposed, and those in whom that divine element within us has retreated because of our sins, all things turn toward evil.

Therefore, the cause of all our evils is sin, which is the disordering and "distemperment" <note>In the medical theory of the time, health was "temperament" (balance), while illness was "distemperment" (imbalance).</note> of our soul. When the soul is thus poorly ruling, or prostrated and falling away from what the celestial influxes require, all things rebel and are thrown into disorder for our ruin. Then, in the human body—otherwise most temperate and composed of the most consonant harmony—there arises a disorder of the elements; evil humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> surge up, and even good ones become disordered and separated from one another, vexing and twisting the body in a cycle. Then a most violent dissonance is felt, either from excess, or from lack, or from some internal accident, or from excessive food, from which superfluous humors are born. For the same reason, illnesses arise, and even the "animal spirits" <note>Refined substances in the body believed to transmit sensation and movement through the nerves.</note>, having lost their restraint, clash in a struggle. Then the celestial influxes, otherwise good in themselves, are rendered harmful to those people, just as the light of the Sun is to poorly disposed eyes. 

Then **Saturn** influences anxiety, weariness, melancholy, delusions, sadness, stubbornness, rigidity, blasphemy, despair, lies, the ghosts of the dead, terrors of the graves, dread of the tombs, and the provocations of demons. **Jupiter**, however, then influences avarice, wicked opportunities for wealth, and tyranny. **Mars** influences impetuous anger, profane arrogance, reckless audacity, and fierce stubbornness. The **Sun** influences imperious pride and insatiable ambition. **Venus** influences the deceptions of concupiscence, lewd loves, and base lusts. **Mercury** influences frauds, deceits, lies, the plotting of evils, and a readiness to sin. The **Moon** influences the unstable progress of all things, and whatever is contrary to human nature. And in this way, man himself, because of his dissimilarity with the heavens, receives harm where he ought to report a benefit. Because of this same dissonance with the heavens (as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on how lower things participate in the divine.</note> says), they are also subjected...

### That a divine character is imprinted on every man, by the power of which he can reach the point of performing wonders. Chapter XL.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'N' featuring a woodcut design of a figure in a landscape within a square frame.</image-desc>
<margin>Why fierce beasts fear fragile man.</margin>
It has been proven by no small amount of experience that there is a certain power of dominating and binding implanted in man by nature. For as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> testifies, an elephant meeting a man wandering in the wilderness is said to show him the way mercifully and peacefully; the same elephant, noticing the tracks of a man before seeing the man himself, is said to tremble with fear of an ambush, to stop, look around, and be terrified. In the same way the tiger, more fierce than all wild beasts, is said to immediately move its cubs upon seeing a man. We read many similar things in various authors who have written great volumes about animals. But from where do these animals recognize that a man is to be feared—one whom they have never seen? And if they have often seen and known him, why do they fear him, when they are so much superior to him in size, strength, and speed? All the historians of animals inquire into and hint at what this nature of man might be that strikes this fear into wild beasts, but they have left it to others to teach and prove. Regarding this, Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note> (as read in Philostratus), upon seeing a boy leading a huge elephant and being asked by Damis why there was such obedience from so vast an animal toward a small child, replied: that it was from a certain "active terror" sent into man by the Creator. Perceiving this, the lower creatures and all animals fear and revere man himself, who is like a terrifying character <note>In this context, "character" refers to a mystical seal or mark of identity</note> and a signet of God imprinted upon man. By this, all things are subjected to him and acknowledge a superior, whether it be a servant or an animal; for otherwise, neither would a boy rule herds and elephants, nor a king terrify a people, nor a judge the accused. Therefore, this character is imprinted on men by the Divine Idea, which the Cabalists of the Hebrews call *Pahad* <term>Fear/Awe: פחד</term>, and the left hand and the sword of God. Nor indeed does man only have a sign by which he is feared, but also one by which he is loved, the Idea of which in the divine numerations <note>The Sephirot or divine emanations in Kabbalah</note> is called *Hesed* <term>Mercy/Kindness: חסד</term>, which signifies clemency, and the right hand and the scepter of God. From these divine numerations, through the intelligences and stars, signs and characters are imprinted upon us, each according to his capacity and purity. These signs the first "protoplast" <note>The first-formed man, Adam</note> undoubtedly possessed in all integrity and fullness, when, attracted by peaceful gentleness and subjected by terror, all living things came to him as to a lord, so that he might impose names upon them. But after the sin of transgression, he fell from that dignity, along with all his posterity; yet not entirely...

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

That divine mark <note>original: "character"; referring to the *Imago Dei* or the spiritual seal of authority given to humanity at creation</note> has been extinguished within us, but the more one is weighed down by sin, the further they are removed from these divine marks and the less they receive of them. Thus, where one ought to receive kindness and reverence, they instead fall into the servitude and fear of others—not only of men, but of animals and demons. Sensing this, Cain was afraid, saying to God: *Everyone who finds me will kill me* <note>Genesis 4:14</note>. Indeed, he feared beasts and demons, for there were very few men then living.
<margin><unclear>How characteristic it is</unclear> <unclear>that innocence prevails</unclear></margin>
In ancient times, however, many men who lived in innocence and led the most excellent lives still enjoyed that obedience and power. Such was the case with Samson, David, and Daniel over lions; Elisha over bears; Paul over the viper; and many anchorites <note>hermits or religious recluses</note> who lived in the deserts, in the dens and caves of wild beasts, neither fearing them nor receiving any harm. For just as that divine mark is darkened by sin, so too, when sin is purged and expiated, it shines forth again more and more.

## Various opinions concerning man after death.
### Chapter XLI.

It is appointed for all men once to die; death is fatal to all. But one death is natural, another violent, another voluntarily undertaken. Another is imposed for a crime by human laws, or inflicted by God because of sin, so that they seem not to have paid a debt to nature, but to have rendered a penalty for their offenses—which (as the masters of the Hebrews say) God remits to no one. Hence the assembly of Hezekiah <note>referring to the Talmudic tradition or the "Men of the Great Assembly"</note> handed down that after the destruction of the Sanctuary, although no order of judicial execution remained, nevertheless the fourfold types of punishment by which men were accustomed to be condemned allowed no one guilty of death to escape without retaliation. For he who deserved death by stoning was, by God’s dispensation, either cast down from a roof, trampled by wild beasts, or overwhelmed by a ruin or an accident. He who deserved fire was consumed either by a conflagration, a venomous bite, the strike of a serpent, or ended his life by poison. He who was to perish by the sword was slaughtered either by the violence of the state, a popular tumult, a faction, or the snares of robbers. He who was to be hanged by a noose was either suffocated in a whirlpool of water or extinguished by some other strangling plague. By this reasoning of doctrine, even the great Origen <note>Early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> judged that Gospel of Christ should be explained: *He who strikes with the sword, perishes by the sword.* Furthermore, the pagan philosophers declare this order of retaliation to be 
<margin>Adrastia.</margin>Adrastia <note>The Greek goddess of "inevitable justice" or Nemesis</note>—namely, the inevitable power of divine laws by which, in future circuits, each person is repaid according to the reason and merits of their prior life. Thus, he who ruled unjustly in a prior life may slide back into a state of servitude in another life; he who defiled his hands with blood is forced to undergo retaliation; he who lived a bestial life is cast down, having rolled back into a brutal body.
<margin>Plotinus.</margin>Plotinus writes of these things in his book *On One's Own Daemon*: "Whosoever among men have preserved their human property are born again as men. But whosoever have used only their senses return as brute animals—yet in such a way that those who lived chiefly by sense joined with anger become animals..."

# BOOK THREE.
## CCXCV.
### B ii

...wild beasts arise. However, those who use their senses only for the sake of lust and pleasure return as lecherous and gluttonous animals. But if they have lived not so much by the senses as by the <term>degeneration of the senses</term> <note>meaning a loss of even basic animal instinct</note>, they sprout again as plants; for in these people, only the vital force was active, and their only care was to be changed into plants. Truly, those who lived too much soothed by musical melodies, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they are infected by some other wickedness. But he who has attained civic virtue returns as a man. And Solomon himself in the Proverbs calls man now a lion, a tiger, a bear, or a boar; now a hare, a greyhound, or a rabbit; now an ant, a hedgehog, a serpent, or a spider; now he names him an eagle, a lizard, a rooster, or some other bird, and many things of this kind. 

Truly, the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Jewish mystics</note> of the Hebrews do not allow that souls are cast down into brute animals; yet they do not deny that those who have utterly shaken off reason are left to animal affection and imagination in another life. They also assert that souls revolve back to this life three times, and no more; 

<margin>
Souls return to this life three times.
</margin>

since this number seems abundantly sufficient for the purging of sins, according to that passage in Job: *He delivered his soul from going into destruction, but that living he might see the light.* <note>Job 33:28</note> Behold, God works all these things three times for each person, so that he may call back their souls from corruption and illuminate them with the light of the living. 

But now at last, let us see what the ancients felt concerning the dead. When a man dies, the body returns to the earth from which it was taken; the mind returns to the heavens from whence it descended, just as Ecclesiastes says: *The dust returns to its earth from whence it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.* <note>Ecclesiastes 12:7</note> Lucretius expressed this in these verses:

->That which came from the earth returns back to the earth; and that which was sent from the borders of the ether, the shining temples of heaven receive again.<-

But Ovid said it better in these verses:

->Man has four parts: the ghost, the flesh, the spirit, and the shadow; these four places receive the four parts. The earth covers the flesh, the shadow flits around the tomb, the Underworld holds the ghost, and the spirit seeks the stars.<-

<margin>Flesh.</margin>

Therefore, the abandoned flesh and the body deprived of life is called a <term>corpse</term> <note>Latin: *cadaver*</note>. As the theologians of the Hebrews say, it is left in the power of the demon **Zazel** <note>Azazel</note>, of whom it is said in Scripture: *You shall eat the earth all your days,* and elsewhere: *The dust of the earth is his bread.* For man was created from the dust of the earth, whence that demon is called the lord of flesh and blood as long as the body has not been expiated and sanctified by the proper funeral rites. Hence, not without cause did the ancient fathers ordain the expiations of the corpse: so that what is greatly unclean may be sprinkled with holy water, perfumed with incense, exorcised with sacred prayers, and honored with lights as long as it is above the earth, until finally it is buried in a sacred place. Hence in Homer, Elpenor says: *I ask you, Ulysses, be mindful of me...*

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<note>original: "DE OCCULTA PHILOSOPHIA"</note>

...fear, nor departing from there, leave me unburied, lest being unsepulchred I become the object of the gods' wrath. The human **Mind** <note>Latin: *mens*; the highest, intellectual part of the soul</note>, however, whose nature is sacred and whose origin is divine, because it is always free from guilt, also escapes all punishment. But the **Soul** <note>Latin: *anima*; the mediating part between mind and body</note>, if it has acted well, rejoices with the mind; departing with its ethereal vehicle, it transcends freely to the choirs of heroes or seeks the higher realms. There, blessed with perpetual happiness in all its senses and powers, it enjoys a perfect knowledge of all things, and moreover, the divine vision and possession of the kingdom of heaven. Becoming a sharer in divine power, it bestows various gifts and benefits upon these lower realms, like an immortal god. 

If it has acted badly, the mind judges it and leaves it to the judgment of a demon <note>In this context, a guiding or punishing spirit, not necessarily a "devil"</note>. Then the mournful soul, without the mind, wanders among the inhabitants of the underworld as an **idol**, which they call the **image** <note>Latin: *imago* or *idolum*; the shadow-self or ghost</note>, just as Dido laments in Virgil:

> And now my great image shall go beneath the earth.

Therefore, this soul, then deprived of its intelligible essence and left to the command of a raging fantasy, is also subjected to the torture of corporeal qualities. It recognizes itself, by the just judgment of God and because of its own fault, to be perpetually deprived of the divine vision for which it was created. This divine vision, as Scripture testifies, is the absence of all evils; its loss is the most bitter punishment of all, which the Sacred Letters call the "outpouring of the wrath of God." And so this image of the soul sometimes enters an aerial body—a shadow—wrapped in which it now consults friends, now haunts enemies, just as in Virgil, Dido threatens Aeneas, saying:

> I shall be present as a shadow in all places; you, wicked man, shall pay the penalty.

For since disturbances, memories, and senses remain in the soul when separated from the body, the Platonists say that the souls—especially of those who were murdered—haunt their enemies. This is effected not so much by human indignation as by divine Nemesis <note>The goddess of retribution</note>, with a demon providing and permitting it. Thus the spirit of Naboth (as the masters of the Hebrews <note>Rabbinical commentators</note> interpret) because he departed at the end of his life with a desire for vengeance, was made (to fulfill that vengeance) a lying spirit. By God's permission, he went forth as a lying spirit in the mouths of all the prophets, until he caused Ahab to go up to Ramoth-Gilead. 

And Virgil himself, along with the Pythagoreans and Platonists—whom our own Augustine also follows—confesses <gloss>confesses</gloss> that separated souls retain the memory and will of those things they did in this life, where he sings:

> The same grace for chariots
> and arms they had when living, the same care to feed
> sleek horses, follows them when laid beneath the earth.

And Al-Ghazali <note>Latin: *Algazel*; a Persian theologian and philosopher</note> in his book *On Divine Science*, and other Arabs and Muhammadan philosophers, feel that the operations of the soul common to the joined body imprint a character of use and exercise upon the soul. Once strongly imprinted, the separated soul will use these for similar operations and passions which were not erased in life. Thus, although the body and its organs are corrupted, the operation will not cease for that reason, but the affections and similar dispositions will remain.

<summary>This page explores the afterlife of the soul's three parts, explaining how the "image" or ghost remains to haunt the living or suffer punishment, while the "mind" returns to the divine. It cites classical poets like Virgil alongside biblical figures and Islamic philosophers to argue that earthly habits and desires persist after death.</summary>

<keywords>afterlife, tripartite soul, ghost, Dido, Aeneas, Naboth, Ahab, Al-Ghazali, retribution, memory after death, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's journey after death, specifically focusing on the state of those who lived virtuously but outside the Christian faith.</meta>

# BOOK THREE. 297.

<margin>The Manes <note>original: "Manes." In Roman mythology, these were the souls of deceased loved ones, often treated as minor deities.</note></margin>
And the ancients called these souls by the common name of "Manes." Among them, those who were innocent in this life, or purified by moral virtues—and as Virgil <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose *Aeneid* describes the underworld.</note> sings:
> Those who suffered wounds fighting for their fatherland,
> And those who were chaste priests while life remained,
> And the pious bards who spoke things worthy of Apollo,
> Or those who refined life through the discovered arts,
> And those who made others remember them by their deserving deeds,
Although they may have departed without grace and the justice of faith, many theologians believe that they are carried away, free from suffering, into certain "fortunate fields." And, as Virgil says:
> They come to joyful places and lovely green glades,
> The dwellings of the fortunate groves and blessed seats,
Where they may enjoy certain wondrous pleasures; and they even rejoice in knowledge, both sensory and intellectual as well as revealed. Perhaps they are even instructed in faith and justice, no less than those spirits to whom Christ once preached the Gospel in prison <note>A reference to 1 Peter 3:19, the "Harrowing of Hell," where Christ is said to have descended to preach to souls trapped since the time of Noah.</note>. For as it is certain that no one can be saved without the faith of Christ, so it is probable that this faith is still preached to many pagans and Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note> after this life in those receptacles of souls for their salvation, and that they are held in those places as if in a common custody until the time arrives when the Greatest Judge shall make an examination of their merits. From this opinion even Lactantius, Irenaeus, Clement, Tertullian, Augustine, Ambrose, and many other Christian writers do not shrink.

However, those souls that depart impure, incontinent, and unjust with sins are not moved by such happy dreams, but wander through horrible phantasms and inferior places. They rely on no free knowledge, except that which is abstracted through concession or manifestation. Then, due to a continuous longing for flesh and blood because of the "rust" of bodily stain, they are even subjected to the sensation of pain, and they fear blades and swords. Homer <note>The Greek epic poet.</note> undoubtedly seems to have perceived this when, in the eleventh book of the *Odyssey*, he introduces the deceased mother of Ulysses <note>Odysseus.</note> standing near him as he offers sacrifice; but she neither recognized nor spoke to him as long as he, with his sword drawn, kept the shadows away from the blood of the sacrifice. But after his mother had tasted of that sacrifice at the persuasion of the prophet Tiresias, and the "cloudy one" drank the black blood, she immediately recognized her son and spoke to him while weeping. Yet the soul of the prophet Tiresias, despite the prohibition of the drawn sword, both recognized Ulysses and spoke to him even before tasting the blood, and pointed out that his mother’s shadow was standing nearby. Therefore, those souls who did not atone for the vices of crimes contracted in the body during this life, carrying their habits with them, are compelled to wash them away among the inhabitants of the underworld <note>original: "inferos."</note> and to pay the penalties for their commissions, which the poet explained in these verses:
> Nay, even when life has left them with the final light,
> Yet not all evil leaves the wretched ones, nor do all
> Bodily plagues depart entirely; it is necessary that
> Many things, long hardened, should grow deep into their ways in strange modes.

<summary>The author discusses the "Manes" or souls of the dead, arguing that virtuous pagans may be instructed in the Christian faith after death, while sinful souls undergo a sensory and psychological purgation.</summary>

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

> Therefore they are exercised with punishments, and for their former sins
> They pay the penalties.
<note>original: "Ergo exercentur pœnis, ueterumq́; malorum / Supplicia expendunt." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, describing the purification of souls in the underworld.</note>

<margin>Lemures <note>Restless ghosts</note>. Lar <note>Household god</note>.</margin>
<margin>Larvae or "fright-inducers."</margin>
For just as the habits and character of men are in this life, so for the most part do these same affections follow the soul after death; the soul revolves these things within a remembering mind, considering what it once did in life. These memories then occur more intensely and sharply, because the various duties of life have ceased—the needs of nourishing, growing, and procreating—as well as the various occupations and comforts of the senses and human business, and the obstacles of the heavy, physical body. At that time, those images occur to the "phantastic" <note>The faculty of the mind that creates mental images or "phantasms."</note> reason all the more turbulently and with great fury, depending on whether the intellectual spark lies more or less dormant, or is entirely extinguished within such a soul. To these souls, the evil demons then introduce images that are either utterly false or terrifying. Hence, in the "concupiscible" power <note>The faculty of the soul related to desires and longing for perceived goods.</note>, the soul is tortured by the longing for an imaginary good and for those things it once craved in life, being deprived of the power to obtain them. Although it sometimes seems to itself to almost reach its delights, it is kept away from them by demons for more bitter punishment—just as among the poets, Tantalus is kept from the feast, Sardanapalus from the embrace, Midas from gold, and Sisyphus from power. These souls are called **Lemures** <note>In Roman mythology, the restless and often malevolent spirits of the dead.</note>. If any of these, caring for domestic matters, dwells quietly in a house, it is called a **familiar Lar** <note>A protective Roman household deity.</note>.

However, they are most sharply tortured in the "irascible" power <note>The faculty of the soul related to anger, fear, and the avoidance of perceived evils.</note> by the hatred of an imaginary evil. At that time, the most false disturbances, suspicions, and horrible phantasms fall upon them. They turn over sad images within themselves: now the sky seems to fall on their heads, now they are consumed by the rush of flames, now they are submerged under a vast whirlpool of water, now they are swallowed by the gaping earth. Now they seem to be transformed into various beasts, now torn apart or devoured by deformed monsters; now they are driven here and there through forests, through seas, through fires, through the air, and through the foulest places of the underworld. Now they perceive themselves being seized and tortured by demons. We believe all these things happen to them after death no differently than they do in this life to those who rave through frenzy, mania, or a "melancholic humor" <note>An imbalance of black bile believed to cause depression or hallucinations.</note>, or those who are tortured in dreams by terrifying visions. They suffer as if these things were truly happening to them, though in truth they are not; rather, they are only the images of such things apprehended in the imagination. Thus, these souls after death are terrified by the horrible images of their sins as if dreaming, and a conscience burdened by crime drives them headlong through various terrors. For this reason, Orpheus calls them the "people of dreams," saying: *The gates of Pluto cannot be unbolted; within are the people of dreams.*

Therefore, such wicked souls, possessing no good resting place, are called **Larvae** or **fright-inducers** when they wander in their "aerial bodies" <note>A subtle, non-physical body believed to clothe the soul after it leaves the physical one.</note> and present any form to our sight. They are empty to the good, but harmful to the wicked. Appearing sometimes in thinner, sometimes in thicker "shucks" <note>The outer layers or "skins" of the spirit body.</note>, they manifest under the appearance of various animals and monsters, whose behaviors they once imitated in life, just as the poet sings:

> Then various forms mock them, and the faces of wild beasts.
<note>original: "Tum uariæ illudunt species, atq́; ora ferarum." Another reference to Virgil, describing the shifting shapes of spirits or the illusions of the underworld.</note>

For the unclean soul of man, which in this life has contracted too much of a habit toward bodies, weaves for itself another body from the vapors of the elements by a certain inward affection for the elemental body. It creates this from easy matter, constantly refreshing that vanishing body as if by a certain draught. To this body, as if to a prison and a sensible instrument, the soul is enslaved by a certain divine law; in it, the soul suffers cold and fire, and whatever things offend the body, spirit, and sense: stenches, wailing, lamentation, gnashing of teeth, lashings, tearing, and chains, just as Virgil sang:

> Therefore they are exercised by punishments, and for the evils of old
> They pay the penalties: some are stretched out empty
> Suspended to the winds; for others, the infected crime
> Is washed away under a vast whirlpool, or burnt out by fire.
<note>original: "Ergo exercentur pœnis..." From Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.739-742), describing the purification of souls in the underworld.</note>

And in Homer, in his *Necyomantia* <note>The "Book of the Dead" or the descent into the underworld in the *Odyssey*.</note>, Alcinous relates to Ulysses:

> We saw also Tityus, the famous foster-child of the earth,
> His body spread across nine acres, whose
> Entrails a vulture, sitting on either side, thrashes.

<margin>Depraved souls are cast down into brutes</margin>
Sometimes those souls do not only inhabit these figurative bodies, but by an excessive affection for flesh and blood, they even cast themselves into animals. Entering the bodies of reptiles and brutes of whatever species, they seize them and haunt them like demons. Pythagoras supports these views, and before him Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*.</note>, asserting that depraved souls are often cast down into reptiles and brutes. Yet they do not give life to or "inform" those bodies as essential forms <note>A technical term in Scholastic philosophy: the "form" is what makes a thing what it is; here, the author argues the human soul doesn't become the animal's soul, but merely stays inside it.</note>; rather, they inhabit them in the manner of a tenant as if in a prison, or they stand by them through local proximity, like an internal motor to its movable part. Or, bound around those things, they are tortured, like Ixion at the wheels of serpents, or Sisyphus at the rock. Nor do they seize only brutes, but sometimes even men, just as we said of the soul of Naboth, who went out as a lying spirit in the mouth of the prophets. Hence some have asserted that the lives or spirits of wicked men, entering into the bodies of certain people, keep them in a bad state for a long time, and sometimes kill them. 

This same thing is perhaps granted much more effectively to blessed souls, so that like good angels they can inhabit and enlighten us, just as we read concerning Elijah: that when he was taken up from among men, his spirit rested upon Elisha. And elsewhere we read that God took from the spirit that was in Moses and gave it to the seventy men. A great mystery lies hidden here, but it is not to be revealed rashly. Sometimes also (which is nevertheless very rare), souls are driven by such great madness—

...so that they do not only perish as the bodies of the living, but by a certain Stygian <note>Stygian: relating to the River Styx in the underworld; here meaning hellish or infernal power.</note> force, they migrate back into their abandoned corpses and, as if revived, commit horrendous crimes.
<margin>History of the Danes, Book 5.</margin>
Just as we read in the writings of Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian famous for the Gesta Danorum.</note>, a certain Asuitus and Asmundus swore a mutual oath to one another: that whichever of them lived longer would be buried together with the one who died. Eventually, Asuitus was consumed by disease and committed to a vast cavern along with his dog and his horse. Because of his oath of friendship, Asmundus endured being buried alive with him, bringing enough food to last a long time. Finally, Eric, King of Sweden, passing through that place with an army and breaking open Asuitus’s tomb (thinking there was treasure inside), opened the cave and restored the rescued Asmundus to the light. Seeing him with a foul appearance, covered in the filth of the grave and bloodied by a flowing, raw scar (for Asuitus, reviving at night, had torn off his left ear in frequent struggles), the King ordered him to explain the cause of the wound. He told the story in these verses:

> Why are you amazed to see me left without color?
> Truly, every living man grows pale among the dead.
> By some daring of a Stygian power, I know not what,
> A spirit sent from the underworld in the form of Asuit
> Ate his swift-footed horse with savage teeth
> And offered the dog to his unspeakable mouth.
> Not content with eating the horse or the dog,
> He soon turned his swift claws upon me:
> Tearing my cheek, he took away my ear.
> Hence the image of my mangled face is a horror,
> And blood flashes in the fierce wound.
> Yet the monster-maker did not act with impunity:
> For with iron I soon cut off his head,
> And pierced his guilty body with a stake.

Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> reports something not unlike this, received from the interpreters of Delphi: namely, that there is a certain infernal demon whom they called Eurynomus, who consumes and devours the flesh of the dead, so that the bones are left barely bare. We also read in the annals of the Cretans that the spirits of the dead, whom they call *Catechanas* <note>original: "Catechanas" — likely a reference to the Greek 'katakhanas', a type of vampire or revenant.</note>, are accustomed to return into their bodies, enter to their abandoned wives, and fulfill their lust. To avoid this, and so that they might no longer infest their wives, it is provided by local laws to pierce the heart of the rising corpse with a nail and burn the entire body. These things are undoubtedly marvelous, and might perhaps seem hostile to common opinion, were they not supported by both established laws and the trusted histories of antiquity. Nor, finally, is it foreign to the Christian religion that many souls can be restored to their bodies before the universal resurrection of the flesh; indeed, we believe many have been taken up into glory with their bodies by the singular benefit of God, and many have even descended alive into hell. And we have heard not infrequently of the bodies of the dead being snatched from their graves by demons, undoubtedly for no other use...

Aristotle relates that near the Aeolian Islands of Italy, there was a certain mound in Lipara to which it was not safe to approach at night; the inhabitants constantly asserted that the clashing of cymbals and the braying of castanets <term>crotalorum: ancient percussion instruments similar to clappers</term> were heard there, along with certain rude laughter, tumult, and empty sounds. A certain drunken youth once approached that place and fell asleep near the cave of the mound toward nightfall; he was finally found there on the third day by those searching for him and was carried away as if dead. When the funeral was being led out with the rites prepared, he suddenly woke up and related many things he had seen and suffered, one after another, to the great admiration of all. There is also in the same region, toward the southern side, a promontory called Nadhegryn <note>Likely a reference to a location in the far north or Iceland, often associated with volcanic activity in medieval lore</note>, where the demons of the place are seen by everyone in their aerial bodies. <margin>Tertullian.</margin>

<margin>Peter the Apostle.</margin>
Indeed, even Peter the Apostle, to Clement <note>Referring to the Pseudo-Clementine literature, early Christian writings attributed to Pope Clement I</note> questioning him about these matters, said: "You compel me, O Clement, to publish some of the ineffable things; nevertheless, as far as it is permitted to bring them forth, I shall not be reluctant. Christ, who was from the beginning and always, was always present through individual generations to the pious, though hiddenly; especially to those by whom he was expected, and to whom he frequently appeared. But it was not yet the time that the resurrection should occur for those with dissolved bodies then; rather, this seemed a greater reward from God: that he who was found righteous should remain longer in the body, or certainly (as is clearly reported in the scriptures concerning a certain righteous man <note>Likely referring to Enoch or Elijah</note>) that the Lord translated him." By a similar example, it was also done with the others who pleased His will, so that being translated to paradise, they are preserved for the kingdom. But of those who were not able to fully complete the rule of justice, but had some remains of malice in their flesh, their bodies are indeed dissolved, but their souls are kept in good and joyful regions, so that in the resurrection of the dead, when they have received their bodies—now purged by that very dissolution—they may possess the eternal inheritance for the things they had done well.

<margin>Irenaeus.</margin>
Irenaeus himself also, at the end of the book which he wrote *Against the Heresies of the Valentinians*, says: Since the Lord went away into the midst of the shadow of death, where the souls of the dead were, and afterward rose again bodily, and after the resurrection was taken up, it is manifest that the souls of his disciples (for whose sake the Lord also performed these things) will go away into an invisible place defined for them by God, and will stay there until the resurrection, awaiting the resurrection; afterward receiving their bodies and rising perfectly, that is bodily, just as the Lord rose again, so they shall come into the sight of God. For no disciple is above his master.

# BOOK THREE. 303.

"But everyone will be perfect, just as his master." <note>original: "perfectus autem erit omnis sicut magister eius." A reference to Luke 6:40.</note> Therefore, just as our Master did not immediately fly away and depart, but waited for the time of His resurrection defined by the Father—which was also made manifest through Jonah—and after three days rose and was taken up; so also we must wait for the time of our resurrection defined by God and foretold by the prophets, and thus rising, be taken up, as many as the Lord shall have deemed worthy of this honor. To these views is added also **Lactantius Firmianus** <margin>Lactantius</margin> <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> in that book of his *Divine Institutes* titled *On the Divine Reward*, saying: "And let no one think that souls are judged immediately after death: for all are detained in one common custody until the time comes when the supreme Judge makes an examination of merits. Then those whose justice has been approved shall receive the reward of immortality; but those whose sins and crimes are uncovered shall not rise, but shall be hidden away with the impious in the same darkness, destined for certain punishments." **Augustine** and **Ambrose** are of the same opinion, of whom the former says in his *Enchiridion*: <margin>// Augustine</margin> "The time which is interposed between a man's death and the final resurrection holds the souls in hidden receptacles, according as each is worthy of rest or of misery, based on what it obtained in the flesh while it lived." **Ambrose**, indeed, in his book *On the Good of Death*, says: <margin>Ambrose</margin> "The Scripture of Ezra <note>A reference to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra), which discusses the 'storehouses' of souls.</note> called the dwellings of souls 'storehouses,' which, meeting the human complaint (because the just who have gone before seem to be defrauded of their due reward for a very long time until the day of judgment), wonderfully says that the day of judgment is like a crown. For the day of the crown is expected by all, so that within that day both the defeated may blush and the victors may obtain the palm of victory. Therefore, while the fullness of time is awaited, souls await their due reward; for some, punishment remains, for others, glory." And in the same chapter, he calls the underworld a "place which is not seen," which souls freed from bodies seek. And in the second book of *Cain and Abel*: "The soul is released from the body," he says, "and after the end of this life, it is still suspended in the ambiguity of the future judgment." That Gospel passage concerning the final judgment supports them, where Christ says in Matthew: "Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many miracles?' And then I will declare to them that I never knew you." From this speech, it seems clear that they were uncertain of their sentence until that day, and through confidence in the miracles they had performed in Jesus' name while they still lived, they were meanwhile suspended in a certain hope of salvation. Because, therefore, the judgment of souls is delayed until the final day, many theologians think that intercessory prayers <term>piacularia suffragia: prayers or offerings intended to appease God or provide relief for the deceased</term> can be of help before the appointed day of judgment, not only for those to be justified but even for the damned. Thus, **Emperor Trajan** was freed from the underworld by **Saint Gregory** and justified unto salvation; although some think he was not freed from the guilt of the penalty, but that the justice of the punishment was deferred until the day of judgment. But **Thomas Aquinas** says it seems more probable that Trajan was restored to life by the prayers of Saint Gregory, and obtained a free grace by which he was [freed] from punishment and the bond of his crimes...

There are some among the theologians who believe that through the intercession of funeral offerings, neither the punishment is removed nor the fine diminished, but rather that only certain comforts and refreshments for the pains are brought forth. They use the comparison of a sweating porter who, by the sprinkling of water, seems to be relieved of the pressure of his burden, or helped to carry it more easily, even though nothing has been taken away from the weight itself. However, the common opinion of theologians denies that prayers and funeral rites offer any help to those guilty in the cavern of Dis <note>original: "Ditis antro" - a classical reference to the Roman god of the underworld, here used for Hell</note>. Truly, since all these matters are of incomprehensible obscurity, many have sharpened their wits upon them in vain. > It is better to doubt concerning hidden things than to litigate over uncertain ones.

<margin>The excellent opinion of Augustine.</margin>
Indeed, I do not doubt that we understand that rich man to be in the heat of punishments, and that poor man in the refreshment of joys <note>A reference to the biblical parable of Lazarus and the Rich Man</note>: but how that flame of hell is to be understood, that bosom of Abraham, that tongue of the rich man, that finger of the poor man, that thirst of torment, and that drop of refreshment, is scarcely found by those who seek gently, and never by those who contend argumentatively. But leaving these things aside now, and hastening to further matters, we shall discuss the restorations of souls.

### By what reasons Magicians and Necromancers thought they were able to evoke the souls of the dead. Chapter XLII.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring floral motifs within a square frame.</note> From these things which have already been said, it is clear that those souls which after death still love their abandoned bodies—such as the souls of those lacking the due burial of their bodies, or those who left their body by a violent death, and still wander in that turbid and moist spirit around their own corpses as if around something kindred attracting them—can be easily evoked and enticed. This is done by knowing those means through which they were once joined to their bodies: through similar vapors, liquids, and scents, and also by employing certain artificial lights, songs, sounds, and the like, which move the imaginative and spiritual harmony of the soul itself. Sacred invocations and such things which pertain to religion are not neglected, on account of the rational portion of the soul which is superior by nature. Thus the Witch <note>original: "Phytonissa" - referring to the Witch of Endor</note> is read to have summoned Samuel: thus the Thessalian prophetess in the works of Lucan raised a corpse. Hence we read among the poets and narrators of such things that the souls of the dead are not evoked without blood and a corpse; but shadows are easily enticed by their fumigations, with the addition of eggs, milk, honey, oil, wine, water, and flour, as if providing a fit medium for the souls to take up bodies, just as Circe teaches Ulysses with long instruction in Homer. Moreover, they judge that these things can only be done in those places where such souls are known to frequent most, either because of something kindred, like the abandoned body attracting them, or because of some affection impressed during life drawing the soul itself to certain places, or because of the nature of the place, which is suited to a hellish <term>Tartarean: relating to Tartarus, the deepest abyss of the underworld</term> nature for purging or punishing souls. Such places are mostly known by the experience of visions, nocturnal incursions, and the occurrence of similar phantasms; some are well enough known by themselves, such as cemeteries and those places in which it is customary for...

For the purification <note>original: "expiatio"</note> and exorcism of a place, as well as the sacred rite of burial properly applied to bodies, often prevents those very souls from approaching and drives them further away to the places of judgment. From this, necromancy <note>literally "death-divination"</note> takes its name, because it works upon the corpses of the dead, and seeks answers through the spirits <note>original: "manes"</note> and shadows of the deceased and subterranean demons, luring them into the corpses of the dead through certain Stygian <note>referring to the river Styx in the underworld</note> songs and infernal invocations, and through funereal sacrifices and impious offerings, such as those we read about in Lucan <note>A Roman poet; the reference is to his epic 'Pharsalia'</note> concerning that sorceress Erichtho, who summoned a dead man to predict to Sextus Pompey the entire outcome of the Pharsalian war.
