For in this way, even the souls of the saints love their own bodies, and are accustomed to hear more readily and promptly where the pledges of their relics are preserved.

<margin>Two types of necromancy.</margin>
There are, moreover, two types of necromancy: one is "necyomancy," which raises a corpse and does not occur without blood; the other is "scyomancy," in which the summoning of a shadow alone suffices. Finally, [the magician] performs all his experiments through the corpses, bones, and limbs of those who have been slaughtered, and things derived from them: because a demonic power friendly to them is present there. Therefore, they easily entice the flow of wicked demons because of a very familiar likeness and property. Since these demons have great power in earthly and human affairs, the necromancers, relying on their labor, kindle illicit loves, send dreams, diseases, hatreds, and similar passions. To these ends, they can also contribute the powers of those souls which, still entangled in a moist and turbulent spirit and wandering around their remains, commit the same acts as the wicked demons. Since, therefore, it has been found by experience that depraved and impure souls, violently torn from their bodies, and the souls of men not purified and lacking burial, linger around their bodies and are drawn to what is kindred to them, sorcerers easily abuse them to accomplish their evil deeds. They lure the unhappy souls by the placement of the body or the taking up of a part of it, then compel them with Stygian invocations, adjuring them by the shapeless corpses scattered over wide fields, and the wandering shadows of those lacking burial, and the spirits released from Acheron <note>A river in the underworld</note>, and the guests of hell whom premature death dragged down into Tartarus, and by the horrendous desires of the damned, and the proud demons, the avengers of crimes.

<margin>What one must know who truly desires to restore a soul to a body.</margin>
He, however, who truly ought to restore souls to their bodies, must be knowledgeable of what the soul's own nature is, from whence it proceeds, with how many and what degrees of perfection it is filled, with what intelligence it is fortified, by what means it is diffused into the body, by what harmony it was joined with it, and what affinity it has with God, with the intelligences, with the heavens, with the elements, and all other things whose image and likeness it holds...

Finally, one must understand by what influences the body is joined together; for all these things are required by the art of the <term>resuscitation of the dead</term> <note>original: "suscitationis mortuorum"</note>, which belongs not to men, but to God alone, and to those with whom He wishes to communicate it—just as with Elisha <note>original: "Helizæo"</note>, who caused the dead son of the Shunammite woman to live again. So too is Alcestis recorded to have been raised by Hercules and to have lived for a long time afterward; and Apollonius of Tyana restored a dead girl to life. <margin>Note this</margin> And here it must be noted that it sometimes happens to men that the life-giving spirit is withdrawn within them, and they appear dead and without sensation, even though the intellectual nature remains united to the body and retains the same form. The body remains the same, although the power of animating it does not actually extend into it at that moment but remains withdrawn in union with the intellectual nature; nevertheless, it does not cease to exist. And although that man may now truly be called dead, insofar as death is the absence of the life-giver, yet that body would not be truly separated [from the soul], and it can be awakened and live again. Thus many miracles appear in these matters, of which many were seen in preceding centuries among the Pagans and the Jews. Among their number is what Plato recites in the tenth book of the *Republic*: namely, that a certain Er <note>original: "Phereū," likely a transcription error for "Er"</note> the Pamphylian lay for ten days among those who had fallen in battle, and two days after he had been taken from there and placed upon the funeral pyre, he returned to life and narrated certain wonders which he had seen during the time of his death. We have spoken of these things partly in the first book, and we shall speak even more extensively below, where we shall discuss the oracles that occur in rapture, ecstasy, and the death-throes of the dying.

### On the power of the human soul, in the Mind, Reason, and the Idol.
->Chapter XLIII.<-

<margin>Of what the human soul consists.</margin>
The human soul consists of the <term>Mind</term> <note>the highest, divine intellect</note>, <term>Reason</term>, and the <term>Idol</term> <note>the "idolon" or image; the lower, animating spirit/astral body</note>. The Mind illuminates the Reason, the Reason flows into the Idol, and all is one soul. Unless the Reason is illuminated by the Mind, it is not immune from error; however, the Mind does not provide light to the Reason unless God—the first light—is shining. For the first light in God transcends all understanding; therefore, it cannot be called an "intelligible light." But when that light is poured into the Mind, it becomes intellectual and can be understood. Then, when it is poured through the Mind into the Reason, it becomes rational, and can not only be understood but also thought upon. Then, when it is poured through the Reason into the Idol of the soul, it is made not only thinkable but also imaginable, though not yet corporeal. But when it migrates from there into the ethereal vehicle of the soul, it first becomes corporeal, yet not clearly perceptible to the senses, until it has passed into the elemental body—whether simple and airy, or composite—in which it becomes a light clearly visible to the eye. Considering this progression of light, the philosophers of the Chaldeans tell of a certain stupendous power of our Mind: namely, that it is possible for the Mind itself, with its whole focus fixed upon God, to be filled with divine power. Thus filled with light, it pours out rays through every medium down to this thick, dark, heavy, mortal body, surrounding it also with abundant light, rendering it like the stars and equally glittering; then also by the abundance of its rays...

<margin>The sense of nature, the ethereal sense, and the vehicle.</margin>

These gifts are not given to all, but only to those whose imaginative and cognitive power is strongest and has reached the height of contemplation. Such a person is fit to perceive and announce all things through the splendor of the universal power, or the spiritual intelligence and apprehension that is over him; and this is the necessary power which must be followed, and which everyone who follows the truth must obey. If, therefore, the power of the imagination is so great that it can insinuate itself into whomever it wishes, hindered by no interval of space or time, and sometimes drags the heavy body along to wherever it dreams and imagines, there is no doubt that the power of the mind is even greater when it has attained its own nature, no longer weighed down by the allurements of the senses, remaining incorrupt and true to itself. For now, souls abound with the copious light of the celestial stars, and a huge abundance of light overflows from there into their bodies. Thus the face of Moses shone so brightly that the children of Israel could not look upon him because of the splendor of his countenance. Thus we read that Socrates was transfigured, surpassing the light-bearing wheels of the sun with his light; thus Zoroaster was transfigured and lifted up bodily; thus Enoch and Elijah ascended to the heavens in a certain fiery chariot; thus Paul was caught up to the third heaven; thus...

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

We can say by this same reasoning that our bodies, after the judgment of the world—which shall then be called "glorified"—will similarly be snatched up and shine like the sun and moon. That this is indeed possible, and has in fact occurred, is admitted and demonstrated by Avicebron the Moor <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century Sephardic philosopher</note> as well as the Arab Avicenna, Hippocrates of Cos, and the entire school of the Chaldeans. Furthermore, it is handed down in historical records that Alexander the Great, when surrounded in India at great peril, burned so intensely in spirit that he appeared to the barbarians to pour forth light. The father of Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths</note> is also said to have poured forth sparks from his whole body. A certain wise man reported the same of himself: that sparkling flames leaped out from him here and there, even with a sound. Nor is this power of the spirit found only in humans, but it has also been discovered at times in brute animals, such as in the horse of Tiberius, which appeared to breathe fire from its mouth. Now, the Mind <term>Mens: the highest, divine part of the human intellect</term> is above fate and within providence; therefore, it is affected neither by the influences of the celestial bodies nor by the qualities of natural things. Thus, religion alone provides its remedy. However, the "Idol" of the soul <note>original: "Idolum autem animæ"</note> is within fate; it is above nature (acting as a kind of knot between body and soul) but below fate and above the body. Therefore, it is changed by the influences of celestial bodies and affected by the qualities of natural and corporeal things.

<margin>
What the Idol of the soul is.
</margin>
By the "Idol of the soul," I mean that life-giving and governing power of the body, the origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of perceiving in this body. It perceives corporeal things through the body, moves the body through space, governs it in its place, and nourishes the body in its stillness.

<margin>
Two virtues in the Idol.
</margin>
In this Idol, two most powerful virtues dominate: one, namely, which is called the phantasy or the imaginative power (of whose power we have already spoken, and also where we treated the passions of the soul); the other virtue is that which is called the "sense of nature," of which we also spoke when we mentioned divination by entrails <term>Aruspicina: the ancient Roman practice of interpreting omens from the internal organs of sacrificed animals</term>. Thus, a human being is under fate by the nature of the body; the soul of a man moves nature through the Idol within fate; but through the Mind, he is above fate, in the order of providence. Reason, however, is free and of its own right. Therefore, the soul ascends through reason into the Mind, where it is filled with divine light; at other times, it descends into the Idol, where it is affected by the influences of celestial bodies and the qualities of natural things, and is distracted by the passions and encounters of sensible things. Sometimes the soul folds itself entirely back into reason, either investigating other things by logic or contemplating itself. For it is possible that the rational part of the soul—which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> call the "possible intellect"—may reach the point where it discourses and operates freely without turning toward mental images <note>original: "phantasmata"</note>.

<insert>The following emphasizes the sovereignty of the rational mind over sensory input.</insert>
Finally, the command of reason itself is so great that whenever anything occurs either in the mind, or in the idol, or in nature, or in the body, it cannot pass into the soul unless reason applies itself to it. In this way, in the external senses, the soul perceives neither seeing, nor hearing, nor feeling, nor that it suffers anything, until the thinking reason first grasps it. It grasps it, however, when it is at leisure, not when it is gasping after something else—as we clearly see in those who do not notice people they meet while they are thinking more intently on something else. Know, therefore, that neither heavenly influences, nor natural affections, nor sensations, nor those of the body...

## On the levels of souls, and their destruction or immortality. Chapter 44.

Because the Mind <term>Mens: the highest, divine part of the intellect</term> is from God, or from the intelligible world, it is therefore immortal and eternal. However, the celestial Reason <term>Ratio: the discursive human intellect</term>, by virtue of its origin from heaven, is long-lived; but the "idol" <term>Idolum: here referring to the lower, animating spirit or shadow-soul</term>, because it depends on the womb of matter and sublunary nature, is subject to destruction and corruption. Thus the soul is immortal through its Mind, and long-lived through its Reason in its ethereal vehicle, yet it is capable of being dissolved unless it is restored in the circuit of a new body. It is therefore not immortal unless it is united to the immortal Mind. Likewise, the "idol" of the soul—or the sensible and animal soul itself—because it was drawn from the womb of corporeal matter, perishes along with the body when it is dissolved; or, it does not survive long as a shadow in the vapors of its dissolved body, participating in nothing of immortality unless it too is united to a higher power. Therefore, that soul which is united to the Mind is called a "standing and non-falling" soul. Truly, not all men have attained the Mind, because (as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings.</note> says) God the Father wished to propose it as a contest and a prize for souls.
<margin>Not all men attain the Mind.</margin>
Those who neglect this, being devoid of Mind and enslaved to the bodily senses, are made like irrational animals and allot for themselves the same destruction as those beasts, just as Ecclesiastes says:
> The death of man and of beasts is one, and the condition of both is equal: as man dies, so they also die. All things breathe alike, and man has nothing more than the beast. <note>original: "Vnus interitus eft hominis & iumentorum..." quoting Ecclesiastes 3:19.</note>
From this, many theologians believe that such souls retain no immortality after being stripped of this body, except for the sole hope of resurrection when all men are to be restored. Augustine records that such was the heresy of the Arabs, who said that souls perished together with the body and would rise again with it at the Judgment. But whoever, supported by divine grace, has attained the Mind, these become immortal according to the comparison of their works—as Hermes says—embracing in their intelligence all things that are on the earth, in the sea, and in the heavens; and if there is anything beyond them above heaven, so that they may behold the Good itself. However, those who happen to live a middle life, although they have not attained divine intelligence but rather a certain rational image of it, when their souls have departed from the body, they are relegated to certain secret receptacles. There, affected by their sensible powers and occupied in a certain kind of activity, based on their opinion...

...imagination, and the irascible <note>the faculty of anger or spiritedness</note> and concupiscible <note>the faculty of desire</note> virtues, they either rejoice excessively or grieve deeply; an opinion also held by Saint Augustine in that book which he wrote, *On the Spirit and the Soul*. The sages of the Indians, Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans handed down the belief that this soul survives its own body for a long time, yet does not immediately become immortal unless through transcorporation <note>original: "transcorporationẽ"; referring to reincarnation or metempsychosis</note>. This is the opinion held by John Scotus <note>likely Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher</note>, and the Parisian theologians decreed in their articles that this is how it must be understood. Hence the Wise Man says: *I was a witty child, and was allotted a good soul* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 8:19</note>, namely, a better one than many others. And according to this inequality of souls in their grades, each is capable of its own duty, which it receives from God as a free gift, just as we read in the Gospels: *Because to one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own particular virtue* <note>Matthew 25:15</note>. And the Apostle says: *He gave some to be apostles, others prophets, others evangelists and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ* <note>Ephesians 4:11-12</note>. For there are (as Origen says) certain invisible virtues to which the dispensing of things upon the earth is entrusted, among which there is no small difference, just as is required among men; for one reaches the highest grade of wisdom or dignity, while another is but a little distance from the beasts, and by feeding beasts becomes a semi-beast. One is abundant in virtues and rich in fortune, while another has either nothing or very little—and often even that little which he has is taken from him and given to the one who has. And such is divine justice in the distribution of gifts, that they correspond to the virtue of each recipient, to whom rewards are also rendered according to their works; so that whatever the proportion of gifts to gifts, and merits to merits, the same is the proportion of rewards to rewards.

<margin>
The fourfold operation of a noble soul.
</margin>
Finally, it must be known that every noble soul has a fourfold operation: one divine, through the image of the divine property; the second intellectual, through the formality of participation with the Intelligences <note>angelic or celestial beings</note>; the third rational, through the perfection of its own essentiality; the fourth animal or natural, through communion with the body and these lower things. Thus, there is no work in the entire series of the world so admirable, so excellent, or so miraculous that the human soul—having embraced the image of divinity, which the Magi call the "standing and not falling soul"—cannot effect by its own power without any external aid. Therefore, the form of all magical power is from the standing and not falling soul of man.

# BOOK THREE.

<image-desc>The letter V is a decorative woodcut initial depicting a figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>Prophecy <note>original: "Vaticinium"</note> is that state by which priests or others are moved, so that they both discern the causes of things and foresee future events; specifically, this occurs when oracles descend into them from the gods or from spirits <note>original: "dæmonibus" - in this context, referring to intermediary spirits or tutelary beings rather than "demons" in the modern sense</note>, and spirits are transmitted by them. The Platonists call these descents the "glidings" of superior souls into our own souls, and Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> calls them the senses and minds of spirits. The ancients called such spirits "Eurideas" and "Pythons," and antiquity firmly believed that they were accustomed to enter the bodies of men and use their voices and tongues for the prediction of future things; Plutarch also mentions these in his *Dialogue on the Obsolescence of Oracles*.

<margin>Foreknowledge of the future belongs to the gods alone.</margin>
However, Cicero, following the Stoics, affirms that the foreknowledge of future events belongs just as much to the gods; and Ptolemy the astrologer says: "Only those inspired by the divine predict particulars." Peter the Apostle agrees with these, saying: "For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit." <note>2 Peter 1:21</note> Furthermore, Isaiah affirms that the prediction of the future is a property of divine "glidings," saying: "Tell us the things that are to come, and we shall say that you are gods." <note>Isaiah 41:23</note> Truly, "glidings" or perceptions of this kind do not transfer into our soul when it is occupied and gasping attentively after something else; rather, they pass in when the soul is vacant. <margin>Three types of vacancy.</margin> There are three types of such vacancy: namely, frenzy <note>original: "furor" - a state of divine madness or ecstasy</note>, rapture, and dreaming, of each of which we shall now speak in order.

### Concerning the first species of frenzy, from the Muses. Chapter 46.

<image-desc>The letter F is a decorative woodcut initial featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or authority figure.</image-desc>Frenzy is an illumination of the soul proceeding from gods or spirits, whence comes this poem by Ovid <note>original: "Nasonis"</note>:

> ->There is a god within us, and we have commerce with heaven,<-
> ->That spirit comes from ethereal seats.<-

Plato defines this through alienation and connection: for it abstracts the soul from those things by which the bodily senses are excited; alienated from the animal man, it adheres to the divine power, from which it receives what it cannot investigate by its own strength. For when the soul is free and loose, the reins of the body having been relaxed—as if from an unguarded prison—it goes out more freely and transcends the bonds of the limbs. With nothing restraining it, driven by its own impulses and stirred by the divine spirit, it comprehends all things and foresees the future. <margin>Four species of divine frenzy.</margin> There are, moreover, four species of divine frenzy proceeding from individual deities: namely, from the Muses, from Dionysus, from Apollo, and from Venus. <margin>Frenzy from the Muses.</margin> Thus, the first frenzy, proceeding from the Muses, arouses and tempers the soul, rendering it divine by drawing superior things to inferior ones through natural forms. The Muses are the souls of the celestial spheres, according to which individual steps are found by which the attraction of superior things to inferior ones occurs. The lowest of these, reflecting the sphere of the Moon, holds those things which are of the vegetable kingdom, such as plants, the fruits of trees, and roots; and those which are of harder materials, such as stones and metals, and their bindings and suspensions. Thus it is said that the moonstone <note>original: "selenites"</note> and the "hyena-stone" <note>original: "lapis hyenæ"</note> provide divination; similarly, vervain and the herb *theangelis* <note>an ancient Persian herb mentioned by Pliny, said to grant prophetic powers</note> provide prophecy.

The **second degree** relates to **Mercury**; it contains those things which come from animals, and those which are composed from the mutual mixing of various natural things, such as drinks and foods. In this manner, the heart of a mole—if someone swallows it while it is still fresh and throbbing—is said to contribute to divination and to the successful outcome of tasks to be performed. And **Rabbi Moses of Egypt** <note>original: "Rabi Moses Cusensis," referring to Maimonides</note> relates in his commentaries on Leviticus that there is an animal called the **Jedua** <note>original: "ידוע" (Yadua). A legendary plant-animal from Jewish folklore, often called the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary</note>, which has a human form. From the middle of its navel, a cord is sent forth by which it is fixed to the ground like a gourd. As far as the length of that cord extends, it devours and consumes everything wandering around it; it cannot be captured, as it deceives the sight, unless the cord is severed by the strike of an arrow. Once the cord is cut, it expires. If someone then places its bones in their mouth according to a certain law, they are immediately seized by a frenzy and utter oracles concerning whatever things are sought.

The **third degree** corresponds to the sphere of **Venus**: this contains the finest powders, vapors, and odors, and the ointments and fumigations made from them, of which we have spoken above.

The **fourth degree** pertains to the sphere of the **Sun**: this contains voices, words, songs, and harmonic sounds. Through their sweet consonance, it drives turbulent discord from the soul and uplifts the mind. Hence **Hermes**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato** command that a dissonant mind be composed and uplifted by song and harmony. Thus **Timotheus** is said to have incited King **Alexander** into a frenzy by sounds; thus the priest of **Calamus** (according to the testimony of **Aurelius Augustine**) used to call himself out of his body into a state of rapture and ecstasy at his own will by a certain plaintive harmony. These matters have also been discussed above.

The **fifth degree** belongs to **Mars**: this contains powerful imaginations and affections of the soul, conceptions, and movements, all of which are explained above.

The **sixth degree** responds to **Jupiter**: this contains the discourses of reason, deliberations, consultations, and moral purifications. Mention of these was made partly above, and partly will be said below. Furthermore, it has under it wonders and venerations, by the awe of which the fantasy and reason are sometimes so bridled that they suddenly cease all their actions. From this, the mind itself—being then free and exposed to the divine power alone, whether to some god or a spirit—conceives heavenly and divine influxes, namely those about which it had previously deliberated. Thus we read that the **Sibyls** and the priests of the **Pythia** were accustomed to receive oracles in the caves of Jupiter and Apollo.

<margin>Contemplation</margin>
The **seventh degree** relates to **Saturn**: this contains the more secret intelligences and the tranquil contemplations of the mind. I call "contemplation" here the free perspicacity of the mind, suspended in admiration at the spectacles of wisdom. For that thinking which occurs through enigmas or images is "speculation," which is a certain discourse pertaining to Jupiter, not contemplation.

The **eighth degree** relates to the **starry heaven**: here one observes the position, motion, rays, and light of the celestial bodies. It also contains images, rings, and similar things which are fabricated according to the pattern of the heavens, of which we have spoken above.

The **ninth degree** corresponds to the **First Mover** <term>Primum Mobile: the outermost moving sphere in the geocentric model of the universe</term>, namely to the ninth sphere or to the universe itself: this contains more formal things, such as numbers, figures, characters, and hidden...

### Concerning the second species according to Dionysius.
## Chapter XLVII.

<image-desc>Ornate historiated woodcut initial 'S' depicting a seated scholar or figure in a landscape with an angelic or divine messenger approaching them.</image-desc>
The second type of frenzy <note>original: "furor" — in this context, a state of divine inspiration or "divine madness" rather than anger.</note> proceeds from Dionysius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note>: this occurs through exterior and interior purifications, and through exorcisms, through sacraments, through solemnities, rites, shrines, and observations. It directs the soul toward the mind—the highest part of itself—and makes it like a worthy and uncontaminated temple of the gods in which divine spirits may dwell. The soul, then possessing these spirits as companions in life, is filled by them with happiness, wisdom, and oracles—not through signs or marks or conjectures, but by a certain arousal of the soul and a loosened, free motion. In this way, Bacchus prophesied to the Boeotians, Epimenides to the Cretans, and the Erythraean Sibyl to the Trojans. Sometimes this frenzy happens through a clear vision, and sometimes through a distinct voice: thus Socrates was ruled by his own demon <note>original: "dæmone" — referring to the 'daimonion' or inner divine voice of Socrates, not an evil spirit.</note>, whose warnings he zealously obeyed, whose voice he frequently heard with his ears, and to whom the form of the demon was often visible. For prophetic spirits are accustomed to offer themselves visibly as companions to well-purified souls; there are many examples of this in the sacred scriptures, as with Abraham and his handmaid Hagar, in Jacob, Gideon, Elijah, Tobias, Daniel, and many others.

<margin>Which angels the ancient fathers had as familiars.</margin>

# Concerning the third species of frenzy, from Apollo. Chapter XLVIII.

<margin>A wondrous art.</margin>
<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial T. The letter is superimposed on a scene featuring a seated figure in a landscape with architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc>The third frenzy indeed proceeds from Apollo, that is, from the mind of the world. This frenzy—through certain sacred mysteries, vows, sacrifices, adorations, invocations, and certain sacred devices, or through certain secret preparations into which the gods have infused the power of their spirit—causes the soul to rise above the mind, joining it with divinities and spirits. We read of this regarding the Ephod <note>A ceremonial garment worn by High Priests in the Old Testament, used for divination</note>, which, when applied, caused men to prophesy immediately. So we read in the *Book of Senators* <note>Likely referring to a Hebrew source or a collection of rabbinical traditions</note>, in the chapters of Eleazar, that Rabbi Ishmael prepared certain small cakes inscribed with certain divine and angelic names and thus consecrated them; whoever ate these with faith, hope, and charity was immediately radiant with the prophetic spirit of wisdom. We read in the same place that Rabbi Johanan, son of Jochahidis, so illuminated a certain unrefined farmer named Eleazar—who was unskilled in all literature—that, surrounded by a sudden brightness, he unexpectedly preached such deep mysteries of the Law in the assembly of the wise that it was a wonder to all standing by. And it is recorded in memory concerning a certain Heraiscus the Egyptian, that he was endowed with such a divine nature that by the mere sight of statues which held some divinity within them, he was immediately stirred by divine frenzy. We also read in the sacred scriptures that when Saul was among the prophets, the spirit of the Lord leaped upon him and he prophesied; and when he departed from the company of prophets, he ceased to prophesy. A similar thing happened to those guards whom Saul sent to capture David: when they saw the company of prophets and Samuel standing over them, the spirit of the Lord came upon them also, and they themselves prophesied. So great is the exuberance of divine light often found in prophets seized by divine frenzy, that it even seizes those near them and compels them to rave with a similar spirit. It is therefore not incredible that someone can suddenly become wise from being ignorant, and again become ignorant from being wise. For there is a certain art (but known to very few) of so informing, adorning, and illustrating the faithful and pure soul of a man, that he is suddenly carried out from the darkness of ignorance to the lights of wisdom and learning. Conversely, there is a faculty to strip the impure and the incredulous of that same gift of wisdom and learning through certain hidden secrets, and restore them to their former ignorance. The human soul can also (according to Apuleius) especially if it is simple and pure, be lulled and externalized by the calling away and enchantment of certain sacred things into a forgetfulness of present matters, so that with the memory of the body removed...

<margin>
Prophets inspired by the divine fear nothing

Hence, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians and Chaldeans</note> says: When prophets are inspired by the power of a god, they fear nothing and respect no danger; for they walk through pathless places, are carried unharmed through fire, and cross over rivers. Thus we read that certain caves, such as those of Apollo and Trophonius, as well as tripods, caverns, springs, lakes, and similar things, were consecrated to the gods in this way, or constructed with such mystery that from them the priests drew the spirit of prophecy. As Iamblichus says to Porphyry: The Sibyl at Delphi was accustomed to receive the god in two ways: either through a thin breath and fire, which broke out from the mouth of the cave in some place; or by sitting herself in the inner sanctuary upon a bronze three-legged chair <term>tripod: a sacrificial seat associated with the oracles of Apollo</term> dedicated to the deity. In both cases, driven by this divine spirit, she poured forth prophecies. Then a great fire, flying out of the cave, surrounds the prophetess on all sides and agitates her as she is filled with his power; or, clinging to the sacred seat through which she is inspired by the god, she immediately breaks out into prophecies. But the prophetic seer among the Branchidae <note>An ancient line of priests who served the temple of Apollo at Didyma</note> either sits upon an axle, or carries a wand in her hand granted to her by some deity, or sometimes washes her feet and the hem of her garment in the waters, or draws the vapor of fire from the waters. By all these means she is filled with divine splendor and, having been brought forth, reveals oracles full of things to come. We also read that in the region of Thrace there was a sanctuary sacred to Bacchus <note>original: "Libero," an Italian deity identified with Dionysus/Bacchus</note>, from which prophecies and oracles were usually given; the priests of this temple performed their duties after drinking wine in abundance. Among the Clarians also, where the temple of Clarian Apollo was located, those permitted to speak divine truths performed their rites after first taking up water. There was also a prophetic spring of Achaean Patrae, situated before the temple of Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture, known as Demeter in Greek</note>, where those consulting about the outcomes for the sick would lower a mirror tied to a thin cord until it touched the surface of the spring's water; and after performing certain prayers and incense-burnings, the outcome of the matter would show itself in the mirror. There was also, not far from Epidaurus, a city of Laconia, a deep pool called the Water of Juno; when grain cakes were cast into it, answers were given: favorable, if the waves calmly retained what was thrown in; but unfavorable if, as if in rejection, they cast them back out. It is recorded that the craters of Etna did something similar, into which coins or sacrificial victims were thrown; they showed the same omen of joy or sorrow by the retention or rejection of the things thrown in. Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian</note> tells similar things in his Roman History about a place he calls the Nymphaeum: where, when incense was cast into the flames in this manner, oracles were received concerning everything one wished to know, except for death and matters pertaining to marriage. It is also a marvel what Aristotle recorded concerning the spring of the Palici in Sicily, to which those about to take an oath approached; whatever they wished to affirm, they threw into the spring written and sealed on tablets. If these were true, they were seen to float upon the waters; but if they were false and sworn with evil intent, they were immediately submerged along with the petitioners; then a fire suddenly leaping out seized the one guilty of perjury...

### On the fourth kind of frenzy, from Venus. Chapter XLIX.

<margin>Why Love is blind.</margin>
<margin>A miracle.</margin>
<margin>The soul of man.</margin>
The fourth frenzy, proceeding from Venus, turns and transforms the soul into God through fervent love, and makes it entirely like God, as if it were God’s own image. Hence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> says: "O Asclepius, man is a great miracle, a living being to be honored and adored: for he passes into the nature of God, as if he himself were becoming God; he knows the race of demons, as he recognizes that he originated from the same source; he despises the part of human nature in himself, trusting in the divinity of the other part." Therefore, the soul having been turned and made similar to God, is so formed by God that, through a certain essential contact with divinity, it knows all things beyond all intellect. For this reason, Orpheus describes Love as being without eyes, because it is above the intellect. And now the soul, having been so turned toward God by love and sublimated above the intellectual sphere—besides the fact that it has attained the spirit of prophecy and prediction by its full power—sometimes performs even more wonderful and greater things than the nature of the world itself, which work is indeed called a "miracle." For just as the heaven, by its image and its light and heat, performs those things which the power of fire does not achieve by its natural quality (which is very well known in Alchemy even by experience), so also God, through His image and light, perfects those things which the world cannot do by its innate power. Now, the image of God is man—at least the man who, having been made like God by the Venerean frenzy, lives by mind alone and "receives Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note> with his whole heart." Nevertheless, the soul of man, according to the teachers of the Hebrews and the Cabalists, is defined as being the light of God, created after the image of the Word, the cause of causes and the first exemplar; a substance of God, figured by a seal whose character is the eternal Word. Beholding this, Hermes Trismegistus says that such a man is either superior to the inhabitants of heaven, or at least possesses an equal lot.

### On rapture, ecstasy, and the prophecies that happen to those seized by the "falling sickness" and fainting, and those in their death-throes. Chapter L.

<margin>What rapture is.</margin>
Raptus <term>Rapture: a state of being "carried away" or seized by divine power</term> is an abstraction, an alienation, and an illumination of the soul proceeding from God, through which God draws the soul—which had fallen from the heights to the lower realms—back again from the lower realms to the heights. The cause of this in us is the continuous contemplation of sublime things; in so far as this joins the soul to incorporeal wisdom by a most profound intention of the mind, it is vehe-

# BOOK THREE.
### 317.

<margin>The soul, when released from the body, encompasses all place and time.</margin>

By its more inward agitations, the soul calls itself away from sensible and bodily things, and (as Plato says) it does so at times in such a way that it either escapes the body itself or seems almost to be dissolved. This is much like what Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> relates concerning the priest of Calama (whom we mentioned above): "He lay there," he says, "exactly like a dead man, without breath; and even when he was burned and cut, he felt nothing." So great, therefore, is the command of the soul—specifically when it has attained its own true nature and is no longer weighed down by the allurements of the senses—that by its own power it suddenly ascends. It does this not only while remaining in the body, but also sometimes, having been loosened from its shackles, by flying outside the body toward a super-celestial dwelling. There, being now most near and most similar to God, and having been made a receptacle for divine effects, it is filled with divine light and vision.

Hence Zoroaster says: "You must ascend to the light itself, and to the rays of the Father, from whence the soul was sent to you, clothed in a great deal of Mind." <note>original: "Ascendendū tibi est ad lumen ipsum..." from the Chaldean Oracles</note> And Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic wisdom</note> says: "It will behoove you to ascend above the heavens, and to be far distant from the choirs of demons." And Pythagoras says: "If you, leaving the body, pass into the free ether, you shall be an immortal god." Thus we read that Hermes, Socrates, Xenocrates, Plato, Plotinus, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, and Zoroaster were accustomed to be called away by rapture, and in this way they learned the wisdom of many things.

We also read in Herodotus that there was in Proconnesus a philosopher of wonderful knowledge named Aristeas <note>The OCR reads "Atheum," but the historical reference is Aristeas</note>, and that his soul would sometimes leave his body, and after seeing distant spaces of travel, it would return into the body more learned. Pliny relates the same thing: that the soul of Hermotimus of Clazomenae was accustomed to do this, and that leaving the body, it used to wander and report many true things from afar. And there are even to this day among the Norwegians and Laplanders <note>original: "Nouergios & Pilappios"</note> very many who call themselves away from the body for a full three days; and having returned, they report many things from distant places. Meanwhile, it is necessary to guard them, lest any living animal should happen to step over them or touch them; otherwise, they say the soul does not return into its body.

It must be known, therefore, that (according to the doctrine of the Egyptians) since the soul is a certain spiritual light, when it is released from the body, it encompasses all place and all time. It is not unlike a light enclosed in a lantern, which, because it is opened, is diffused everywhere and does not fail; for it is everywhere and always. And Cicero, in his book *On Divination*, says: "The mind of man never divines, except when it is so loosened that it has absolutely nothing or very little to do with the body."

When, therefore, it has reached that state which is the highest degree of contemplative perfection, it is then snatched away from all created forms, and it understands not through acquired appearances, but through an inspection of the Ideas <note>The Platonic archetypes or eternal forms</note>, and it knows all things in the light of the Ideas. Plato says that very few men become participants in this light in this life, but almost all the gods do. Fainting fits and the "falling sickness" <note><term>comitiales</term>: Epilepsy, historically called the "comitial disease" because its occurrence was seen as an omen that could stop public assemblies (comitia).</note> also imitate rapture in a certain way, and in these states, just as in rapture, prophecies very often come forth; we read that Hercules and many Arabs excelled in this kind of prophesying. And there are certain prophecies which are intermediate between the boundaries of natural divinations and trans-natural oracles: namely, those which arise from an excess of some passion, such as excessive love, or sadness, or amidst frequent sighs, or in the agony of death...

For there is within our souls a certain clear power capable of all things, but it is obscured and hindered by the fog of the body and mortality. However, once it has attained immortality after death and is released from the body, it possesses full and perfect knowledge. From this, it happens that those near death and those weakened by old age sometimes experience an unusual light, because the soul is then less hindered by the senses and understands more sharply. Now, as if slightly loosened from its chains and no longer entirely subject to the body—being, as it were, a neighbor to the place where it is about to migrate—it easily perceives revelations which, mixed with its own death-agonies, are then offered to it. Whence Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> says in his book *On Faith in the Resurrection*: "Our soul yearns to escape this bodily prison-house <term>ergastulum</term> <note>A Roman term for a private prison or workhouse for slaves; here used metaphorically for the body</note>; being free in its airy motion, it knows not where it goes or whence it comes. We know, however, that it survives the body, and having now cast off the barriers of its own senses, it beholds with a free gaze those things which it did not see while situated in the body. We can judge this by the example of those who sleep, whose souls—while the body is buried in rest—raise themselves to higher things and report to the body visions of absent or even celestial matters."

<margin>Whence it happens that one sees dreams and understands them.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'S' depicting three classical or biblical figures in a landscape, used to begin the word "Somnium".</image-desc> **S**leeping-vision <note>original: "Somnium"</note> I call that which proceeds from the phantastic spirit <term>spiritu phantastico</term> <note>The "imagination" or the faculty that processes mental images</note> and the intellect united with one another, either through the illumination of the active intellect upon our soul, or through the wondrous revelation of some divinity, with a purged and tranquil mind. For from this, our soul receives true oracles and abundantly provides us with prophecies. Indeed, in dreams we seem to ask questions, to learn, to read, and to find; many doubts, many counsels, many unknown and unexpected things never before attempted by our minds are opened to us in dreams. Images of unknown places appear, as do likenesses of men both living and dead. Future things which have not yet happened are foretold, and things are revealed to have happened elsewhere which have not yet been made known by any report of knowledge. These dreams require no other art of interpretation, like those of which we spoke in the first book (which belong to divination, not foreknowledge). It often happens that those who have seen them do not understand them because (as Abdala the Arab <note>Likely referring to a medieval Arabic source or commentator</note> says): "Just as seeing dreams comes from the strength of the imagination, so understanding them comes from the strength of the intellect." Therefore, he whose intellect is drowned in too much commerce with the flesh and is asleep, or whose imaginative or phantastic spirit is so dull and unpolished that it cannot receive the species and flowing images of the higher intellect, nor retain them once received—such a person is plainly useless for the prophecies of dreams. It is necessary, therefore, for one who wishes to receive true dreams to keep the phantastic spirit pure, unshaken, and undisturbed, and to compose it so that it is made worthy for the mind and intellect to preside over it and make things known to it. For such a spirit is most fit for prophecies, receiving all the images <term>idola</term> <note>In the Epicurean sense: thin films or "idols" shed by objects that strike the senses</note> flowing from things on every side (as he says...

# BOOK THREE.

<margin>Note</margin>
Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who wrote "On Dreams."</note> says the soul is a most clear mirror. Therefore, when we are healthy in body, undisturbed in mind, not weighed down by food, nor grieving from poverty, and with no vices of lust or anger clamoring within us, we go to bed chastely to sleep. Then our soul—pure and divine, released from every harmful thought and now free through sleep—relies upon this divine spirit as an instrument. It receives into itself the radiating and shining beams and images from divine minds. As if in a deific mirror, the soul beholds these things far more certainly, clearly, and effectively than through any common investigation of the intellect or discourse of reason. The divine powers instruct the soul, which is invited into their assembly by the opportunity of the night's solitude; nor even then will the propitious divinity be lacking to the waking person to moderate their actions. Whoever, therefore, keeps their spirit pure through tranquil and religious meditation, and through a temperate and moderate diet according to nature, uses this spirit as a well-prepared tool to become divine and knowledgeable in this manner. But whoever, on the contrary, languishes with a disordered <term>phantastic spirit</term> <note>The "spiritus phantasticus" was believed to be a subtle substance in the body that mediated between the soul and the senses.</note>, does not receive clear and distinct visions.

<margin>A simile.</margin>
Just as a one-eyed man judges confusedly and indistinctly because of weakness, so also when we are filled with gluttony and wine, our spirit is oppressed by harmful vapors (just as turbid water is affected differently under the same form). It is deceived and grows dull. For this reason, the seer Amphiaraus <note>A legendary healer and seer of Greek myth.</note> 
<margin>Philostratus, Book 2, Chapter 14.</margin>
(as we read in Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus, author of "The Life of Apollonius of Tyana."</note>) ordered one wishing to receive oracles to abstain from food for an entire day, and from wine for three days. This was because the soul could not prophesy rightly unless it were freed from wine and food; for the gods are accustomed to grant oracles to sober and religious souls who are devoted to divine worship. Whence Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet of Greek mystery religions.</note> exclaims:

> Greatest prophet and messenger of things to come,
> You approach souls soothed by quiet sound.
> Addressing them, you rouse the mind,
> You suggest the meanings of the blessed deities to them through sleep,
> Silent, you announce the future to silent souls—
> To those souls, I say, whose minds are most rightly devoted to divine worship.

Hence it was the custom among the ancients that those about to receive responses would first celebrate certain sacred expiations and sacrifices. Having performed the divine worship, they would lie down religiously in a consecrated bedchamber, or at least upon the fleeces of their own sacrifices. Virgil <note>The Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> mentions this rite in these verses:

> In times of doubt they seek responses; here the priest
> Brought gifts, and beneath the silent night
> Lay upon the spread skins of slaughtered sheep and sought sleep.
<note>original: "In dubiis responsa petunt..." from the Aeneid, Book VII.</note>

And a little later he sings:

> Here then father Latinus himself, seeking responses,
> Ritually sacrificed a hundred wool-bearing sheep,
> And lay supported upon their backs and spread
> Fleeces.
<note>original: "Hic et tum pater ipse petens responsa Latinus..." from the Aeneid, Book VII.</note>

### Page 320

And because the Spartans were in charge (as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman statesman and philosopher</note> says), they were accustomed to lie down in the temple of Pasiphae for the sake of dreaming; the same was done in the temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note>, by whom true dreams were thought to be sent. And the Calabrians, wishing to consult Podalyrius, the son of Aesculapius, would fall asleep near his tomb upon the skins of lambs; for in this way, one was advised in dreams concerning whatever they desired to know.

<margin>The time for dreams is night.</margin>
Furthermore, the most familiar time for dreams is the night, when the senses are freed from wandering objects, midday errors, and vain emotions; when fear does not strike the soul, nor thought waver, and the mind is most peaceful, it may perseveringly cling to the divine.

<margin>Four types of true dreams.</margin>
There are, however (as Rabbi Johanan <note>original: "Rabi Iohenan"; likely referring to Yochanan bar Nafcha, a famous Talmudic sage</note> says in the *Book of Senators* <note>likely referring to the Sanhedrin</note>), four types of true dreams: First, the morning dream, which occurs between sleep and waking; second, that which one sees concerning another; third, the interpretation of which is shown to the dreamer himself in a nightly vision; fourth, that which is repeated to the same dreamer, according to what Joseph said to Pharaoh, saying: "As for the dream having been seen a second time pertaining to the same matter, it is a sign of its certainty." <note>Genesis 41:32</note> Moreover, the most certain dream is that which concerns those things which one revolves within oneself and agitates in the mind when going to sleep, just as it is written: "O King, thoughts began to come to you in your bed regarding what would happen hereafter." <note>Daniel 2:29</note> It is necessary, however, for an interpreter of others' dreams to possess the knowledge by which he can distinguish and discern the likenesses of all things, and know the customs of all nations, according to the laws they have received concerning God and the angels.

<margin>Vain things mixed with dreams.</margin>
Furthermore, it should be known that there is scarcely any dream, or none at all, without some vain matter, just as no grain of wheat is without chaff; which even the dream of the patriarch Joseph himself testifies, which his father Jacob interpreted, saying: "What does this dream mean that you have seen? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down to you on the earth?" <note>Genesis 37:10</note> which indeed was not fulfilled regarding his mother, who had died shortly thereafter. These things also Rabbi Johanan says in the aforementioned book; to which Rabbi Levi <note>A medieval Jewish scholar</note> adds, saying that every prophetic dream can be delayed in its effect for no more than twenty-two years: thus Joseph dreamed in the seventeenth year of his age what afterwards came into action in the thirty-ninth year of his age.

<margin>What is required for the reception of divine dreams.</margin>
Therefore, one wishing now to receive divine dreams should be well-disposed in body, the brain free from vapors, and the mind free from disturbances; on that day let him abstain from supper, nor drink anything that can intoxicate. Let him have a clean and bright bedroom, even exorcised and consecrated, in which, having performed a fumigation <note>burning of incense or herbs</note>, anointed the temples, and placed rings of dreams upon the fingers, with a celestial image and a sacred parchment placed under the head, and the divine power invoked with sacred prayers, let him seek his bed with his thought intent upon the matter he desires to know. For thus he shall see most true and indubitable dreams, with a true illumination of the intellect. Whoever, therefore, knows how to join together those things which we have said dispersedly in these books concerning this matter, shall easily obtain the gift of oracles and dreams.

### PAGE CCCXXI.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'S' containing a figure in a landscape holding a staff, used for the beginning of the word "Sunt".</image-desc> There are also certain lots <note>original: "fortes"; here referring to the practice of cleromancy or casting lots</note> possessing a divine power of oracles, acting as judges of divine judgment. These are sought out only after much prayer and entreaty by those who inquire of them; sometimes they are even commanded to be performed by God himself. We read of this in Leviticus regarding the goat to be offered to the Lord and the scapegoat, and in the Book of Numbers regarding the rods of the tribes of Israel. Furthermore, both Moses and Joshua, having cast lots in the sight of the Lord, divided the lands and inheritances among the tribes of Israel according to the decree of God. The Apostles of Christ, after first offering prayers, chose Matthias by lot to take the place of the traitor Judas. When the prophet Jonah was sailing to Tarshish while fleeing from the face of the Lord, and a storm arose, the sailors discovered by lot that he was the cause of the danger; once he was cast into the sea, the storm ceased. Caesar relates that when Marcus Valerius Procillus was captured by enemies, the lots were consulted three times to determine whether he should be killed by fire immediately or reserved for another time; by the benefit of the lots, he escaped unharmed. There was formerly at Bura, a town of Achaia, an oracle of Hercules established by means of dice <note>original: "talis"; specifically knucklebone dice</note> and a counting board <note>original: "abaco"</note>. There, one wishing to consult on any matter would first perform prayers to the god and then throw four dice; the priest, observing their positions and shapes, would find what was to come written upon the board. These dice were all fashioned from the bones of sacrificial victims.

<margin>The ancient fathers did not cast lots rashly</margin> Indeed, it should be known that the ancient fathers were not accustomed to cast lots for any light cause, but only when urged by necessity or great utility, and never without great religion, reverence, purifications, fasts, cleanliness, prayers, invocations, vows, sacrifices, consecrations, and other sacred mysteries of religion. For these sacred rites, when duly performed before our works, are most effective in invoking the divine will and benevolence, and the presence of divine spirits; by their dispensation, the lot is directed, and we receive a true judgment on the matter sought.

<margin>The disposition of one who wishes to work through lots.</margin> Therefore, whoever works through lots must approach with a well-disposed mind—not troubled, not distracted—and with a strong desire, firm deliberation, and a constant intention of knowing that which is sought. Furthermore, being distinguished by purity, chastity, and holiness toward God and celestial things, and with undoubting hope and firm faith, he should invoke through sacred prayers so that he may be made worthy for the divine spirits to join him and for the divine will to be made known. For if you are so disposed, the greatest secrets will be opened to you by the power of the lots, and you will be a truth-telling prophet of things past, present, and future, concerning which you have inquired. What we have said here regarding lots must also be observed in the auguries of omens and signs <note>original: "ominum & notaminum"</note>; namely, when with awe, yet with firm expectation, we set before ourselves certain signs for the sake of prophesying, or ask for a sign, as we read that Abraham’s servant Eliezer and Gideon the judge in Israel did. There was formerly in Pharis, a city of Achaia, a statue of Mercury in the middle of the forum; there, one about to receive an omen would burn incense and light the lamps that stood before it, and after offering a local coin into the statue's right hand, would whisper into the statue's ear whatever he wished to ask. ### How one wishing to receive oracles ought to dispose himself. Chapter LIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a putto or cherub-like figure within a leafy architectural frame.</image-desc>

Whoever desires to approach the supreme state of the soul and sets out to seek oracles must approach disposed in a chaste and holy manner, pure and clean, so that his soul is defiled by the stain of no foulness and bears no scars of sins impressed upon his breast. It will be necessary to thoroughly segregate and purge the soul—as far as the necessity of nature permits—from every disease, dullness, malice, and similar passions, and from every irrational condition which follows the soul just as rust follows iron. This is done by rightly composing and arranging those things which pertain to the tranquility of the mind; for in this way, he will receive truer and more effective responses. By what means the soul may be purged and restored to its divine purity must be learned by us from religion and wisdom; for wisdom is not without religion, nor is religion to be approved without wisdom. For wisdom (says Solomon) is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her <note>Proverbs 3:18</note>; and Lucretius says that it is a discovery of God, or a breath of God, where he sings:

> He was a god, that illustrious Memmius,
> Who first discovered that reasoned way of life which
> Is now called wisdom, and who through his art
> Rescued life from such great waves and such great darkness
> And placed it in such tranquility and such clear light.
> <note>original: "Hic deus ille fuit..." from Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book V.</note>

<margin>Man is the temple of God.</margin>
He understands also that wisdom is a divine illumination, whence Democritus judges no men to be wise except those who are stirred by a certain divine frenzy <note>term: divine frenzy (furor divinus) — a state of inspired madness or ecstasy believed to be the source of poetic and prophetic insight</note>, just like that Minos of Crete, whom they say learned all things from Jove <note>Jupiter</note> when he had frequent conversation with the god on Mount Ida. So also the Athenians say that Melesagora of Eleusis was instructed by the nymphs. Thus we also read that Hesiod, when he was a shepherd of cattle in Boeotia and had driven his flock near a certain Mount Helicon, was presented by the Muses with several reeds; having received these, he suddenly acquired the art of poetry. Indeed, to attain such things in a moment is certainly not the work of the human mind, but of one divinely inspired—namely, one in whom God is present, performing all things. For God himself, transferring himself into holy souls, appoints prophets and workers of wonders, powerful in deed and word, as Plato and Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius" referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> assert, and even Xystus the Pythagorean himself, asserting that such a man is the temple of God, and God moreover...

# BOOK THREE.

...guest: in which our Paul <note>original: "Paulus"; referring to the Apostle Paul</note> also agrees, calling man the temple of God, and elsewhere says of himself: *I can do all things in him who strengthens me, God* <note>Philippians 4:13</note>: for He is our virtue, without whom (as He himself asserts) we can do nothing. This is even admitted by Aristotle in his *Meteorology* and *Ethics*, that there is no virtue, whether natural or moral, except through God. And in his secrets <note>likely referring to the pseudo-Aristotelian *Secretum Secretorum*</note> he adds that a good and healthy intellect can penetrate the secrets of nature, provided that the influence of divine power is present; otherwise, it is by no means possible. We receive this influence only when we release ourselves from burdensome impediments, from carnal and earthly occupations, and from all external agitation. For a bleary and unclean eye cannot gaze upon things that are too bright, nor can he who is ignorant of the purification of the soul grasp divine matters.

<margin>One must arrive at purity of soul step by step.</margin>
However, it is necessary to arrive at this purity of soul gradually and, as it were, through certain steps. For not everyone newly initiated into these mysteries immediately comprehends all things clearly; rather, the mind must be accustomed little by little, until the intellect stands out within us and, applying itself to the divine light, becomes mingled with it. Therefore, when the human soul has been rightly purified and expiated, then, released from all variety, it flashes forth with free movement, ascends upward, grasps divine things, and even instructs itself, even when it seems perhaps to be instructed from elsewhere. For it then requires neither recollection nor demonstration because of its natural skill; then, through its mind—which is the head and charioteer of the soul—having imitated the angels by its very nature, it attains what it desires not by succession or time, but in a sudden moment.

<margin>David, Solomon, and the other prophets and apostles were taught suddenly.</margin>
For David did not learn letters, yet from a shepherd he was made a prophet and most learned in divine matters. Solomon, in the dream of a single night, was filled with the wisdom of all things above and below. Thus Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the rest of the prophets and apostles were instructed. For the soul (which is the common opinion of the Pythagoreans and Platonists) can, through the purgatorial way without other study or investigation, acquire a perfect knowledge of all knowable things through only a small and very easy comparison and an external addition to the intelligible things already held from above. It can also arrive at this through external expiation, so that it understands all things indivisibly through its own substantial form.

<margin>How the soul is to be expiated.</margin>
The soul is purified and expiated through cleanliness, through abstinence, through penitence, and through almsgiving. Certain sacred institutions also contribute to the same end, as will be shown below; for the soul must be cared for through the study of religions—which are generally hidden—so that, restored to health, strengthened by truth, and fortified by divine protections, it does not fear the shocks that arise.

### On cleanliness, and how it is to be observed. Chapter 54.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop cap 'M' containing a scene of a traveler in a landscape with hills and a distant town or tower.</image-desc>

For such external cleanliness is believed to help the purity of the soul in no small measure. For this reason, the Pythagorean philosophers, captivated by the greed for oracles, having celebrated divine praises, washed in rivers—

<margin>The dress and gestures of the Brahmans.</margin>
Brahmans <note>The "Bragmani" or Brahmins, the priestly caste of India, often idealized in Renaissance occult texts as ancient keepers of wisdom.</note>, the wise men of the Indians, were accustomed to wash in the spring called Dirce in Boeotia <note>The author likely conflates Greek mythology with Indian geography here</note>, having stripped off their clothes and first anointed their heads with amber drops and scents suited for that purpose. Then, after they were sufficiently clean according to the rite, they would go out around midday dressed in white linen with a white miter, wearing rings on their fingers and carrying staffs in their hands. In a similar way, among the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian ascetics</note>, it was a holy law to wash three times a day and twice at night in cold water before entering the inner sanctums of the sacred rites; they also used linen garments washed fresh every day. We also read of this same rite of washing in Hesiod, in the book *Works and Days*, where he sings:

> *No one dares to pour out wine to Jove at dawn*
> *With unwashed hands, nor to any of the other immortals,*
> *For they do not wish to hear such prayers, and they spurn the petitioners.*

->And elsewhere:<-

> *When a wicked man crosses a river with unwashed hands,*
> *The gods are angry at this, and grant him sorrows thereafter.*

Hence, in Virgil, Aeneas speaks thus to his father:

> *You, father, take the sacred objects and our ancestral gods in your hand;*
> *For me, having come from such a great war and recent slaughter,*
> *It is a sin to touch them, until I have washed myself*
> *In a living stream.*

For it was the custom among the nations, when they were about to perform sacrifices to the gods above, to purify the body by washing; but when a sacrifice was to be made to the gods of the underworld, a mere sprinkling was sufficient. Hence in Virgil, when Dido was instituting sacrifices to the gods of the underworld, she says:

> *Dear nurse, bring my sister Anna here to me,*
> *Tell her to hasten to sprinkle her body with river water.*

And elsewhere, where he describes Aeneas bringing the branch to Proserpina <note>The Golden Bough offered to the Queen of the Underworld</note> in the land of the dead, he sings:

> *Aeneas reaches the entrance, and sprinkles his body*
> *With fresh water.*

And also where he tells of the burial of Misenus, he sings:

> *Three times he went around his companions with pure water,*
> *Sprinkling them with a light dew from a branch of a fruitful olive.*

For when cleanliness is achieved, a man becomes celestial and spiritual, and is thus prepared for the vision and union with God, provided he serves God with a clean body and a pure mind. He should embrace cleanliness in all things: in his internal organs, in his skin, in his clothes, in his tools, in his dwellings, in his gifts, offerings, victims, and sacrifices. The cleanliness of all these things even purifies the air and attracts that most pure influence of celestial and divine beings; it entices and draws the clean ministers of God and good spirits <note>original: "dæmones," here used in the classical sense of guiding spirits or intermediaries, not necessarily evil entities</note>. However, sometimes even unclean spirits and evil demons—acting as the apes of the good, or so that they might be worshiped and dece—

## Concerning abstinence, fasts, chastity, solitude, tranquility of mind, and ascent.

### Chapter 55.

Abstinence also everywhere familiarly fortifies and protects its observers against vices and evil demons; it renders the soul like an uncontaminated temple of God and joins the mind to God. Nothing is better for health and the balance of the temperament <note>original: "complexionis," referring to the four humors</note> than to avoid gathering superfluities and not to exceed the measure of necessary food. For nourishment should not be taken that is more powerful than nature, but rather that by which nature becomes more powerful—just as some assert regarding Christ, that he took food in such a measure that it did not generate the waste of the "fourth digestion" <note>In medieval medicine, the fourth digestion was the final process where nutrients became part of the living tissue; the author suggests Christ's body was so efficient it left no waste.</note>. Many others also rejoiced in agility of body and health through the sparing use of food, such as Moses and Elijah, who extended their fasting until the fortieth day. Hence, the former’s face shone with splendor, and the latter, being uplifted, led his body as easily as a spirit at his command. For the Magi and philosophers assert that our spirit is not nourished like the earthly body through the digestion of food or drink in specific organs, but rather, like a sponge, it draws its nourishment from everywhere through the whole body—namely, from the thinnest vapors penetrating the body on all sides. Therefore, those who desire to have this spirit pure and powerful use drier foods, and they thin out this thick body with fasts, making it easily permeable so that the spirit is neither thickened nor suffocated by the body's weight. Then, through washings, rubbings, exercises, and clothing, they keep the body itself clean, and they strengthen the spirit with purifications and incense, leading it to a pure and thin sincerity. We ought, therefore, to be pure and abstinent in taking food, just as the Pythagorean philosophers, who, keeping a sacred and sober table, prolonged their lives in all temperance. <margin>The effects of temperance.</margin> For temperance of life and temperament—because it brings us no tumult of any overriding humor that might stir the imagination toward any [false] image—ensures that our soul, very often while dreaming and sometimes even while awake, is always subjected to celestial influences. Furthermore, the Pythagoreans promise perpetual health of both and even a long life to anyone who, through abstinence, wisely moderates every motion of both soul and body. Thus, the Brahmans <note>original: "Bragmani," referring to the Hindu priestly caste</note> admitted no one to their college unless they abstained from wine, meat, and vices, saying that no one can understand God except he who emulates Him through divine conversation; Phraotes also taught this to the lower Indians in the works of Philostratus. <margin>From what things a man must especially abstain.</margin> Moreover, it behooves us to abstain from all things whatsoever that infect the soul and spirit: from lusts and envy, which are the handmaidens of injustice (as...

# BOOK THREE.

...wrote and performed many things concerning the art of divining and prophesying. His writings to Musaeus <note>Musaeus was a legendary polymath and disciple of Orpheus</note> declare that Orpheus performed similar works in the deserts of Thrace. Thus we read that Epimenides of Crete was instructed by a certain very long sleep, for they say he slept for fifty years: by this they understand that he lived in concealment. Pythagoras also is said to have remained hidden in a similar way for ten years, and Heraclitus and Democritus were delighted by solitude for the same reason. For the more we leave behind the animal and human life, the more we live as angels and God; joined to them and restored to a better lot, we are capable of all things, ruling over all. Proclus, in his commentaries on the *Alcibiades*, teaches how our soul is to be separated from the animal life and from all multiplicity, and how it is to be raised until it ascends to the One itself—the Good, the True, and the Beautiful—through each level of both things known and ways of knowing. He shows how, <margin>What things man must especially flee.</margin> first of all, sensible things <note>Objects perceived by the physical senses</note> must be fled, so that we may transfer ourselves to the incorporeal essence. There, it is necessary to overcome the order of souls—which is nevertheless multiplied through many reasons, various habits and proportions, many chains, and a multiform variety of powers—and to strive toward the intellect and the intelligible realms, contemplating by how great an interval these are better than souls. Furthermore, it is permitted to leave behind even that intellectual multiplicity, though it be united and indivisible, and to reach the super-intellectual and essential Unity, absolute and free from all multiplicity, the very fountain of the Good and the True. By a similar reasoning, it behooves us to flee all knowledge that distracts and deceives in manifold ways, so that we may follow the simplest truth. Therefore, the multitude of affections, senses, and imaginations must be left behind, as well as opinions, which are so diverse in themselves that some are contrary to others in any given person. We must ascend to the sciences, in which, although there is a varied multitude, there is nevertheless no contrariety; for all are connected to one another, and alternately one ministers and serves the other, up to the one science presupposed by all, which presupposes no other further, and to which all others must be referred. Yet even there is not the highest peak of knowledge; rather, above it is the pure intellect. Therefore, having laid aside all composition, division, and multiform discourse, ascending to the intellectual life and simple intuition, and speculating upon the intelligible essence with indivisible and simple perceptions, let us follow the highest existence of the soul itself, through which we are "one," and under which our own multiplicity is united. Thus, let us reach the first "One"—from which union is in all things—through that "one" which is, as it were, the flower of our essence. This we finally achieve when, fleeing all multiplicity, we rise up into our own unity, are made one, and act with uniformity.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>What repentance is.</margin>
...a familiar path leading back to the higher realms. Therefore, repentance is not only the mortification <note>The "killing off" or subduing of bodily desires</note> of vices, but also a spiritual martyrdom of the soul, which is pierced on every side by the sword of the spirit: and the sword of the spirit is the word of God. Whence the prophet Jeremiah says, and also Paul writing to the Ephesians: *Cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood* <note>Jeremiah 48:10; here interpreted allegorically as the struggle against sin</note>: and the Psalmist sings: *A sword is in their lips.* Therefore, the thoughts and affections of the mind, and all the evils that come out of our heart and mouth, must be laid open to the priest in confession, so that he may judge them according to the word of God, and according to the power granted to him by God, cleanse and purge them by the penance enjoined, and direct them toward the good. Indeed, in religion, no sacrament is found more powerful for abolishing sins than repentance: hence the gods themselves (as Ovid witnesses in *Letters from the Black Sea*)

->Often lighten the punishments, and restore the sight that was taken away,<-
->When they see that one has truly repented of the sin.<-
<note>original: "Sæpe leuant pœnas, ereptaq; lumina reddunt, / Quum bene peccati pœnituisse uident."</note>

<margin>Praise of almsgiving.</margin>
There is yet another sacrament of expiation, namely almsgiving itself, about which I remember reading little or nothing among the philosophers; but the Supreme Truth <note>referring to Christ</note> taught it to us, saying: *Give alms, and all things are clean unto you*: and in Ecclesiasticus it is read: *As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin*: and Daniel taught the king of Babylon to redeem his sins with alms, and the angel Raphael testifies to Tobias: *Because alms delivers from death, and it is that which purges sins and makes one find eternal life.* Hence Christ commanded us to pray to the Father, *forgive as we forgive, and give as we give*: concerning which he said elsewhere: *You shall receive a hundredfold, and possess eternal life.* The same one, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, will reproach the damned above all else for neglected alms and works of mercy, when he says: *I was hungry and thirsty and you gave me nothing to eat or drink*: and yet in another place, speaking of the poor, he says: *What you have done for one of these, you have done for me.* It seems to me that Homer also felt this, where he introduces a youth speaking to the suitor Antinous in these words: *Antinous, you did not do well to strike a wretched beggar; a god in heaven will destroy you if there is one, for even the gods, taking the likeness of foreign guests and going out into the world, overturn the cities of men, looking upon both injuries and wickedness.*
