Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> also writes that priests were accustomed to use sulfur and bitumen in purifications, or a washing of seawater; for sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its scent, while seawater purifies because of its fiery portion. In a similar way, the herb cinquefoil <term>pentaphyllon: literally "five-leafed" herb</term> purifies, which is why the ancient priests used it in their cleansings due to its inherent purity. They likewise used olive branches: for this tree is said to be of such great purity that they say an olive tree planted by a prostitute will either remain forever fruitless or wither away entirely. In a similar manner, frankincense, myrrh, vervain, and Valerian—which is also called the herb of light <note>herba lucia</note> and is called *Fu* in Arabic—contribute to expiation. Likewise, the "blessed herb" <note>herb bennet</note> and cloves; similarly, the smoke of a black dog’s gall is said to be most effective in these matters, both for driving out evil demons and for undoing sorcery wherever it may be. Likewise, the smoked feathers of a hoopoe bird drive away phantoms.

However, there is a wonder, scarcely believable unless it were told by that grave and not-to-be-despised author Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> in his *History of Jerusalem*, concerning the Baaras root, 

<margin>Wonders of the Baaras root.</margin>
named after a place near Machaerus, a town in Judea. He says this root is flame-colored and emits a glow at night, yet it is very difficult to catch, as it deceives the hand of the one trying to grab it and flees from the eyes; nor does it stay still until it has been sprinkled with the urine of a menstruating woman. Even when held in this way, it is not pulled up without danger, for instant death follows the one extracting it unless they are protected by an amulet made of that same root. Those lacking this, having dug around the earth, tie the root with a cord to a dog and then quickly move away. Finally, the dog, following with great effort, pulls out the root and, as if paying the price for its master, dies on the spot. Afterward, that root can be handled by anyone without danger. Its power in expiations is most excellent, as it has been found to immediately liberate even those who are vexed by unclean spirits. They believe that materials of this kind act upon spiritual substances—by putting them to flight, or attracting them, or soothing them, or inciting them—no differently than the fire in Sicily acts upon souls. This fire 

<margin>The fire in Sicily.</margin>
(according to William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, a 13th-century theologian</note>) does not harm bodies but causes intolerable torment to the souls of those who approach it. However, these matters have been partly treated above.

### On Adorations and Vows. Chapter LVIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, framed by vines and architectural scrolls.</image-desc>
Adorations and vows, sacrifices and offerings, are indeed steps in the sacred rites for seeking out God. They are the primary things that provoke the divine will and forge a sacred and indissoluble communion between souls and the gods. For from the prayers which we utter with true and sacred words, and with feeling and mind, we acquire great power; when we apply these to some divinity, they move that divinity to direct its speech and response toward us through a divine ray. By this ray (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> says) God speaks with men, but so secretly that only a few perceive it. That king and prophet David, however, perceived it very often. When (he says) shall I hear what the Lord God speaks within me? Therefore, long-continued adoration...

<margin>
How man returns to God.
</margin>
Man returns to God through prayers: reaching Him (as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*), he halts his horses and enters the banquet chamber, where he feeds on ambrosia and drinks nectar. Therefore, those who desire to possess any virtue must pray and supplicate frequently to Him who contains all virtue within Himself. However, the better and best prayer is not that uttered by the mouth, but that which is offered to God in holy silence and with an untainted mind; crying out with the voice of the mind, it venerates the presiding gods with the words of the intellectual world.

<margin>
What a vow is.
</margin>
A vow is an ardent affection of a chaste soul dedicated to God, which, by vowing, desires that which appears good. This affection (as Iamblichus and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote extensively on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine.</note> testify) joins souls to God in such a way that at some point the operation of God and the soul becomes one: namely, God as the craftsman and the soul as the divine instrument. Hence, all antiquity testifies that through vows, miracles are sometimes performed, diseases cured, storms averted, and similar things. Thus we read that the most excellent and wisest men among all nations—the Brahmans of the Indians, the Magi of the Persians, the Gymnosophists <note>term: Gymnosophists (literally "naked philosophers"), ancient Indian ascetics known for their wisdom.</note> of the Egyptians, and the theologians of the Greeks and Chaldeans who established the festivals of the gods and hidden mysteries—devoted themselves chiefly to divine vows and prayers and achieved many wonderful things.

<margin>
Two things are required for the perfection of a vow.
</margin>
For the perfection of a vow and of adoration (for there is no vow without adoration, nor is adoration anywhere perfect without a vow), two things are chiefly required: first, the knowledge of that which is to be adored and to whom the vow is to be made, and by what reason, order, and means it should be worshipped. For there are many co-operators and instruments of God—namely the heavens, the stars, administrative spirits, celestial souls, and heroes—whom he who proceeds toward the Archetypal God <note>The ultimate, original source of all being.</note> (who alone is the final end of adoration) must first implore as gatekeepers, interpreters, administrators, and mediators. All other divinities are like entrances to God Himself. Know therefore that adorations and vows must be made principally with a pure and pious mind to the one God alone, the highest Father, King, and Lord of all gods. When, however, they proceed to the lower gods, it should not be intended unless as an administration delegated by the highest Father. Thus, Zoroaster and Orpheus thought it permissible to use fumigations, characters, and the like in adorations and vows when directed to lower divinities; but when they are raised to the majesty of the supreme Jupiter <note>Used here as a name for the supreme Godhead.</note>, they should not be done at all. Hermes and Plato also forbid this. Whence Hermes says to Tatius: "This is like sacrilege, when you pray to God, to wish to light incense and such things; for these are foreign" (as Porphyry says) "to all piety." For nothing material can be found which is not [unsuitable] to the immaterial God...

Secondly, however, a certain assimilation of our life to the divine life is required, proceeding from purity, chastity, and holiness, along with a lawful desire for that which we hope for: for by this we especially capture divine benevolence and are subjected to divine bounty. For unless we are worthy to be heard because of a purged mind, and unless those things which we ask for are worthy to be done, it is manifest that the gods are not present at our prayers at all; whence the divine Plato says that God is turned toward no unjust things by any prayers or gifts. Let us therefore ask nothing of God which is unbecoming for us to want: for we see very many people frustrated in their prayers and vows for this reason alone—because they themselves are not religiously disposed, nor are their desires and petitions made concerning those things which are pleasing to God, nor do they know how to discern in what order he must be adored, and through which mediators God himself must be approached. Ignorance of these things very often reduces our prayers and petitions to nothing and causes vows to be denied to our supplications.

### Concerning sacrifices and offerings, and their kinds
### and modes. Chapter LIX.

<margin>Many kinds of sacrifices.</margin>
<margin>The sacrifice of expiation.</margin>
Sacrifice is an offering which is both made sacred by the act of offering and which sacralizes or sanctifies the one offering it, unless irreverence or some other sin hinders him. Therefore, these sacrifices and offerings provide us with much confidence, make us of the household of God, and repel many evils threatening us. Indeed, the teachers of the Hebrews <note>referring to Kabbalistic or Rabbinic scholars</note> confirm this above all others, saying: by the fact that we slaughter our animals and dissipate our possessions in sacrifice, imminent evils are deflected from us toward such things. Then, just as this mortal priest in this lower world sacrifices the souls of irrational animals to God through the destruction of the body from the soul, so Michael the Archangel, the priest of the higher world, sacrifices the souls of men; and he does this through the separation of the soul from the body—not the body from the soul—except by accident, as happens in fury, rapture, ecstasy, sleep, and similar vacations of the soul, which the Hebrews call the "death of the kiss" <note>original: "mors osculi," a mystical term for a peaceful death or ecstatic union with the Divine</note>. Truly, sacrifices and offerings are to be made first and principally to the highest God; however, when they are directed toward secondary powers <note>original: "secunda numina," such as angels or celestial intelligences</note>, understand this to be done in the same manner as was said concerning prayer and vows; then, whatever was said there, we shall also understand here by similarity. Truly, there are several kinds of sacrifices: for one is called a "holocaust" <note>term: holocaust (from Greek 'holokaustos'), a sacrifice completely consumed by fire</note>, when the victim is consumed by fire; another is an "immolation" on account of the pouring out of blood. Furthermore, some are called "salutary sacrifices," which are made for obtaining health; some are "peaceful," for obtaining peace; some are "praises," for liberation from evils or the granting of goods; some are "congratulatory," for divine veneration and the giving of thanks. Some are even made neither for the honor of God nor out of good will, such as was the "sacrifice of jealousy" among the Hebrews, which was made solely for the sake of detecting hidden adultery. And there was formerly among the nations a "sacrifice of expiation," by which cities were purged of famine or pestilence, or other...

<margin>Kinds of sacrifices</margin>
There were, furthermore, many kinds of sacrifices and victims, such as the *Agonalia* <note>festivals for Janus or the gods of the state</note>, *Dapsa* <note>sacred banquets</note>, *Farreations* <note>grain offerings or ancient marriage rites</note>, *Hecatombs* <note>the sacrifice of a hundred cattle</note>, *Hostia* <note>sacrificial victims</note>, *Hyacinthia*, *Armilustra* <note>purification of arms</note>, *Janualia*, *Lucalia*, *Lupercalia*, *Munychia*, *Novendinalia* <note>nine-day festivals</note>, *Nyctiluca* <note>night-shining rites</note>, *Palatialia*, *Pastillaria*, *Popularia*, *Protervia*, *Scenopegia* <note>Festival of Tabernacles</note>, *Suovetaurilia* <note>original: "Solitaurilia"; the sacrifice of a pig, sheep, and bull</note>, *Stata*, *Rubigalia* <note>to avert mildew</note>, *Fontanalia* <note>honoring springs</note>, *Ormia*, *Parentalia* <note>honoring deceased parents</note>, *Inferiae* <note>sacrifices to the underworld</note>, *Consualia*, *Lampteria*, *Amburbia* <note>city purification</note>, *Ambarvalia* <note>field purification</note>, *Vivalia*, *Thyia*, *Holocausts* <note>burnt offerings</note>, *Orgia*, *Latialia*, *Dianetaurica*, *Bacchanalia*, *Trieterica*, *Liberalia*, *Cocytia*, *Cerealia*, *Thesmophoria*, *Adonia*, *Theonia*, *Laurentalia*, *Opalia*, *Palilia*, *Quirinalia*, *Vertumnalia*, *Gynecia*, *Panathenaea*, *Quinquatria*, *Diapalia*, *Diasia*, *Horma*, *Hormea*, *Nemea*, *Mytriaca*, *Palogygia*. There were also specific and diverse victims for these: for the he-goat and the ass were for Bacchus, the sow for Ceres, the horse for the Sun, the doe and dogs for Diana, the ass for Priapus, the goose for Isis, the rooster for Night, the she-goat for Faunus, the bull for Neptune, the she-goat for Minerva, the bull for Hercules, a boy for Saturn, a pregnant sow for Maia, and a rooster for Aesculapius; indeed, sacrifice was even made to the Gnidian Hercules with insults and reproaches. There were also various orders of priests: Pontiffs, Flamens, Arch-flamens, Phylades, Salii, Hierophants, and various names for religions and superstitions, sacrifices, ceremonies, feasts, consecrations, dedications, vows, devotions, atonements, oaths, victims, and offerings, by which the misled Gentiles sacrificed to false gods and demons.

<margin>True sacrifice is twofold</margin>
But the true sacrifice, which purifies man and unites him to God, is twofold: one which the High Priest Christ offered for the remission of sins, purifying all things through the blood of his cross; the other, by which man offers himself pure and immaculate as a living sacrifice to God, just as Christ the High Priest offered himself, and taught that we ought to be offered together with him just as he was offered, saying of the sacrament of his body and blood: *Do this in remembrance of me* <note>original: "Hoc facite in meam commemorationem"</note>: namely, that we, having been mortified together through the passion of the mortal body and quickened in the spirit, might offer ourselves together. Concerning this, Porphyry says: "Let us labor to offer the holiness of our life as a sacrifice; for no one can be a good priest of God except he who, presenting himself as a victim, builds up his own soul like a certain image, and establishes his mind and intellect into a temple in which he can receive the divine light." External sacrifices, however (as Heraclitus says), are certain healings of souls, instituted by the Supreme Physician; for an evil demon possesses a man (as Proclus says) until he is purified through sacrifices.

<margin>Sacrifices are necessary to appease God.</margin>
Sacrifices are therefore sought out to appease God and the celestial virtues, and to purify man, who himself bears the image of God and the world. But our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Pontiff and High Priest, concluded every sacrifice...

<margin>Which victims were usually slaughtered for which gods.</margin>
Furthermore, white victims were slaughtered for the celestial and ethereal gods; but for the terrestrial and infernal ones, black: but for the terrestrial upon altars, and for the infernal in pits; for the aerial and aquatic gods, birds were used: but white for the former, and black for the latter. Finally, birds were immolated to all gods and spirits except for the terrestrial and infernal ones, for to those only quadrupeds were given, for like rejoices in like. Finally, of those things which were immolated to the celestial and ethereal gods, it was permitted only to eat the flesh, the extremities being reserved for the deity, but of the others not at all. Aristotle, asserting this, says that sacrificing to God is inherent in man by nature. Therefore, they say, these are intermediaries which savor of the nature of both, and represent divine things by analogy. They possess certain most suitable symbols both with the deity to whom they are offered and with those who are being purified—yet these are so hidden that the human intellect can scarcely grasp what God and the deities specifically require for our expiation, by which the celestial virtues may be appeased and restrain themselves from executing the punishment which our sins deserve. And these are what Orpheus calls the "keys" that open the gates of the elements and the heavens, so that through them man may penetrate to the super-celestial realms, and the intelligences of the heavens and the spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note> of the elements may descend to him. However, men who are perfect and truly religious do not need these things, but only those who (as Hermes Trismegistus says) "having fallen into harmony" <note>A reference to the soul becoming entangled in the physical laws and planetary influences of the material world.</note> have been made servants of the heavens and of created things. Because they are subjected to the heavens, they think they must be strengthened by the favor of celestial virtue until, flying higher, they are released from that presidency and emerge more sublime than they.

### How these things are to be presented both to God and to the lower powers. Chapter 61.

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a figure seated in a landscape, reaching upwards toward a light source or cloud.</image-desc>Every adoration, offering or sacrifice, prayer, and invocation is distinguished by this difference: namely, that it is either made to God alone, or to the lower powers <note>original: "numina"</note>, such as angels, stars, and heroes. In these matters, you must observe such rules that whenever a prayer is to be offered to God alone to obtain some effect, this should be done with the commemoration of some work, miracle, sacrament, or promise drawn from the holy scriptures. For example, if a prayer is made for the destruction of enemies, let it be commemorated how God destroyed the giants in the flood of waters, and the attempts of Babel in the confusion of tongues, Sodom and Gomorrah in the rain of fire, the army of Pharaoh in the Red Sea, and the like: adding to these whatever curse can be gathered from the psalms and here and there from the sacred writings. By a similar reasoning, when about to pray against the dangers of waters, let us commemorate the salvation of Noah in the flood, the passage of the children of Israel through the midst of the Red Sea, and Christ walking with dry feet upon the waters, and the same one having saved the little boat in danger, having commanded the winds and the waves, and having led the sinking Peter out of the waters of the sea, and such things. But if prayer is necessary for seeking oracles or dreams, whether to God or to angels and heroes, there now offer themselves innumerable places from the Old Testament where God is read to have spoken with men, with very many verses promising presages and revelations, then various prophetic dreams of Jacob, Joseph, Pharaoh, Daniel, and Nebuchadnezzar: then whatever is found in the New Testament and in all religion concerning the revelations of John, Paul, the Holy Magi, then of Helen, Constantine, and Charles: then things...

From this same root, the method of consecrating can also be taken, of which we shall now speak consequently.

### On consecrations and their rationale. Chapter LXII.

<margin>The efficacy of consecrations is perfected by two things.</margin> <image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a male figure, possibly a scholar or magician, holding a celestial sphere or globe.</image-desc> Consecration is the sublimation of experiments, through which a spiritual soul—drawn by proportion and conformity—is infused into the matter of our works (rightly and lawfully prepared according to the tradition of the magical art), and our work is quickened by the spirit of the intellect. The efficacy of consecrations is perfected chiefly by two things: namely, by the virtue of the person consecrating, and by the virtue of the prayer itself. Regarding the rites by which consecration is administered, there is required in the person a holiness of life and a power of sanctifying. The first is provided by nature and merit; the second is acquired through initiation and dignification <note>The process of becoming "worthy" or "dignified" through spiritual rank</note>, of which we have spoken elsewhere. Next, it is necessary that the consecrator himself recognizes this virtue and power within himself with a firm and undoubting faith. <margin>Prayer and its power.</margin> What is required in the prayer, however, is my present intention to describe. Prayer itself is a certain power of sanctifying divinely implanted in it—either if it is so ordained by God for this very purpose (such as many we read in the holy utterances of the Bible), or if it is instituted for this by the ordinance of the Church through the power of the Holy Spirit (many of which kind exist everywhere). Or, this holiness is inherent in the prayer not by virtue of institution, but by the commemoration of sacred things—such as sacred writings, histories, miracles, works, effects, graces, promises, sacraments, and sacramentals—which seem to belong to the thing to be consecrated either properly, improperly, or through some similarity. We shall now give some examples of this, through which the way to this entire consideration will easily lie open. <margin>The consecration of water.</margin> Thus, in the consecration of water, a commemoration is made: how God placed the firmament in the midst of the waters; how in the earthly paradise He established a sacred fountain from which the entire world is irrigated by four sacred rivers; how He made the waters the instrument of His justice...

You will find many more things of this kind in the prophets and the Book of Revelation, such as the sacred names of the "sword of God," the "rod of God," the "staff of God," the "vengeance of God," and similar terms. Let these examples of the consecrations and blessings of objects suffice; from these, the consecrations and blessings of persons are easily understood. <margin>Another rite of consecrating and expiating.</margin> But there is yet another rite of consecrating and expiating, powerful and of great efficacy, which belongs to the types of superstitions: namely, when the rite of some sacrament is transferred to some thing intended to be consecrated or expiated—for example, the rites of baptism, confirmation, funerals, and the like. It should be known, moreover, that a vow, an offering, or a sacrifice possesses a certain power of both real <note>original: "realis," meaning pertaining to physical objects</note> and personal consecration, insofar as things or persons are devoted and offered to specific deities.

### What things are called sacred, and what are called consecrated: and how these relate to us and the gods, and concerning sacred times. Chapter LXIII.

<margin>Sacred things.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' depicting a seated man in a landscape setting.</image-desc> Those things are called sacred which have been hallowed by the gods themselves or by their assisting spirits, being (so to speak) dedicated to us by the gods themselves. In this way, we call spirits "sacred" because God dwells in them, and they are often said to bear His name. Hence we read in Exodus: *I will send my angel who shall go before thee; observe him, and do not think him one to be despised, for my name is in him.* <note>Exodus 23:20-21</note> <margin>Mystery.</margin> In this way also, mysteries are called sacred. For a mystery is that which possesses a hallowed and hidden power and grace bestowed by the gods or spirits, or dispensed by the Supreme God Himself—just as are the sacred names and characters <note>term: characters — symbolic sigils or marks believed to hold magical power</note> mentioned above. Thus the Cross itself is sacred and mysterious, hallowed by the passion of Jesus Christ. For this reason, certain orations and prayers are called sacred and mystical, which were instituted not by human devotion but by divine revelation—just as we read in the Gospels that Christ instituted the Lord's Prayer. In a similar way, certain preparations are called sacred, into which God has infused a singular ray of His power, as we read in Exodus concerning the incense and the oil of anointing; and as among us there is the sacred font, the sacred chrism <note>term: chrism — a mixture of oil and balsam used in Christian sacraments</note>, the oil of the catechumens, and such like. There is also another kind of sacred things, which we call sacred because they have been dedicated and consecrated to God by men, such as the vows and sacrifices mentioned above. Whence Virgil says:

> ->But Caesar, entering the Roman walls in triple triumph,<-
> ->Consecrated an immortal vow to the Italian gods.<-
<note>Virgil, Aeneid, Book VIII</note>

**And Ovid sings in the books of the Metamorphoses:**

> ->The feast day had arrived, on which Achilles, the swan-borne,<-
> ->Appeased Pallas with the blood of a slain heifer;<-
> ->When he placed the offering upon the hot altars,<-
> ->And the smoke, accepted by the gods, rose into the air:<-
> ->The sacred rites took their share, the rest was given to the tables.<-
<note>Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book XII</note>

<summary>Agrippa defines the nature of "sacred" and "consecrated" things, distinguishing between those hallowed by divine revelation and those dedicated to God by human ritual. He cites both Biblical authority and classical poets like Virgil and Ovid to illustrate the power of sacrifice and ritual objects.</summary>

# BOOK THREE.

In a similar way, sacred likenesses, shrines, idols, statues, images, and paintings are called "sacred" when they are made in the likeness of the gods or dedicated to the gods themselves, just as Orpheus sings in his hymn to Lycian Venus:

> For our leaders, protecting the divine things of the fatherland,
> Established a sacred colossus near the little town.
> <note>original: "Noſtri nanq; duces patriæ diuina tuentes / Oppidulum propter ſacrum ſtatuere coloſſum."</note>

->And Virgil:<-

> You, father, take the sacred objects and the ancestral household gods in your hand.
> <note>original: "Tu genitor cape ſacra manu patriosq; penates." A quote from the Aeneid, Book 2.</note>

Hence the divine Plato, in the eleventh book of *The Laws*, commanded that the sacred statues and images of the gods ought to be honored—not for their own sake, but because they represent the gods to us. In this way, the ancients venerated that famous likeness of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, interpreting it thus: for by the fact that it bears the likeness of a man, it signifies that <margin>Interpretation of the likeness of Jove.</margin> he is Mind, which produces all things through "seminal reason" <term>seminal reason: the Stoic concept of 'logoi spermatikoi', or the creative seeds/principles that organize matter</term>. He is depicted sitting so that his stable and immutable power may be expressed. He has his upper parts naked and open because he is visible to the intelligences and superior beings; his lower parts, however, are covered because he is hidden from inferior creatures. He holds a scepter in his left hand because the most spiritual home of life is found in those parts of the body. Moreover, the creator is the intellect, the king and life-giving spirit of the world. In his right hand, he extends both an eagle and a Victory: the former because he is the lord of the other gods, just as the eagle is of other birds; the latter because all things are subject to him.

In a similar way, we also venerate the figure of a lamb because it represents Christ; and the figure of a dove because it denotes the Holy Spirit; and the figures of a lion, an ox, an eagle, and a man, signifying the Evangelists <note>The traditional symbols for Mark, Luke, John, and Matthew</note>, and other similar figures which we find expressed in the revelations of the prophets and in various places in the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, these very things contribute to similar revelations and dreams, and for that reason are called sacred paintings.

There are also sacred rites and sacred observations which are performed for the veneration of the gods and religion, such as devout gestures, genuflections, the uncovering of the head, washings, the sprinkling of holy water, fumigations <note>the burning of incense</note>, outward purifications, and likewise processions of supplication. There is also the outward adornment of divine praises, such as musical resonance, the lighting of candles and lamps, the ringing of signals and bells, and the decoration of temples, altars, and images. In all of these, the highest and most beautiful worship and grace are required; therefore, whatever is most beautiful, fair, and precious—gold, silver, precious stones, and the like—is employed for these purposes. Indeed, these venerations and outward sacred acts are like instructions and invitations to spiritual sacred things, for the purpose of obtaining benefits from the gods, as Proserpina testified concerning these things in these verses:

> For who among men would ever neglect forms of bronze,
> Or the yellow gifts of gold, or the white gifts of silver?
> Who would not marvel? Who would not say these very things
> Belong to the gods?
> <note>original: "Quis nam hominum formas æris neglexerit unq̃..."</note>

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

They are also called sacred priests, the ministers of the spirits <note>original: "numinum"</note> and gods, and are consecrated to them: as well as those administering any sacred rites and consecrating things. Whence Lucan <note>A Roman poet, author of Pharsalia</note> says:
> Sacred pontiffs, to whom power is granted.

And Virgil says of Helenus, the priest of Apollo:
> He prays for peace from the gods, and unbinds the fillets
> Of his consecrated head.

Indeed, sacred rites of this kind are like certain pacts between the gods and us, offered under praise, or veneration, or obedience, through the mediation of which we often obtain some wonderful virtue from that spirit to whom such veneration is paid: such are sacred hymns, and speeches, and exorcisms, and incantations, and voices, which are composed and dedicated to the praises and venerations of the gods. Whence Orpheus, in a song composed to the stars:

-> Therefore with sacred voices, I now invoke the pure spirits. <-

And the primitive church used certain sacred incantations against diseases and storms, all of which—either by praying and pronouncing them under the veneration of some spirit, or even sometimes carrying them written, hung, or bound upon themselves—often obtain some virtue from such a spirit, which men greatly admire. In this way there are also sacred names, figures, and characters, and seals, which contemplative men have vowed, dedicated, and consecrated with a pure mind for their secret desires <note>original: "votis"</note> toward the veneration of God; which indeed, if someone later pronounces them with the same purity of mind with which they were first instituted, they will similarly effect wonders, provided also that the manner and rule handed down by the first institutor is observed: for those who are ignorant of these things lose their labor and work in vain. In this way, we sometimes effect wonders not only with foreign <note>original: "barbaris," often referring to non-Greek or non-Latin magical words</note> words, but also with Hebrew, Egyptian, <margin>There is sometimes a wonderful power in names.</margin> Greek, Latin, and names of any other language, devoted to God and attributed and dedicated to His essence, or virtue, or operation. Thus among Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> there are names such as Osiris, Ieto, Emepht, Ptha, Epies, Amun: so among Plato and the Greeks, *He who is* <note>original: "ὢν"</note>, *of beings* <note>original: "ὀντῶν"</note>; so the Greeks call Jupiter *Zena* <note>original: "ζῆνα"</note> from *to live* <note>original: "ζῆν"</note> because he provides life to individuals: similarly *Dia* <note>original: "Δία"</note>, which signifies *through*, because through him all things are made: so *athanaton* <note>original: "ἀθάνατον"</note>, which signifies immortal. So among the Latins he is called *Jupiter*, as if a *helping father* <note>original: "juvans pater"</note>, and things similar to these, just as certain proper names are also given to men according to a wish, such as Eutychides, Sosia, Theophilus—that is, prosperous, a savior, and dear to God. Similarly, certain material things receive no small amount of holiness and virtue from consecration, especially priestly consecration, just as we see those wax seals <note>known as Agnus Dei</note> on which the figure of lambs is inscribed, receive virtue through the blessing of the Roman Pontiff against lightning and storms, so that they do not harm those carrying them: for divine virtue is breathed into consecrated images of this kind, and is contained in them, as if in a certain sacred letter which holds the image of God. <meta>This page continues the discussion of sacred objects and times from the previous section, focusing on how specific days acquire spiritual power through historical events or divine decree.</meta>

# BOOK THREE. 341.

Through their consecration and blessing, [bells] receive power so that they may ward off and restrain lightning and storms, lest they cause harm in places where their sound is heard at that time. In a similar way, salt and water, through their own blessings and exorcisms, receive the power of purifying and driving away evil demons, and so <margin>Sacred times.</margin> it is with similar things. There are also sacred times, observed with the highest veneration among the peoples of every religion, which were either commanded to be sanctified for us by the gods themselves, or dedicated to them by our fathers and ancestors in perpetual commemoration and thanksgiving for benefits received from the gods. Thus the Hebrews have their Sabbaths; thus the heathens have their festivals; thus we have received the solemn days of our own sacred rites to be venerated always with the greatest celebration. There are also contrary times, which <margin>Expiatory times.</margin> we call expiatory, and those days we call "black days" <note>original: "dies atros"</note>, because on those days the state suffered some notable slaughter or calamity. Of this sort among the Romans was the day before the fourth Nones of August <note>August 2nd</note>, because on that day they suffered that most vast slaughter of the Battle of Cannae. For a similar reason, all days following a festival were called "black days," <margin>Black days.</margin> on which they very often fought with ill success. Thus among the Jews there are black days: the seventeenth of the month of June, because they hold that on that day Moses broke the tablets, Manasseh erected an idol in the Holy of Holies, and the walls of Jerusalem were destroyed by enemies. Similarly, the ninth of July is a black day for them, because on that day both destructions of the Temple were carried out. By this reasoning, the "Egyptian Days" <note>Days considered unlucky for medical or magical work in medieval calendars</note> were named, having once been observed by the Egyptians; and any nation can easily fashion for itself a similar <margin>Egyptian days.</margin> calculation of lucky and unlucky days by this method. The Magi command that these sacred and religious days be observed no differently than planetary days and celestial arrangements; indeed, they claim those days are much more effective, especially for attaining spiritual and divine powers. This is because their power and influence descend not so much from elemental or celestial bodies, but from the intelligible and super-celestial world. Aided by the common prayers of the saints, this power is not broken by any opposing arrangement of the heavenly bodies, nor frustrated by the corruptible contagion of the elements—provided there is no lack of firm belief and religious veneration (that is, joined with fear and awe, for that is what "religion" properly means). Hence those days are called "religious" which it is a sin to violate, and which we observe anxiously, fearing some great evil if anything should be done on them otherwise than it ought to be.

Moreover, that times have great power in natural things can be shown by many examples. On the same day, they say that inflated bladders burst, and the leaves of willow-thickets and the seeds of apples turn and rotate. That Crete does not bear owls; that in the territory of Naples cicadas are not heard; that in Venice no kind of flies enter the public barbershops; that at the public meat market in Toledo, throughout the whole year, no more than one fly is seen, and that one of a notable whiteness. Turnips also become larger if, while they are being sown, they are prayed to so that they might provide generously for oneself, the family, and the neighbors. The peacock is also praised, and soon it spreads its feathers; on the contrary, it is found that if the herb basil is planted with great curses and reproaches, it brings forth more choice fruit. ## Conclusion of the entire work. Chapter LXV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' showing a person or figure within a landscape of rolling hills and trees.</image-desc>
**H**ere are the things which we have gathered into this book for an introduction to magic <term>magiæ introductionem: the foundational entry into the sacred art</term> from the tradition of the ancients and various compilations, in a brief discourse indeed, but sufficient for those who are to understand. Some of these things are written in order, some without order; some are handed down in fragments, some even hidden and left to the investigation of the intelligent, who, by looking more sharply and searching through those things which are written, can attain the complete teachings of the magical art as well as infallible experiments. For we have handed down <note>original: "tradidimus"</note> this art in such a way that it might not happen to be hidden from the prudent and intelligent: but it should not admit the wicked and the incredulous to the secrets of those mysteries; rather, it should leave them struck with wonder, abandoned under the shadow of ignorance and desperation. You, therefore, sons of learning and wisdom <term>sapientiæ filii: a traditional term for initiates or dedicated students of philosophy</term>, search through this book by gathering our dispersed intention, which we have set forth in various places; and what was hidden by us in one place, we have made manifest in another, so that it may be opened to you who are wise. For we have written for you alone, whose souls are incorrupt, established in the right order of living; whose chaste and modest minds and unstained faith fear and revere God; whose hands are separated from every wickedness and crime, and whose manners are modest, sober, and temperate. For you alone will find the doctrine preserved for you, and the secrets hidden by many riddles, which are not drawn out except by hidden intelligence <term>intelligentia abscondita: an intuitive or spiritual understanding beyond literal reading</term>. When you have attained this, the complete and invincible science of the magical discipline will instill itself into you, and those virtues will appear to you, such as Hermes, Zoroaster, Apollonius, and the rest of the workers of wonders once attained.
<margin>Abstain from [the] below, do not have / [unclear]</margin>
But you, malevolent slanderers, sons of perverse ignorance and foolish wickedness, flee from these our writings, for they are hostile to you, and placed on a precipice, so that you may wander and fall into misery. If anyone, therefore, because of his own incredulity and sluggishness of intellect, does not obtain his desire, let him not impute the fault of his ignorance to me, nor say that I have erred, or written false things on purpose, or lied, but let him accuse himself—

But he who does not understand our writings: for they are obscure, and covered over with various mysteries, in which it will easily happen that many will err and lose their way. ## THER, MASTER OF SACRED THEOLOGY
->Aurelius of Aquapendente, of the Order of St. Augustine, from Henry<-
->Cornelius Agrippa. Greetings.<-

<margin>Namely</margin>
<note>The decorative initial 'E' begins the word 'Ex' (From/Out of).</note>
From the letters which you sent to me on the second of this month, I have perceived the sincerity of your mind toward me, Reverend Father, and I have recognized you as a man of all-encompassing learning <note>original: "cyclice doctum," referring to the circle of liberal arts</note>, and a curious explorer of those things which still lie hidden in darkness. I rejoiced immediately, and I congratulate myself that I have obtained the friendship of such a man, with whom I might one day cultivate both my spirit and my intellect: and I now receive you (as this handwritten note bears witness) among my closest friends. But hark! Who are your leaders whom you follow, you who dare to enter the inescapable house of Daedalus <note>The Labyrinth</note> and of the fearsome Minos, to pass through the sentries, and to commit yourself to the Fates? Who are your teachers, you who occupy yourself with immense things, daring to attempt to make the wandering stable, the treacherous faithful, and the most fleeting of all gods more constant than Adrastia <note>A goddess of inevitable fate or Nemesis</note> herself? Beware lest you be deceived by those who were themselves deceived. For no amount of reading books will be able to direct you here, since they sound of nothing but pure enigmas. Oh, how many writings are read concerning the impregnable power of the magical art, concerning the prodigious images of the astrologers, concerning the monstrous metamorphosis of the alchemists, and concerning that blessed stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> by which, like Midas, all things touched are soon changed into gold or silver;
<margin>Namely</margin>
all of which are found to be vain, fictitious, and false as often as they are practiced according to the literal word. And yet these things are handed down and written by great and most serious philosophers and holy men, whose traditions who would dare to call false? Indeed, it would be impious to believe that they wrote lies on purpose: there is, therefore, another sense than what is handed down in the letters, and that sense is covered by various mysteries, but so far explained openly by none of the masters; I do not know if anyone, without a skilled and faithful teacher, can attain it by the reading of books alone, unless he be enlightened by a divine power, which is granted to very few. Therefore, many run in vain who pursue these most secret mysteries of nature, applying their minds only to the bare sequence of the reading. For, having fallen away from the true understanding by an unpromising intellect, into...

### TO THE SAME.

From your most kind letters (venerable father), I have looked into your whole soul as if into a mirror, and I embrace it entirely. I wish you to be so persuaded that you are more dear to me than can be demonstrated by letters, and that you dwell in the deepest part of my soul. I am truly such a man as writes this from the abundance of my heart, and one who is never accustomed to desert those who have committed themselves to my friendship, no matter the storm. Therefore, so that you may attain your wishes (which are no less than my own), I shall come to you shortly. When it is granted for us to hear and return our voices to one another in person, I know our friendship shall be indissoluble and endure forever.

Now, as pertains to the Philosophy you requested, I want you to know that to know God himself, the craftsman of all things, and to pass into him with the whole image of likeness (as if by a certain essential contact or bond)—by which you yourself may be transformed and made a god, just as the Lord said of Moses, saying: *Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh* <note>original: "Ecce ego constitui te deum Pharaonis." A reference to Exodus 7:1.</note>—this is that true and supreme most hidden philosophy of wonderful works. Its key is the intellect. For the higher the things we understand, the more sublime the virtues we put on, and the greater the things we perform, both more easily and more effectively. 349.
# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>No</margin> <note>The margin note "no" appears to be a fragment or a marker for the start of the sentence "noperuidendis" (thoroughly examining).</note> For the purpose of thoroughly examining those most hidden secrets of God and nature, [human effort] is entirely ineffective; and "this is the task, this is the labor: to emerge into the upper air." <note>original: "hoc opus, hic labor est, superas euadere ad auras" — a famous quote from Virgil's Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note> For how shall he who has lost himself in ash and mortal dust find God himself? How shall one immersed in flesh and blood apprehend spiritual things? Shall a man see the Lord and live? What fruit shall the grain of wheat bring forth if it has not first died? For it is necessary to die—to die, I say, to the world and the flesh, and to all the senses, and to the entire "animal man" <note>The "animal man" (homo animalis) refers to the soul driven by base instincts rather than spirit.</note> who wishes to enter into these inner chambers of secrets; not that the body should be separated from the soul, but that the soul should leave the body. Concerning this death, Paul writes to the Colossians: "You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ." And elsewhere he says more clearly of himself: "I know a man—whether in the body or out of the body, I know not, God knows—who was caught up even to the third heaven," and what follows. In this death, I say, which is "precious in the sight of the Lord," one must die; which happens to very few, and perhaps not always. For "the few whom impartial Jupiter has loved, or whom glowing virtue has lifted to the heavens, being born of the gods, were able to do it." <note>Another Virgilian reference (Aeneid VI) regarding the rare few who achieve divine ascent.</note> First, those who are born not of flesh and blood, but of God; next, those who, by the benefit of nature and the gift of their birth-chart <term>genethliaco dono: a gift determined by one's astrological horoscope at birth</term>, have been made worthy of it. The rest strive by merits and by art, concerning which a living voice shall make you more certain. 

But I wish you to be warned of this: do not be deceived regarding me, as if I—having at some time experienced divine things—preach these things to you, or wish to claim such a thing for myself, or hope it could be granted to me. For I have been until now a soldier consecrated by human blood, almost always a courtier, bound by the bond of the flesh to a most dear wife, and exposed to all the blasts of unstable fortune. Being driven crosswise entirely by the flesh, by the world, and by domestic cares, I have not attained such sublime gifts of the immortal gods. But I wish to be accepted as a signpost <note>original: "indicem"</note> which, always remaining before the doors itself, shows others which path must be entered. Furthermore, concerning my love for you, you are indeed not at all deceived; what you may owe to my favors, I do not see, since I have not bestowed anything upon you, except that I am ready, when the occasion is given, to bestow everything. Now, most happily, Farewell. From Lyons, November 19, Year 1527.

# LETTER.

I shall explain its theme to you. Hear now, therefore, a matter both foolish and impious: A certain man of the demons—that is, a <term>cacomagus</term> <note>From the Greek 'kakomagos', meaning an evil magician or sorcerer</note>—has been summoned from Germany at no small expense. In him, the power of demons dwells, so that just as Jannes and Mambres <note>The traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in Exodus</note> resisted Moses, so this man might resist the Emperor. For they have been persuaded by the father of lies <note>The Devil</note> that he possesses foreknowledge of all future events, is privy to any secret counsels whatsoever, and is an interpreter of deliberate thoughts. Furthermore, he is said to be endowed with such great power that he can transport the royal children through the air, just as one reads that Habakkuk <note>Referring to the story in the apocryphal 'Bel and the Dragon', where an angel carries the prophet by his hair</note> was carried with his pottage to the lions' den. He is supposedly able, like Elisha when besieged in Dothan, to show mountains full of horses and chariots of fire and a vast army; moreover, he can reveal and transfer the treasures of the earth, compel or dissolve marriages and loves as he wishes, and cure even the most desperate diseases with a Stygian <note>Hellish or underworld</note> medicine—suppose it be deep-rooted consumption, confirmed dropsy, or elephantiasis that has reached the bone, and that which:

->Medicine knows not how to loosen the knotty gout,<-
->And many things besides which obscure rumor hides.<-

You see where their faith is placed, where their hope is laid up—they who attempt to subject the elements, the sky, the fates, nature, providence, God, and all things to the command of a single magus. They seek the safety of the kingdom from the demons, the enemies of public safety, saying in their hearts with Ahaziah: "Is there no God in Israel, that we go to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?" And just as Saul spoke to the Pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor</note>, saying: "The Philistines fight against me, and the Lord has departed from me and would not hear me; therefore I have called you." Has God been so despaired of even among these men that they have judged it necessary to seek the aid of demons? Is this not, according to the word of Jude and Peter, to deny our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, who redeemed us, and to bring upon themselves swift destruction? Do they not store up for themselves the wrath of the Lord's indignation, which sends among them infestations by evil angels? Have they not been given over to a reprobate mind, since they seek the truth of secret counsel from the father of lies, the devil, and demand victory from elsewhere than from the Lord of Hosts? 

And yet, to this so nefarious practitioner of idolatry and sacrilege, audacity is provided by that "Orthodox Mother" <note>Likely a sarcastic reference to the Queen Mother or the Church hierarchy supporting the faction</note> who favors these men so lavishly; the authority of the "Most Christian Sons" is granted to him, and gifts are bestowed from the sacred funds. Even the pillars of the Church—the bishops and cardinals—connive and hire such wicked labor, and the impious nobles applaud the minister of impiety, just as crows congratulate the works of the wolf. What greater sin did Pharaoh, Balak, Saul, Ahab with his Jezebel, Ahaziah, Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Sennacherib, and the other worshippers of Baal commit? Pharaoh called his magicians against Moses, and they, defeated at the third plague, confessed "the finger of God"; but the obstinate king perished in the Red Sea after ten plagues. Balak the Moabite called Balaam the soothsayer to curse Israel, and God himself turned the curse into a blessing, while Balak himself was cursed. Of what use to Saul were the responses of his Samuel or of the Pythoness? Was he not pierced through on Mount Gilboa? Ahab and Jezebel, joined in nefarious marriage, put their trust in the prophets...

Baal, and according to the word of God, a lying spirit went out into the mouths of all the prophets <note>original: "prophetag₂" (prophetarum)</note> who promised success to Ahab as he was about to go up into Ramoth-Gilead; and Ahab fell, and Jezebel was cast down, and the dogs devoured them. Asa, King of Judah, was rebuked by the prophet of the Lord because in his illness he did not seek the Lord, but put his trust in the skill of physicians. Will not those be held in greater sin who, abandoning God the Savior and the healthy forces of nature, seek salvation from Satan? Ahaziah once did so, and for that reason he heard from the prophet of the Lord: "You shall not come down from the bed you have climbed, but you shall surely die." Let the series of other unfaithful kings be run through, even the histories of the pagans: Zoroaster, Deiotarus, Croesus, Pompey, Pyrrhus, Crassus, Nero, Julian—what did they gain from their mages and diviners who lied to them about happy outcomes? Were they not all reduced to nothing and perished miserably in their sins? Thus those impious trifles are always accustomed to bring destruction to those who cultivate them; indeed, those who trust in them most are rendered the most unhappy of all. I do not
<margin>note</margin>
deny that there are natural sciences, there are metaphysical arts, and there are hidden talents by which—without offending God and without injury to faith and religion—kingdoms can be protected, plans explored, enemies conquered, captives rescued, riches increased, the goodwill of men won over, illnesses driven away, health preserved, life prolonged, and the strength of youth restored. There are, moreover, the intercessions of holy religion, public supplications, and the private prayers of good men, by which we are able not only to turn away the wrath of God but also to obtain His favor for ourselves. But if there is, besides these, a certain art of foreknowledge and of miraculous works, which the ancients call "Good Magic" <note>original: "Calomagia"</note> or "Theurgy" <term>Theurgy: a form of high magic intended to draw down divine influence or commune with the divine</term>, certainly this is unknown to those triflers and slaves of demons. For indeed, to investigate the future or imminent events or other hidden things, and to provide true judgments on what is portended to men by divine will, and to perform works of power exceeding the common custom of nature, belongs only to profound and perfect learning and to a life and faith of the greatest integrity—not to men who are frivolous and unlearned. For to men who are innocent and learned in the law of the Lord, every creature serves according to the vow of faith, and they are heard in whatever they ask. Thus a raven fed Elijah <note>original: "Heliam"</note>, and at his prayers the earth withheld its fruit, the heaven denied rain, and vomited its fires upon the impious. Thus bears served Elisha <note>original: "Helisaeo"</note>, angels fought for him, and rivers were crossed with dry feet. For Daniel, the lions—their ferocity set aside and their hunger ignored—fawned
<margin>haha <note>This marginalia appears to be a later reader's reaction to the lions fawning over Daniel.</note></margin>
upon him; and the fire kindled in the furnace did not burn the boys. Works of this kind belong not to "Evil Mages" <note>original: "Cacomagorum"</note>, nor to "Sorcerers" <note>original: "Geoticorum"</note>, nor to demons, but to faithful and divine men; for it is not demons, but the spirit of God that ministers to them. I confess there are some, even to this day (and perhaps many), men grave in wisdom, distinguished in knowledge, prevailing in virtues and powers, upright in life and character, invincible in prudence, and even well-disposed in age and strength, so that they might be of great benefit to the state by their counsel and labor. # CCCLII
## LETTER

Right is replaced by mere counsel, cunning and craftiness stand in for knowledge, and deception and treachery are used instead of prudence. Superstition occupies the place of true religion, and in times of affliction, God is blasphemed. That faith which (as the Apostle says) <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:9, "My strength is made perfect in weakness."</note> is made perfect in infirmity, is instead held in contempt; people turn instead to the invocation of evil demons. Every good man among them is mocked, bold hypocrisy is promoted, truth is treated as a crime, and praise and rewards are reserved for folly and wickedness. O foolish and impious men, who wish to stabilize a kingdom with those very arts by which the most powerful empires of old fell and were utterly overturned! Of such men it was truly said through Jeremiah: *The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned.* <note>Lamentations 5:16</note> I wish that verse did not fit you as truly as the ingenious calculation devised against you. For that very verse, when its Roman numeral letters are collected—M, C, V, I—expresses the year 1524 <note>original: "M. D. XXIII II." This is a chronogram, a popular Renaissance word-puzzle where certain letters are read as numbers to reveal a date.</note> in which, according to your own reckoning, your King was captured at Pavia. <note>The Battle of Pavia (1525) saw the capture of King Francis I of France by the forces of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note> Did you not see these things and marvel at them—things you judged impossible before they happened? And yet you remain proud and hardened in your misfortunes. You despise the prophets, and God’s threats are like fables to you.

Behold, the time is near, and you shall yet see and feel the great wonders of God in the world, and having collapsed into your fate, you shall tremble, because a misery you do not know shall come upon you. Where will you flee then? Stand with your enchanters and with the multitude of your sorcerers, to see if they might benefit you or if you might become stronger. Will the summoned German <term>cacomagus</term> <note>From the Greek 'kakomagos', meaning an evil magician or sorcerer.</note> save you? Will he make the prophets liars, prevail against the wrath of the Lord, and deliver you from evil? Not so, you impious men, not so! Unless the Lord builds and guards the cities and the kingdom, all its watchmen labor and wake in vain. It belongs to God alone, not to demons or magi, to suspend or change the sentence of the prophets—if you, turning with your whole heart to His mercy, change your malice and treachery.

For in this way Nebuchadnezzar, by the counsel of Daniel, redeemed his sins with alms and his iniquities with mercy toward the poor, escaping the imminent wrath of God for a time, until he called it back upon himself in the court of Babylon by the voice of his own pride. <margin>3 5</margin> Even the most impious Ahab with his Jezebel, to whom the Lord announced death through Elijah—because he turned to God, the word of the Lord came again to Elijah: *Because Ahab has humbled himself before my face, I will not bring the evil in his days.* <note>1 Kings 21:29</note> The Ninevites, because they performed penance at the preaching of Jonah by the edict of the king and princes, were immediately delivered from imminent destruction. <margin>3</margin> Isaiah informed Hezekiah of his sentence, that he should set his house in order as he was soon to die; but he prayed and wept, and was healed, with fifteen years added to his life. For thus the Lord spoke to him through the same prophet: *I have seen your tears, and I have heard your prayer; behold, I will add fifteen years to your days. Moreover, I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the King of the Assyrians, and I will protect it.* So great was the conversion and prayer of a pious king, that he who prayed for himself alone nevertheless obtained his request not only for himself, but also for the city and the people. It is the Lord alone who has saved the king,

# EPISTLE.

...and who gives wisdom to the son of the king. <note>A reference to God as the source of true royal wisdom, likely echoing Psalm 72.</note> Those who seek salvation must flee to this Master, not to mages and soothsayers. Clothe yourselves in justice, and fear the Lord, you who seek happiness. If the stability of a kingdom is sought, it is written: *The just shall inherit the land* <note>original: "Iusti hæreditabunt terram"</note>: *The just man shall be in eternal memory, and shall not be moved forever.* If security is sought: *Those who fear the Lord shall not fear an evil report, but shall look down upon all their enemies.* If honor and wealth are sought: *Glory and riches are in his house.* If praise and favor: *The generation of the upright shall be blessed.* If power: *He and his seed shall be mighty upon the earth: his strength shall be exalted in glory.* If marriage and the prosperity of wedlock: *His wife shall be as a fruitful vine on the sides of his house, and his children like olive plants.* If health and strength of body: *The Lord will not allow his holy ones to see corruption.* Finally, in all things, blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who is immaculate in his way, who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, who has mercy on the needy and the poor: for in the evil day the Lord will deliver him, and will not hand him over into the hands of his enemies: but sinners shall see and be angry, they shall gnash their teeth and waste away, and their desire shall perish. It is enough to have given these warnings now. For I do not wish to pursue this matter too inquisitively, lest perhaps the malice of the subject matter push my pen further than is expedient. ### ON MAGIC IN GENERAL.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'E' depicting a figure sitting in a landscape or study.</image-desc>

Even this place demands that we speak of Magic, for it is so joined and related to astrology that he who professes magic without astrology achieves nothing, but wanders entirely from the path. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> thinks that magic derived both its name and origin from the Maguseans. The common opinion is that the name is Persian, which Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> and Apuleius <note>Author of 'The Golden Ass' and a famous defense against charges of magic.</note> support, and that in their language it signifies the same as a priest, a wise man, or a philosopher. Magic, therefore, embracing all of philosophy, Physics, and Mathematics, also joins the powers of religions to them. Hence it also contains within itself both <term>Goetia</term> <note>Low magic or sorcery involving the invocation of spirits.</note> and <term>Theurgy</term> <note>High magic or "divine work" aimed at union with the divine.</note>. For this reason, most people divide magic into two parts: namely, into natural and ceremonial.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'N' depicting two figures, possibly classical or biblical.</image-desc>

Natural magic they consider to be nothing other than the highest power of the natural sciences, which they therefore call the highest peak of natural philosophy, and its most absolute consummation; it is the active portion of natural philosophy, which [harnesses] the natural...

# 355.
## ON NATURAL MAGIC.

...with the aid of virtues, through their mutual and timely application, it produces works beyond all grasp of admiration. This was the magic most used by the Ethiopians and Indians, where there was an abundance of herbs, stones, and other things pertaining to this faculty. They wish to remember this in Jerome's letter to Paulinus, where he says that Apollonius of Tyana was a magus <note>original: "magum"</note>, or a philosopher, like the Pythagoreans. Of this kind also were the Magi who, visiting with gifts, adored the newborn Christ, whom the interpreters of the Gospels explain were the philosophers of the Chaldeans. Such were Hiarchas among the Brahmans, Tespion among the Gymnosophists <note>A sect of ancient Indian philosophers who lived naked and practiced asceticism</note>, Buddha among the Babylonians, Numa Pompilius among the Romans, Zamolxis among the Thracians, Abbaris among the Hyperboreans, Hermes among the Egyptians, and Zoroaster the son of Oromasus among the Persians. For the Indians, Ethiopians, Chaldeans, and Persians especially excelled in this magic. Because of this (as Plato relates in the *Alcibiades*), the sons of Persian kings are imbued with it, so that they may learn to administer and distribute their own republic according to the image of the world's republic. And Cicero, in his books *On Divination*, says that no one among the Persians obtains the kingdom who has not first learned magic. Therefore, natural magic is that which, having contemplated the powers of all natural and celestial things, and having scrutinized their sympathies through curious investigation, brings forth into the open the powers hidden and latent in nature. It joins lower things to the endowments of higher things as if they were certain allurements, through their mutual application to one another, so that from there, stupendous miracles often arise—not so much by art as by nature, to which this art shows itself as a servant while nature performs these things.

<margin><unclear>how they are made</unclear></margin>
For magi, as the most accurate explorers of nature, by bringing together those things which have been prepared by nature and applying active things to passive ones, very often produce effects before the time ordained by nature. The common people think these are miracles, when they are nevertheless natural works, occurring only through the intervention of "anticipating the time." For example, if someone should produce roses in the month of March, or ripe grapes, or make sown beans or parsley grow into a perfect plant within a few hours; and greater things than these, such as clouds, rains, thunders, and various kinds of animals, and many transmutations of things—many of which Roger Bacon boasts he performed through pure and natural magic. Concerning its works wrote Zoroaster, Hermes, Evanthes the King of the Arabs, Zacharias the Babylonian, Joseph the Hebrew, Bocus, Aaron, Zenotenus, Kiranides, Almadal, Thetel, Alchindus <note>Al-Kindi</note>, Abel, Ptolemy, Geber, Zahel, Nazabarub, Thabit <note>Tebith</note>, Berith, Solomon, Astaphon, Hipparchus, Alcmaeon, Apollonius, Triphon, and many others, of whose works some remain whole and many fragments still exist, and have sometimes come into my hands. Among the more recent authors, however, few have written on natural magic, and those indeed wrote little, such as Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, Arnold of Villanova, Raymond Lull, Bacon, and Abano <note>Pietro d'Abano</note>, and the author of the book dedicated to Alfonso, published under the name of *Picatrix*, who nevertheless mixes much superstition in with natural magic, which indeed others have also done.

...[They] claim that by adopting the influences of the heavens, they can produce works similar to those of nature, such as bodies that move or speak, yet do not possess animal souls. Boethius excelled in these matters, a man of the greatest genius and manifold erudition; Cassiodorus, writing to him about such things, said: "It is your purpose to know difficult things and to show miracles; by the genius of your art, metals low, Diomedes sounds a trumpet in heavy brass, a bronze snake hisses, birds are imitated, and those which do not know how to have their own voice are proven to emit the sweetness of song; we report small things of him for whom it is lawful to imitate the heavens." I think it was said of these crafts what we read in Plato in the eleventh book of the *Laws*: "Art was given to mortals so they might generate certain later things, not indeed participants in truth and divinity, but might lead down certain likenesses related to themselves." And the magi, most audacious men, progressed so far as to perpetrate all things, favored especially by that ancient and powerful serpent, the promiser of knowledge <note>A reference to the Serpent in Eden.</note>, so that like apes, they might strive to emulate God and nature.

<note>original: "DE MAGIA VENEFICA"</note>

And Exodus relates many such things concerning the magi of Pharaoh. # ON GOETIA AND NECROMANCY

<margin>Note:
how this is done</margin>
These magicians scrutinize not only natural things, but also those things which accompany nature and, in a way, strip it bare—such as motions, numbers, figures, sounds, voices, harmonies, lights, the passions of the mind, and words. Thus the Psylli and Marsi <note>Ancient tribes renowned for their power over snakes</note> used to summon serpents, while others drove them away by suppressing them. Thus Orpheus calmed the storm of the Argonauts with a hymn, and Homer tells of blood being restrained by words for Ulysses. Even in the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE</note>, a penalty was established for those who had enchanted harvests away. Thus there is no doubt that magicians, by words and passions alone and other similar means, often produce a wonderful effect not only upon themselves but even upon external objects. They believe that all these things pour an innate power into other things, drawing them toward themselves or repelling them, or affecting them in any other way, just as a magnet draws iron and amber draws chaff, or as a diamond and garlic bind the magnet <note>A common medieval belief that garlic or diamonds could neutralize magnetic force</note>. And so, through this gradual and linked sympathy of things, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Synesius <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote on theurgy and the soul</note> confirm that, according to the opinion of magicians, not only natural and celestial gifts but even intellectual and divine ones can be received from above. Proclus confesses this in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, namely that through this kind of consensus of things, magicians were also accustomed to evoke deities. For some of them have fallen into such madness that they think an image, constructed from various constellations of stars at specific intervals of time and rightly observed by a certain ratio of proportions, will receive a spirit of life and intellect by the nod of the heavens, so that it may answer those consulting it and reveal the secrets of hidden truth. From this it is clear that this Natural Magic, having sometimes leaned toward Goetia <note>term: Goetia; from the Greek 'goeteia', meaning low magic or sorcery involving the conjuration of spirits</note> and Theurgy <note>term: Theurgy; 'god-working', or high magic intended to unite the practitioner with the divine</note>, is very often ensnared by the deceits and errors of evil demons.

### ON GOETIA AND NECROMANCY

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a small figure, likely a cherub or putto, nestled within dense foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>The parts of Ceremonial Magic, however, are Goetia and Theurgy. Goetia is ill-omened by its commerce with unclean spirits, composed of the rites of wicked curiosity, illicit incantations, and prayers; it has been exterminated and execrated by the decrees of all laws. To this class belong those whom we today call necromancers and sorcerers.

> *A race hated by the gods, skilled in staining the heavens,*
> *Whom nature brought forth as an evil; who the stars of the world,*
> *And the laws of fixed things are able to pervert.*
> *For now they know how to make the poles stand still, and to send back rivers,*
> *They drive the heavens beneath the earth, and tear up mountains.*

These are they, therefore, who call upon the souls of the dead, and those whom the ancients called *epodoi* <note>Greek for 'enchanters' or 'singers of spells'</note>, who enchant boys and draw them into the speech of an oracle, and those who carry about attendant demons <note>original: "dæmones paredros"</note>, such as we read regarding Socrates. There are also those who, as it is said, feed spirits in glass vessels, through whom they falsely claim to prophesy. And all these proceed in two ways. For some strive to call and compel evil demons by the power of certain divine names, especially since every creature fears and reveres the name of Him who made it; it is no wonder if practitioners of Goetia—even those who are infidels, Pagans, Jews, Saracens, and any profane...

# 356.
## ON GOETIA AND NECROMANCY
<note>original: "DE GOETIA ET NECROMAN." Goetia refers to low magic or sorcery involving the summoning of spirits, often contrasted with Theurgy or high magic.</note>

<margin>2</margin>
...of this sect or school, men constrain demons by the invocation of the divine name. Others, however, most wicked and deserving of punishment by every fire for their detestable crime, submit themselves to demons, sacrificing to and adoring them; they have become practitioners of idolatry and the most vile abasements. Even if the former group <note>those who merely constrain spirits</note> are not liable for these specific crimes, they nevertheless expose themselves to manifest dangers. For even when coerced, demons remain vigilant, always seeking to deceive us as we wander. Indeed, from this assembly of <term>goetic</term> <note>sorcerous</note> practitioners have flowed all those books of darkness, which the legal consultant Ulpian calls "writings of disapproved reading," and which he decreed should be immediately destroyed. A certain Zabulus, devoted to illicit arts, is said to have first devised such things, followed by a certain Barnabas of Cyprus. Even today, books are circulated under forged titles, using the names of Adam, Abel, Enoch, Abraham, and Solomon; likewise Paul, Honorius, Cyprian, Albert, Thomas, Jerome, and a certain person of York. Their trifles have been foolishly followed by King Alfonso of Castile, Robert the Englishman, Bacon <note>Roger Bacon</note>, and Abano <note>Petrus d'Abano</note>, and many other men of lamented genius. Furthermore, they have not only made men, saints, patriarchs, and the angels of God the authors of such execrable doctrines, but they even show off books delivered by the angels Raziel and Raphael to Adam and Tobias. Yet, to one looking more sharply, these books—by the rule of their own precepts, their ritual, custom, the kind of words and characters used, the order of construction, and their tasteless phrasing—openly betray themselves to contain nothing but mere trifles and impostures. They were forged in later times by the most abandoned masters of perdition, who were ignorant of all ancient magic, mixing profane observations with the ceremonies of our religion and grafting in many unknown names and seals to terrify the unlearned and simple, and to strike wonder into the senseless and those who do not know good literature. Nevertheless, it is not evident from this that these arts are mere fables; for unless they were real, and many wonderful and harmful things were done through them, divine and human laws would not have decreed so strictly that they must be exterminated from the earth.

The reason why these goetic practitioners employ only evil demons is because good angels rarely appear; they wait for the command of God and do not associate with any but those pure of heart and holy of life. Evil spirits, however, present themselves easily to be invoked, falsely favoring the caller and lying about their divinity, always ready to deceive by their craft so that they might be venerated and adored. And because women are more greedy for secrets, less cautious, and prone to superstition, the spirits present themselves more easily to them and perform great wonders. The poets sing of such things regarding Circe and Medea; Cicero, Pliny, Seneca, Augustine, and many others—both philosophers and Catholic doctors and historians—bear witness to this, as do the Holy Scriptures themselves. For in the Books of Kings, we read of the <term>pythoness</term> <note>the Witch of Endor</note>, the woman who was in Endor, who summoned the soul of the prophet Samuel, although many interpret this to mean it was not the soul of the prophet, but a malignant spirit who took on his image.
